stories.Headline: OCC issues examiner framework for bank AI use without creating new requirements
stories.Summary:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued Bulletin 2026-54 and a Supervisory Framework on Bank Use of Super Intelligence on November 4, 2026. The framework is an examiner resource addressing banks' use of artificial intelligence, particularly generative AI and AI agents that can act on their own. The OCC states the framework creates no new legal requirements or supervisory expectations. The OCC also states banks are not expected to use it to assess their own AI use or risk management. The framework identifies as higher risk several AI uses common for banks that are already governed by binding law.

The framework organizes 16 components under six pillars: purpose, risk, control, oversight, resilience, and assurance. It applies to generative and agentic AI, which the OCC's prior April 2026 interagency model risk management guidance expressly excluded. It provides illustrative risk-tier definitions, with Tier 1 Critical covering autonomous payment agents, real-time credit decisioning, fraud-hold release, and market access. Tier 2 High covers AI-assisted underwriting, agent-initiated customer communications, AML alert disposition, and code assistance for internal code or data access changes. Tier 3 Moderate covers internal document summarization for credit memos and agent-assisted research, and Tier 4 Low covers internal productivity tools, code assistance, and general employee Q&A.

The OCC has instructed examiners to tailor reviews to the bank's size, complexity, and risk profile and the nature and consequences of its AI uses. The framework states that activity an AI system undertakes outside its approved purpose may be treated as a control failure even when the resulting output or action appears reasonable. It states that institutions should ensure human roles are not reduced to a nominal click where a risk assessment relies on human review. The framework distinguishes agents supplied by the bank's providers from customer and other external agents outside the bank's control. Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould pledged Wednesday to double down on tailoring supervision to emphasize material financial risk, ensuring the regulatory burden doesn't hinder economic growth, and embracing innovation.

The framework creates no new enforceable standards, so departing from its illustrative practices does not by itself establish a legal violation or grounds for an MRA. Under the OCC and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's new MRA standards, effective November 2, 2026, an MRA requires an actual violation of banking or banking-related law or regulation or an imprudent practice meeting the rule's material-financial-risk criteria. The Federal Reserve has addressed its examiners' approach to MRAs separately, in a statement of supervisory operating principles. Regulation E, which governs electronic fund transfers, may apply to consumer payments initiated through AI agents if the account and transfer fall within Regulation E's scope. Banks' underlying activities remain subject to existing consumer protection, fair-lending, Bank Secrecy Act, and payment requirements.

The framework is written for OCC examiners overseeing national banks, federal savings associations, and federal branches and agencies. Reuters reported in October that all three federal banking agencies were asking about banks' AI controls. The Conference of State Bank Supervisors released its own AI supervisory framework in September, which each state agency may decide whether and how to use. NYDFS's cybersecurity regulation applies to covered entities subject to exemptions, and its October 2024 and May 2026 AI letters address cybersecurity risks but do not themselves impose new requirements. Colorado S.B. 26-189 adds notice, human-review, and record-retention requirements beginning January 1, 2027, subject to its scope, exemptions, and alternative-compliance provisions.

The NYDFS noted in a May 2026 AI advisory that secure programming practices may include additional testing, validation, and human oversight of AI-generated code before production deployment. Banks are taking different approaches to customer-directed agents, including restricting credential-based access and revising customer agreements to address agent activity. How Regulation E's existing authorization and liability rules apply to particular AI-agent arrangements raises interpretive questions. Giving an agent access does not by itself resolve whether a disputed transfer was authorized or who bears liability. State-law coverage and federal preemption remain provision- and activity-specific, and nonbank affiliates and agents do not automatically inherit National Bank Act protection.

Institutions may wish to record who can invoke each system, the system's access to data and tools, permitted actions, human checkpoints, and associated legal obligations. Institutions may wish to test the detection and suspension of inappropriate activity, continuity arrangements, and reviewer capacity. Institutions may wish to assess independence and correlated-failure risks where secondary agents or judge models provide a backstop. Institutions may wish to keep internal audit's assurance role distinct from management's testing and validation. Institutions may wish to include AI-related failures in incident-response procedures and assess whether they trigger existing notification obligations.

stories.Headline: AI finds security flaws faster, forcing rushed patches that cause tech outages
stories.Summary:
In the roughly two and a half months before Microsoft's massive outage last week, the company patched 3,554 security flaws in its software, more than it had in 2025 and 2024 combined. The rapid increase is largely thanks to AI's remarkable ability to find flaws in code, according to the article dated Nov. 21, 2026. Federal officials and business leaders say that unlocked skill has led to numerous high-profile tech outages in recent weeks. The United States experienced a series of high-profile tech outages in November, impacting critical services from mail to banking and aviation. US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated that these crashes are not the work of hackers, citing no digital footprint of attacks.

The trouble began on November 12, when Microsoft services, including Outlook, went down. On November 13, a telecommunications error forced a nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration, halting over 10,000 flights. HR and payroll software giant Workday also suffered major disruptions on the same day. On November 16, United Airlines was hit by a widespread system outage, and at the exact same time, major online banking services from JPMorgan Chase crashed, temporarily locking users out of their bank accounts. High-profile tech outages at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, and Charles Schwab have disrupted businesses and consumers.

Mullin revealed in a Fox News interview that an unnamed technology expert believes "SI" is trying to automatically fix problems inside older systems too quickly. This expert's theory suggests that modern SI, by writing code and fixing things rapidly, creates a massive ripple effect in programs not designed to run as fast. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed that the nationwide flight groundings on November 13 were caused by a contractor upgrading an outdated 1980s copper wire system to fiber-optic cable. When the new router was installed, the technology overloaded the old air traffic control system, causing it to crash. Duffy strongly rejected rumors that the FAA's new AI-based air traffic tool, SMART, caused the flight groundings, confirming the new AI tool is completely separate from the failed older system.

Politicians and tech executives, including Armadin CEO Kevin Mandia, suggest that organisations are using AI to discover software vulnerabilities in their systems. This has led to a "mad rush" to apply patches quickly, according to Senator Mark Warner, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee. Mandia stated that updating at speed may prevent testing all potential outcomes of an update. Nicole Perlroth, a former cybersecurity reporter, noted that pressure to patch faster increases the likelihood of "breaking things in unexpected, cascading ways" via an X post. Mandia added that while nobody wants an outage, organisations will become operationally better at updating in the AI age, and he anticipates near-term cybersecurity pain will lead to long-term gains.

Last month, AI discovered significant flaws in a programming language used by up to 70 per cent of websites, contributing to the increased patching activity. The FBI has been asked to investigate the ground stop to confirm it was an installation error and not a cyberattack. The FBI is investigating the FAA incident to confirm it was an installation error, not cyberattack. A temporary ground stop at US airports also caused chaos, though Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cited aging air traffic control infrastructure. Organisations are rolling out a higher volume of fixes, potentially overwhelming systems, and fast updates may hinder full testing, leading to system disruptions, experts say.

More tech outages are expected as firms accelerate patching in the AI era, according to the article dated Nov. 19, 2026. Recent tech outages at major US banks, Microsoft, and the FAA may stem from a rush to fix cybersecurity flaws discovered by AI. The article states that organisations are rolling out a higher volume of fixes, potentially overwhelming systems. Experts say fast updates may hinder full testing, leading to system disruptions. The articles leave open the identity of the unnamed technology expert cited by Mullin and the outcome of the FBI investigation.

stories.Headline: Most people trust AI answers without checking them, F-Secure survey finds
stories.Summary:
A survey of 1,500 consumers in the US and UK, published in F-Secure's Digital Trust Report Fall 2026, found that around 90% of respondents believe people have a responsibility to verify AI-generated information. The report also found that 70% of respondents say they only sometimes, rarely, or never check AI answers before using them. The research found that 47.3% of respondents stopped questioning an AI answer because it sounded right. One in four respondents told the researchers they have followed AI advice on a major real-life decision. The findings were published on 20 November 2026 in an article by Dr. Amel Bourdoucen on Cybersecurity Insiders.

The data showed that the main barriers to checking are not having a reliable source to check against at 37.5%, checking taking too long at 19.2%, and not knowing how to check at 15.4%. Among people who use AI across a wide range of tasks, 59.7% rarely or never check its answers, compared with 28.6% of those who use it for a narrower set of tasks. Among people who do not currently use AI, scam detection mattered most at 46.1%, followed by keeping personal data from being stored or shared at 45% and blocking harmful content at 42.9%. Sources and confidence scores ranked far lower, at 14.6% and 11.4%. The article was published on 20 November 2026.

The article argues that the fix belongs with the people building these tools, saying trustworthy AI starts with citations and links that lead to real, trusted sources. It says builders should make uncertainty visible when an answer isn't reliable, rather than delivering a guess with the same confidence as a fact. It says builders should optimize for the quality of an answer, not simply the ability to produce one. It says digital service providers should make clear sourcing, meaningful control over personal data, and honesty about not knowing a design priority from day one. It says AI providers can keep asking people to work around their products' limitations, or build products that don't need workarounds.

A separate article by a practitioner who completed an 18-month deployment of 25 production agents across a large travel and cruise group, published on CIO.com on 18 November 2026, says the window is rarely stated and the denominator almost never. It says concurrent initiatives that could have produced the same movement go unnamed. It says the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001 tell you to measure, not what a reportable number looks like. It says medicine and ML research already have reporting standards such as CONSORT-AI and REFORMS, while agentic deployments don't. It says the practitioner used three outcomes internally to justify further investment, and two came out weaker under the CLEAR standard.

The CLEAR standard has five tests: concurrent changes registered, locked window, evidentiary custody, attributable baseline, and reference volume. The practitioner says the locked window asks for pre-commitment, which is costly because it forecloses discovering later that a different period tells a better story. One outcome survived because the six-month window was fixed to include peak season, contact volume was flat year over year, and counts came from the system of record reviewed by finance rather than the agent team. One outcome did not survive because the 23 days included time in a standing backlog, and part of the gain came from clearing that queue rather than shortening the process. The weakest outcome was reported without the caveat that a marketplace rebuild and opt-in dynamic pricing ran in the same window as the AI-native search capability credited with most of the uplift.

The practitioner says the most important control in the deployment cost nothing to build: any line-of-business manager, from the wholesale desk to the cruise operations floor, could stop an agent within ninety seconds with no ticket and no approval. The practitioner says being wrong cost an hour of throughput, while being slow could cost a customer. The practitioner says CLEAR isn't a validity standard, because a result that passes all five is still a single-organization observation. The practitioner says CLEAR assumes the operational record is complete, and in agentic systems one gap quietly breaks that assumption. The F-Secure article says people who don't currently use AI value practical protections over tools that help them assess an answer's reliability.

stories.Headline: Sarvam AI launches Token Factory to provide AI inference services for Indian developers and enterprises
stories.Summary:
The Bengaluru based startup Sarvam AI launched a commercial platform called Token Factory on November 16. This new service allows developers and enterprises to access multiple AI models through its computing infrastructure. The launch focuses on the emerging Indian market for inference as a service. Other companies like L&T and Utho Labs are also building token based infrastructure. Mirror Security and E2E Networks through Jarvislabs are also creating similar offerings.

The platform hosts the Sarvam 105B model and open weight models like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Kimi K3.1 Pro. It also includes GLM 5.3 and Google Gemma 4 31B, with billing conducted in Indian rupee. Sarvam 105B costs ten rupees per million input tokens and twenty five rupees per million output tokens. Other model prices range from fourteen rupees for input to nine hundred fifty rupees for output tokens. The system uses a common API to handle hosting and optimization without requiring customer GPU procurement.

Sarvam clarified that the Token Factory runs on privately procured GPUs rather than government subsidized ones. The company stated that its access to IndiaAI Mission GPU capacity ended in March 2026. They noted there are no commercial arrangements for royalties or data sharing with hosted model developers. Sarvam explained that these open weight models can be downloaded and deployed on private infrastructure. The company also stated that zero data retention is available only upon an explicit request.

Sanchit Vir Gogia of Greyhound Research said the factory keeps the B200 cluster busy between training runs. He noted that founders must show by late 2027 that DeepSeek customers stay for Sarvam. Manoj Dhanda of Utho Cloud called this a positive development that proves Indian model operation is feasible. Enterprise users are affected because Sarvam uses data for training unless the end user disables the feature. Businesses processing sensitive information may find this default data usage a significant concern.

The company was selected under the IndiaAI Mission to develop homegrown foundation models using 4,096 Nvidia H100 GPUs. This six month computing allocation was worth 247 crore rupees, including a government subsidy of 98.68 crore rupees. Sarvam currently serves over 450 billion tokens daily through the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model. The platform carries SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certifications and promises 99.95 percent uptime. E2E Networks expanded its own capabilities by acquiring Jarvislabs assets in August 2025.

Introductory pricing for the Token Factory will remain in effect until the end of 2026. Utho Cloud intends to enter the domestic inference space by early 2027 to meet growing demand. OpenAI is also moving to bring its own inference services directly to the Indian market. The articles leave open whether the service is a revenue play or a data play. It remains unclear how many GPUs Sarvam runs or the actual utilization of its B200 cluster.

stories.Headline: AI coding tools reduce engineer satisfaction and change valued skills
stories.Summary:
Software engineers say artificial intelligence coding tools are reducing the satisfaction they get from solving difficult problems, and the shift is changing which technical skills are valued while raising concerns about how junior developers are trained. Gemma Rodgers, a UK-based software developer, told CNBC that reaching a working solution feels less rewarding when AI produces it quickly, and she worried that engineers could lose essential technical abilities if they lean too heavily on automated answers. A 2026 Stack Overflow survey found that 83 per cent of software developer respondents use at least one AI tool. Rodgers, who began studying computer science in 2002, said the joy of spending weeks fixing a hard bug has been somewhat removed by AI, and she described the satisfaction from AI-generated solutions as a breadcrumb of joy rather than a full meal of joy.

The growing use of AI is also changing what companies expect from developers, who are now more often required to review AI-produced code for usefulness rather than write every line themselves. James Broadhead, Chief Technology Officer at Taktile, told CNBC that developers who once took three weeks to build a prototype can now generate ten in an afternoon, and he said the challenge lies in identifying which versions are effective. He added that engineers are no longer reading all the AI-generated code, which can complicate understanding how a project is organised. Joshua Whle, Chief Executive Officer of Mindstone, believes the trend is creating a widening gap between employees who can use AI effectively and those who cannot, and he suggested AI could foster what he called 100X engineers compared with the earlier idea of 10X engineers. Whle acknowledged that developers who enjoy traditional coding might find the change difficult, because skills they honed for years are no longer necessarily the most valued.

The shift also poses concerns for people entering the software industry, since junior engineers typically learn by writing basic code, debugging and solving problems, and AI could automate those tasks and cost them crucial chances to develop practical skills. Chris Sees, Chief Executive Officer of Hoxton Mix and a software engineer with more than 20 years of experience, said routine tasks are vital for young developers' learning. He advised companies to integrate AI into training rather than let it become a shortcut, and he described AI as a junior engineer that requires human supervision. Rodgers, while not against AI, prefers using it for repetitive tasks and keeping challenging problems for herself, because she believes struggle is essential for job satisfaction.

stories.Headline: Incoming Democratic Congress plans stricter AI oversight and safety regulations
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence industry is preparing for more aggressive oversight as a Democratic-controlled Congress takes power on November 20, 2026. These incoming lawmakers intend to use their control over congressional committees to investigate tech companies and demand that executives testify in hearings. The new majority plans to introduce various bills that establish safety guidelines for capable models, protect the labor force, and address child safety. These legislative efforts require federal safety requirements for advanced developers and the mandatory reporting of safety breaches. Some proposed rules would force companies to maintain the ability to shut down AI systems if they spiral out of human control.

This shift follows two years of minimal regulation under a Republican-led Congress and President Donald Trump, who believes the industry can self-police. Trump has prioritized winning the AI race against China and has favored voluntary commitments over federal restrictions. Representative Don Beyer of Virginia stated that the government cannot wait for a major catastrophe before implementing meaningful safeguards. Representative Nathaniel Moran of Texas argued that the United States does not have to choose between innovation and safety. Senators Maria Cantwell of Washington and Mike Rounds of South Dakota recently urged National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to take immediate action against cyberattacks.

They claimed that current defenses are not keeping pace with the ability of AI to exploit software weaknesses. The push for regulation comes as voters express negative attitudes regarding how data centers impact electricity prices and jobs. Recent tech outages at Apple, JPMorgan Chase, and Microsoft have further highlighted the vulnerabilities of interconnected digital infrastructure. While these outages were not linked to cyberattacks, they have spurred calls for a more proactive federal role in protecting financial institutions. Lawmakers are now forming bipartisan caucuses to create legislation that balances industry growth with necessary risk mitigation.

stories.Headline: ALIVE: Making Streaming Video Models Interactive
stories.Summary:
Jinzhao Li and fifteen other authors posted a paper titled ALIVE: Making Streaming Video Models Interactive to the arXiv repository on 22 November 2026, describing an interactive streaming video model that supports proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination and feedback-seeking interaction. The authors say streaming video large language models can continuously observe the world yet often handle user requests in isolation, which the new model is meant to address. To train it, the team built two datasets, ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K, for a two-stage process. The first stage, contrastive supervised fine-tuning, teaches the model when and how to respond, according to the abstract.

The second stage applies reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment, or BACA, which combines trajectory-level and local advantages to refine decisions, responses and silence across multi-turn interactions. The authors also introduce FSI-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating feedback seeking and the task completion that follows it. ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among the compared models on four public benchmarks and on FSI-Bench, the abstract states. The authors present those results as evidence of strong streaming understanding and interactive capabilities.

The paper lists Jinzhao Li, Yuan Xu, Jinxuan Wu, Yukun Wang, Yijia Lei, Hanyu Ji, Yinuo Chen, Zining Huang, Chi Zhang, Hang Ye, Yiwu Zhong, Honglei Yan, Panwang Pan, Yizhou Wang, Yin Li and Miao Liu as its authors. Their abstract describes the work as an effort to make streaming video models interactive rather than handling each user request in isolation. The posted pages also describe arXivLabs, a framework that lets collaborators develop and share features directly on the arXiv website. The listing says individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have accepted values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv works only with partners who adhere to them.

The listing includes an invitation for ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community and points readers to learn more about arXivLabs. The abstract gives no dates for future releases, no plans for a public demo and no further details beyond the training sets, the benchmark and the reported benchmark scores. The full paper is available as a PDF and as a TeX source from the arXiv page.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act turns AI ethics principles into binding duties for financial firms in 2026
stories.Summary:
In 2026, the regulation of artificial intelligence shifted from voluntary ethical principles and high-level supervisory expectations toward binding legal duties. This change brings active regulatory scrutiny and the real prospect of enforcement for firms using these advanced technologies. The transition is especially significant for financial services where AI is already embedded in credit decisioning and insurance underwriting. It also impacts fraud detection, customer servicing, and internal risk management across the global financial services market. These applications raise regulatory concerns at a scale and speed that existing frameworks were not designed to address.

The EU AI Act became generally applicable on 2 August 2026, with core high-risk requirements starting 2 December 2027. Product-related systems under Article 6(1) and Annex I must satisfy these high-risk obligations starting on 2 August 2028. Annex III classifies AI for credit scoring and life or health insurance risk assessment as high-risk, requiring fundamental-rights impact assessments. In October 2026, the Financial Stability Board released 12 non-binding sound practices for the responsible adoption of AI. Indonesia's OJK issued Regulation No. 6 of 2026 regarding the conduct of financial sector information providers.

Jaime Bofill stated that human oversight becomes more important as AI becomes more autonomous, requiring clear accountability for decisions. Hywel Jenkins noted that the lack of specific regimes leaves supervisors and investigators to define appropriate levels of scrutiny. The Financial Stability Board strongly encourages firms to reference its sound practices when refining AI governance and control frameworks. The Financial Conduct Authority intends to regulate AI through existing technology-neutral frameworks like the Consumer Duty and SMCR. The OJK expects boards of directors and commissioners to take substantive oversight of critical and high-risk AI systems.

Cross-border institutions are affected by a compliance landscape that is converging in substance but diverging in form across jurisdictions. The EU uses a horizontal statutory regime, while the UK, Singapore, and Australia rely on existing obligations and expectations. In the United States, federal oversight is increasingly complemented by various state-level initiatives, creating a more fragmented regulatory model. Technology providers and financial institutions must reconcile these varying legal requirements without fragmenting their own internal governance arrangements. Compliance teams must navigate layers including the EU AI Act, NIST standards, ISO 42001, and sector-specific guidance.

The articles explain that AI governance is moving from voluntary principles to concrete regulatory and supervisory expectations for financial firms. Regulators are converging around common priorities such as accountability, transparency, human oversight, third-party risk, and general risk management. The EU AI Act operates alongside the Digital Operational Resilience Act, which imposes its own ICT risk and governance duties. Indonesia uses a cross-sector ethical framework from the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs Circular Letter No. 9 of 2023. The UK's FCA uses the Mills Review and AI Live Testing programme to focus on outcomes and real-world deployments.

Firms must now demonstrate through testing and documentation that risks are managed throughout the entire AI lifecycle in practice. Compliance will depend on the ability to prove that policies operate effectively rather than just having the policies exist. Institutions that embed these controls into existing risk management frameworks will be better positioned to navigate the regulatory divergence. The articles leave open how firms will reconcile fragmented technical controls and shared responsibility for AI models and hosting. It remains unclear how supervisors will define standards in jurisdictions that lack a specific regulatory regime for artificial intelligence.

stories.Headline: Congressional researchers propose marijuana tax rules as model for taxing AI data centers
stories.Summary:
A report from the Congressional Research Service released on November 18 identifies the federal tax treatment of marijuana businesses under Section 280E as a possible model for taxing artificial intelligence companies and data centers, according to The Marijuana Herald. The report, titled Taxing AI: Alternative Approaches, examines several methods Congress could use to tax the growing artificial intelligence industry. Among the options discussed is applying restrictions similar to those that have long prevented marijuana businesses from deducting ordinary operating expenses on their federal tax returns. Under Section 280E of the Internal Revenue Code, businesses trafficking in Schedule I or II controlled substances are generally prohibited from deducting standard business expenses, even when operating legally under state law. They can subtract the cost of goods sold from their revenue when calculating gross income, but generally cannot deduct expenses such as rent, employee wages, utilities and depreciation.

The CRS report dedicates an entire section to marijuana tax treatment, explaining that the restrictions make the resulting tax resemble a value-added tax. Researchers discuss whether comparable limitations on business expense deductions could be applied to participants in the artificial intelligence market, although they acknowledge uncertainty about the feasibility of such an approach. The report returns to marijuana taxation in a separate discussion of potential gross receipts taxes on AI data centers, describing an alternative that would apply the same general tax treatment as marijuana businesses. Under this approach, companies would be taxed on receipts minus the cost of goods sold, without the full range of ordinary operating expense deductions available to most businesses. CRS notes that because data centers generally do not manufacture or sell physical inventory, applying this approach would effectively function as a gross receipts tax, subjecting nearly all their revenue to taxation rather than just their profits.

The analysis comes as members of Congress consider multiple proposals to increase taxes on AI-related businesses. Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR), for example, has separately proposed a gross receipts tax on data centers, along with restrictions on depreciation deductions and other tax benefits. CRS identifies the marijuana-style tax treatment as a closely related alternative to the gross receipts approach. Other proposals discussed in the report include taxes on electricity consumption, computer processing power, digital advertising revenue and AI-related services. The report also examines arguments against additional AI taxes, including concerns about reduced investment, economic productivity and international competition.

The comparison comes as Section 280E remains a major financial issue for marijuana companies. An April federal order moved certain qualifying medical marijuana activities to Schedule III, generally removing those activities from Section 280E's restrictions. However, marijuana activities that remain classified under Schedule I continue to face the deduction limitations, and federal tax guidance addressing businesses with multiple activities remains pending.

stories.Headline: House committee sends Walberg bill to measure AI use in the workplace to the floor calendar
stories.Summary:
The AWARE Act, H.R. 9381, a bill directing the federal government to measure how artificial intelligence is used in the workplace, has been placed on the House Union Calendar and is eligible for floor consideration. Rep. Tim Walberg (R-MI) introduced the measure, which would direct the Bureau of Labor Statistics to collect and report the data. No floor vote has been scheduled, leaving lobbyists and congressional staff tracking workforce and AI policy without a date for the next legislative action. The bill is a measurement proposal that would amend the 1913 law establishing the Department of Labor to require federal labor statistics to include AI use, workplace conditions, and productivity. The House Education and Workforce Committee held a markup June 25 and ordered the bill reported, as amended, by a 19-14 vote.

The bill would require BLS to begin collecting the data within 18 months of enactment, and it identifies gaps in existing data on employer adoption of AI, worker-level use, changes to job tasks, training needs and effects on hiring, wages and employment. It says existing BLS surveys do not adequately capture those developments, and policymakers, employers, workers, educators and researchers are among the groups that could benefit from the information. The measure would not directly regulate employers or AI developers. It was reported Nov. 18 as H. Rept. 119-887 and placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 782, and the bill has no cosponsors from either party. The committee's markup record covers 11 bills, and the transcript shows Walberg offered a substitute amendment before the chair moved to report the bill.

Republicans argue that better data on artificial intelligence's impact on the workforce is essential to shaping effective policy, and Walberg, announcing the legislation on June 22, said information about its impact is needed as AI transforms the workplace. The House Education and Workforce Committee echoed that position, saying the bill would help generate data to support workers, inform policy, and keep America competitive. Democrats have raised concerns that the legislation would duplicate existing federal research without providing additional resources. Rep. Bobby Scott (D-VA), the committee's ranking member, argued that the bill would burden the already underfunded BLS with responsibilities largely already being performed by other agencies, and he warned that the measure would force BLS to conduct duplicative work and urged lawmakers to oppose it.

The bill's reach is narrow, establishing a federal data-collection requirement without directly imposing new rules on employers, and the dispute centers on agency resources and potential overlap with existing surveys. Obstacles include the 19-14 committee vote, the lack of cosponsors, and Scott's funding objection. At the markup, Scott cited the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey as an example of work other agencies already perform, and he said the bill provides no additional funding for BLS. The legislation was reported as amended, and the reported version retains the requirement to begin collecting statistics within 18 months. Next developments to watch include the House floor schedule and any Rules Committee notice on H.R. 9381.

stories.Headline: Colorado adopts rules requiring chatbot age checks beyond government ID and AI disclosures to users
stories.Summary:
Colorado's Department of Law adopted 76 pages of rules on November 19, 2026, governing two new state laws at once, the Automated Decision-Making Technology in Consequential Decisions Act, enacted as SB 26-189, and the Conversational Artificial Intelligence Services Act, enacted as HB 26-1263 and called the "Chatbot Safety Act" in the rules. The text is numbered 4 CCR 904-6 and titled "Automated Decision-Making Technology & Conversational Artificial Intelligence Service Rules." It sets out how companies using algorithms in lending, hiring, housing and education must explain adverse decisions. It also sets out how operators of consumer chatbots must estimate users' ages, remind them they are talking to a machine, and report on suicide and self-harm safeguards. The rules are not yet in force.

The rules require a company that uses such a tool and turns someone down to say so in plain language within 30 days, and require chatbot operators to check users' ages without relying only on government ID, remind them they are talking to AI, and file safety metrics with the state by July 1, 2027. Deployers must respond to a request for more information about the AI system within 15 days, give instructions for accessing or correcting data within 15 days when requested by email, mail or phone, and list third parties holding the data within 15 days when the deployer holds none. Access to or correction of personal data must come within 45 days, extendable once by 45 days, and a request for meaningful human review must be acknowledged within 10 days and completed within 45 days, with one extension of up to 45 days, though no extension is available where the decision affects food, shelter or required medical care. Records of human review must be kept three years, printed disclosures sent by post must use not less than 12-point font, a continuous chatbot interaction ends when sixty consecutive minutes pass without the user interacting, AI disclosure to minors must come at the start of each interaction and at least once every three hours, AI disclosure to adults must come at the first interaction of each calendar day and then persistently or at three-hour intervals, the first annual report to the Attorney General is due on or before July 1, 2027, covering the preceding calendar year, and documents verifying the annual report must be produced within 30 days of a Department request.

The Department posted the adopted text as a double redline dated November 18, and the Secretary of State's docket lists November 19 as the adoption date and November 20 as the date the Attorney General's opinion was requested, with the filing shown as pending. The adopted Rule 1.3 reads that the rules "shall become effective by the effective date published by the Secretary of State in the Colorado Code of Regulations," a change from the August 11 proposal and the October 6 interim draft, which both set a fixed effective date of January 1, 2027. The statutes themselves still take effect on January 1, 2027, and SB 26-189 requires the Attorney General to adopt rules on post-adverse outcome disclosures before that date. The adopted definition of a continuous interaction says it begins when a user starts a conversation, thread, project or chatbot profile and "Ends when sixty (60) consecutive minutes pass without the User interacting with the Conversational Artificial Intelligence Service," and a pause of less than 60 minutes does not end it. That definition drives every disclosure timer in the chatbot half of the rules.

Rule 6.2 presumes an output materially influences a consequential decision if it "constrains an option set, sets a threshold, or produces a rank, score, classification, recommendation, prediction, or other inference that pertains to the individual about whom the decision is being made," and it is reviewed by the deployer during the decision, used to screen the data the deployer sees, or used to decide without human involvement. The presumption can be rebutted by showing the output was a "De Minimis Factor," through evidence that the deployer never consulted the output, that the decision rested on a hard cut-off documented beforehand, not derived from the ADMT and applied consistently, or that a person conducted an independent review with enough time, authority and subject matter understanding. Tools used "solely to summarize, organize, translate, draft, route, or present information for human review of administrative processing" are not ADMT, and an AI system that sorts applications from highest to lowest grade point average "without any subjective input" is excluded, as is a tenant-placement tool that sorts applicants by unit size and date, though that tool becomes covered ADMT once it labels applicant data "positive" or "negative." A private college that uses an AI system to "predict how that student would respond to different amounts of institutional aid" and sets aid accordingly is making a consequential decision, because the aid amount is "a differentiated price that is reasonably likely to materially limit or fundamentally alter a consumer's access to education." In hiring, an algorithm that ranks candidates from "strongest" to "weakest" without showing a numeric score still triggers the presumption, because it "produced a non-objective conclusion about the applicants."

A developer that integrates another developer's covered ADMT into its own product must either pass the upstream documentation to downstream customers or fold it into its own disclosures, and downstream parties "may reasonably rely on information made available by preceding Developers absent actual knowledge that the information is materially inaccurate or incomplete." A company whose general AI product is integrated into covered ADMT "without the party's knowledge" and without having designed, marketed or contracted for that use is not a developer, and developer documentation must name the decisions for which a system's use "is known to be inappropriate or harmful" and say whether training data includes sensitive or biometric data. Trade secrets may be withheld, but the developer must cite its legal authority and still provide "a summary, categorical description, or other generalized information," and when a third party runs the system on a deployer's behalf, the deployer remains responsible, as in the rules' example of an employer that has a staffing agency shortlist applicants. Rule 7 supplies sample sentences including "Bank ABC closed your checking account," "Leasing Company ABC was unable to approve your application to rent 123 Main Street," and "Credit Union ABC has denied your loan application," and states that "a statement that the role of the Covered ADMT was to automate a review of the Consumer's Personal Data is insufficient," while a statement that the system reviewed "credit report information and employment verification information" is specific enough. Where a factor was an automatic denial, such as criminal history, credit score or years of work experience, the disclosure must say so, and where the decision followed incomplete information, it must say that too, with a college awarding a 50% tuition scholarship writing "You are only eligible for a 50% tuition scholarship, covering $16,850 in your first year."

According to the Department's rulemaking page, informal comments were accepted through July 13, 2026, and the proposed rules were filed with the Secretary of State on August 11 under tracking number 2026-00360, followed by an interim draft on October 6, a regulatory analysis on October 21, and a formal hearing on October 26 at 10:00 a.m., the same day written comments closed at 11:59 p.m. Mountain time. SB 24-205, the original Colorado AI Act signed on May 17, 2024, was repealed and replaced by SB 26-189, which the Colorado House passed 57-6 on May 9, 2026. According to the General Assembly's record, Governor Jared Polis signed SB 26-189 on May 14, 2026 and HB 26-1263 on May 29, 2026. The rules themselves carry no date, and their effective date clause points to whatever date the Secretary of State publishes in the Colorado Code of Regulations. The article's table collects the deadlines from the text of 4 CCR 904-6, including the 30-day adverse outcome disclosure under Rules 7.4(A) and 7.7 and the 15-day response under Rule 7.6(A)(1).

The Department has asked for a formal opinion from the Attorney General, after which the rules go to the Secretary of State and become final twenty days after publication. A federal court order in xAI's lawsuit already limits when the state can start enforcing the automated-decision law. The Secretary of State's docket shows the filing as pending. The article leaves open what still stands between the 76 pages of rules and enforcement, and it does not say when the Attorney General's opinion will issue or when publication will follow.

stories.Headline: NHAI deploys AI dashcam analytics to detect road damage and track contractor repairs
stories.Summary:
The National Highways Authority of India is deploying an artificial intelligence-powered analytical tool to assess road conditions, identify damage to roads and pavements, communicate the information to contractors, follow up on the complaints and ensure that the issues are rectified. NHAI officials announced the system during a series of technical sessions at the 85th Indian Roads Congress in Hyderabad on November 20, 2026. Dashcam Analytics systems have been mounted in patrol vehicles to monitor highways for infrastructure-related issues. The system captures geotagged, high-resolution photographs of road conditions, pavements and road signage and uploads them to a dashboard, where each photograph is uniquely numbered. The system then communicates the information to the relevant contractor, who proceeds to rectify the issue, and NHAI officials described it as an end-to-end detection to rectification system.

Key road conditions identified by the system include potholes and road rutting, which refers to the formation of depressed surfaces on the road. Other issues identified include edge dropping and uneven road shoulders, streetlights that are not working, signage, and gaps in road medians. The Indian Roads Congress also deliberated on whether India could take a lead in road safety globally. Samrat Valani, vice-president of Development, Operations and Customer Experience, North America, Transurban, made a case for a clear mandate to halve road deaths by 2030, in line with the Stockholm Declaration on road safety adopted in 2020. He emphasised the need for a strong framework based on the four Es of education, engineering, enforcement and emergency care, along with political will and evidence that the initiatives were working.

Sharing examples of road safety interventions from across the world, Valani said that data show that in India, 54,000 people who did not wear helmets lost their lives last year. Citing the case of Vietnam, which he described as a motorcycle country, he said a government-led awareness programme at around 100 schools had increased helmet use from 36% to 69% in one year. As the programme continued, they saw in the next year that the usage dropped to 50% and stabilised at around 57%, and he said the point was not the number of injuries but the helmet use and the ability to count, because when you count, you get to know the effectiveness of the programme. Touching upon the importance of quick incident and accident detection, leveraging technology to respond to incidents and clearing them as quickly as possible, he said that in the US, for every minute an incident remains on the roadway, the likelihood of a secondary accident increases by 2.8%. Informing road users, creating awareness and measuring outcomes, adopting a fair approach by issuing warnings, particularly in cases of speeding, followed by firm enforcement, and using data to prevent crashes are important metrics, he said.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose GameWM to split game engine and video model roles for next-generation games
stories.Summary:
Bing He, Runze Wang, Fei Zha, Zhongyuan Wu, Ke Xu, Tao Zhuang, Yuxuan Xie and Zhongyuan Liu posted a paper titled GameWM: Toward Next-Generation Video Games with Interaction-Centric World Models to the arXiv preprint server on November 22, 2026. The paper proposes a design for next-generation video games built on a division of labor between a game engine and a generative video model. For more than half a century, the authors write, video games have pursued better graphics, more natural interaction and more engaging gameplay, and generative video models now bear on all three. Neural networks already draw most of the pixels in shipped games, and recent world models let a lightweight game engine keep the world state while a video model turns the engine's coarse proxy video into final frames. Those systems, however, treat the video model as a renderer that only restyles motion the engine has already authored, which the authors say leaves most of its generative capacity unused and limits the diversity a game can offer.

Under the proposed division of labor, the GameWM-engine keeps what must be exact, namely the rules, state, camera and layout of the world, which also spares the video model from having to remember that layout. The GameWM-VM generates what is expensive to author by hand, namely the look of the world and the detail of the player's interactions. One game mechanic can then be realized in many visually and physically distinct ways, while its outcome stays exactly as the engine computed it. To realize this division of labor, the authors build GameWM as a complete system with three parts. The first is a data engine centered on interactions rather than exploration, the second is an interface through which authored character sheets, scene art and skill descriptions enter the model, and the third is a model family from 5B to 33B parameters with a real-time causal variant for play.

The authors state that together these parts give every player a fresh version of the same game, with each player's own character, world and skills turning the same engine mechanics into a new experience. They add that every event keeps the timing and outcome the GameWM-engine computed. The paper is listed under the identifier 2611.19247, and the full text is available as a PDF, as experimental HTML and as TeX source. The posting page also carries a standard description of arXivLabs, a framework that allows collaborators to develop and share new arXiv features directly on the website, and states that arXiv is committed to openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. The articles give no further details on publication venue, code release or follow-up work.

stories.Headline: Google workers petition Pichai to drop school search cutoff
stories.Summary:
Hundreds of workers at Google are pushing senior leadership to retract a policy that would block schools who turn off its Gemini AI tools from access to the company’s search engine starting next year. Google made the surprise announcement two weeks ago, on Election Day, with executives saying they wanted to address teachers and parents’ concerns around AI in the classroom. Since then, communities across the country have protested Google’s tight hold on tech in many schools. The push came in a petition brought by the Alphabet Workers Union, which represents more than 1,000 workers at Google’s parent company. A software engineer in Google’s education department told Mother Jones on Thursday that most workers did not know about the Google Search decision before it was publicly announced.

The policy would block schools that turn off Gemini AI tools from access to Google’s search engine starting next year. School districts across the country use the company’s software and Chromebooks, which were more affordable than Windows and Apple computers when many were quickly assembling remote learning programs during the early years of the Covid pandemic. The Chromebooks have built-in AI classroom tools, and Google Search embeds AI Overview and AI Mode powered by Gemini. Responding to the backlash, three of the largest school districts in the US, New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago, are now discussing alternative search engines. Protests took place in New York City and in six other cities, Los Angeles, Chicago, Boston, Portland, Oregon, Boulder, Colorado, and Durham, North Carolina, all organized by a nationwide alliance of parent and community advocacy organizations.

The petition was addressed to Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Google vice president and general manager of education Chris Phillips, and Elizabeth Reid, its vice president and head of search. Employees wrote that any opportunity to drive positive change with AI in education will rely on educators having the freedom to choose how to implement it in their curriculum. They wrote that cutting off access to Search for schools that don’t wish to use AI will not help persuade users and will more likely result in them shutting out Google products altogether. They continued that it is their job as Googlers to respect the user and listen to them when they have concerns about products.

Corporate leadership has now acknowledged the letter but has not responded to any of its specific demands. A Google engineer said AI classroom tools should be built responsibly and prioritize the best interests of the students, not the company’s bottom line. Another engineer and union member in New York, who also signed the petition, said the executive team seems convinced that resistance to AI adoption is because people don’t see the vision. That goes beyond teachers, parents, and students, the Google staffer said, with colleagues also concerned about how the company is implementing their work on AI tools.

The engineer asked why, if the tech is really as useful and desirable as they think it is, they don’t trust workers to choose to use it on their own terms. Google has been contacted for comment. Attendees of a rally in New York City of all ages held signs reading “NO AI IN MY SCHOOL!”, “A.I. Gets an F,” “Stop stealing our imaginations,” and “SCHOOL Librarians = THE BEST Search Engines.” Some students handed out fliers to passersby while younger children ran around and drew pictures off to the side.

Many cars driving by honked their horns in support, and a few construction workers on the other side of the one-way street cheered the protesters on. Chromebooks are distributed to students through a fence at a Los Angeles Unified School District high school during the Covid quarantine. Google made the announcement on Election Day, two weeks before the petition was reported on November 20, 2026. More to follow.

stories.Headline: US education unions condemn Google for tying school search access to AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Google announced earlier this month that it plans to turn off search engine access as soon as next year for K-12 schools that toggle off its AI tools, claiming the decision is necessary based on the technologies' recent fusion. Education unions in the United States strongly criticized Google's reported decision to require schools to adopt its AI tools if they wish to continue using the company's search and education services. The American Federation of Teachers condemned the move, arguing that schools should not be presented with an all-or-nothing choice. The National Education Association echoed those concerns, stressing that schools must remain free to decide whether and how AI technologies are used. The criticism follows reports that Google is pressuring schools to choose between access to its search and education ecosystem and the adoption of its AI products.

Google disclosed that it would turn off its Gemini AI program and search engine for schools until schools decide which services to enable. Google has only offered school districts more ways to interact with AI, such as AI Mode and AI Overview, which provides users with chatbot search functions and summarized results. Potential options include DuckDuckGo and Microsoft's Bing, both of which offer users the option to disable AI-generated answers. Some of the country's largest school districts, including in Los Angeles, New York, and Chicago, are considering doing away with Google altogether. A January report by the Brookings Institution's Center for Universal Education found that AI can undermine children's foundational development.

Kamar H. Samuels, the chancellor of New York City schools, said in a statement that if Google doesn't reconsider their position, they will explore other search options. Samuels said they refuse to accept the false binary Google has laid out. Google told the Times in a statement Wednesday that it is actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure its products support students and teachers. The AFT said it is unfortunate that Google has prioritized its business interests over the education of children. The AFT said that instead of working with educators and parents to uphold privacy and ensure their tools are safe and useful, Google throws the baby out with the bathwater and bans access to its tools altogether.

The NEA said educators, school districts, and parents should have the freedom to decide which AI tools are right for their students. The NEA said they deserve the time and opportunity to make sure these tools are useful, safe, fair, accessible, protect student privacy, and keep educators involved in how they are used. Rebecca Winthrop, one of the report's authors, told NPR in January that when kids use generative AI that tells them what the answer is, they are not thinking for themselves. Winthrop said they are not learning to parse truth from fiction and are not learning to understand what makes a good argument. Winthrop said they are not learning about different perspectives in the world because they are actually not engaging in the material.

Education International has consistently argued that the adoption of artificial intelligence in education must be guided by pedagogical needs and democratic governance, not by commercial profit making. EI General Secretary David Edwards said no technological product or platform can replace the trust, care, and professional judgement at the heart of teaching and the lifeblood of our societies. Edwards said we demand transparency, accountability, meaningful teacher consultation, and the right to say no to technologies that undermine professional judgement, educational quality, equity, or student privacy. The reported decision by Google also raises concerns about vendor lock-in and the growing dependence of schools on a small number of technology companies. The Google announcement comes at a time when schools around the world are grappling with how to harness new technologies while safeguarding students' rights.

The AFT has called on Google to engage constructively with educators and families and to demonstrate its commitment to protecting students by adopting stronger safeguards for privacy and data protection. Education International emphasizes that education is not a site for technological innovation and product testing. Clear public regulatory frameworks are needed to ensure transparency, accountability, data protection, human oversight, and respect for educators' professional judgement. As governments and education systems develop policies governing artificial intelligence, education unions continue to advocate for transparent regulation, meaningful consultation with education workers, strong privacy protections, and the right of schools to determine whether AI tools serve their educational mission. Studies conducted over the last several months have indicated that the risks attached to the use of AI in schools outweigh the potential benefits.

stories.Headline: Trump orders federal contractors to clear congressional requests with the White House
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump on Friday ordered every company holding a federal contract to notify the White House and its contracting agency immediately of any pending or future congressional request about its communications or work with the executive branch, and to withhold material the administration determines is protected by executive privilege. Executive Order 14438, titled "Protecting the Executive's Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting," was posted on the White House website late on Nov. 20. The requirements extend to subcontractors, and prime contractors are made responsible for ensuring their subcontractors comply. Each agency must promptly inform its contractors and subcontractors of the new obligations and require compliance, and the Office of Management and Budget is to write guidance on how agencies check that contractors are complying. Agencies are directed to coordinate with the White House and contractors on responses to congressional requests, including the assertion of privileges.

If a contractor or subcontractor fails to comply, contracting agencies shall consider all appropriate actions consistent with applicable law, including the potential termination or cancellation of contracts and the potential debarment or suspension of contractors. The order cites the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act and the common law as its legal basis, and it states that it creates no right or benefit enforceable at law against the United States and must be implemented consistent with applicable law. It does not mention existing federal whistleblower protections for contractor employees. The White House defended the order as necessary to protect sensitive government communications, including on national security, and said contractors answering congressional requests on their own could expose privileged information and force the administration into costly legal disputes, according to a Reuters report published by CNBC. The order itself frames the rule as an efficiency measure, saying separate litigation strategies by contractors and the government over the same requests waste taxpayer money.

The move follows a directive issued this week by White House Counsel Will Scharf requiring federal agencies to obtain White House approval before employees agree to testify before Congress. Democrats, who won both chambers in this month's midterm elections, have vowed to investigate the administration, the Trump family's business dealings and its relationships with private companies. Representative Robert Garcia of California, who is set to lead the House Oversight Committee, this week asked 12 of Trump's allies, former aides and family members to preserve documents related to alleged Trump family corruption and government misconduct. The offices of Garcia, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senator Elizabeth Warren did not respond to requests for comment on Friday night, Reuters reported. The restrictions could face legal challenges, particularly if contractors are told to withhold information sought through congressional subpoenas, according to the Reuters report, which notes that executive privilege lets presidents protect certain confidential communications but courts can step in when Congress and the White House dispute access to information.

stories.Headline: Israel introduces AI into courtrooms to ease judges caseloads
stories.Summary:
Israel has begun introducing artificial intelligence into its courtrooms in a country that sanctifies innovation, according to a Haaretz report published on November 21, 2026, by Shay Aspril. The article describes the technology as a means to ease the caseloads that judges currently carry. It raises the prospect that such systems could ultimately replace judges altogether. The report frames the change as one that has already entered the judicial system rather than one that remains only a proposal.

The article sets out what a trial conducted by a machine would involve, describing a process in which the pleadings are input into a system. That system would also analyze the evidence and determine the verdict in the case. No judge would sit across from the person on trial, and there would be no expression to read and no silence to interpret. No one would have to bear the cost of what is decided under such an arrangement.

The report does not name the officials or courts responsible for the introduction, and it records no statement from any judge, ministry or developer about the systems. It presents the shift as one that eases the work of judges while carrying the possibility that they could be replaced. The article offers no date for when an algorithm might deliver verdicts. It gives no figures on how many courts or judges are involved.

The context the article supplies is the country's attitude toward innovation, which it describes as sanctifying, and the pressure of judges' caseloads that the technology is meant to relieve. Beyond that, the report does not say what happens next, and it names no pilot program, budget or timetable for further adoption. It leaves open whether an algorithm will soon deliver verdicts, which its headline poses as a question. No further steps are described in the article.

stories.Headline: Sony and Warner sue Anthropic over pirated lyrics used to train Claude
stories.Summary:
Sony Music and Warner Music's publishing arms sued Anthropic in California federal court on August 28, 2026, a filing reported September 1, accusing the company of pirating song lyrics and sheet music to train its Claude AI chatbot. The suit claims Anthropic misused copyrighted song compositions, including hundreds of lyrics and sheet music from The Beatles, Taylor Swift, Michael Jackson and hundreds of other artists. The labels say Anthropic downloaded millions of pirated books from LibGen and PiLiMi, including books containing copyrighted lyrics and sheet music. The case names CEO Dario Amodei and co-founder Benjamin Mann individually. It was filed in the U.S. District Court, Northern District of California.

The labels seek damages of up to $150,000 for each infringed copyright, covering tens of thousands of compositions, and a court order barring Anthropic from using their works. Universal Music Group and Sony Music filed a second copyright lawsuit against Suno on September 18, 2026, in the U.S. District Court, District of Massachusetts, a 45-page complaint targeting Suno's v6 model. The labels claim v6, which Suno said is trained exclusively on licensed music, actually uses their recordings without consent, and that because the new models are partly built on users' outputs derived from former models, they remain in violation. Jason Isbell filed a proposed class action against Suno on August 31, 2026, with David Lowery, Guy Forsyth and Eduardo Calle, on behalf of musicians whose names Suno has accepted as prompts. SOCAN, the Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada, filed a statement of claim reported September 15, 2026, citing 150 Suno songs it says are identical or nearly identical to works by Joni Mitchell, The Weeknd, The Tragically Hip and others, seeking $20,000 per work and $10,000,000 total.

Universal Music Group sued DistroKid, in a filing reported September 15, 2026, accusing the distributor of flooding streaming platforms with AI-generated slop and of violating federal copyright laws and Delaware's Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Germany's Federal Court of Justice issued its Metall auf Metall VI decision on September 3, 2026, ruling the disputed use permissible under the pastiche exception for the period from June 7, 2021, when the relevant German provision came into force. The US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit heard arguments on September 25, 2026, in SoundExchange's appeal against Music Choice, and has not yet ruled. SoundExchange says SiriusXM's alleged underpayment now exceeds USD $400 million, a claim SiriusXM denies, and the complaint claimed Music Choice invented its own formula for allocating BES receipts, which the CRB's regulations do not permit. The appeal has put SoundExchange's $3.4 million lawsuit against Sonos on hold.

Music Choice has denied underpaying, arguing that under the rule it owes royalties only on revenue from music it provides exclusively to business customers. Suno is asking a federal judge to dismiss the Isbell lawsuit, arguing that using an artist's name to describe a musical style is protected speech, comparing its technology to a producer asking musicians to create something with more of a Jason Isbell vibe. District Judge Angel Kelley has not ruled on Suno's dismissal request, and the musicians are scheduled to respond by December 1, with Suno's reply due December 15. Putting Jason Isbell into Suno created a song called Paper Bell, described by the AI software as a contemporary Americana singer-songwriter track with fingerpicked acoustic guitar, featuring a male voice imitating Isbell's vocal elements. Warner broke away from the $500-million joint copyright lawsuit originally launched by Warner, Sony and Universal against Suno and has since signed a licensing deal with Suno.

Universal Music Group sued Anthropic in 2023 and earlier this year over the alleged use of copyrighted song lyrics in AI training, and Anthropic already paid $1.5 billion to resolve a class action from a group of authors. Suno launched v6, its first model trained on licensed music, weeks before the second suit, after partnering with Warner Music Group, BMG and Believe. The original label suit against Suno was filed over two years earlier. The Kraftwerk case is the legal ancestor of basically every sampling lawsuit filed in the United States since, including early cases like Bridgeport Music v. Dimension Films. The SoundExchange dispute with Music Choice is more than seven years old, originally filed years ago.

The second UMG and Sony suit against Suno is still in early stages, so no settlement talk yet. Suno has responded to each suit differently, settling with some labels while fighting others in court. SOCAN's lawsuit raises questions about the place of Canadian artists in a music industry increasingly shaped by American tech companies. The articles leave open how Judge Kelley will rule on Suno's dismissal request, how the Second Circuit will decide the SoundExchange appeal, and how the Anthropic, DistroKid and SOCAN cases will proceed.

stories.Headline: Delhi high court justice Arora urges law firms to keep hiring fresh graduates despite AI cost savings
stories.Summary:
Delhi High Court Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora urged law firms not to stop recruiting fresh law graduates to save costs amid the growing use of artificial intelligence, warning that the legal profession cannot afford to stop training its next generation of lawyers. She was speaking at the first meeting of the Indian Commercial Litigators' Forum, hosted by JSA Advocates and Solicitors in New Delhi on November 20. Justice Arora said she had heard that some law firms in India had stopped hiring A0 associates, even as concerns grow over the potential impact of AI on employment opportunities for young lawyers. She asked who would train new lawyers for three years if firms only took on people after they had gained experience, and told the audience that while they are saving costs they should not cut down on the future, because firms that do not take in A0 associates today will not have themselves tomorrow.

Responding to her observation, JSA Managing Partner Amar Gupta said firms were conscious of the need to retain training opportunities for fresh graduates even as the firm integrates AI into its operations. He said the firm has in mind to reserve some kind of work entirely without any AI aid or assistance, and that this first-level training will continue to be imparted to new associates who join the firm. Gupta said that roadmap is quite clear in their minds, and that the firm has onboarded AI models deliberately, with some method and planning. Justice Robin Knowles of the High Court of England and Wales moderated the session virtually from London, and he emphasised the value of bringing insights from both the judiciary and legal practitioners to the upcoming seventh full meeting of the Standing International Forum of Commercial Courts.

Delhi High Court Justice Prathiba M Singh shared global figures from a recent WIPO IP Judges Forum survey in Geneva covering 146 courts and tribunals. The survey stated that 35% of courts worldwide already have AI policies in place, 19 courts reported that 30% of their drafting involves AI, and an on-the-spot poll revealed that 52% of judges want to use AI for drafting. Delhi High Court Justice Anish Dayal, who is leading the Indian judiciary's input on SIFOCC's AI workstream ahead of the seventh meeting in Zambia, pointed to the Supreme Court of India's draft AI regulations alongside existing guidance from the High Courts of Kerala and Gujarat. Justice Dayal highlighted the need to guard against hallucinations and confidentiality breaches, while identifying where human decision-making remains irreplaceable, and he also advocated for peer-to-peer judicial training and standardised operating procedures.

Justice Prateek Jalan welcomed CLF India and encouraged the forum to eventually expand its membership to include individual and small-firm practitioners who form a vital part of the Indian bar.
