stories.Headline: Law Society issues practice note tying solicitors' AI use to existing duties and insurance checks
stories.Summary:
The Law Society published a new practice note on 21 October 2026 that brings together existing professional obligations and practical guidance on using AI in legal practice. It follows the SRA's strongly worded warning notice in August, which Hogan Lovells Cadwalader examined at the time. The note distinguishes AI used in the "practice of law", such as legal research, drafting and analysis, from AI used in the "business of law", such as billing and marketing. It states that there is no AI-specific regulator for the legal sector, so solicitors' use of AI sits within existing professional, data protection and cybersecurity frameworks, including the SRA Standards and Regulations. The note also addresses insurance, highlighting the potential implications of firms' use of AI for both professional indemnity and cyber insurance.

The note says the SRA has not certified AI products and that responsibility for work produced using AI remains with the solicitor and cannot be transferred to the technology provider. It states that AI cannot reliably verify its own output, so lawyers should check AI-generated material against authoritative sources rather than asking the same, or another, AI system to confirm it. It cites Ayinde v London Borough of Haringey and Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank [2025] EWHC 1383 (Admin), in which the High Court addressed the use of false authorities and emphasised lawyers' responsibility for material put before the court. It cites SRA v Kumar, in which a Registered Foreign Lawyer was removed from the Register of Foreign Lawyers after repeatedly relying on false or unsupported AI-generated authorities, including following an express warning. It cites R v FGD [2026] EWCA Crim 918, in which the Court of Appeal warned that using AI to prepare a witness for cross-examination may amount to coaching and, in an extreme case, create sufficient unfairness for the court to consider excluding evidence.

The note states that although there is currently no general obligation to disclose the use of AI, transparency may be appropriate where AI has been used materially in preparing documents. It states that a witness statement must remain the witness's own evidence and accurately reflect their recollection. It cites the Civil Justice Council's final recommendations on AI use in court documents, published on 29 October 2026, which propose that factual witnesses should declare that AI has not generated or influenced the substantive content of their statements, with a different disclosure requirement for expert evidence. It cites R (Munir) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2026] UKUT 81 (IAC), in which the tribunal highlighted the potential confidentiality and privilege consequences of uploading client material to a publicly available AI tool. It states that using an "enterprise" or specialist "legal AI" product does not remove these risks, and that information described as anonymised will only fall outside data protection law where individuals are genuinely no longer identifiable.

The note states that AI may create new categories of potentially relevant material, including prompts, draft outputs and audit logs, whose treatment under existing privilege principles remains largely untested. It states that a business user may ask AI for legal advice and create unprivileged material, even if it is later sent to the legal team. It states that professional competence increasingly includes understanding the systems lawyers use and their limitations, and that one particular concern is automation bias, where users place undue confidence in an output simply because it has been produced by technology. It states that professional liability could eventually arise from failing to use AI where a reasonably competent lawyer would have done so, and that there is currently no positive professional duty to use AI, but the applicable standard of care may evolve as increasingly reliable tools become embedded in legal practice.

It states that the risks become more significant with AI agents and agentic AI, which can take actions and carry out multi-step processes across systems with reduced human intervention. The note states that firms should limit systems' permissions to what is genuinely necessary and build in appropriate human review and approval points as autonomy increases. It states that firms need effective AI governance even if they have not formally adopted AI, because staff may independently use publicly available tools, creating the risk of "shadow AI". It states that appropriate controls may include an AI-use policy, approved-tools list, restrictions on the information that may be entered into AI systems, staff training and clear processes for escalating errors or data breaches.

It states that clients should receive appropriate information about how AI may be used on their matters, which firms can address upfront through engagement letters or terms of business. It states that where work is billed by time, firms should not charge for the hours the task would have taken without AI, and that any separate AI or technology charge should be transparent, agreed appropriately and should not duplicate other fees. The note states that AI risks extend beyond hallucination and confidentiality, and include bias and discrimination, cybersecurity, operational resilience and concentration risk arising from dependence on particular technology providers. On professional indemnity insurance, it recommends that firms consider whether their use of AI changes their professional indemnity risk profile or falls outside the considerations upon which their insurance was arranged.

It recommends that firms check whether their existing professional indemnity policy, proposal form or renewal documentation asks about matters such as the use of AI, automation and legal technology. It recommends that firms consider their disclosure obligations including in respect of risks that the firm ought to be aware of, in addition to those which the firm is aware of. It recommends that firms maintain clear supervisory documentation and evidence of risk management, as insurers may be interested in the firm's AI governance processes and may ask about the extent of human oversight of AI-assisted work. More to follow.

stories.Headline: From administrative reforms to AI policy to green economy, Keralam’s fifth Administrative Reforms Commission has a wide-ranging mandate
stories.Summary:
Keralam’s Congress-led United Democratic Front government constituted the fifth Administrative Reforms Commission through an order issued on October 1, 2026, and the Personnel and Administrative Reforms department published its terms of reference through a separate order dated November 19, 2026. The commission is headed by former Minister and Indian Union Muslim League leader M.K. Muneer, according to The Hindu. The panel’s mandate is more expansive than that of the fourth commission, which was headed by former Chief Minister V.S. Achuthanandan. The fifth commission is required to recommend a State artificial intelligence policy and a connected legal framework, and to examine emerging challenges that range from demographic ageing, migration, urbanisation, disaster and climate resilience and public health preparedness to the green economy, Centre-State relations and fiscal federalism.

The terms of reference require the panel to review the structure and processes of the State administration against the backdrop of policy changes, institutional developments and technological advances since the previous commission’s tenure. The commission must also update the Manual of Office Procedure and the Rules of Business of the government in line with current policy, Acts and Rules. It will assess how earlier commission recommendations were implemented, while suggesting reforms to make the State administration adaptive, citizen-centred, efficient, accountable and future-ready. In budgeting and planning, the panel should recommend agile planning and budgeting mechanisms that help the government adapt to unforeseen sectoral requirements, and it will look into barriers to inter-departmental coordination and the interface between departments and local governments.

The Personnel and Administrative Reforms department has issued orders creating 12 posts for the new commission, including those of an Additional Secretary and a Deputy Collector, and there will be four daily-wage posts in addition. The number of posts for the fifth commission and for the chairman’s personal staff will be the same as that of the fourth commission. The ARC chairman will have 12 personal staff whose appointments will be on a co-terminus basis. The commission’s wide-ranging terms of reference cover administrative reform, artificial intelligence policy and the green economy, among other areas.

Articles.Title: From administrative reforms to AI policy to green economy, Keralam’s fifth Administrative Reforms Commission has a wide-ranging mandate

stories.Headline: Rep. Vince Fong introduces bipartisan bill to place private AI experts inside CISA
stories.Summary:
Representative Vince Fong introduced a bipartisan bill on November 20, 2026, to strengthen cybersecurity in the United States. This legislative action follows several widespread technical outages that have recently impacted various systems across the entire country. These outages included a nationwide plane ground stop and issues affecting the National Security Agency and multiple banks. Other entities impacted by these technical failures included Apple, United Airlines, and the Outlook service provided by Microsoft. The bill aims to bolster national defenses against a surge of cyberattacks that are related to artificial intelligence.

The Bridging Resources for Innovative Defense and Government Expertise in Artificial Intelligence Act is the formal name of the bill. It would authorize the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, known as CISA, to collaborate with private sector AI professionals. The legislation calls for a pilot project that would allow about 100 private sector workers to serve within CISA. If approved, the bill would also require a semi-annual report regarding the status and potential improvements of the program. These measures are designed to help the government better defend critical infrastructure from sophisticated and frequent AI-related attacks.

Representative Vince Fong, a Republican representing Bakersfield, stated that communities and critical industries are struggling to keep up with AI attacks. He noted that cyberattacks in the Central Valley have increasingly targeted water systems, hospitals, and schools to steal sensitive data. Fong argued that bringing in emerging technology specialists ensures that national experts have the tools needed to modernize systems. He believes these specialists will help address vulnerabilities and protect the essential services that Americans rely on every day. Fong emphasized that these real threats are not waiting for the government to catch up to the technology.

Representative Josh Gottheimer, a Democrat from New Jersey, co-authored the bill and stated that adversaries use AI to attack networks. He claimed that the agency on the front lines of defense does not have enough capacity to keep pace. Gottheimer described the act as a common sense fix to bring in the best tech minds to hunt intruders. He believes these experts can patch vulnerabilities and stress-test AI tools before they are exploited by any hostile actors. He stated that protecting national security, water systems, and families should not be treated as a partisan political issue.

The articles provide background on the necessity of the bill by citing recent technical failures across various American sectors. These failures include the aforementioned ground stop for planes and the outages at the National Security Agency and several banks. The legislation is a response to the increasing frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks targeting critical infrastructure and sensitive data. Specifically, the text highlights how schools and hospitals in the Central Valley have become targets for these digital attacks. This context establishes the perceived urgency for the government to integrate private sector expertise into its cybersecurity framework.

The next step for the legislation is to seek approval to authorize the pilot project for the private sector workers. The bill would then establish the requirement for semi-annual reports to monitor the progress and effectiveness of the program. The articles do not state if the bill has been scheduled for a vote or a formal debate. They leave open whether other members of Congress support the measure beyond the two named authors of the bill. It remains unclear how the 100 private sector workers will be selected or compensated for their service.

stories.Headline: ICC re-elects Jay Shah as Silicon Valley Unicorns use AI to make mid-match cricket decisions
stories.Summary:
The article, a Guardian opinion column by Barney Ronay published on 20 November 2026, concerns Jay Shah, who was re-elected unopposed this week as president of the International Cricket Council. The article also concerns the San Francisco Unicorns, a Major League Cricket team that uses artificial intelligence in making mid-match decisions on the field. Ronay first heard about this in an interview with Ravichandran Ashwin in the Cricketer Magazine. The article also discusses Jensen Huang, president of Nvidia, and proposals to regulate new global T20 leagues.

The proposals to regulate more aggressively the rush of new global T20 leagues were postponed to the next ICC conference. The Unicorns are the brainchild of Anand Rajaraman and Venky Harinarayan, Silicon Valley types whose stated aim is treating a cricket team like a startup. Their key tool is called Cric Lens, which provides real-time stats, pitch data and player information plus the predictive power of every T20 game ever played. The process is described as Human-in-the-Loop Execution. The Unicorns' roster includes celebrity endorsements such as Pat Cummins.

Shah was re-elected unopposed at a meeting in Bali, where the article says he wore his usual glazed facial expression. The article says Shah is the son of Indian prime minister Narendra Modi's oldest political ally. Rajaraman and Harinarayan are Stanford graduates of the mid-90s turned Bay-Area digital rainmaker types, like Huang. One of the founders says the ideas are at the level of human civilisation and cannot be kept contained, and that it is cricket for now but why not the NFL, football or soccer. The article says Huang has spent years perfecting a machine that can make every other person's job vanish.

Finn Allen, a New Zealand batsman for the Unicorns, spoke enthusiastically about the effect of the tool in the season just past. Allen said it is not all AI or no AI but the perfect amount of contribution, after an eight-wicket win against Washington Freedom. The article says the Unicorns' backstory reads like a pitch for an app, with endless giddy chat about scaling up the product. The article says AI is already present in elite football scouting systems, and that Formula One is already a machine-led activity now embracing robo-integration. The article says there is a theory big tech companies have begun to buy into sport, citing Bezos at Liverpool, as a hedge against AI.

The article says the latest suggestion being punted about is that Huang is irreplaceable as president of Nvidia. The article says the ICC conference was widely seen as disappointingly inconclusive. The article says captaincy is a skill and sport is a live test of human capacity, and that using a machine to make captaincy decisions should obviously be regulated, understood, debated and capped at source. The article says the Unicorns may be the tiniest twinkle in the sporting sky right now but carry a potentially significant contagion. The article says AI would undoubtedly be better at managing Manchester United than the lost souls currently passing through those gates.

The article says the 20th century gave visions of a flowering of culture and the death of human drudgery. The article says the current version is one in which four people become incredibly wealthy while the rest live in an asbestos box, face clamped into a smartphone. The article says the Luddites actually had some pretty good points about the industrial loom. The article says sport, the human spectacle, is seen as safe from new technology, like buying gold when currencies go haywire. The article says so much of football is essentially guesswork, sniff-test and hunch-based, all of the stuff artificial intelligence exists to replace.

The article asks whether we will ever have the will and the collective backbone to resist and regulate this stuff and police its limits. The article ends by urging readers to resist the machines and release Finn Allen from the Phantom Zone. The article says the proposals on T20 leagues will go to the next disappointingly inconclusive ICC conference. The article does not say when that conference will be held. The article gives no response from Shah, the ICC, the Unicorns or Huang to its claims.

Articles.Title: Forget rogue robots, it’s tech billionaires and AI cricket that should really terrify us | Barney Ronay

stories.Headline: Gomumari adds contracting authority selection to its Target List Creation AI agent
stories.Summary:
Gomumari Co., Ltd., based in Arakawa, Tokyo and led by representative director Yuta Murayama, announced on November 22, 2026 that its business AI agent "Target List Creation" now supports the selection of contracting authorities for companies selling to government agencies and local governments. The company began offering the new business development agent in October 2026, and the new function starts on November 22, 2026. If a customer sends a list of contracting authorities it has won orders from, even names alone, along with information on its products and target areas, the AI analyzes the conditions shared by the authorities that placed orders. It then lists likely contracting authorities from among those posting notices on the government procurement information portal site, with a selection reason for each authority, and returns the list together with the selection criteria. Initial setup starts at 500,000 yen over a period of four weeks or more, followed by operation from 100,000 yen per month.

The articles give the scale of the problem the function addresses. Notices for government and local government tenders exceed 300 on a single weekday, and when Gomumari pulled notices from October 1 to 30, 2026 through the portal site's search API across all 47 prefectures, it found 8,916 notices in one month, or 306 to 626 per weekday, issued by 1,055 authorities. Notices arrive by case, but sales visits are decided by authority, and filtering methods used for private companies, such as industry or employee count, do not work for contracting authorities. Among the October notices, 418 cases had "system" in the title, issued by 187 of the 1,055 authorities, so names and sizes alone do not show which authorities buy a company's products. The know-how about which authorities buy often stays only in the head of the person who has tracked tenders, and when that person is transferred, the successor starts over by reading notices from the top.

The processing runs in four stages. The customer submits its past order list, which can be names of contracting authorities alone, with product and target area information, and about 30 orders are enough to derive conditions, with no need to standardize formats in advance. The AI analyzes the conditions common to authorities that placed orders and puts into words, with reasons, why authorities meeting those conditions buy. It then selects likely authorities from among the 1,055 that posted notices in October 2026 and ranks them by priority with a reason for each. It outputs the list with reasons, an order analysis memo, the selection criteria themselves, and data in a format that can be imported into a CRM, so the company can later build lists on the same criteria internally. The criteria are re-read each time new orders accumulate, and no dedicated system installation or operation training is required.

Murayama said that strong salespeople in the public sector decide which authorities to approach before notices appear, and that this difference lies less in how they read notices than in whether they remember which authorities bought and why. He said the company added the function of selecting the next contracting authorities from a list of past orders to its existing method of reading the conditions of buyers from order records, and that it actually pulled the 8,916 notices from 1,055 authorities in one month and counted which items are usable as sales material. He said the company aims to increase sales teams where a successor can explain in his or her own words which authority to visit next even after a personnel change. The articles also describe the base service: in a customer's sales department, about 2,000 negotiations and about 2,000 activity records were read to redesign customer segments into six groups and apply them to about 4,000 clients, producing a list narrowed to about 300 sales targets. Gomumari also counted the October notices itself, finding 1,294 notices located in Tokyo, 14.5 percent of the national total, but only 83 of them were issued by the metropolitan and ward governments, with the rest from national institutions, independent administrative agencies and national universities, so counting notices by location does not represent the number of cases a local government issues.

The same Target List Creation is also offered as a specialist AI-BPO service that returns deliverables, starting at 200,000 yen and taking seven business days from the day after materials are ready, for either a one-time or monthly engagement. Customers can choose between AI agent introduction to run the process internally and the AI-BPO deliverable list, and Gomumari also offers adjacent services such as data enrichment that organizes CRM company information and assigns customer ranks. The company presents itself as an FDE company that enters customer sites and builds AI agents, providing introduction of AI agents with initial setup and monthly operation, and it says its lineup will be added in order from work refined in actual fields. The articles state that prices and periods are as of the time of release and may be revised, with the latest conditions on the company website.

stories.Headline: Stuttgart AI factory pairs startups with concierge support to avoid lock-in
stories.Summary:
The HammerHAI AI factory in Stuttgart, Germany, is being built around a Hewlett Packard Enterprise system that uses Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips, and it is aimed especially at small and medium-sized businesses and startups rather than only at large industrial users. Bastian Koller, managing director of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart, described the effort during an exclusive broadcast with theCUBE Research's John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, a livestream from SiliconANGLE Media's studio. Koller said some startups already know what they want from such a system while others need help and support to try things out, which is why the center pairs each customer with a consistent contact in what he called a concierge model. The center has already worked with customers on its existing systems while it waits for the new hardware, and several of those customers have produced success stories.

The design is meant to avoid lock-in, because Koller said the services are built so that workloads can simply move from the Stuttgart center to a hyperscaler and back again, with the center giving customers a boost and pushing them forward. The center runs an ISO-certified environment and holds TISAX Level 3 certification for automotive work, and Koller said full independence down to European chips is not realistic in the near term, so the focus has to be on the data rather than waiting years for a sovereign processor or GPU. The new system doubles the performance of its 3.2-megawatt predecessor at about 700 kilowatts, and the center reuses its waste heat. Koller said the bigger lesson is human, because the concierge model lets the center learn how users work and think, and a highly fancy system nobody uses would be worthless if the user's needs were never considered.

Koller is responsible for the center as its managing director, and he framed the approach as pragmatic rather than absolute, saying the center cannot tell customers to come back in 10 years when a sovereign processor exists. He said industrial users no longer want shell programming and expect the look and feel of a hyperscaler, which raises fresh demands on security and access. The interview was part of SiliconANGLE's and theCUBE's coverage of SC26, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise sponsored that segment of theCUBE, with the disclosure stating that neither the sponsor nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the center continuing to evolve its system and services while it waits on the new hardware.

stories.Headline: Yuehua Li and Pengfei Li review explainable AI methods for hepatocellular carcinoma research
stories.Summary:
A comprehensive narrative review by Yuehua Li and Pengfei Li was published in the Journal of the Egyptian National Cancer Institute on explainable artificial intelligence in hepatocellular carcinoma research. The review synthesizes recent methodological advances and clinical translation challenges in applying explainable artificial intelligence to hepatocellular carcinoma research. Hepatocellular carcinoma is a malignancy with significant global incidence, mortality, substantial inter-tumor and intra-tumor heterogeneity at molecular, pathological, and imaging levels, and poor clinical prognosis. Deep learning and machine learning models have shown considerable diagnostic and prognostic accuracy across oncology workflows. Their clinical deployment has been constrained by an opaque black-box architecture where decision-making logic remains concealed.

The authors examine how explainable artificial intelligence methods turn opaque predictions into interpretable findings across four clinical domains: imaging diagnosis, multi-omics biomarker discovery, treatment response prediction, and postoperative prognostic evaluation. The review systematically outlines technical bottlenecks that prevent post-hoc explanations from functioning as direct, actionable clinical interventions. In imaging diagnosis, explainable frameworks visualize model focus and align automated classifications with established clinical frameworks such as the Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System. Techniques like Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping and SHapley Additive exPlanations decode internal feature activations into standardized clinical indicators, including non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement. Post-hoc attribution methods accurately highlighted the tumor margin and peritumoral boundary zones as decisive features for predicting microvascular invasion, aligning artificial intelligence outputs with histopathological realities.

Multi-task learning frameworks have linked routine macroscopic magnetic resonance imaging performances with underlying tumor grading. Specialized ultrasound and magnetic resonance sequence evaluations confirmed the adaptability of explainable systems across diverse imaging acquisitions. In whole-slide image analysis, explainable architectures apply attention-based visualizations and activation maps to render histological evaluations of nuclear atypia, tissue architectural distortion, and stromal alterations transparent. Explainable systems have successfully decoded the biological foundations of specific magnetic resonance imaging phenotypes by linking macroscale imaging features to underlying cellular microenvironments. This integration marks an evolution toward multi-scale explainability that unifies radiological, histopathological, and spatial molecular data layers into an auditable diagnostic continuum.

Explainable artificial intelligence functions as a high-dimensional mining engine and hypothesis generator across multi-omics data layers, including genomics, single-cell transcriptomics, metabolomics, pathomics, radiomics, and routine clinical records. Methodological frameworks using tree-based feature attribution, automated machine learning, and multi-model feature selection have established reproducible pipelines to pinpoint robust candidate biomarkers while reducing false discoveries. Intrinsically interpretable deep learning structures and pathway-directed post-hoc models have mapped prediction weights directly to known biological cascades, including the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase and stimulator of interferon genes signaling pathway. Interpretable deep learning models processing hematoxylin and eosin slides have identified aggressive macrotrabecular structural patterns to predict microvascular invasion. Multimodal architectures such as token-guided fusion mechanisms and dual-branch exploratory networks simultaneously evaluate whole-slide morphological features, quantitative tumor-stroma ratios, and bulk gene expression profiles.

In transarterial chemoembolization, attribution modeling with SHapley Additive exPlanations has unraveled drivers of variable patient responses. Studies analyzing pre-treatment contrast-enhanced computed tomography parameters and dynamic trajectory tracking of albumin-bilirubin scores have identified distinct responder subtypes and revealed that splenic and renal imaging characteristics significantly inform outcome estimates by reflecting systemic inflammatory states. For systemic therapies encompassing targeted agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors, explainable models have linked baseline radiographic features and cellular pathomic signatures, such as tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte density, to therapeutic responsiveness and specific molecular pathways. Multimodal nomograms and random survival forest models incorporate computed tomography and magnetic resonance radiomics to quantify the biological invasiveness of tumors, reliably forecasting postoperative recurrence in hepatitis B-related malignancies and large hepatocellular carcinomas. Explainable models tailored to specific sub-populations have provided personalized outcome forecasts for alpha-fetoprotein-negative patients, individuals with concurrent diabetes mellitus, and patients at elevated risk for spontaneous tumor rupture or post-hepatectomy liver failure.

The review highlights three fundamental methodological bottlenecks inherent to the prevailing post-hoc explanation paradigm. Post-hoc methods remain fundamentally correlational rather than causal, highlighting statistical dependencies within historical datasets without confirming whether highlighted features represent genuine biological drivers or incidental epiphenomena. A persistent semantic gap separates low-level, pixel-oriented saliency heatmaps from the high-level semantic reasoning utilized by clinicians, leaving models vulnerable to shortcut learning where predictions rely on artifacts rather than disease mechanisms. Current predictive architectures operate as static snapshots trained on historical cohorts, rendering them incapable of self-updating alongside evolving clinical guidelines or actively comparing alternative therapeutic outcomes. The authors delineate a paradigm shift centered on causal inference, concept-driven interpretability, and dynamic collaborative systems.

Methodologies such as double machine learning and causal forests provide mathematical rigor to control for high-dimensional confounding, enabling the estimation of true treatment effects and identifying heterogeneous patient cohorts that derive differential survival benefits from specific interventions. Concept Bottleneck Models offer an architectural solution to bridge the semantic divide by forcing intermediate network layers to predict human-interpretable clinical concepts, such as arterial phase washout or histological nuclear atypia, prior to generating final classifications. Mechanistic interpretability techniques utilizing sparse autoencoders show promising capability in disentangling the complex, polysemantic latent representations of large-scale pathology foundation models into individual, monosemantic biological concepts. The review concludes by emphasizing that the ultimate maturation of explainable artificial intelligence depends on transitioning from passive, retrospective explanatory tools into active, interactive clinical decision partners. stories.Headline: Standard Bank Group automates generative AI risk checks in its own AWS account
stories.Summary:
Standard Bank Group, working with AWS Professional Services, deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies, as described in an AWS blog post dated November 20, 2026. The post is co-written by Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard showing what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. The bank already had a model risk practice covering explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case by its level of risk before it goes live. Generative AI increases complexity because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case must still meet the same high security and compliance bar.

The assessment runs entirely in Standard Bank Group's own AWS account, with documents, code, and test results kept in an Amazon Simple Storage Service bucket there. The AWS Well-Architected Tool handles intake, AWS Step Functions orchestrates the pipeline, and a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock evaluates the evidence using a technique called LLM-as-a-judge. The custom lens in the Well-Architected Tool holds about 40 questions, each covering a risk event such as incomplete technical documentation or insufficient human oversight, and Standard Bank Group customized the lens with judge questions built from its own standards, bringing the total to more than 300. A pre-assessment agent running on AWS Fargate scans the use case's code repository and documentation, maps relevant files to each question, and pre-populates the lens with answers and links to the evidence. The pipeline calls the application through its AWS Lambda function or API, adds a built-in set of jailbreak attempts and off-topic questions, sends the same prompt several times in original and reworded forms, and uses an embedding model on Amazon Bedrock to check that answers stay consistent in meaning.

Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer at Standard Bank Group, said the assessment demonstrates how the bank is working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into its AI journey, allowing it to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. He said the bank believes responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, which now bases each decision on consistent evidence collected the same way across use cases. Sri Elaprolu, Director of Frontier AI Science & Engineering at AWS, said most organizations treat policy as something you read, while Standard Bank Group treats it as something you run. He said that when every rule becomes a check that runs against the live system, a policy update stops being a memo and becomes a test, which fundamentally changes how fast a bank can scale AI responsibly.

Each risk receives a likelihood score, the share of required evidence the model couldn't find, and a fixed severity level that the bank's risk team can adjust, together producing a rating from Very low to Critical. Each missing piece of evidence maps to a specific mitigation and to the clause of the standard or policy it came from, so a risk officer can trace any findings back to their source when explaining decisions to a regulator. The checks cover eight AWS responsible AI dimensions: veracity and robustness, privacy and security, transparency, fairness, safety, controllability, governance, and explainability. Every AI model interaction is protected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, and each evaluation runs multiple times to measure how consistent the answers are, with inconsistent findings flagged in the review interface. The pipeline delivers results as an executive presentation, a mitigation checklist, a detailed technical report, and an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that tracks scores across use cases over time.

The assessment fits into three stages of the use case lifecycle: during a proof of concept it is optional, at the build stage it becomes mandatory, and the approval gate draws on its results as formal evidence. Today the assessment runs in Standard Bank Group's production environment, evaluating use cases before they go live, and after live workloads are connected it will rerun on a schedule or whenever code or configuration changes. The bank's teams already trigger assessments on their own through a central system where use cases flow from intake to evaluation in a single workflow. The assessment produces evidence against controls but does not certify compliance with any regulation, and Standard Bank Group remains responsible for its own regulatory determinations. Model availability varies by AWS Region, so the post advises checking the supported models by Region before deploying.

At Standard Bank Group, the assessment reduced a traditionally manual two-week review to a comprehensive risk report generated in approximately two hours, demonstrated across six assessments. It also delivered a 14% improvement in use-case risk scores after remediation, which the post says strengthens responsible AI governance and reduces compliance bottlenecks. The post states that Amazon Bedrock doesn't share the bank's prompts or model outputs with model providers and doesn't use them to train models, and that the bank controls access to the model through AWS Identity and Access Management. Because Amazon Bedrock offers many foundation models through one API, the team can move to a newer judge model by changing a configuration setting instead of rebuilding the pipeline. The assessment uses the judge model as-is with no fine-tuning or customization, and a question factory generates extra judge questions from internal documents so that a policy change becomes a test change.

stories.Headline: Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase outages and a US flight grounding stem from technical upgrades, not attacks
stories.Summary:
A series of technical failures disrupted American infrastructure and global services starting on Friday, November 14, 2026. Federal aviation authorities ordered a nationwide grounding of planes, while a Microsoft outage affected millions of users worldwide. These events were followed by a widespread outage at United Airlines on Monday afternoon and significant transaction slowdowns at several top United States banks. Other strange occurrences on Friday included a tanker hitting a cruise ship in New Orleans, drones over a British air base, and a bomb discovery in Illinois.

The aviation crisis required a ground stop lasting more than four hours because a technology upgrade overloaded antiquated air traffic control equipment. Microsoft reported that its own service disruption resulted from a network capacity upgrade that surfaced after a recent network change. Financial instability began when a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase created ripple effects across the broader banking system. United Airlines stated that its Monday technical problems specifically impacted departing flights rather than aircraft already in the air.

Bryan Bedford of the Federal Aviation Administration and representatives from Microsoft both stated that no malicious activity caused these failures. A spokesperson for Chase confirmed that their banking issues were not the result of a cyberattack and that they were working to restore services. While some citizens expressed fear that these events signaled a coordinated attack on the economy, officials maintained that the causes were prosaic. The Federal Aviation Administration indicated that airline schedules should have returned to normal by late Sunday.

stories.Headline: Manufacturers face a data gap that blocks physical AI rollout on factory floors
stories.Summary:
Robotics and physical AI companies raised nearly 48 billion dollars so far in 2026. These companies want to roll out fully autonomous machines in industrial settings. Robots need real world data to move beyond controlled environments onto manufacturing floors. Most production facilities are not currently set up to provide this necessary information. This data gap may prevent manufacturers from achieving expected efficiency and quality improvements.

Manufacturers must capture complex interactions between process parameters and quality outcomes to help systems make reliable adjustments. They need to connect equipment and quality management systems that were not designed to communicate. This requires creating a digital thread connecting production conditions with inspection results and finished part quality. In medical device manufacturing, regulatory requirements often mandate validation of production processes to ensure consistent quality. This limits how freely AI systems can modify production parameters in those specific environments.

Michael Kenworthy, chief technology officer at VulcanForms, says manufacturers must understand what information robotic systems will rely on. He suggests identifying production conditions that systems need to recognize and respond to early. Kenworthy believes manufacturers should focus investments where they will have the greatest impact. He states that a system cannot make independent decisions if it cannot evaluate resulting quality. He advises linking existing process records to inspection results rather than just collecting more data.

Lior Susan of Eclipse says a physical asset is a dead asset if it does not generate real time operational data. The Manufacturing Leadership Council conducted a 2026 Smart Factories and Digital Production Survey. This survey found that 37 percent of manufacturers cited a lack of data interoperability as a major roadblock. This figure is an increase from 22 percent in 2025. These silos affect manufacturers who want to implement smart factory strategies.

Technicians develop understanding of welding angles, travel speed, and workpiece position through years of hands on experience. Much of this knowledge is not captured in a form robotics partners can use. Operational data is often collected but never reviewed or structured for autonomous learning. Relevant contextual information often sits in separate systems, such as quality management systems. In metal additive manufacturing, powder characteristics and processing temperatures can influence a component's final properties.

Manufacturers should now identify the specific data needed for a targeted robotic application. They must work with technology partners to establish consistent part identifiers. Companies need to define acceptable operating limits and establish how systems verify results. They must also develop clear criteria for when an unexpected outcome requires engineering review. The articles leave open how long it will take to overhaul existing production infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Dutch court bans BYD Ti7 SUV sales in EU for infringing Land Rover Defender design
stories.Summary:
A preliminary relief judge at the district court in The Hague barred the sale of the BYD Ti7 SUV in the European Union on November 20, 2026. The court ruled that the seven-seat vehicle infringes upon the design rights held by Jaguar Land Rover for the Land Rover Defender. This legal action followed the launch of the Ti7 in China under the Fangchengbao brand during 2025. The judge determined that the distinctive and characteristic elements of the Defender are reflected in the design of the BYD model. This decision came during summary proceedings rather than a full trial to address the immediate design conflict.

The injunction takes effect one week after the ruling because BYD currently lacks concrete plans to place the vehicle on the market in the European Union. Until the legal case is resolved, BYD is prohibited from producing the Ti7 at its new factory in Hungary, which was scheduled for mass production early next year. The court stated it had no jurisdiction over the UK affiliate of BYD, meaning the order does not reach Britain. JLR filed the suit after BYD listed the Ti7 on its UK website with deliveries planned for January 2027. Media reports highlight the boxy flat-roof shape, squared-off wheel arches, and upright proportions as key points of contention.

BYD stated that it strongly disagrees with the ruling and maintains that the Ti7 resulted from its own independent design work. The company intends to appeal the decision and will pursue every available legal avenue to challenge the ban. Jaguar Land Rover, which is owned by Tata Motors, stated that proceedings are ongoing and that the company protects its intellectual property. JLR declined to provide further comments beyond these statements regarding the current status of the litigation. The Defender remains a critical asset for JLR, with more than 100,000 units sold worldwide in 2025.

This unusual early ruling occurs as BYD expands its presence, with European sales doubling to over 280,000 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026. According to ACEA data, BYD has recently outsold other major manufacturers including Ford, Tesla, and Nissan in the region. Major automakers rarely sue over design rights in Europe, making this specific court decision a rare occurrence in the industry. The outcome of the appeal will determine if BYD can eventually bring the Ti7 to the European market. The legal battle highlights the growing tension between established European brands and expanding Chinese automotive firms.

stories.Headline: Study finds European Union uses AI Act to seek global influence through governance
stories.Summary:
Vasiliki Koniakou published a scholarly investigation in Information Systems Frontiers on November 21, 2026. The study evaluates if the European Union can gain global influence through its Artificial Intelligence Act. This strategy is described as leadership through governance within an intensifying global competition. The researcher used doctrinal legal analysis, policy review, and perspectives from information systems scholarship. This work examines how a horizontal statute functions as a domestic framework and geopolitical instrument.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 uses a risk-based scheme for a market of 450 million consumers. Article 5 prohibits social scoring, workplace emotion recognition, and untargeted facial image scraping. High-risk systems under Article 6 and Annexes I and III require continuous risk management and human oversight. Article 27 mandates Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments for specific public or high-impact sectors. Article 50 requires machine-readable markings for synthetic audiovisual content and biometric categorization systems.

Koniakou says the Union uses its single market to induce multinational adaptation via the Brussels Effect. She states that the AI Act functions as a sociotechnical regime reshaping corporate workflows. The author notes that signing compliance codes does not prove firms integrated European ethical norms. She argues that the Union promotes Trustworthy AI as a premium commercial standard. Koniakou warns that compliance could become superficial documentation rituals without integration into technical decisions.

Major firms including Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon, and Cohere signed a July 2025 code. Mistral AI also signed, while xAI endorsed only safety chapters and Meta declined participation. Other polities like South Korea borrow European vocabulary but often strip out heavy compliance obligations. The study notes that the United States leads through capability and dominant private technology firms. China pursues leadership through coordination using state-directed development plans and national champions.

The European Union lacks frontier models, private venture capital, and native digital platform giants. This situation is called the European Paradox where strong research fails to reach commercial supremacy. The strategy involves strategic intent, anticipatory rulemaking, governance instrumentation, and external uptake. The framework relies on the European AI Office and notified bodies to translate legal principles. It targets machine learning opacity, system autonomy, and algorithmic inscrutability through design stage traceability.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 deferred high-risk obligations due to administrative bottlenecks and lagging national authority readiness. Annex III requirements were postponed to 2 December 2027, and Annex I obligations to 2 August 2028. The new statute adds prohibitions against child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate imagery. Fines under Article 99 can reach 35 million euros or 7 percent of annual turnover. The articles leave open whether the Union can overcome gaps in operational enforcement capacity.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act amendment delays high-risk rules but adds new prohibitions and enforcement powers
stories.Summary:
The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026 and amends the AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, on a number of points. It is widely described as a postponement, and in one important respect it is, because the obligations for high-risk AI systems will now apply later than originally planned. That description is incomplete, however, because much of the AI Act already applies and the Omnibus also introduces new prohibitions and stronger enforcement tools. The note by Logan & Partners sets out the main changes and what they mean in practice for companies that develop, procure or use AI systems in the European Union. The AI Act is not a future regime, since its first provisions have applied since 2 February 2025.

Since 2 February 2025 the practices prohibited under Article 5 have been unlawful, including manipulative or deceptive techniques, social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images, and emotion recognition in the workplace and in education, subject to limited exceptions. Infringements may lead to fines of up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Providers of general-purpose AI models have been subject to Chapter V since 2 August 2025 and must maintain technical documentation, put in place a copyright policy and publish a summary of the content used for training. The Commission's power to fine these providers has applied since 2 August 2026, and the transparency obligations in Article 50 have also applied since that date. Users must be informed when they interact with an AI system, synthetic content must be marked in a machine-readable format, and deepfakes must be disclosed.

Under new Article 111(4), providers of generative AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 to comply with the marking obligation in Article 50(2). The requirements and obligations in Sections 1 to 3 of Chapter III will apply from 2 December 2027 to the systems listed in Annex III, which covers areas such as recruitment and workforce management, creditworthiness assessment, risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, education, biometrics, critical infrastructure, law enforcement, migration and the administration of justice. They apply from 2 August 2028 to AI systems that are safety components of products, or are themselves products, covered by the EU legislation listed in Annex I, such as medical devices, toys and lifts. The recitals explain that the postponement responds to the late availability of harmonised standards and to delays in setting up national authorities, and the legislator chose fixed dates. The Omnibus does not link application to the publication of standards, so companies should not plan on the assumption of a further extension.

The transitional rule in Article 111(2) has also been adjusted, so high-risk systems placed on the market or put into service before the relevant application date fall within the AI Act only if their design is significantly changed after that date. According to the recitals, this assessment is made per type and model, and systems intended for use by public authorities must in any event comply by 2 August 2030. The Omnibus adds two prohibitions to Article 5, which apply from 2 December 2026, the first covering AI systems that generate or manipulate realistic intimate images or sexually explicit content of an identifiable person without that person's explicit consent and the second covering AI-generated child sexual abuse material. Under new Article 5(1a), a provider may be caught even where its system was not designed for this purpose, where such output is a reasonably foreseeable outcome that can be reproduced without significant technical modification and the system lacks adequate safeguards to prevent it.

A deployer, by contrast, is caught only where it uses the system for the purpose of generating such material, so providers of general-purpose image and video generation tools should review their technical safeguards. Article 25 now specifies the information, technical access and assistance that an initial provider must give to the party that becomes the provider of a high-risk system, and it also requires written agreements with suppliers of AI models, tools and components. A breach of these obligations may now be fined up to EUR 15 million or 3% of turnover under new Article 99(4)(da). At EU level, the AI Office has obtained exclusive competence over certain AI systems, including systems based on a general-purpose AI model where the model and the system are developed by the same provider, and AI systems that constitute or are integrated into very large online platforms or search engines, with some exceptions.

The AI Office now has inspection powers and may impose periodic penalty payments. Article 4 on AI literacy now requires providers and deployers to take measures to support the AI literacy of their staff, and it states expressly that no specific level of literacy has to be guaranteed. SMEs and the new category of small mid-cap enterprises may provide technical documentation in a simplified form and apply a quality management system proportionate to their size, and where they are fined, the lower of the fixed amount and the percentage of turnover applies. New Article 4a allows providers of high-risk systems to process special categories of personal data where this is strictly necessary to detect and correct bias, subject to specific safeguards, and in exceptional cases the same possibility extends to deployers of high-risk systems and to providers and deployers of other AI systems and models.

The Commission has published draft guidelines on classification under Article 6, the consultation closed in July 2026 and, at the time of writing, the final guidelines have not been adopted. Article 6(3) allows certain Annex III systems to be treated as not high-risk, for example where they perform only a narrow procedural or preparatory task, but this exception never applies to systems that perform profiling. Providers relying on it must document their assessment before placing the system on the market and register the system. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Delaware court fines partner personally for filing unverified GenAI output but spares his firm over its AI policy
stories.Summary:
The Delaware Court of Chancery sanctioned a senior partner personally under Court of Chancery Rule 11 for filing a brief containing unverified GenAI output, in Leiske v. Kidd, C.A. No. 2025-0426-CDW (LWW), on November 13, 2026. The underlying proceeding concerned advancement, and on January 22, 2026, the plaintiffs filed an answering brief opposing the defendants' exceptions to a Magistrate in Chancery's final report. Five days later, the defendants' reply brief pointed out that the brief contained fabricated quotations, inaccurate citations and hallucinated legal propositions. The following day, the plaintiffs' lead counsel, who had signed the brief, filed a letter acknowledging that a GenAI tool had been used and submitted a corrected brief.

The letter attributed the failure to catch the errors to an oversight during a paralegal's cite-check, but the corrected brief removed quotation marks around the nonexistent quotes while retaining the inaccurate descriptions of the underlying cases. When defence counsel wrote to the court identifying the remaining misrepresentations, the plaintiffs' counsel responded by faulting opposing counsel for failing to "meet and confer" before alerting the court and insisting that the cited authorities were real and supported the arguments advanced. After resolving the exceptions dispute on the merits, the court issued an Order to Show Cause concerning the GenAI issues, which directed both the signing partner and his law firm to explain why sanctions should not be imposed under the applicable court rule and the court's inherent authority. The partner and the firm filed detailed affidavits, and the court determined the matter without an evidentiary hearing. The court emphasized that the use of GenAI in legal practice is neither forbidden nor inherently problematic, and that these tools offer substantial benefits and efficiencies, but they must be used with the care required by the court's Rule 11 and the Delaware Lawyers' Rules of Professional Conduct, including ensuring the accuracy of every authority and citation presented to the court.

Under Court of Chancery Rule 11(b)(2), an attorney who presents a paper to the court certifies that, after an inquiry reasonable in the circumstances, its legal contentions are warranted by existing law. The court said that "[a]n attorney's signature on a court filing is not a procedural formality; it is a certification to the tribunal," and that a fake quotation or a fabricated legal synthesis generated by an algorithm is not "existing law," so presenting unverified GenAI output violates the rule. Rule 11(c)(1) provides that, absent exceptional circumstances, a law firm must be held jointly responsible for violations committed by its partners, associates or employees. Drawing on Rule 5.1(a) of the Delaware Lawyers' Rules of Professional Conduct and the American Bar Association's Formal Opinion 512, the court asked whether the firm had made reasonable efforts to put in place measures giving reasonable assurance of compliance. The court concluded that it had, because the firm had barred the use of unapproved GenAI tools in March 2023, formed a working group in 2024 to evaluate tools and study ethical guidance, and adopted a comprehensive GenAI policy in July 2025 requiring an experienced lawyer to review GenAI output for accuracy and completeness.

The firm had also developed an accredited ethics training program that over 200 employees had completed by January 2026, and the court said the firm "did the right thing" and should not be sanctioned for an individual lawyer bypassing those controls. The signing partner, as Chair of his firm's AI subcommittee, had been piloting a GenAI tool that was not approved for general firm use, yet he used that tool to draft and condense arguments in the brief. He then delegated cite-checking to a junior lawyer and a paralegal and filed the brief without personally verifying the authorities, and the court held that the duty of candour and the obligation to conduct a reasonable inquiry under Rule 11 are personal and nondelegable. The court held that a senior lawyer who signs a brief cannot disclaim responsibility for unverified GenAI output where the lawyer knowingly introduces text generated by GenAI into a draft, and the signatory must ensure that the underlying authorities have been reviewed and that those authorities actually support the propositions for which they are cited.

The court rejected the argument that it was sufficient that the cases cited were real or that the overarching propositions were arguably consistent with general principles of law, noting that GenAI tools not only invent case names but also fabricate plausible-sounding quotations and stretch real decisions to stand for propositions they never addressed. The court stated that counsel has an affirmative duty to review the underlying authorities and correct the errors if GenAI errors are detected, and that "[i]t is not enough to remove quotation marks and leave a fabricated legal synthesis in place." As to the sanction, the court weighed the partner's initial deflection of blame and the retained mischaracterizations against his subsequent acceptance of full responsibility, sincere contrition and long record of practice before the court. It imposed a fine of US$2,500, consistent with fines in comparable proceedings, and given the nondelegable nature of the duty, the partner was required to pay it personally.

Additional mandatory continuing education was considered redundant, since the lawyer had already completed several GenAI ethics programs and led internal training. The court noted that GenAI tools are now widely used in everyday legal practice and can assist with drafting, condense and refine written material, and outline arguments in a fraction of the time it would otherwise take. At the same time, courts across North America have been faced with a steady stream of briefs and factums containing fabricated cases, invented quotations and mischaracterized holdings, and the question is no longer whether such errors will attract judicial scrutiny but what happens when they do. The article states that although this is a Delaware decision, the reasoning will resonate with litigators and their firms in any jurisdiction where courts are confronting the same problem.

It states that a lawyer who signs a factum or other document citing authorities owns every citation in it, and reliance on a cite-check by others will not shift that responsibility, particularly where the signatory knows that GenAI-generated text was used. It states that verification must go beyond confirming that a case exists and requires reading the authority to confirm that any quotation is accurate and that the decision supports the proposition for which it is cited. For law firms, the article states, the decision underscores the value of a clear GenAI policy, verification requirements, restrictions on unapproved tools and documented training for members of the firm. The article states that its content is intended to provide a general guide to the subject matter and that specialist advice should be sought about specific circumstances.

stories.Headline: NYC schools chancellor Kamar Samuels says Google refuses an AI-free search option for schools
stories.Summary:
New York City schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said on Thursday, November 19, 2026, that Google is refusing to offer schools a version of its search engine without artificial intelligence features, which is forcing districts to evaluate other options. New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago are all weighing alternatives to Google search because of the dispute over AI in classroom search tools. Samuels said Google is trying to give the district an ultimatum by saying schools must either use student generative AI in its search engine or get nothing at all. He said the city is not buying into that binary choice, and he described the disagreement as a reason the district is looking at what else is available.

The concern among school leaders is that AI-generated answers and chatbots could undermine students' critical thinking and interfere with the learning process. Samuels said the district does not want guided learning from a chatbot and wants relearning from a teacher instead. Google says it is giving schools more control over which AI tools they use, but the company says AI features are now deeply integrated into its search engine and that it cannot offer a chatbot-free version. Among the alternatives being considered are Microsoft's Bing and DuckDuckGo, both of which offer options to disable AI-generated answers.

Samuels said New York City has other options available and is continuing discussions with Google despite the disagreement. He said the city will definitely take a look at those options when the time is right. For now, he said the city remains in talks with Google and is seeking greater collaboration, and he said no decision has been made about whether the district will continue using Google's search platform. He also said the city does not plan to change its existing policy on student AI use, noting that parents and teachers love the current policy and that the district will continue along those lines.

stories.Headline: Zhong-Ren Peng proposes a framework that binds urban AI to human primacy and equity
stories.Summary:
A featured perspective published in Frontiers of Urban and Rural Planning examines an eight-year research trajectory led by Professor Zhong-Ren Peng. The research investigates how municipal planning institutions can expand computational capabilities without compromising democratic legitimacy, public accountability, or spatial justice. The intellectual arc spans from early symposium inquiries in 2018 to recent foundational treatises. The research addresses the growing capability, legitimacy tension confronting contemporary municipal governance. Urban administrations face pressure to navigate severe housing shortages, transit inequities, cumulative environmental hazards, and climate risks under severe temporal constraints and deep uncertainty.

The analysis draws a conceptual distinction between Urban AI as a broad scientific discipline and Urban Planning AI as a distinct, institutionally bounded practice. Urban AI is organized around three primary functions: discovering spatial patterns, evaluating causal relationships, and optimizing physical urban subsystems through computer vision, deep neural networks, and machine learning models. Urban Planning AI operates strictly within democratic plan-making and policy formation, where automated systems intervene in the allocation of public resources, zoning configurations, land development rights, and municipal investments. A 2024 pathway study published in the Journal of Planning Education and Research established a typology of four stages: AI-assisted, AI-augmented, AI-automated, and AI-autonomized planning. That study was grounded in a scoping review of 881 peer-reviewed publications cataloged in the Web of Science by May 2023, with 74 percent published after 2020.

Symbiotic Planning Theory was published in the Journal of the American Planning Association in 2026. It posits that artificial intelligence should be configured as a governed co-creator operating under absolute and binding human primacy. The theory articulates three mandatory governance conditions: normative triggering, binding agency, and time-bound primacy. Normative triggering mandates that computational workflows explicitly extract and formalize normative value judgments, compelling vague aspirations such as equity into explicit mathematical boundaries. Binding agency requires that community priorities function as non-negotiable hard constraints rather than advisory suggestions.

Governed friction executes across a three-step cycle commencing with generative provocation, followed by normative recalibration, and concluding with binding reauthorization. The CORE framework translates theoretical principles into a four-stage municipal workflow consisting of Collaboration, Options, Refinement, and Execution. A micromobility deployment study conducted in Gainesville, Florida, uncovered a severe institutional compliance trap. Under existing municipal regulations, shared electric scooter vendors met formal requirements by staging at least 10 percent of their vehicle fleets within designated equity zones. Empirical telemetry revealed that this spatial zone generated only approximately 3 percent of total community trips, whereas roughly 84 percent of all rides concentrated exclusively around the university campus.

Traditional oversight mechanisms, centered entirely on administrative checklists and spatial placement metrics without outcome-driven feedback triggers, proved structurally incapable of identifying or correcting the spatial isolation experienced by underserved residents. Initially, researchers employed a deep reinforcement learning model to construct an efficiency-optimized deployment baseline, which automatically concentrated vehicle allocations around the high-density campus area. Through subsequent normative recalibration, marking the municipality’s first systematic public engagement on micromobility in four years, workshops and surveys uncovered that unbanked households, transit schedule misalignments, affordability barriers, and pedestrian access gaps suppressed utilization. Planners translated these community findings into binding model constraints, shifting the computational objective from unconstrained revenue maximization to maximizing service access subject to an inviolable spatial equity floor.

The perspective candidly delineates major technical, institutional, and epistemological risks that constrain the broader adoption of artificial intelligence in urban planning practice. Pervasive training data bias represents a fundamental challenge, as historical municipal datasets regularly reflect decades of disinvestment, socioeconomic segregation, and institutional neglect. The analysis underscores that while artificial intelligence offers unprecedented speed in synthesizing complex spatial patterns, unsupervised algorithmic optimization risks quietly displacing public judgment, formalizing administrative opacity, and entrenching historical inequities within municipal decision-making procedures. Because plan-making inherently involves state authority, contested social values, and administrative accountability to diverse publics, computational accuracy alone cannot justify deployment.

Traditional paradigms, including rational comprehensive planning, participatory planning, and iterative co-design, were formulated under the historical condition that human cognition set the practical upper boundary of analytical capacity. None provided mechanisms for governing machine-generated alternatives or turning community priorities into enforceable algorithmic constraints. The Execution stage treats implementation as an ongoing monitored governance protocol sustained by mandatory artifacts including transparent model cards, equity-disaggregated dashboards, public grievance pathways, and empirical reauthorization files. The pathway paper clarified how administrative structures shift as computational autonomy increases, transitioning human planners from being in-the-loop, to on-the-loop, and in highly constrained circumstances, out-of-the-loop.

The CORE framework is anchored by the fundamental operating axiom that accountability must precede algorithms, prohibiting optimization modeling until public objectives, harm definitions, community participation rights, and procedural challenge avenues are established. During Collaboration, planning agencies and publics formulate the social contract governing computation, treating baseline data gaps not merely as technical oversights but as structural equity signals. In the Options phase, multi-model pluralism generates competing alternative trajectories balanced across conflicting objectives such as efficiency, environmental resilience, and spatial justice. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Symbiotic Planning Framework Governs Artificial Intelligence to Protect Urban Equity and Legitimacy

stories.Headline: US travelers trust banks over Meta to run AI payment agents, TubStays survey finds
stories.Summary:
A TubStays survey of 5,000 US travelers, released on November 21, 2026, found that 48% would trust their own bank or credit card company to run an AI agent that pays for travel, while only 13% would trust Meta, the maker of the Muse agent, which ranked seventh among eight options. The survey ran online from October 27 to November 6, 2026, through SurveyMonkey Audience in English and Spanish with 68 questions, and responses were weighted by age, gender, region, household income, education, and race and ethnicity. Muse was the most-used agent among travelers who have used a personal AI agent, at 57%, yet four in ten of those users said they would not trust Meta at all with their payment details. An airline's or hotel brand's own assistant drew 43%, a travel booking site such as Expedia or Booking.com drew 38%, Apple drew 37%, Google drew 31%, OpenAI drew 24%, and a new AI start-up drew 9%.

The results show that travelers accept AI agents only when the agent asks for approval before paying, since 43% are comfortable letting an agent book and pay after they review and approve the details, while just 13% would let it pay without asking each time. Willingness to skip approval depends on the amount, as 30% would let an agent pay for a $25 ride without asking, against 6% for a $2,000 vacation package. Before approving a hotel payment, 66% want to see the total price including taxes and fees, and 50% want the cancellation terms. Most travelers still book for themselves, since only 11% have used a personal AI agent, and on the most recent trip where travelers used any AI, 61% used it only for ideas or information while the AI made the booking for 4%.

Of the 2,520 travelers who used AI for a trip in the past year, 41% got wrong or out-of-date information and 17% were told a hotel had a feature it did not have, such as a bathtub, pool or parking. If an agent books the wrong hotel, 64% say the company that made the agent should pay, either alone at 38% or shared with the hotel or booking site at 26%. Ritesh, founder of TubStays, said travelers will let AI plan the trip but still want to hold the card, and that trust is something AI agents will have to earn one accurate booking at a time. TubStays, founded in 2024 and based in San Jose, California, lists more than 9,000 verified properties in more than 1,600 cities and destinations, and the full survey and questionnaire are available on its website.
