stories.Headline: Amazon launches Textract Insights to extract document fields from natural language descriptions
stories.Summary:
Amazon announced on November 20, 2026 the general availability of Amazon Textract Insights, a new generative AI feature of Amazon Textract available through a new API within Amazon Textract. The announcement was published on the AWS blog at aws.amazon.com. With it, users describe the fields they want in natural language and submit a document or a mixed, multi-document packet. They receive structured results in which each value carries a confidence score and page-level grounding. No model training is required.

Users define what to extract in a blueprint, a JSON Schema in which each field carries a natural language description and an inference type. Users can begin with an AWS public blueprint for a common document type, such as a W-2, Form 1040, Form 1098, a passport, or a birth certificate. For a mixed packet, users add the blueprints for each expected document type to the same project and submit a single file of up to 3,000 pages from their own Amazon S3 bucket with splitting enabled. The service splits the packet into logical sub-documents, matches each to the fitting blueprint, extracts the requested fields, and returns a confidence score and grounding for each value. In the example given, a 26-page PDF mortgage application containing a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a loan officer's handwritten notes is submitted with a single StartDocumentInsights call.

Vijay Agrawal, Vice President, Information Systems, Symbeo, A CorVel Company, said his firm evaluated Amazon Textract Insights and was excited about its potential. He said its medical bills and forms come from a wide variety of sources and often have different layouts and formats, so extraction rules developed for one source do not always transfer effectively to another. He said that with the service his team can describe the fields it needs in plain language and the service identifies and extracts the corresponding data. He said each extracted value is returned with a confidence score, allowing the team to focus review efforts only on fields where the service has lower confidence. He said the firm is also excited to explore the document splitting capabilities, which could help automatically separate multi-document files into individual documents.

Amazon Textract Insights returns two kinds of fields: explicit fields read directly from the page and inferred fields derived from the document's content. Both return with a confidence score and with grounding that identifies the page and the coordinates the value was drawn from, so a reviewer or auditor can confirm any result against the original document. Organizations across financial services, insurance, healthcare, and the public sector depend on document processing and want dependable, auditable answers from complex documents. The service supports PDF, PNG, JPEG, and TIFF inputs and processes documents in English, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish. It is priced per page rather than per token, with no minimum commitment.

AWS updated Amazon Textract's reading engine, Amazon Textract Core, improving accuracy, strengthening the handling of dense tables and handwriting, and expanding language coverage to 40 languages for the DetectDocumentText and AnalyzeDocument APIs. These benefits are available to Amazon Textract customers today with no changes, and the Amazon Textract APIs remain unchanged. Amazon Textract Core is now generally available in two additional AWS Regions, Asia Pacific (Tokyo) and Europe (Zurich), bringing in-region processing to a total of 18 AWS Regions. Amazon Textract Insights isn't yet available in these AWS Regions. Amazon Textract Insights encrypts projects and blueprints at rest with AWS owned keys, and users can specify their own AWS Key Management Service customer managed key in EncryptionConfiguration when calling CreateProject or CreateBlueprint.

Getting started takes four steps: define what is needed from an AWS public blueprint or by describing fields in natural language, create a project and add blueprints to it, submit documents from an Amazon S3 bucket with one API call, and review results by accepting values that meet a confidence threshold and routing the rest for review. AWS advises tuning the threshold on a representative sample of the user's own documents. Intermediate job data is encrypted at rest with AWS owned keys, is transient, and is deleted when the job completes, and a project's key does not apply to its jobs. Amazon Textract Insights automatically selects the optimal AWS Region within the user's geography to process inference requests, and inference requests originating in the United States are processed within the United States. AWS points readers to the Amazon Textract documentation guide for the list of destination AWS Regions and to a re:Invent session titled Accelerate intelligent document processing with Amazon Textract.

Articles.Title: Announcing Amazon Textract Insights: Verifiable generative AI for documents

stories.Headline: Justice Department charges 15 people over $3.4 million in VA fraud
stories.Summary:
The Justice Department announced charges and convictions against 15 individuals, including multiple people charged in Florida who allegedly defrauded the Veterans Affairs Department. That included convictions of individuals who promised to build a cancer center for veterans in St. Petersburg. The legal actions were part of a surge in fraud investigations by Justice officials, the VA and the VA Office of Inspector General. The individuals are collectively suspected of defrauding, or trying to defraud, the agency of $3.4 million. The Justice Department said the surge in enforcement from September through this month included sentencings, pleas, and trial verdicts totaling more than $19 million in intended loss.

Authorities took Matthew West and Kevin Kutina to trial for securing an $8.9 million contract to build the Cancer Infusion Therapy Center at Bay Pines VA Medical Center. Only Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Businesses could bid on the contract, but a secret side deal steered most of the work to a company that did not qualify. Co-conspirators Robert Gonzalez, who did qualify as a service-disabled veteran, and William Gonzalez already pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Of roughly $4.8 million that Maxon Groupe collected from the U.S. Treasury under the contract, about $4.2 million went to West, who then paid more than $350,000 to Kevcon, a company run by Kutina. West and Kutina were convicted of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, and major fraud against the United States.

Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald of the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division said veterans' benefits are earned through service, sacrifice, deployments, injuries, time away from loved ones, and a willingness to serve something larger than themselves. He said today's results demonstrate the department's commitment to protecting those who have served, safeguarding taxpayer resources, and preserving the integrity of federal programs. Rep. Gus Bilirakis, a Palm Harbor Republican, applauded the Justice Department, the VA and the VA Office of Inspector General for the coordinated enforcement actions targeting fraud against veterans' benefits programs. He said the men and women who served earned these benefits through sacrifice, dedication, and commitment to protecting freedoms, and that fraud targeting veterans is particularly reprehensible. Rep. Kathy Castor, a Tampa Democrat, said anyone who tries to steal or exploit veterans' benefits must be held accountable and that corrupt actors must be held accountable.

Michael Christopher Comiskey was charged in Florida's Southern District with theft of government funds and aggravated identity theft after allegedly scheming for benefits paid after the death of a veteran beneficiary. A jury in Florida's Middle District convicted Zachary Somers Hiscock and Arif Hasan Sayed of wire fraud and conspiracy to commit wire fraud in a scheme that rewarded recruiters based on the GI Bill tuition dollars each enrolled veteran produced, which federal rules prohibit. Veterans attended a short course and received a certification with little value for employability, Justice officials said. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tiffany Fields and Samantha Newman are prosecuting the Bay Pines case for the Middle District of Florida. The work supports the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, run by Vice President JD Vance.

Sen. Rick Scott, a Naples Republican, called on the Senate to pass the Banning Lobbying and Safeguarding Trust (BLAST) Act, which would impose a lifelong ban on former members of Congress becoming federal lobbyists. Scott introduced the bipartisan bill in May with Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat. Sen. Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican retiring at the end of this Congress, objected to Scott's request to pass it by unanimous consent. Tillis said on the floor that he had no plans to become a federal lobbyist but considered the bill too broad, Just the News reported. The Senate passed the Charlotte Woodward Organ Transplant Discrimination Prevention Act (HR 1520) on Thursday, legislation championed by Sen. Ashley Moody that bars transplant centers from using intellectual and other disabilities as factors in denying referrals for organs.

Moody, a Plant City Republican, carried the bipartisan bill with Sen. Maggie Hassan, a New Hampshire Democrat, and said it was hard to believe that in America, in 2026, a person could be denied consideration for a lifesaving organ transplant simply because they have a disability. The legislation was named for disability rights activist and heart transplant recipient Charlotte Woodward, who said receiving a heart transplant 14 years ago saved her life and allowed her to pursue her dreams. Paris Hilton stumped on Capitol Hill for the Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Non-Consensual Edits (DEFIANCE) Act (HR 3562), alongside its co-sponsor, U.S. Rep. Laurel Lee. Lee, a Thonotosassa Republican, crafted a bipartisan bill with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat, and said the images may be fake but the victims are real. Rep. Kat Cammack, a Gainesville Republican who founded and chairs the Republican Women's Caucus, endorsed the legislation, which would let victims sue those who make deepfake pornography from real people's likenesses.

The House passed Castor's Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act (HR 9084), which would require timely public disclosures of key safety and authorization decisions for advanced nuclear test reactors. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, an Iowa Republican, co-sponsored the bill, which was introduced in response to an Energy Department pilot program to advance investment in nuclear power. The legislation requires public notice of any changes to covered nuclear facility directives or safety standards, as well as of preliminary and documented safety analyses, within 72 hours. It also calls for annual reporting to Congress on the state of those nuclear facilities. The articles leave open whether the BLAST Act, the DEFIANCE Act and the nuclear transparency bill will become law.

stories.Headline: Dan Ives views recent AI sell-off as a generational buying opportunity
stories.Summary:
Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives discussed a significant artificial intelligence sell-off during a CNBC interview on Friday, November 21, 2026. He described this recent downturn as one of the most disconnected technology crashes he has witnessed since starting his career in the late 1990s. The market experienced a sharp swing in investor expectations, causing the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF to drop over 6 percent. Meanwhile, the iShares U.S. Technology ETF fell nearly 7 percent during the same trading session.

This volatility requires investors to look past current political uncertainty and concerns regarding chip export restrictions to China. Ives believes the market is incorrectly pricing stocks as if the AI revolution will not happen, despite the cycle being less than 15 percent complete. He noted that demand for chips from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Nvidia Corp. remains so high that new orders might not be filled until the end of 2028. Furthermore, he stated that roughly 75 percent of data center projects have already received the necessary permits.

The Yorkville Ives partner argued that the current market sentiment is an overreaction to spending concerns and a political backlash against data center expansion. He characterized the situation as a white-knuckle roller-coaster moment but maintained that the broader technology bull market remains intact. Ives suggested that this period represents a generational opportunity to buy winning companies before the market realizes its mistake in eighteen months. He believes the infrastructure boom will eventually benefit financial services, industrials, and energy companies.

The current turbulence follows a blue tidal wave of political opposition that acted as a gut punch to technology investors. While retail sentiment on Stocktwits remained bearish toward the S&P 500 ETF, some indices showed recovery in after-hours trading. The Invesco QQQ Trust ETF rose 1.53 percent, and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF gained 1.11 percent. Ives expects the long-term potential of the industry to eventually outweigh these temporary shocks.

stories.Headline: Akamai turns away AI infrastructure deals as power limits constrain capacity
stories.Summary:
Akamai Technologies is turning away some potential AI infrastructure business because of limited power availability, Chief Financial Officer Ed McGowan said at an event hosted by RBC software analyst Rishi Jaluria, MarketBeat reported on Saturday, November 21, 2026. The company has signed $14 billion in large deals this year, McGowan said. He said its pipeline is the largest he has seen in its history. Demand comes from enterprises, foundation-model developers, startups and other AI companies. Power constraints make it difficult to take on additional large projects requiring capacity in 2027.

McGowan said power is the most important and scarcest element today, and that availability should improve in the second half of 2028 and into 2029. Akamai closed a $2.5 billion offering the prior week and is funded for its committed deals without returning to debt markets through 2028, Jaluria said, and McGowan confirmed that. McGowan said Akamai has investment-grade ratings from Fitch and Moody's, while S&P downgraded the company. He attributed the difference to the agencies' assumptions about future leverage and growth. He said Akamai expects to deleverage over the next two years as it pays down debt and expands EBITDA margins.

McGowan declined to set a firm date for a sustainable return to positive free cash flow, saying faster cloud infrastructure growth would require more capital spending before revenue arrives. Depending on the pace of growth, he said, the company could reach that point in 2028 or later. He said three large customer projects expected to start in the fourth quarter are now generating revenue. Data center construction, customer-specific fit-outs and equipment issues can affect the precise date revenue begins, he said, calling it spreadsheet risk. Asked about an approximately 13% internal rate of return calculation for a large infrastructure contract, McGowan said Akamai included data center fit-out and network connection costs, as well as spare capacity, in its analysis.

McGowan said those costs could be shared as other customers are added to the same facilities. He said the calculation assumed revenue only for the contract's duration, although the company may be able to continue using the equipment afterward. He described the return as a floor, noting that a customer committing to a deal of that size receives Akamai's best pricing. McGowan said Akamai sees substantial demand for CPUs alongside GPUs in AI applications and will supply the hardware customers need. He pointed to potential uses for its distributed infrastructure in latency-sensitive applications, including robotics and other forms of physical AI.

Akamai is already supporting workloads from central cloud to the edge, including post-training work, McGowan said, but does not plan to build gigawatt-scale facilities for large-scale model training. Its development work includes making applications easier for customers to run without specifying the underlying hardware. In security, McGowan said AI-related bot activity is increasing demand for bot management tools, although traffic volume does not translate directly into revenue. Customers are also seeking broader web application firewall coverage, he said. McGowan described security as a healthy, recurring-revenue business but stopped short of predicting an acceleration in its growth rate.

Akamai acquired cloud provider Linode in March 2022, and McGowan said the company has since more than quadrupled the revenue it acquired in that transaction. McGowan said Akamai's own rising third-party cloud costs, along with customer requests to run their code on Akamai's platform, helped prompt its entry into the broader compute market. He said Akamai would continue to consider acquisitions, while weighing potential deals against returns from investing in its fast-growing cloud infrastructure business. McGowan said the company's financing needs after 2028 would depend largely on how quickly it chooses to grow. Akamai provides cloud computing, cybersecurity and content delivery services through Akamai Connected Cloud.

stories.Headline: Elementl Power and Google use Gemini AI to speed nuclear project delivery
stories.Summary:
Elementl Power and Google said on Tuesday that they have agreed to work together to use Google Cloud's artificial intelligence technology to help bring nuclear projects onto the grid sooner, according to a press release from the Washington, D.C. headquartered project development company. The collaboration will build on Elementl Power's project delivery tool, which is named Elementl Lattice, and the company's AI system is based on Google's Gemini. Elementl Power said the system will continue to leverage Google Cloud's technological expertise to create a standardized and scalable project approach for nuclear development. The companies are additionally working together to create a single, controlled record of a nuclear plant's design, licensing requirements and approved changes, according to the release. Elementl Power said this effort will directly assist with creating shorter timelines and more regulatory certainty for future projects, which the company framed as the purpose of the arrangement.

The collaboration deepens the partnership between Google and Elementl Power after the companies signed a strategic agreement last year. In May 2025, the two companies agreed to develop three advanced reactors, with each project being at least 600 megawatts. The Tuesday announcement did not give a value for the new agreement, a schedule for the work, or a date for when any reactor project might reach the grid. The articles do not name the executives who signed the agreement or give direct statements from either company beyond the release language paraphrased above. Elementl Power is described as a nuclear power project development company headquartered in Washington, D.C., and Google's role is through its cloud computing unit and its Gemini AI system.

The release casts the AI work as a way to standardize how projects are delivered and to keep design, licensing and change records in one controlled place. No independent party is named as overseeing or reviewing the collaboration. The context given is the earlier May 2025 agreement between the two companies to develop three advanced reactors of at least 600 megawatts each, which the new collaboration builds on. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the work described in the release, and they give no timeline for the AI tools or for the reactor projects themselves. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Valar Atomics raises $1 billion and powers an Nvidia AI chip with its nuclear reactor
stories.Summary:
Isaiah Taylor left high school at 16 without completing his formal education, and eleven years later, at 27, he leads Valar Atomics, a nuclear energy startup based in El Segundo, California. Valar Atomics has attracted a $1 billion investment from Sequoia Capital and reached a reported valuation of $6 billion. The company demonstrated that its small nuclear reactor can generate electricity to power an Nvidia AI processor. Valar Atomics is developing small modular nuclear reactors, compact, factory-built power plants designed to supply electricity to data centres and industrial facilities. The demonstration came in July 2026, when the company showed its Ward 250 nuclear reactor could power an Nvidia Blackwell-based system.

According to a July 2026 TechCrunch report, the three-year-old startup was initially in talks to raise $1 billion at a valuation of around $6 billion, and the round closed in August with Sequoia Capital leading. Valar Atomics announced on August 4, 2026, that it had closed a $1 billion Series B round led by Sequoia Capital, and Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire joined the company's board. The company also announced a $200 million credit facility led by Erebor Bank, with participation from JPMorgan, Crescent Cove and Hercules Capital. Bloomberg reported the transaction valued the company at $6 billion including the new investment, and TechCrunch and the Los Angeles Times subsequently reported the same valuation. Reuters reported on July 1 that Valar Atomics and Nvidia were working towards developing a 30-megawatt AI facility in Utah, powered by Valar's helium-cooled nuclear microreactors.

Taylor founded Valar Atomics after leaving high school at 16, and before starting the nuclear company he had launched two other startups, according to TechCrunch. Taylor has said his great-grandfather was a nuclear physicist who worked on the Manhattan Project, the US-led programme that developed the first atomic weapons during World War II. Among the investors backing Valar Atomics are Palmer Luckey, founder of defence technology company Anduril, and Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of Palantir Technologies. The funding is expected to support the company's plans to move beyond individual reactor demonstrations towards manufacturing multiple small modular reactors. According to TechCrunch's August 3 report, the demonstration involved using electricity generated through a nuclear fission reaction to operate an Nvidia AI processor and host a website.

Around the same time as the demonstration, Valar Atomics and Nvidia announced a partnership to explore nuclear-powered infrastructure for artificial intelligence data centres. The collaboration comes amid growing demand for electricity from AI data centres, which require substantial power to operate computing infrastructure. Technology companies are increasingly exploring alternative energy sources as existing electricity networks face pressure to accommodate expanding data centre capacity. Valar Atomics joined several US states and competing startups in a legal challenge against the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, arguing that the regulator applies lengthy licensing procedures to small test reactors that are also used for larger commercial facilities. According to TechCrunch, the legal dispute remains unresolved, with proceedings having been paused multiple times as the parties pursue the matter.

Valar Atomics is among several companies developing advanced nuclear technology for industrial and data centre applications, and other players in the sector include Kairos Power, Bill Gates-backed TerraPower and NuScale Power. The company's Ward 250 reactor demonstration used electricity generated through a nuclear fission reaction to operate an Nvidia AI processor and host a website. The three-year-old startup was initially in talks to raise $1 billion at a valuation of around $6 billion before the round closed in August. Taylor left high school at 16 without completing his formal education, and by 27 he was leading the company. The company is based in El Segundo, California, and is developing small modular nuclear reactors designed to supply electricity to data centres and industrial facilities.

The funding is expected to support plans to move beyond individual reactor demonstrations towards manufacturing multiple small modular reactors. The legal dispute with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission remains unresolved, with proceedings having been paused multiple times as the parties pursue the matter. Valar Atomics and Nvidia announced a partnership to explore nuclear-powered infrastructure for artificial intelligence data centres. Reuters reported on July 1 that the companies were working towards developing a 30-megawatt AI facility in Utah, powered by Valar's helium-cooled nuclear microreactors. The articles do not say when the legal dispute will be resolved or when the Utah facility will be built.

stories.Headline: Researchers recover pruned MoE experts without training through gated reuse
stories.Summary:
Linliang Chen, Yan Zhong, Wang Kang, Sai Li, Ji Wu and Ji Liu posted a paper to arXiv on 21 November 2026 describing a method for recovering the work of pruned experts in Mixture-of-Experts large language models. Mixture-of-Experts models activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all experts in GPU memory for high efficiency, and expert pruning reduces that memory footprint but discards the contribution of the pruned experts. The authors report that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. They propose GEAR, which stands for Gated Expert Activation Reuse and reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. They also propose GEAR$^2$, which adds an ultra-lightweight residual to further recover what reuse cannot express.

The work was tested on five Mixture-of-Experts large language models ranging from 16B to 106B parameters, with 25% and 50% of experts pruned. GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting, by up to 4 percentage points in terms of accuracy. GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches by up to 2.75 percentage points in every setting across nine zero-shot benchmarks. The authors report larger advantages, up to 2.72 percentage points higher, under more aggressive pruning of up to 50%. The paper contrasts its approach with existing remedies that rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training.

The paper lists Linliang Chen, Yan Zhong, Wang Kang, Sai Li, Ji Wu and Ji Liu as its authors, and the abstract presents the findings and the two proposed methods in the authors' own account. The authors state that GEAR reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation, and that GEAR$^2$ adds an ultra-lightweight residual for what reuse cannot express. They describe the reconstruction of pruned experts' functionalities from the activated remaining experts as a finding of the paper. The abstract frames the motivation around the GPU memory footprint that expert pruning reduces and the discarded contribution of pruned experts that existing remedies handle in other ways.

The articles provide no information on what happens next, such as release of code, further testing or publication beyond the arXiv posting. The abstract reports results on nine zero-shot benchmarks and on models from 16B to 106B parameters, with pruning at 25% and 50%. The arXiv listing notes that a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source are available for the paper. It also describes arXivLabs as a framework allowing collaborators to develop and share features directly on the arXiv website, and states that arXiv is committed to openness, community, user data privacy and partnership with organizations that adhere to those values.

stories.Headline: Senator Mark R. Warner leads a bipartisan bill requiring AI-using companies to disclose governance and financing risks
stories.Summary:
A bipartisan group of senators plans to introduce a sweeping securities disclosure bill. This legislation targets companies that use artificial intelligence or are involved in the AI industry. The announcement regarding this new bill was made on November 21, 2026. It aims to increase transparency regarding AI operations and transactions. The group also wants to know if board committees provide AI oversight.

The AUDIT AI Act is led by Senator Mark R. Warner of Virginia. Senators John Kennedy, Angela Alsobrooks, and Mike Rounds are co-sponsors of the proposed legislation. Section 3 requires the SEC to issue rules within 180 days of enactment. Covered issuers are companies required to file annual reports under Exchange Act Section 13 or 15(d). These companies must disclose AI governance policies and board expertise or explain their absence.

Senator Mark R. Warner stated that AI has enormous potential to transform the economy. He noted that trillions of dollars pouring into the technology come with real financial risks. Warner believes investors and policymakers deserve to know where that money is going. He also wants clarity on how deals are financed and what risks are involved. These statements were provided in a press release from the senator.

The bill affects non-financial covered issuers, excluding banking, insurance, lending, investment management, and securities trading. It targets round-trip financing arrangements between AI chip providers and other hardware or software components. Some AI industry observers have described these specific financing arrangements as a concern. The bill protects private fund investor identities unless they are defined as covered entities. Covered entities include joint ventures, special purpose vehicles, or variable interest entities.

Some group members previously served on a small team under then-Majority Leader Chuck Schumer. That team was tasked with creating a legislative framework for AI several congresses ago. Prior legislation proposing similar board expertise disclosures for cybersecurity never advanced beyond the introductory stage. The SEC previously rejected cybersecurity expertise rules, noting that broad business knowledge is often sufficient. The Commission stated that cybersecurity processes are largely administered at the management level.

The SEC must amend Form 10-K within 180 days to include standardized AI risk sections. This section will cover foundation model dependence, compute provider concentration, and training cost volatility. The SEC must also study AI research and development reporting and publish results after one year. A report on automated investment strategies and market efficiency is due within 120 days. The articles leave open whether the bill will pass or how the SEC will implement flexibility.

stories.Headline: Julie Menin leads New York City Council plan to vote on AI bills in January 2027
stories.Summary:
The New York City Council plans to begin 2027 by voting on a set of artificial intelligence bills, according to two people with knowledge of the timing who were granted anonymity to discuss private deliberations. The legislation is being led by Council Speaker Julie Menin, a Manhattan lawmaker who has become a foil to Mayor Zohran Mamdani on several issues, including AI regulation. The package would place the city at the forefront of efforts to rein in frontier AI technology, amid growing concern about its existential threats to society. The measures are meant as a counterpoint to federal inaction on AI, which the article describes as amounting to a regulatory vacuum. The vote is expected in January, though a spokesperson for Menin said the bills are still undergoing review and that no exact date has been set for a vote.

The article gives no other numbers, dates or names beyond the January timing, the 2027 start, Menin, Mamdani and the two anonymous people. It does not specify how many bills are in the package or what any of them would require. The article also does not say what penalties or obligations the legislation would create. Menin is the lawmaker responsible for shepherding the legislation, and her spokesperson said the bills remain under review while confirming that a vote date has not been fixed.

The article does not include further comment from Menin, Mamdani or other council members on the substance of the bills. It also does not say whether the mayor supports or opposes the package. The two people who confirmed the January timing spoke on condition of anonymity because the deliberations were private. The context given is federal inaction on AI, which the article says has left a regulatory vacuum that the city measures are intended to counter.

The article does not say what happens after a January vote, such as whether the mayor would sign the bills or whether further steps are required. It also does not describe any federal proposals that the city effort is responding to. No other details on the next steps are provided. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop compact visual latents to improve remote sensing for large language models
stories.Summary:
Meng Tang, Siyuan Du, Yuxin Liu, Shuaishuai Cao, Di Wang, and Haonan Guo published a research paper on November 21, 2026, regarding ultra-high-resolution remote sensing. The researchers developed a method to compress detailed image crops into short sequences of continuous visual latents to help multimodal large language models. This approach addresses the problem where global overviews hide small objects and detailed crops use too much computational context. By encoding high-resolution crops into latent memory tokens, the team sought to determine if these compact forms could retain fine-grained evidence.

The system utilizes a 64-token memory that achieves a compression rate between 7.6 and 9.9 times compared to retained crop tokens. When tested across two generations of Qwen-VL on the LRS-GRO dataset, this method improved accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over using only downsampled global images. The researchers also observed consistent behavior on the XLRS-Bench to validate the predictive utility of the latent memory. Substituting memory from different images or regions reduced accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points, which was worse than removing the memory entirely.

The authors explained that these results prove predictions depend directly on the encoded regional evidence stored within the compact visual latents. They noted that restoring the original source crop within the same model reduced the accuracy loss caused by zeroing or removing the memory. This evidence suggests that the availability of specific local data is the primary factor governing how these latents contribute to model performance. The findings establish that compact visual latents can successfully retain useful local evidence for complex remote sensing tasks.

Articles.Title: Out of Sight, Into Memory: Compact Visual Latents Retain Local Evidence in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing

stories.Headline: Principals lobby Congress for school funding increases and AI limits
stories.Summary:
Three hundred school leaders and students from across the nation fanned out across Capitol Hill on Nov. 17, 2025, as part of a two-day National Advocacy Summit organized by the National Principals Association. They met with their state representatives and senators to ask for more funding to support public education. The summit took place in Washington, D.C., and the principals met with their state representatives on Capitol Hill. On their agenda were requests to raise federal funding to expand student mental health services, curb school choice programs, and put guardrails on how schools use artificial intelligence. After a long day of lobbying, most principals said they felt hopeful, a decided vibe shift from when they last appealed to Congress in March 2025.

Principals asked their representatives for an increase in Title I funding to $19 billion from $18.4 billion to help high-poverty school districts meet students' needs. They sought an increase in Title II funding to $2.4 billion from $2.14 billion and Title IV-A funding to bolster teacher and principal pipelines and support and expand access to quality mental health care for educators and students. The Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027, and individuals can claim a federal income tax credit up to $1,700 for qualified cash contributions to certain scholarship-granting organizations. Scholarships can be used for students' approved expenses such as tutoring at a public school or tuition at a private school. Governors of 31 states have opted into the program, fifteen states and the District of Columbia are still undecided, and four have said they will not participate.

Erin Sieh, the principal of Freeman Elementary School in Adams, Neb., said the March 2025 layoff announcement came out hours before they were going to go to the Hill and it felt like their bubble had been burst. Sieh said it felt very defeating and like education wasn't valued, with a lot of uncertainty that was very frightening. Mike Rubin, who leads Uxbridge High School in Uxbridge, Mass., said there's a palpably positive feeling around the willingness to support education and to hear their messages more than the last two or three times they've been here. Rubin said he feels like there's an alignment with what are students' needs and actual next steps to support these needs. Lucas Pugh, the principal of Connolly Middle School in Tempe, Ariz., said the current funding levels are insufficient to retain high-quality educators, provide wraparound student services, and meet testing and graduation requirements.

Jeff Linden, the principal of the approximately 1,000-student Hastings High School in Nebraska, said schools are doing everything they can to work with what they have and find the resources to get creative, but at the same time we need help. At Hastings High School, 54% of students belong to low-income households and 30% require special accommodations in school. Jay Dostal, the principal of Westside High School in Omaha, Neb., said his family is in generational debt trying to teach the youth of tomorrow and asked how we incentivize the youth to continue teaching. Anna Thoma, the assistant principal of Millard High School in Millard, Neb., told an aide to Republican Sen. Pete Rickett that the funding is finite and school vouchers dilute the funding for public schools. Greg Johnson, the longtime principal of West Liberty-Salem High School, an hour outside Columbus, said even policymakers who supported private school choice were open to his view that these programs pull money away from public school students.

Over the past two years, the Trump administration has gutted the Education Department and frozen several federal grants that help schools cover food and medical costs for students. There were cuts to teacher and principal training programs as well, though some grant funding has been restored. The Trump administration has argued that in shutting down the Education Department, they are returning power to the states and to parents by giving them the right to choose the type of education they want for their children. The principals' top fear, of reduced Title 1 and other federal funding, has somewhat dissipated since Congress voted to maintain the existing levels of funding for public education for fiscal year 2026. A group of Republican senators has also proposed a spending package that again preserves virtually all current federal education funding for fiscal year 2027.

Other principals credited the shift in mood to the Democratic takeover of both houses of Congress after the midterm elections and the rise of the so-called blue wave. Rubin and Wiltshire, from Massachusetts, told an aide in Democratic Sen. Ed Markey's office that multiple students from their schools had been hospitalized for mental health conditions. An aide for Markey said their office had written to Google about its decision to bundle AI features with the search function, a move that several prominent school districts have pushed back against. Democratic Rep. Jim McGovern indicated to the Massachusetts contingent that he intends to push to regulate AI sooner than Congress had acted on curbing social media exposure for students. Virginia's newly elected governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, reversed her Republican predecessor's decision and pulled out of the program this week.

stories.Headline: Senate passes permitting bill that limits environmental laws and requires data centers to pay for grid impact
stories.Summary:
The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, S.5653, on Nov. 19, 2026, by a 62-33 vote, with 14 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent joining most Republicans. Thirty Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent voted against the bill. The bill's sponsors are Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Republican Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance vouched for the legislation in a Nov. 20 news conference. The bill must win approval in the House to advance, and the House could amend it, which would require the Senate to approve the new text. The bill would limit the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act. The Natural Resources Defense Council's analysis concluded that under the bill a court "can never invalidate a permit" based on a violation of the National Environmental Policy Act or the National Historic Preservation Act. The bill would cut the time to build a major new transmission line from 10-plus years to five or six.

About 2,000 gigawatts of proposed generation and storage are waiting to connect to the grid, and 85 percent of that capacity is solar, wind, or storage. The bill requires data centers to pay for their impact on electricity supply rather than shifting those costs to ratepayers. Juniper Katz, a University of Massachusetts-Amherst assistant professor of public policy, said there are priorities both sides want and the bill "is not perfect." Geoffrey Henderson, a University of Michigan assistant professor of environmental policy and planning, said it is reasonable to be concerned that development of each kind of project Ruffalo mentioned could be facilitated by the bill. Henderson also said the bill's impacts are highly uncertain, depending on political, market, geopolitical and legal outcomes.

The NRDC analysis said that if the Trump administration issued a blanket grant of all permits for oil and gas infrastructure without any environmental review, the bill provides no clear mechanism for a future administration to revoke those permits. Ruffalo's representative did not respond to an inquiry for the article. Mark Ruffalo said in a Nov. 18 video viewed 22 million times that the bill would fast-track AI data centers, pipelines, mines, power plants and ICE camps while sacrificing clean water, tribal rights, public lands and endangered species. Groups supporting the bill include the Solar Energy Industries Association, the AFL-CIO, the American Petroleum Institute and the Edison Electric Institute.

Groups opposing it include the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Climate Justice Alliance, a range of tribal organizations, the NAACP and the American Civil Liberties Union. Opponents say their concerns about ICE facilities stem from the use of the National Environmental Policy Act to oppose ICE facilities in court in Maryland, Arizona and Florida. Ezra Klein, a New York Times columnist considered left of center, said he was "unnerved" by conflicting interpretations of certain provisions but still supported the bill. The bill grew out of concerns from both fossil fuel backers and renewable energy supporters that opponents could stymie projects for years in the courts.

Supporters said growing energy demand and rising electricity prices meant a failure to build new infrastructure would consign the United States to a spiral of insufficient energy supplies and higher costs. Critics say the bill effectively guts tools to prevent local governments, citizens, Native American tribes and other local interests from blocking harms caused by such projects. Critics also say the Trump administration, which refuses to acknowledge the possibility of emissions-driven climate change, could wield the law to advance fossil fuel projects over renewable energy infrastructure. The NRDC analysis devotes almost 1,000 words to describing what it considers the bill's positive features, including improving electric capacity by increasing how much power existing transmission lines can carry and enabling construction of new lines.

The bill's fate in the House is uncertain, and the potential for updated language and the difficulty of predicting how courts would interpret its provisions make it difficult to know whether Ruffalo's scenario will come to pass. The bill could also boost non-energy projects that have faced long-running challenges in the courts, including rail and transit, affordable housing and broadband access, Klein wrote. The bill does not directly address ICE detention facilities. The articles leave open whether the House will amend the bill and whether the Senate would then approve new text.

stories.Headline: Federal contractors face False Claims Act liability for overstated AI capabilities, BCLP partners say
stories.Summary:
Federal contractors that exaggerate or misrepresent artificial intelligence capabilities in bids and billing for government work could face liability under the False Claims Act, according to a Bloomberg Law analysis published on November 20, 2026 by Emmet P. Ong and Susan Carney Lynch, both partners at BCLP. The authors point to regulators who have already pursued misleading claims about AI, including the Securities and Exchange Commission, which has acted against companies for misrepresenting their AI use, and the Federal Trade Commission, which has challenged deceptive claims about AI-enabled products. They describe examples such as a defense contractor claiming its drones can autonomously identify and track targets despite testing that showed undisclosed human intervention, or a medical-device manufacturer overstating diagnostic capabilities to win placement on government supply schedules. The risks also extend to contracts for AI development, where a contractor might falsely report completed model training or successful testing to obtain milestone payments, or bill for AI-enabled analysis never performed.

The analysis says not every promotional claim supports liability, since vague descriptions such as AI-powered differ from specific representations about autonomous operation, detection accuracy or deployed safeguards. It cites the Department of Justice's Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative as a precedent, noting a university-affiliated defense research contractor that settled allegations last year that a cybersecurity assessment score submitted under defense contracts was based on a fictitious or virtual environment rather than an actual covered system, and a medical-services contractor that settled allegations in 2022, including failing to disclose that patient records were not consistently stored in the secure electronic medical-record system for which it billed the government. Applying established False Claims Act theories would raise questions about materiality, scienter and damages, complicated by the technology's evolving capabilities, and the authors note that under United States ex rel. Escobar v.

Universal Health Services a contractual or regulatory violation does not automatically establish liability because a misrepresentation must have a natural tendency to influence, or be capable of influencing, the government's payment decision. They also cite United States ex rel. Schutte v. SuperValu Inc. for the point that a defendant's subjective beliefs matter, so an objectively reasonable interpretation does not necessarily protect a contractor whose internal communications show it understood its AI representations were false.

On damages, the authors cite United States v. Science Applications International Corp., where the court applied a benefit-of-the-bargain measure to account for the value of services received, and they say evidence that the government would have withheld payment does not itself establish damages. They recommend that federal contractors incorporate reviews of material AI representations into existing contracting and compliance controls, and they set out four practical steps: substantiate claims before making them by comparing proposals, demonstrations and billing submissions with documented testing and actual capabilities; ensure testing supports representations by documenting testing conditions, limitations and results; preserve records connecting commitments to performance, including milestone reports, acceptance tests, deployment records and internal assessments; and reassess representations during performance, since model updates, disabled controls or changes in human oversight may make later claims or certifications inaccurate even if earlier statements were sound. The authors conclude that DOJ may not need a dedicated AI-washing initiative to pursue misrepresentations about AI capabilities, and that as AI becomes embedded in federal procurement and healthcare, contractors should expect greater scrutiny of the gap between promised capabilities and actual performance.

stories.Headline: Yunhong Han and co-authors present ReactNexus, a generative framework that maps reaction networks from reactants alone
stories.Summary:
A paper posted to arXiv on 21 November 2026 by Yunhong Han and 18 other authors describes ReactNexus, a generative framework that produces transition-state candidates directly from reactant graphs without requiring products to be specified in advance. The framework then predicts the chemical species those candidates connect and refines the resulting pathways using a reactive machine-learned potential to guide exploration of the reaction network. Its models were trained on a quantum-chemical database of 130 million structures drawn from 1.1 million reaction records, covering 11 elements and multiple charge and spin states. The authors say the work shows how generative models can extend mechanistic analysis to increasingly complex reaction mixtures.

On held-out reactions, 93.6% of the generated candidates refined to valid transition states at the density functional theory level, and 83.3% connected the supplied reactants to distinct products. Across decomposition, complex rearrangements and organocatalysis, ReactNexus showed how competing mechanisms shape product formation and uncovered pathways that previous studies had missed. In a multisite nucleophilic aromatic substitution, it identified diarylation products that explained LC-MS signals which had initially gone unassigned, with the structural assignments supported by NMR after isolation. ReactNexus also predicted an additional product family that was not detected under the initial conditions, and later experiments at higher temperature provided LC-MS evidence supporting its formation.

The authors frame the work as a response to a specific difficulty, noting that automated saddle-point searches can explore from reactants alone but their computational cost rises sharply as competing pathways accumulate across successive steps. They also observe that machine-learning approaches to transition state generation typically require predefined products, even though identifying those products is a central goal of exploration. ReactNexus is presented as a way around both constraints, generating candidates from reactants and then refining the pathways with the reactive potential. The abstract highlights the potential of generative models to extend mechanistic analysis to increasingly complex reaction mixtures.

The paper is titled Generative discovery of chemical reaction networks, and its author list runs from Yunhong Han and Gaopeng Ren through Chenru Duan and Qiyuan Zhao. The work was posted on arXiv along with a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, and the posting carries the standard arXivLabs notice describing that framework for collaborators who develop and share features on the site. That notice states that individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have accepted values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv works only with partners who adhere to them. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the higher-temperature experiments already reported.

stories.Headline: Software factory creator builds Squid to automate coding while humans steer planning and final review
stories.Summary:
A software factory is a system that automates software creation by turning raw inputs such as bug reports and feature ideas into shipped software, according to an O'Reilly Media article reported by TechGig on November 21, 2026. The author of that article built a software factory named Squid to manage small and medium projects with reduced human oversight. The approach focuses on combining good software principles with coding agents rather than on constantly changing labels like prompt engineering or context engineering. The article says the concept is gaining traction for automating development and aims to generate clean, maintainable code with minimal human intervention. The factory runs through eight stages grouped into three categories, which are what to build, actual building and checking, and self-improving.

The first category covers triage, brainstorming and planning, the second covers implementation, review, CI and release, and the third covers monitoring and incident response, which feeds production signals back in as new tasks. A context layer supplies user analytics, competitor analysis, research and documentation to guide agent decisions across the stages, and the article says this layer is often implemented as an LLM Wiki. Humans stay indispensable during brainstorming and planning, where taste and high-leverage decisions are made, while agents handle implementing, testing and initial review, and humans return for the final pull request review and merge. Zach Lloyd, the CEO of Warp, is quoted as saying that software engineering will become factory engineering. The article says effective planning with powerful models like Fable lets cheaper models such as Opus or Sonnet execute tasks efficiently, while a weak plan can lead to more retries, more tokens and higher overall costs.

The author advises against overbuilding factories and stresses the need for granular control and human intervention points so workflows can be debugged or redirected. The article presents the shift as a move toward actionable outcomes over evolving engineering labels. The article does not say what happens next beyond describing the structure and roles, and it gives no timeline for adoption. It frames the software factory as a way to redefine roles in the Software Development Life Cycle, with humans steering the early and final decisions and agents doing the intermediate work. The author's guidance is to keep human checkpoints in place rather than removing oversight entirely.

stories.Headline: Madras High Court directs Keralam to install AI cameras along railway tracks to prevent elephant deaths
stories.Summary:
The Madras High Court on November 13 directed the Keralam government to install artificial intelligence enabled cameras along railway tracks in that State, adopting the system Tamil Nadu has implemented between Madukkarai and Walayar to prevent elephants from being hit by trains. A Division Bench of Justices N. Sathish Kumar and G.K. Muthukumar issued the direction while hearing a 2019 public interest writ petition filed by S. Muralidharan. The court gave the State two months to implement the measure, noting that Tamil Nadu's camera based surveillance system had been successful in preventing elephant deaths along railway tracks. It also referred to a recent incident in Palakkad in which a train ran over an elephant and its calf, killing both animals.

The direction followed a memo from the Keralam government detailing its discussions with the Palakkad Divisional Railway Manager on measures to prevent elephant deaths. These included sanctioning three elephant underpasses, rail fencing between Madukkarai and Kanjikode, extension of rail barricading between Ettimadai and Walayar, real time sharing of elephant movement information with Station Masters and Section Controllers, an Elephant Intrusion Detection System and clearance of vegetation along vulnerable stretches. The court directed Keralam to grant immediate written approval for the construction of two elephant underpasses agreed upon with the Railways, and asked the Railways to complete the construction and submit an action taken report at the next hearing. On a third proposed underpass, the court expected Keralam to take a decision within two weeks, and the matter was posted to February 5, 2027, for a status report.

Senior Railway and Forest Department officials had inspected vulnerable locations and Tamil Nadu's AI based Forest Control Office, and the court had earlier directed Keralam officials to visit the control room between Madukkarai and Walayar and adopt its model. In the same order, the court directed the Coimbatore District Collector to conduct a detailed inspection of three establishments among the 33 resorts and establishments inspected in the Anaikatti area. A joint team of DTCP, Rural Development, Revenue and Forest Department officials conducted the inspection and document verification, and Aara Jungle Resort and My Village Eco Tourist Resort were reported to have DTCP approval. The third establishment, a café with Panchayat approval for a 1,322 sq ft building, was alleged to attract large crowds, operate beyond 10 p.m.

and sit on an elephant migratory path. The court also ordered periodic inspections of resorts directed to close, to ensure they were not operating indirectly under another guise, and posted that matter to January 8, 2027. Separately, the court directed the State to file a response to a petition by Darza Resorts challenging the sealing of its premises on November 11, and that petition was posted to December 11. The Collector had earlier informed the court that over 20 resorts in and around Anaikatti had closed.

stories.Headline: Marc Miller and Evan Solomon name members of Canada's AI and culture advisory council
stories.Summary:
On November 19, 2026, the Honourable Marc Miller, Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture and Minister responsible for Official Languages, and the Honourable Evan Solomon, Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario, announced the members of the new Advisory Council on Artificial Intelligence and Culture. The announcement was made in Gatineau, Quebec. The ministers also convened the council for its inaugural meeting. The members were selected based on their expertise and experience. The council follows Canada's first-ever National Summit on Artificial Intelligence and Culture, held in Banff, Alberta last March.

The council includes technology experts, researchers, industry and labour leaders, cultural practitioners and civil society stakeholders. Its membership will rotate over time to ensure a broad range of expertise informs its work as new questions and emerging issues arise. The members are Samuel Bischoff of the Directors Guild of Canada, Jeremy de Beer of the University of Ottawa, Jonathan Dewar of the First Nations Information Governance Centre, Stéphanie Hénault of the Association nationale des éditeurs de livres, Yves Jacquier of Ubisoft La Forge, Samantha Kaine of the Independent Media Producers Association of Creative Talent (IMPACT), Pascale Landry of Compétence Culture, Margaret McGuffin of Music Publishers Canada, Brenda O'Farrell of the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media / Quebec Community Newspapers Association, Sean Power of Musical AI, Amor Provins of the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, and Afsoon Soudi of the Creative AI Hub at Toronto Metropolitan University. The council will provide ongoing advice and insight to guide implementation of Canada's National AI Strategy, with a focus on the unique challenges facing the sector as well as the opportunities for adoption and innovation that responsible AI development can create for Canada's creative industries. The National Summit on Artificial Intelligence and Culture was held in Banff, Alberta, from March 15 to 17, 2026.

Miller said that at the Banff Summit, they heard clearly that building trust in AI will require the cultural sector to play a role in shaping how these technologies are developed and used. He said they are establishing this council to ensure that AI reflects the values, priorities and realities of Canada's cultural sector. Solomon said the future of Canadian culture cannot be shaped by technology alone. He said it has to reflect the voices and value of the people who create it. Solomon said the council brings creators, researchers and technology leaders together to help seize new opportunities, protect the value of human creativity and build a stronger cultural economy.

Solomon said their goal is clear: AI that earns trust, expands opportunity and strengthens Canada's culture and identity. The articles state that AI is changing how Canadians create and experience culture. They state that Canadian creators, cultural organizations and creative businesses must have a voice in ensuring it strengthens our cultural sector, protects Canadian creativity and diversity of expressions, and delivers shared prosperity. The summit was presented in partnership with the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity. The summit convened leaders from the cultural, government, technology, academic and civil society sectors to shape a shared vision for the future of culture in the age of artificial intelligence.

Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy: AI for All sets out six pillars to build a strong, trusted AI ecosystem that creates opportunity and strengthens Canada's sovereignty in AI. The strategy brings together actions to support AI adoption and skills, build infrastructure and advance the safe and responsible development of AI. It includes a $50-million investment in a new Creative Technology Program. The articles state that the council will help the government and the cultural sector navigate the rapid changes driven by AI. The source of the announcement is Canadian Heritage.

The articles state that the council will provide ongoing advice and insight to guide implementation of Canada's National AI Strategy. They state that its membership will rotate over time as new questions and emerging issues arise. The articles do not state when the council will next meet. stories.Headline: Anthropic shares fall 6% in premarket trading after record Nasdaq debut
stories.Summary:
Anthropic experienced a stock slide on November 20, 2026, following its market debut. The company went public on November 19, but investor enthusiasm for the AI sector failed to revive. This listing was widely viewed as a proxy for the broader artificial intelligence trade. The stock fell after a strong start that initially made it a very valuable company. This stumble delivered a reality check for investors who had eagerly anticipated the listing.

The stock traded at US$88.87, US$91.24, and US$87.28, falling about 9 to 10 percent below its November 19 close. Anthropic has a market capitalisation of US$1.2 trillion and a fully diluted valuation between US$1.6 trillion and US$1.7 trillion. It raised US$93.5 billion in its IPO, surpassing the US$85.7 billion raised by SpaceX in June. The valuation is about 40 times sales over the past 12 months, with an IPO price of US$83. Shares closed 13 percent below their opening price on Thursday, November 19, in New York.

Kaush Amin of US Bank Asset Management recommends patience and evaluating the company as it reports its public results. Harrison Rolfes from PitchBook stated that the growth plan is largely priced in and the valuation is not cheap. Tejal Patel of SOC Investment Group noted that a decline after a high-profile listing is normal but could raise alarms. Robert Pavlik from Dakota Wealth believes investors are skeptical of the market rather than the company or its management. David Miller of Catalyst Funds said investors believe in AI but are becoming more selective about growth payments.

Retail investors traded US$772 million of shares on November 19, the most since Vanda Research began tracking in 2012. Nvidia fell about 6 percent and Meta Platforms dropped nearly 3 percent, while Amazon and Microsoft lost less than 1 percent. Chip stocks slid, with AMD and Sandisk down 7 percent and Marvell Technology down over 8 percent, while Intel lost 3 to 5 percent. Wall Street indexes ended sharply lower on November 19, and futures pointed to further declines on November 20. Apple is developing an AI agent, entering a market already pursued by Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic.

The AI boom faced pressure as spending, expected to top US$1 trillion this year, may not generate returns quickly enough. Concerns include political hurdles for data center construction and leadership turmoil at the chipmaker Nvidia. Some investors compared Anthropic to Elon Musk's SpaceX, which saw sharp swings after its June listing. SpaceX shares fell about 5 percent, leading Rob Hackel of RF Lafferty & Co to warn against FOMO. Large IPOs have historically delivered modest returns during their first year, according to research from PitchBook.

Index-tracking funds could purchase up to 30 percent of shares by year-end, according to estimates from London-based firm Intropic. Options trading begins next week, which Carsten Hesse of Berenberg suggests could add to the current market volatility. Morgan Stanley closed a position that was intended to stabilize the shares after the initial debut. The focus now shifts to OpenAI, which has indicated it may go public in 2027. The articles leave open whether the current valuation can be sustained as the initial listing euphoria fades.

stories.Headline: Om Birla urges AI and digitisation to protect India's defence land
stories.Summary:
Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla spoke on Friday, November 20, 2026, regarding the management of land used for national defence. He addressed the centenary celebrations of the Defence Estates Organisation during an event held in the city of New Delhi. Birla called upon the organization to strengthen the protection of defence land using digitisation and Artificial Intelligence. He stated that securing assets and curbing encroachments must remain top priorities for the agency. The speaker emphasized that the Armed Forces require timely land availability to meet their various operational needs.

The mandate of the Defence Estates Organisation involves managing and safeguarding more than 1.7 million acres of defence land. Birla noted that accurate, secure, and accessible land records are vital for the effective governance of these vast areas. He commended the digital upgrades already underway and suggested that emerging technologies can address long-term administrative challenges. The speaker highlighted that the original character, forests, and green cover of military cantonments must be protected. He cautioned that development should be planned thoughtfully to preserve the identity of cantonments amid rapid urban growth.

Om Birla said that timely access to land and conducive conditions for personnel are essential to national security. He appreciated the efforts to carry out accurate surveys and measurements while avoiding unnecessary hardship for civilian residents. The speaker encouraged staff to study the laws, rules, and administrative frameworks built over the past century. He suggested that pairing institutional wisdom from former officers with the agility of younger personnel will build stronger systems. Birla expressed confidence that innovation and transparency will help the organization safeguard the nation's valuable defence land.

The speaker lauded civic initiatives for cantonment residents, including schools, healthcare facilities, and computer education for the local community. He mentioned that skill training, water conservation, recycling, and environmental protection are important services provided to the residents. Birla called for sustained engagement with civil society to respond to the evolving needs of these community members. The Armed Forces are affected by these policies because they rely on the operational preparedness provided by land. Civilians are also affected as the organization seeks to protect properties without creating unnecessary disputes.

The articles state that the Defence Estates Organisation is currently entering its second century of institutional existence and operation. This organization has spent the last hundred years building the laws and administrative frameworks that govern defence land management. The agency is tasked with the large scale responsibility of managing over 1.7 million acres of land. It provides various social services to those living in cantonments to maintain a relationship with the civil society. The organization is currently implementing digital upgrades to modernize how it handles its extensive land records.

The organization will now focus on building an institution that combines its rich legacy with a forward-looking vision. Officers and employees were called upon to carry their responsibilities forward with dedication, foresight, and a shared national purpose. The agency aims to strengthen the operational preparedness of the Armed Forces through renewed commitment to public service. The articles leave open how the specific AI solutions will be implemented to curb land encroachments. They do not specify the exact timeline for completing the digital upgrades or the budget for these technologies.

stories.Headline: Anthropic completes largest IPO in history with 1.5 trillion dollar valuation
stories.Summary:
Anthropic completed the biggest initial public offering in history on November 19, 2026. The San Francisco company became the first major artificial intelligence lab to list publicly. This record breaking debut occurred despite recent jitters among some investors regarding the AI sector. The company raised a total of US$81 billion through this massive Wall Street offering. This event marks a superlative debut for the maker of the Claude AI system.

The company offered 980 million shares at a price of US$83 each before trading began. Shares opened at US$111.50, pushing the valuation to US$2.01 trillion by noon Eastern time. Trading closed at US$97.17 per share, resulting in a final first day value of US$1.75 trillion. This exceeds the US$75 billion raised by SpaceX in June and US$26.5 billion by SK Hynix in July. It also beats the US$25.6 billion raised by Saudi Aramco during its 2019 public debut.

CEO Amodei is the person responsible for taking the safety approach of the company public. He decided to proceed with the listing despite growing unease among the general public. The company leadership moved forward even with fears that artificial intelligence might be running amok. They ignored the jitters regarding market volatility and the possibility of an AI bubble. The company now joins a small group of tech giants with thirteen digit wealth figures.

Investors expressed worry about wider risks from the technology and the potential for a market bubble. Some people are affected by the general unease surrounding the risks of artificial intelligence technology. The debut shows the power of the AI boom despite these lingering fears of market volatility. The company is not yet part of the S&P 500 index but joins the trillion dollar club. This club includes eleven companies, with Apple leading at US$5.1 trillion and Microsoft at US$3.8 trillion.

Apple was the first company to pass the trillion dollar threshold back in 2018. Nvidia follows Microsoft with a value of US$3.6 trillion among the current S&P 500 leaders. SpaceX also debuted with a value over one trillion dollars just months before the Anthropic listing. SpaceX ended its first day at US$2.1 trillion, though its cap fell to US$1.95 trillion. One trillion dollars is a thousand times greater than one billion and a million times more than one million.

The market will determine how Anthropic ultimately fares as a publicly traded company over time. The articles leave open whether the current AI boom is actually a bubble that will burst. They do not state if Anthropic will eventually be added to the S&P 500 index. The text does not explain how the company will address the public's growing unease about risks. It remains unclear if the company can maintain its value above the trillion dollar mark.

stories.Headline: US investors flee AI stocks for value shares as Nasdaq falls 5%
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 20, 2026, Wall Street fled from the AI boom into bonds and lower-priced shares outside the tech sector, with the Nasdaq composite dropping over 5% for its third decline of 2% or more that week and its biggest weekly decline since March 2020. Anthropic's sharp decline took it within a whisker of its IPO price before recovering to trade down over 8%, just a day after a record debut that briefly valued the AI lab above $2 trillion. The S&P 500 lost 3.7% for the day, leaving it down 12% from its record high close on October 6 and confirming the benchmark is in a correction, while the pullback left the Nasdaq lower for the year for the first time since April. The retreat partly reflects expectations that high inflation readings will force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in coming months, likely further increasing borrowing costs and compressing valuations, and making Treasuries and so-called value stocks look like a better bet. The median S&P 500 stock now is up 5% in 2026, which beats the 1% year-to-date gain in the S&P 500, an index hobbled of late by a 48% slump in Nvidia and deep declines in other AI stocks, including a 12% drop in Broadcom on Friday.

The S&P 500 value index is up 7% in 2026, compared to a 4% drop in the S&P 500 growth index, putting cautious value investing on track to beat growth for the first time since 2022, when inflation fears sent Wall Street into its worst slump since the 2008 financial crisis. Nvidia, the onetime market leader whose shares have been in free fall since the Nasdaq composite hit its most recent record in October, has shed more than $2.2 trillion of market value. Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera in El Segundo, California, said the prior day's AI IPO was a valuation test and that with the 10-year around 5% and the Fed still hiking, investors are asking how much of the AI story is already priced in. Philip Palumbo, CEO of Palumbo Wealth Management, said Kevin Warsh represents a different approach to monetary policy that has introduced additional uncertainty regarding interest rates, inflation and economic growth, and that markets do not like uncertainty.

Jim Awad, senior managing director at Clearstead Advisors LLC in New York, pointed to questions about the health of the underlying business at Nvidia and said the fundamentals have not deteriorated as much as the stock prices have, viewing it as a normal violent correction in a long-term upward trend in AI spending and in the markets. Lawrence Gillum, chief fixed-income strategist at LPL Financial, called it a classic flight-to-safety trade in which investors concerned about the AI trade move out of those stocks and into Treasury securities, and noted the Treasury market has rallied on the back of any hiccup in the AI trade. Many analysts and portfolio managers said they did not view the AI trade as impaired, and instead said an occasional washout can improve valuations and draw in investors with a longer-term perspective. The flight to value stocks and Treasury notes, which rallied sharply on Friday, is the latest sign of markets grappling with the extent to which a slowing buildout of AI infrastructure will hit US growth, a debate that has been going on all year, if not to this extreme.
