stories.Headline: Researchers find elderly health monitoring AI lacks human centered privacy features
stories.Summary:
An international research team published a comprehensive review in Discover Artificial Intelligence on November 21, 2026. They found that health monitoring AI for the elderly rarely uses human centered privacy features. The researchers examined how algorithmic safeguards align with human centered artificial intelligence dimensions. They discovered that most systems rely on technical data transformations rather than user controls. These systems often fail to involve elderly end users directly in the design process.

The team analyzed forty-five primary studies published between 2020 and 2025 from IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and Web of Science. They retrieved 202 initial records during search cycles in May 2025 and May 2026. Research was concentrated in Asia, with India providing eight studies, China six, and Japan five. The United States and Taiwan contributed three each, while Australia and Canada provided two each. Fourteen other nations and two multi-country partnerships also contributed to the reviewed literature.

The authors stated that nominal transparency is not meaningful human oversight if elderly users cannot comprehend the feedback. They noted that technical explainability must become actionable, low-burden indicators to protect vulnerable populations. The researchers argued that most studies rely on inferred alignment rather than explicit human relevant considerations. They found that ethical awareness is often reduced to mathematical data perturbation or privacy-by-design engineering. The team highlighted that personal autonomy and patient dignity remain largely unexamined in the literature.

Older adults are affected by cognitive, accessibility, and digital literacy barriers when navigating complex privacy settings. Patients are vulnerable to risks from unprocessed audio, video feeds, thermopile arrays, wearable telemetry, and smart-home sensors. The review found that 85 percent of papers designed systems specifically for older populations. These users face threats from cybersecurity breaches and the use of untrusted third-party cloud infrastructure. Only four studies provided explicit documentation of human relevant considerations, but none evaluated them with elderly participants.

Remote health monitoring gathers sensitive physiological, behavioral, and environmental information to reduce frequent in-person medical examinations. Systems focus on Android-based Ambient Assisted Living, smart home care, nursing facility dementia monitoring, and gait analysis. Most models concentrate on prediction and detection tasks, specifically fall detection and activities of daily living. Technical approaches include federated learning, edge AI, and data minimization using LiDAR or millimeter-wave radar. International conferences accounted for 60 percent of the literature, while journals provided 34 percent and preprints 6 percent.

The researchers performed a sensitivity analysis showing that alignment with human values decreases when rigorous standards are enforced. Only one study addressed more than one human centered dimension simultaneously. Future work must address the psychological impact of persistent ambient surveillance on elderly patients. The articles leave open how to effectively translate technical explainability into user-facing controls for seniors. The study was limited to English-language literature, potentially omitting relevant research on responsible artificial intelligence.

stories.Headline: Writer disables all Galaxy AI features for a week and misses only two
stories.Summary:
Shimul Sood, a writer for MakeUseOf, published an article on November 21, 2026, describing a week-long experiment in which she turned off every Galaxy AI feature on her Samsung phone running One UI 9. She undertook the test after hearing chatter that Samsung might someday put some Galaxy AI features behind a paywall, although Samsung has not officially confirmed anything of that kind. She said she had been using a Samsung phone for months and could not immediately say which AI features she would be willing to pay for. Rather than guessing which features she could live without, she disabled all of them and went about her usual routine for an entire week. By the end, she found she wanted to turn only two features back on, and she said neither had anything to do with One UI 9 itself.

The two features she missed were Circle to Search, which she noted is technically a Google feature also available on Samsung phones rather than something Samsung built for Galaxy AI, and Object Eraser, an existing Galaxy AI tool in Samsung's Gallery app. She said Circle to Search proved useful on Pinterest, where she looks for home decor and interior design inspiration, because images often carry no product link and the feature let her circle a lamp or coffee table and find the item or similar alternatives. She said several of her furniture purchases began with a random picture she found on Pinterest, and that going back to manual searching felt unnecessarily tedious. Object Eraser, she wrote, let her remove unwanted elements from photos in the Gallery app instead of discarding a picture or using a third-party editing app, and while results were not always perfect with complicated backgrounds, it handled her usual fixes convincingly. Sood stressed that the experiment was not a criticism of One UI 9 or of how Samsung has implemented AI across its smartphones, but rather a reflection of how she personally uses her phone.

She wrote that she enjoys trying new AI features when they arrive, but very few become part of her routine, and she would rather have a handful of well-thought-out features than a whole suite of tools she tries once and forgets. She also said that what she missed during the week was not necessarily the AI itself but the convenience she had grown accustomed to. Once the week ended, she was in no rush to turn everything back on, and her device felt just as capable without most of its AI features. She concluded that if Samsung ever decides to charge for Galaxy AI, she at least knows where she stands, and that it would take a lot more than a growing list of AI features to convince her to open her wallet. The article does not say that Samsung has announced any pricing, timeline or other change to Galaxy AI, and it gives no further details on what happens next beyond her own intention to keep most features off.

stories.Headline: OpenAI requires prior approval for platforms that give third parties direct access to its models
stories.Summary:
OpenAI began requiring operators of platforms that give third parties direct access to its models to obtain the company's prior review and approval, under a rewritten version of its Usage Policies. The new text carries an effective date of November 20, 2026, and replaces the version that had applied since October 29, 2025. OpenAI announced the changes in a changelog entry dated October 21, 2026, which gave customers 30 days before the rules took hold. The rewrite also adds a section barring the use of OpenAI models and outputs to prepare training material for rival AI systems. The policy body grew from about 830 words in the October 2025 version to about 1,400 words in the new one, according to a PPC Land count of the two texts.

The policy states that operators of a model-access intermediary platform or other service enabling third parties to directly access OpenAI models must obtain prior review and approval. It states that this requirement does not apply solely because an application integrates OpenAI models to power its features or functionality. The rewrite rewrites the child safety rules and widens the human review rule from automated decisions to automated actions, with a definition covering actions, decisions, transactions, submissions, and other steps. Three headed sections are new: Training and developing models, OpenAI-approved use, and Providing access to our models. The training section states its restrictions do not prohibit uses expressly permitted by an applicable Agreement with OpenAI, including any Permitted Exception under the Services Agreement.

The changelog entry states that OpenAI updated its Usage Policies to clarify restrictions on using OpenAI models and outputs to train other models. It states that OpenAI also clarified protections for children and teens and requirements for high-stakes uses, and that the update incorporates existing national security principles and sets out approval requirements for national security and law enforcement uses, as well as for model-access intermediaries. A help center notice titled "We're updating our Usage Policies" lists the same four themes and describes the training language as a clarification of restrictions that already existed rather than a new prohibition. It describes the intermediary rule as an added approval requirement and states that existing agreements and other applicable terms, including any express permissions granted in them, continue to apply. Under the heading "OpenAI-approved use," the policy states that OpenAI may grant specific partners case-by-case exceptions to certain restrictions, naming the factors reviewed as the partner, proposed use, applicable safeguards, and the partner's compliance commitments.

Elena Gurevich, an AI and intellectual property attorney who advises companies on AI governance, wrote in a LinkedIn post on November 20 that OpenAI's updated usage policies kicked in that day. She summarized the intermediary rule as meaning that a business providing customers direct access to OpenAI's models needs OpenAI's approval first, while using the models to power an application's features does not trigger the requirement. She gave OpenRouter, which she described as a platform that streamlines access to multiple AI models from different providers, as an example of the kind of service in scope, and OpenAI's policy names no company. The changelog records that on October 25, 2022, developers no longer needed to wait for approval after submitting as long as they complied with the policies.

It records that on November 9, 2022, OpenAI no longer required developers to register their applications, using a combination of automated and manual methods to monitor for policy violations instead. In August, data drawn from OpenRouter showed AI agents using nearly five times as many tokens per task as human users, with agent usage up about 14 times since February 2026 and more than 85% of agent token spend going to cached prompts. When Anthropic's rewritten Usage Policy took effect on November 12, 2026, it added a prohibition on reselling, proxying or otherwise providing access to Claude through unauthorized means, naming services that route requests through consumer subscriptions or misrepresent which product or client is in use. The training section opens with a rationale stating that capable models must have safeguards proportionate to the risks they pose before they are deployed, and that training another model on OpenAI outputs can transfer capabilities without carrying those safeguards over.

The operative prohibition states that users must not use OpenAI models or their outputs to generate, prepare, select, or supply training material or signals for models intended as alternatives to or substitutes for OpenAI models or services. The policy lists what that covers, including creating or preparing training data, training tasks, rubrics, or reinforcement-learning environments, and providing feedback used in training, including labels, scores, rankings, preferences, rewards, or corrections. Neither the policy page nor the help notice describes how to apply, how long a review takes, whether services already running on November 20 have a transition window, or whether any intermediary has already been approved. The policy gives no application route, form or review time for the access rule.

OpenAI's documents do not state a rationale for the intermediary section. The introductory text remains unchanged word for word, including the statement that OpenAI reserves all rights to withhold access where it reasonably believes it necessary to protect its service or users or anyone else. The privacy section still bars uses such as facial recognition databases built without data subject consent and reads exactly as before. More to follow.

stories.Headline: EU consortium 2DFIRE develops graphene and barium titanate modulators for AI data center optics
stories.Summary:
A new European Union project called 2DFIRE has officially started with seven partners from five European countries, and the Universitat Politècnica de València in Spain coordinates the consortium. The other partners are Lumiphase from Switzerland, KU Leuven from Belgium, Graphenea from Spain, Annealsys from France, Riga Technical University from Latvia and PNO Innovation from Spain. The project has a total budget of €4.92 million, which is about US$5.4 million, and it will run for 36 months. The work is funded by the European Union under the Graphene Flagship. The project aims to develop faster, smaller and more energy-efficient photonic devices for artificial intelligence and high-performance computing.

Its approach is a hybrid platform that combines barium titanate, a ferroelectric material, with two-dimensional materials such as graphene and MoS₂. The core target is electro-optic modulators for optical interconnects in data centers, and the consortium points to electricity use in AI data centers, which it expects to more than double by 2030. According to the project page, the devices are barium titanate coupled-modulated ring modulators, and the target is data transmission at 400 Gbps per wavelength. Besides graphene and MoS₂, the work covers hydrogen-doped indium oxide as a transparent conducting oxide. The aims include thermal phase shifting with low optical losses and new electrode designs that cut driving voltage and energy use.

The partners will work on reliable methods to deposit and transfer the two-dimensional materials and integrate them with barium titanate devices. The project also aims to show that the modulators are compatible with existing semiconductor manufacturing processes and value chains, including 200 mm wafer technology. The consortium says this compatibility should support industrial adoption and strengthen Europe's semiconductor and photonics supply chains. The articles do not name individual people or give direct statements beyond the consortium's published positions on the project page. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the 36-month work plan and the stated aims.

stories.Headline: AI spending concerns and high rates push Dow and Nasdaq sharply lower
stories.Summary:
The Dow Jones 30 and Nasdaq 100 dropped significantly last week as uncertainty in the Middle East, concerns about AI spending and high interest rates continued to pressure US stocks, according to FXEmpire analyst Muhammad Umair. The Dow Jones closed at 48,350.30, down 1.52%, and the S&P 500 closed at 6,954.55, down 3.09%, both on Nov 20 at 21:59 UTC. The US Tech 100 closed at 25,237.55, down 4.68%, on Nov 20 at 21:59 UTC. Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) lost 13.8% and closed at 125.53, down 14.01%, on Nov 20 at 20:59 UTC. Caterpillar Inc. (CAT) dropped 5% and closed at 510.45, down 5.01%, on Nov 20 at 20:59 UTC.

The Nasdaq 100 dropped 9.38% last week to close at 25,237.50 and broke key support at 26,200, which suggests a decline towards 23,500. A break below 23,500 may trigger a deeper decline to the 200-week SMA near 21,000, and the index must recover above 28,000 to initiate the next rally. The Dow Jones broke below key support at 50,000 last week and closed with a loss of 7.24%, which suggests a drop towards 45,000 if it remains below 50,000. A break below 45,000 may trigger a deeper correction towards 38,500, a break below 48,000 may continue momentum towards 45,000, and a break above 50,000 may open the way towards 55,000. The Fed minutes released on 18 November kept the risk of higher interest rates in the near future, and officials discussed the risk of AI spending and rapid growth of related debt.

President Donald Trump said the US is very close to agreement with Mexico after meeting Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum in Asia, and Sheinbaum said talks about vehicles, steel and aluminum have made progress. She mentioned that agreement can be made during the next meeting at the G20 summit in December. The White House mentioned that The Boeing Company (BA) and GE Aerospace have finalized a $12 billion sale to Philippine Airlines for up to 20 Boeing 787 aircraft with GE engines. Boeing (BA) traded at $157.09, down 1.09%, on Nov 21 at 09:44 UTC. Umair wrote that confirmed relief in tariffs may provide clear benefits to industrial sectors of the Dow.

The final University of Michigan survey released on Friday showed consumer sentiment increased to 51.5 in November from 48.0 in October. One-year inflation expectations dropped to 3.7% from 4.7% while long-term expectations eased to 3.3% from 3.5%. Initial jobless claims increased by 1000 to 203,000 and continued claims increased by 70,000 to 1.763 million for the first week of November. The 10-year US Treasury yield dropped to 4.91% on Friday after a strong spike to 5.17% following US consumer inflation data, and the 10-year yield lies at 0.96% above the three-month bill rate.

WTI crude oil closed at 84.9520, up 0.94%, and gold (XAU) closed at 3,538.19, down 1.92%, both on Nov 20 at 21:59 UTC. The weekly Nasdaq 100 chart shows a cup and handle formation from November 2021 to November 2023, and the RSI is approaching oversold levels as the index drops towards 23,500. The daily chart shows a broadening wedge pattern from June 2026, and the index broke the 200-day SMA at 28,000 and dropped 4.63% on Friday. The Dow Jones long-term support at 38,500 is defined by an ascending broadening wedge pattern from January 2024, and 45,000 represents the neckline of an inverted head and shoulders pattern formed from December 2024 to August 2025.

Iran may make the US blockade of Iranian ports as difficult as possible with the hope that the US will withdraw, and shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz are shrinking. The recent selloff in WTI oil, gold and US stocks may be the symptom of shrinking liquidity. Umair wrote that the Nasdaq 100 and Dow Jones remain under extreme pressure in the short term and that a lasting recovery needs strong confidence in corporate profits and returns from AI investment. He wrote that concerns about profitability from AI spending outweigh the benefits of cheaper long-term funding.

The articles leave open whether the US-Mexico agreement will be announced and whether the Fed will raise rates in December. stories.Headline: GlobalWafers ramps new 12 inch fabs in Texas, Italy and Japan as retail investors watch
stories.Summary:
Retail investors began watching GlobalWafers after panic selling hit Nvidia and other AI leaders on November 21, 2026. This market shift followed the exit of Jensen Huang, which turned previous excitement into doubt for many investors. The company provides silicon wafers to chip manufacturers and offers upstream exposure to data center and AI demand. GlobalWafers operates across the Americas, Europe, Northeast Asia, and other Asian regions to serve its global customers. It currently holds a market capitalization of NT$233.2 billion according to the provided financial data.

The company generates NT$58.4 billion from its Semiconductor Business Group and NT$0.2 billion from its Renewable Energy operations. It is currently moving its global capacity buildout from construction into qualification and ramp at new 12 inch fabs. These new facilities are located in Texas, Italy, and Japan to expand the company's overall production capabilities. Phase 1 tool installation is nearly complete in Texas, while the Italy line has achieved automotive grade certification. The facility in Utsunomiya, Japan, has already turned profitable and is currently operating with high utilization.

Analysts from Simply Wall St are responsible for the narrative regarding the company's global expansion and earnings potential. They stated that the company is transitioning its capacity buildout into the qualification and ramp phase for new fabs. These analysts link the company's cost base and earnings potential to its strategic expansion in three different countries. They believe the current progress in Texas, Italy, and Japan supports the company's growth in the semiconductor market. The report suggests that these developments are core threads linking the company's global capacity and future success.

The report notes that retail investors are watching the stock as a potential opportunity after recent market pullbacks. These investors are affected by the broader volatility in AI chip stocks following the leadership change at Nvidia. The analysis suggests that solid businesses can move from being crowded to ignored when market expectations reset. Some investors may see the current weakness as a signal of mispricing rather than permanent damage to the business. The text indicates that these investors are seeking established leaders in the AI and semiconductor sectors.

GlobalWafers is described as a large and profitable wafer producer tied into broader semiconductor spending and AI demand. The company's business model relies on supplying the essential silicon wafers needed by chip manufacturers worldwide. It has diversified its sales across multiple continents to mitigate risks and capture various regional market opportunities. The company's current financial standing includes significant revenue from its primary semiconductor business group. This background positions the firm as a key upstream player in the global AI hardware supply chain.

The company will continue the ramp of its new 12 inch fabs in Texas, Italy, and Japan. Future success depends on how quickly these new lines fill and the pricing the company can achieve. The articles leave open whether unseen pressures will change the speed of utilization for these new facilities. It remains unclear how the wafer mix and subsidies will reshape the company's long term financial story. Investors must wait to see if the current ramp speed leads to lasting profitability and margin growth.

stories.Headline: Benton Harbor approves City Detect AI system to scan for code violations
stories.Summary:
Benton Harbor City Commissioners approved a contract at their regular meeting this past week that will allow the city to use a more automated method of detecting code violations citywide, according to News/Talk/Sports 94.9 WSJM. The service, called City Detect, is offered to municipalities and uses vehicle-mounted cameras and artificial intelligence to spot things like building violations and illegal dumping. The department of public safety says the camera would be mounted on a city code compliance truck to conduct inspections. Commissioners amended the resolution approving the contract by adding a requirement that the Public Safety Committee receive regular reports on the program's results, and it was then approved five to three with Mayor Marcus Muhammad not present.

The contract will cost $55,000 per year and will be paid with Community Development Block Grant funds, and commissioners will be asked to renew it yearly. Public Safety told commissioners that City Detect conducted a demonstration for the inspection department, scanning 896 parcels in just a half hour and identifying issues like tall grass, sidewalk problems, boarded up windows, and trash. City Manager Alex Little said the city is not in a position to hire enough people to handle all these inspections, but technology like City Detect can help. Commissioner Sharon Henderson said the city's inspection department will only use City Detect as a first step when issuing potential citations, and that staff get a photograph and review the information rather than writing a ticket immediately.

Commissioner Juanita Henry took issue with the program, saying residents should not be burdened with surprise tickets and little human oversight, and she said she knows AI can do a lot of things but does not think this will work out well for residents because there is no human in it. Henderson said inspectors are still looking at what has been sent to them to make sure, and are not just giving people a ticket based on the system. Henry also said it is all about policy. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the yearly renewal request and the regular reports to the Public Safety Committee.

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook warned against delaying interest rate hikes before an expected increase in December. Governor Michael S. Barr stated that on-balance-sheet debt for the seven largest AI firms could exceed 800 billion dollars by the end of the year. The current downturn follows a period of extreme volatility for companies like DigitalOcean, which reached a 52-week high of 181.29 dollars in June 2026. stories.Headline: Apple adds non-AI features to iOS 27 including better AutoMix and Find My redesign
stories.Summary:
Apple released iOS 27 in September 2026, and while the new Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features drew most of the attention, the update also brought a long list of non-AI changes that 9to5Mac editor Chance Miller highlighted in a piece published on November 21, 2026. In the Music app, Apple updated AutoMix with new transitions that Miller described as noticeably better and more immersive than the version that launched in iOS 26. The Photos app now offers full-resolution sharing in iCloud Shared Albums, and it also lets users save a specific video frame as a photo without taking a manual screenshot. The Clock app gained an independent alarm volume option found in Settings under Sounds & Haptics, so alarms and timers no longer have to match the ringtone volume.

The Home Screen adds an all-new extra-large widget size, including full-screen widgets for apps like Music, Photos, Weather and Calendar, and users can now swipe away the Now Playing widget from the Lock Screen. On the Lock Screen, the clock can be moved to the top widget row so it no longer covers the wallpaper. The Apple Pay checkout flow was significantly overhauled to make switching between payment cards easier, and landscape support arrived in more apps, including Music, Reminders and Weather. The Find My app has a new design with more flexible sharing options that show more specific location information without tapping on a specific person, and a built-in paste shortcut now appears above the keyboard in the next text field after something is copied. CarPlay also gained an audio scrubber for skipping to different parts of a song or podcast on the car's display.

Miller, the editor-in-chief of 9to5Mac who also hosts the site's Daily and Happy Hour podcasts, wrote that he had come to really enjoy these features and called the landscape support great as someone who keeps his iPhone docked at his desk all day. He said he was a big fan of the initial AutoMix in iOS 26 and finds the new transitions better, and he singled out the Find My redesign for showing more specific location information without extra taps. He closed by asking readers to share their own favorite non-AI features in the comments. The article does not say what happens next beyond that invitation.

stories.Headline: US export rules restrict a wider range of chips including those for consumer electronics
stories.Summary:
The United States government introduced tighter export controls on Thursday, November 20, 2026, to restrict the flow of semiconductor technology. Industry insiders report that these new rules are causing a much wider disruption across the global supply chain than was first anticipated. The restrictions are not limited to advanced artificial intelligence chips but also impact system on chips used in common consumer electronics. Consequently, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. has already suspended some of its shipments to various clients.

These updated regulations affect a diverse range of developers, including those who are not based in China and do not create AI hardware. The rules target mobile and everyday consumer applications, which forces companies to change how they source and distribute their semiconductor components. Because the world's largest contract chipmaker is involved, the changes impact major customers like Nvidia who rely on leading-edge processors. Every developer using these specific types of integrated circuits must now navigate these stricter American trade requirements.

Multiple industry executives told Nikkei Asia that the scope of these controls is unexpectedly broad and damaging to the supply chain. They expressed concern that the rules extend far beyond the intended targets of high-end AI technology to hit general electronics. These leaders believe the current environment creates significant uncertainty for developers who were previously unaffected by trade wars. They warned that the sudden suspension of shipments could lead to larger shortages of essential components for mobile devices.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike discusses acquiring Zscaler to expand AI-powered cybersecurity defenses
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. is in talks to acquire Zscaler Inc. according to a Bloomberg report on Friday, November 21, 2026. This potential combination would be one of the largest deals in the cybersecurity industry. The two companies are discussing a deal that could come together soon. This move follows a wave of multibillion-dollar takeovers in the security market. These companies are racing to expand defenses against sophisticated attacks powered by artificial intelligence.

The deal involves Austin, Texas-based CrowdStrike and Santa Clara, California-based Zscaler in the 244 billion dollar security market. Zscaler had a market value of 32 billion dollars at the end of regular trading Friday. CrowdStrike has a market capitalization of around 235 billion dollars. Zscaler reached record revenue of 3.35 billion dollars in fiscal 2026 but has not turned an annual profit since 2018. Zscaler serves 11,000 customers in over 185 countries, including more than half of the Fortune 500.

People familiar with the matter said deliberations are ongoing and a transaction is not certain. These sources asked not to be identified because the information is confidential. Representatives for CrowdStrike and Zscaler did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The report caused Zscaler shares to rise about 16 percent after the close of trading. The deal would allow CrowdStrike to monitor threats across more parts of a company's technology infrastructure.

Cloudflare co-founder Matthew Prince said in June that AI agent traffic surpassed human internet traffic for the first time. Businesses are grappling with risks from AI-enabled attacks, benefiting providers like Palo Alto Networks Inc. and Cloudflare Inc. Zscaler's cloud-based products replace traditional VPNs from companies like Citrix and Ivanti Inc. that suspected Chinese hackers have targeted. The "SaaSpocalypse" fear suggests AI tools could allow competitors to recreate software services more cheaply. This threatens the business models of established providers.

CrowdStrike's Falcon product had a botched software update in 2024 that triggered a global IT meltdown. Alphabet Inc. bought Wiz for 32 billion dollars last year, and ServiceNow Inc. bought Armis for 7.75 billion dollars in December. Palo Alto Networks took over CyberArk for 25 billion dollars in February and bought Applied Compute for 4.5 billion dollars this month. Recent US outages affected Microsoft Corp., JPMorgan Chase & Co., United Airlines, and the National Security Agency. Gartner Inc. projects global information security spending will grow nearly 12 percent this year.

The companies will determine if these ongoing deliberations result in a final transaction. A combination would give CrowdStrike a broader role in defending corporate networks and applications. The deal would accelerate a shift toward fewer companies protecting more of the world's computers. The articles do not state when a final decision will be reached. They also do not provide a specific purchase price for the potential acquisition.

stories.Headline: Governor Kathy Hochul pauses a proposed AI data center project in Niagara Falls
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul paused a proposed artificial intelligence data center project in Niagara Falls. She signed an executive order on July 14, 2026, to freeze certain permits. This action affects the Niagara Digital Campus proposed by Niagara Falls Redevelopment. The developer first proposed this specific data center project back in 2021. The freeze on state environmental permits can last for up to one year.

The project requires a state air permit for backup diesel generators and costs 1.5 billion dollars. It involves nine buildings using 140 megawatts near the Robert Moses plant. The Milstein family owns Niagara Falls Redevelopment, which wants to build on vacant South End land. National Grid confirmed in 2023 that transmission lines could accommodate the 140 megawatts. The developer requested an interconnection from the New York Independent System Operator in April 2024.

Governor Hochul said the pause allows the state to study effects on water and electric bills. She stated that developers should pay for the infrastructure they require rather than households. Niagara Falls Redevelopment says it will pay for its own grid upgrades and substation. The state council of building trades urged the governor not to adopt the freeze. A consultant projects 675 annual construction jobs and 550 permanent positions for the campus.

Opponents of the project expressed worries about noise, water use, and higher electric bills. Residents across the country have fought data centers over water and power bills. A noise study by the developer concluded sound levels at nearby residences would not increase. The builder, Urbacon, designs cooling systems that use little or no water for the facility. The project would use city sewers and water, which the sewer district can accommodate.

China added 543 gigawatts of generating capacity in 2025, mostly through wind and solar power. The U.S. faces a projected 44 gigawatt power shortfall for data centers by 2028. In early 2026, local opposition delayed 75 American data center projects worth 130 billion dollars. China's data centers pay about 3 cents per kilowatt hour, which is one third of American prices. Stanford University found American and Chinese chatbots were nearly equal by March 2026.

The State Legislature passed the Responsible Data Center Development Act to pause permits for 20 megawatts. Governor Hochul has until December 31 to act on this broader legislative restriction. The project's target date for interconnection was June 2027, but the current freeze creates delays. The articles leave open whether the project will move to Virginia, Texas, or Ohio. It remains undecided if the state will impose conditions or reject the project entirely.

stories.Headline: Seven senators question whether Meta's $6.6 billion AI data center R&D tax credits qualify under Section 41
stories.Summary:
A New York Times article has renewed attention on the tax credits that Meta claimed for its artificial intelligence data centers, according to a report published by Accounting Today on November 20, 2026. In a letter dated October 14, 2026, Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden of Oregon and six other senators said Meta claimed about $6.6 billion in federal research and development tax credits between 2023 and 2025. The senators questioned whether Meta described its AI data centers as experimental pilot models in those claims and asked the company for a breakdown of the credits tied to the data centers. The inquiry highlights two separate questions, which are whether the development activities count as qualified research and whether the claimed expenditures count as qualified research expenditures for the credit. Treasury Regulation 1.174-2(a)(4) defines a pilot model as any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty about the product during its development or improvement.

The rules say production costs paid or incurred after the uncertainty is eliminated are not eligible, and a pilot model must involve genuine uncertainty in the design that the model is needed to resolve. Meeting that definition does not by itself satisfy Section 41 of the tax code, which sets additional requirements for the credit and for eligible expenses. Only wages, supplies, computer leasing and contractor costs tied to qualifying research activities can be claimed as qualified research expenses. Section 41(b)(2)(C) excludes land, improvements to land and property subject to depreciation from the definition of qualified supplies, so a taxpayer cannot turn depreciable equipment into qualified supplies by calling it experimental or by not claiming depreciation on it.

For Meta's data centers, the treatment of purchased servers, chips and other equipment is a central issue, because using equipment for qualified research does not by itself make its purchase price a qualified supply expense. Meta asserts that uncertainty existed in the data centers and that it could only be resolved by building a physical data center and testing it. To support that claim, Meta would need to show the technical uncertainty that existed before the data center was built and how building it resolved that uncertainty. The article says taxpayers claiming pilot model costs should build a record that connects the technical work to the claimed expenditures, including initial design questions, alternative designs, simulation results, test plans, test findings and engineering designs.

Cost records for employee activities, materials and contractor charges should be traceable to the relevant development work and should complement the technical evidence. The article, written by David Seibel, a senior manager in the research and development tax credit practice at Indianapolis-based McGuire Sponsel, says the credit is one of the most fact-intensive and subjective areas of tax law. It says the questions raised by the Meta claim extend well beyond AI infrastructure, because manufacturers, equipment developers and other businesses face similar challenges in showing why a model was built, how its development involved experimentation and which costs the credit permits. The articles do not say what happens next in the Senate inquiry or whether Meta has responded to the senators' request.

stories.Headline: Luca Guadagnino says Altman has guns as Artificial opens Christmas Day
stories.Summary:
Neon is releasing Luca Guadagnino's film Artificial, about OpenAI co-founders Sam Altman, Ilya Sutskever and Elon Musk, on Christmas Day, 2026. The film premiered at the New York Film Festival and the BFI London Film Fest before its theatrical release. Deadline published its Crew Call podcast interview with Guadagnino on November 21, 2026. The film stars Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman, Monica Barbaro as Mira Murati and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever. Artificial currently holds a 95% fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes.

The film opens limited on Christmas Day, a date Deadline calls perfect for a sophisticated adult skewing awards contender. Amazon MGM Studios originally backed the movie but exited out of fear of OpenAI, because Amazon has a $50 billion investment in the Altman non-profit. CAA screened the project for Neon, which Guadagnino says was first and front and center in its passion to take over. The Simon Rich script was shot outside Altman's house in San Francisco. Dario Amodei's Anthropic went public earlier this week creating a $1.18 trillion company, with shares falling from a $111 day-of-market price to $88.91 EOD Friday.

Altman told the Vanity Fair podcast he "did not" coerce Amazon to drop Artificial, adding "I don't know anyone else who did" and "I didn't speak to Jeff Bezos." Altman said he felt like he was in a weird glitch or a simulation when he saw Garfield dressed exactly like him with the same backpack, and emphasized that Garfield "did walk like me." Altman said of the trailer, "I don't think they're going for accuracy," and called the bunker loaded with guns "an example of an inaccuracy," saying "There's no bunker with firearms on the wall." Altman admitted "I have a survivalist mindset" but said "I don't have a setup that is depicted in that trailer."

Guadagnino told Deadline, "I have validated the validating information that has been vetted: He does have guns." Guadagnino said "We were very careful that everything that was in the movie had to be approved legally," and that "the truth in this case is more extraordinary than any fiction." On Amazon exiting, Guadagnino said "I was cool because I like disruptions, very much," and called the decision to let the movie find another home "truly honorable." Guadagnino said of speculation that no studio wanted the movie, "I like to think that there was the need (by the media) to fill blank pages with nothing."

On AI as a doomsday threat, Guadagnino told Deadline, "I don't have trust and I don't have faith in humans." Guadagnino's suspicions stem from growing up during the Cold War, and he remembers "very well in 1985 when Chernobyl happened." Deadline contrasts Artificial with Sony's recent theatrical release The Social Reckoning, which it says arguably didn't resonate with the current tech era. Deadline notes the film arrives as people fear the technology will end us, whether in regards to existence or financial livelihoods.

Deadline says there has been zero ill will from Altman or OpenAI about the film, unlike the Facebook camp when The Social Network was released in 2010. Deadline cites concerns about AI including a Chatbot being at the center of 16-year old Adam Raine's suicide, and AI trespassing and impostering another company's security space. The Crew Call episode also covers why Andrew Garfield was right to play Altman and Altman's sincerity about creating guardrails for the technology. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Council of Europe trains 20 local authority teams to govern AI responsibly
stories.Summary:
The Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe organised the first-ever Academy on responsible AI governance at local level, held in Paris from 17 to 19 November 2026. Twenty teams from local and regional authorities, selected in an open call, took part in the academy. The teams came from 18 municipalities and two counties, spanning the continent from Diyarbakır in Türkiye to Fingal in Ireland. The academy was organised by the Centre of expertise for multilevel governance (CEMG) at the Congress, in partnership with the Council of Europe's Steering Committee for new and emerging digital technologies (CDNET). It put into practice the Congress's call to strengthen local and regional authorities' capacity to use and manage AI.

Participants were provided with practical tools for responsible AI governance, based on the Council of Europe's HUDERIA methodology for assessing the impact of AI systems. Over three days, participants applied the methodology to a fictional AI-supported public consultation, identifying and analysing risks, mapping stakeholders and developing mitigation measures. The programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services on everyone they serve, from a human-rights, democracy and rule-of-law perspective. The participating authorities were Amaroussion (Greece), Bălți (Republic of Moldova), Bergen (Norway), Bitola (North Macedonia), City of Arezzo (Italy), City of Vigo (Spain), Diyarbakır (Türkiye), Fingal County (Ireland), Harghita County (Romania), Kutaisi (Georgia), London Borough of Camden (United Kingdom), Lviv (Ukraine), Nõo (Estonia), Resen (North Macedonia), Rivne (Ukraine), Shkodër (Albania), Szentendre (Hungary), Turnišče (Slovenia), Valongo (Portugal), and Ventspils Education Board (Latvia). The academy was also an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme, leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit.

Opening the discussions, Congress co-rapporteur on AI Annika Vaikla (Estonia, ILDG), Deputy Mayor of Viimsi, urged authorities to use AI to give public servants more time for people, while keeping people in control. She called for AI literacy among political leaders, staff and citizens. She also called for smaller municipalities to have access to shared expertise. Deputy Mayor Vaikla is co-rapporteur for the 2026 Congress report on strengthening the capacities of local and regional authorities in the use of artificial intelligence. The articles give no further remarks from her.

The articles state that local and regional authorities are on the frontline of the AI revolution in Europe's town halls. Faced with shrinking budgets, they see real potential in efficiency gains promised by AI. They also face hard questions such as planning applications for data centres and democratic accountability for decisions informed by AI. The articles say they lack capacity in understanding and governing AI technologies, particularly smaller municipalities.

The academy served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe and was held in support of the implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence. The articles give no further background beyond the academy's organisation and aims. They state that artificial intelligence is already in Europe's town halls. They describe the academy as the first-ever of its kind at local level.

They state that the twenty teams were selected in an open call. They state that the programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services. They give no further details on the Congress report or the Framework Convention. The articles state that the academy was an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme, leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit.

They state that it was held in support of the implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence. They state that it served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe. They give no further details on what follows the academy. They leave open what the participating authorities will do next and what the 2026 Congress report will contain.

stories.Headline: One engineer runs an AI podcast network producing over 300 sports shows daily for about 5 cents
stories.Summary:
Beatline Sports, an AI-generated podcast network, launched in August and began flooding the market with daily episodes covering dozens of professional and college teams, but the shows drew little attention until their heavy use of keywords gave them traction on Apple and Spotify's search functions in November 2026, according to a Boston.com column by Chad Finn. The podcasts are hosted by AI voices trained on basic facts about a given team, and the network's graphics look suspiciously like those of the Locked On Podcast Network. A New York-based engineer named Ibnul Jaif Farabi claimed on X.com that Beatline Sports is his creation, writing that one person is producing more than 300 sports podcasts daily using custom models and agents running on CPU only. Finn listened to part of a Friday Patriots episode hosted by voices called Monica and Frank, and he wrote that the product is so lousy that even intentional promotion would not help it. The network's output requires no human hosts, as the episodes are described as an AI reading of a script of keywords about a real team rather than an actual conversation.

Farabi wrote that the whole operation costs him about 5 cents daily, a figure Finn responded to by suggesting Farabi is getting robbed. Finn noted that on a phony Jets podcast, edge rusher Will McDonald IV was referred to as Will McDonald Four, and he said he hoped for something similarly unintentionally funny on the Patriots episode but found no such luck. In the snippet Finn quoted, Monica said the offense was completely suffocated against Detroit and asked whether the team is competitive or just surviving on momentum and hope, while Frank said he felt cautious after a 35-10 loss to the Lions and that without Drake Maye at full health the ceiling is lower than most people will want to admit. Farabi is the person responsible for the network, and in his X.com post he told doubters to question their profession and said the choice is to compete or perish. Finn wrote that the podcasts entirely miss why people enjoy podcasts in the first place, which he described as hearing a conversation with knowledgeable and often humorous people listeners enjoy spending time with.

He added that Monica and Frank will never make listeners wish they were part of the conversation because it is not a conversation at all. Finn wrote that he worries about what happens when AI-generated content starts to look decent and people can no longer tell what is authentic, though he said these Beatline pods are fortunately not that. In separate media news, a Deadline report cited in the column said ESPN and ESPN2 dropped from 61 million pay-TV subscribers in 2025 to 54 million this year, down from a peak of more than 100 million fifteen years ago. Finn attributed the decline mostly to pay-TV subscriber losses across the board rather than to programming decisions. He also answered a reader question about Boston sports radio shows discussing the Celtics, ranking WEEI's Jones and Keefe and The Sports Hub's Zolak and Bertrand as the top two midday shows and Felger and Mazz at the bottom.

stories.Headline: AI selloff creates new opportunities for Enablence, CETC Chips and Aeva
stories.Summary:
Sasha Jovanovic wrote an article on November 21, 2026, about a sharp repricing of artificial intelligence and semiconductor stocks. This selloff caused Nvidia to drop about 48 percent from its peak and the SOXX ETF to fall over 40 percent. The Nasdaq also experienced its roughest week since 2020 during this period of market volatility. This reset punished crowded trades while creating new opportunities for investors who felt they arrived too late. The author identified several stocks that could benefit from this specific shift in market sentiment.

Enablence Technologies, listed as TSXV:ENA, has a market cap of CA$130 million and designs silicon based optical chips. The company generates about 8 million dollars, with roughly 7 million dollars coming from customers in Asia Pacific. CETC Chips Technology, listed as SHSE:600877, has a market cap of CN¥10.9b and makes analog semiconductor chips. Aeva Technologies, listed as NasdaqGS:AEVA, has a market cap of US$669 million and sells 4D LiDAR sensors. Aeva reports about US$24.7 million from industrial automation and controls across North America, EMEA, and Asia.

The author states that Enablence Technologies is positioned in the core infrastructure of the AI trade. This company supplies planar light wave circuits and multiplexers used in high speed optical links for hyperscale computing. Regarding CETC Chips Technology, the author notes that the company provides exposure through chips used in satellite links. The author explains that CETC Chips Technology has seen profitability turn weak and earnings shift to a loss. These details help professionals map risks and potential upside before market sentiment changes again.

A bearish analyst from Simply Wall St focused on the high risk nature of Aeva Technologies. This analyst noted that Aeva has a current cash burn of more than US$28 million per quarter. The analyst warned that any slip in achieving planned 2027 initial volumes could leave this burn unsupported. Furthermore, the analyst mentioned a 2028 ramp to multiple millions of units as a critical future goal. These factors make the company sensitive to changes in confidence and hedging flows.

Enablence Technologies has a fragile balance sheet and small revenue, though its products tie directly to AI infrastructure. CETC Chips Technology produces analog chips for power management, smart devices, communications, and navigation. Aeva Technologies uses FMCW based sensors and autonomy software to track auto tech and AI sentiment. Aeva also launched an optical connectivity business through a joint development agreement targeting a major hyperscaler. These companies represent a sample of 37 listed products tied to semiconductor short or inverse exposure.

Investors may now use a Global AI and Semiconductor Short/Inverse Exposure screener to find high conviction trades. The articles leave open whether Aeva Technologies can successfully meet its volume targets for 2027 and 2028. It remains uncertain if Enablence Technologies can overcome its fragile balance sheet and small revenue streams. The text does not state if CETC Chips Technology will return to profitability after its recent losses. Future movements depend on whether sentiment turns faster than expected for these specific hardware and software operators.

stories.Headline: RingCentral CFO says AI products drive growth as paid AI ARR doubles
stories.Summary:
RingCentral Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Agarwal spoke at an RBC conference, and MarketBeat reported the remarks on Saturday, November 21, 2026, describing a strategy centered on an AI customer engagement platform. He said the platform handles communications between people and increasingly between people and AI. He said the company expects AI to address routine inquiries and automate workflows, with humans stepping in when more judgment or expertise is required. He said the core business is durable and that RingCentral goes into the base to address new sales with more AI products. The conference interviewer said RingCentral AI annual recurring revenue represented about 15% of total ARR and had doubled year over year.

The measure covers customers using at least one paid AI-native product, and Agarwal said it helps the company track paid AI adoption within its customer base. RingCentral's AIR product has more than 22,000 customers, while ACE has nearly 7,000, Agarwal said. The interviewer said the Customer Engagement Bundle had 14,000 paying customers, up 50% sequentially. Agarwal said RingCentral's overall gross margin is 80%, with AI product gross margins close to that level. He identified approximately 40 billion voice minutes flowing through the platform annually as a competitive asset.

Agarwal said RingCentral is spending more than $250 million on AI investments and manages AI costs through model orchestration, inference efficiency and infrastructure efficiency. He said the company uses multiple frontier models and routes work to lower-cost models, and could evaluate open-source models over time for additional cost efficiencies. He said RingCentral sells through direct representatives, in-product discovery, a network of 16,000 partners and global service carriers. He corrected the interviewer's suggestion that about half of AI ARR comes through the partner channel, saying RingCentral had not disclosed that mix. He said an expanded partnership with NiCE gives RingCentral greater access to enterprise customers as NiCE resells its RingEX product.

Agarwal described RingCentral's enterprise business as close to $1 billion, with a generally stable demand environment, win rates and retention. He said the company continues to face comparisons with COVID-era contracts that have undergone seat and pricing rationalization and expects to move past those comparisons into the first half of next year. He declined to provide guidance for next year. He said AI products are growing from a smaller base and could contribute more to overall growth as their share of the business increases. Based on its latest guidance, he said the company expects margin expansion of about 200 basis points this year.

Agarwal said stock-based compensation is declining by about 200 basis points, supported by discipline in new share grants and the fading impact of older grants. He said RingCentral has previously stated a longer-term goal of bringing stock-based compensation to 3% to 4%. Asked about potential AI-related pressure on customer seat counts, he said RingCentral is not seeing much seat rationalization among small businesses, though it sees some at the high end of the enterprise market following headcount actions. He said selling additional products to existing customers can help offset that pressure. He said AIR, which addresses missed calls, has initially found traction with small businesses but is also being sold to larger customers.

Agarwal said AIR Pro is designed for more complex workflows, using voice AI to understand intent and take actions before handing interactions to a human when needed. He said CEB targets businesses whose employees communicate with customers but do not have a dedicated contact center, and that once customers adopt it they can also buy AIR to address missed calls and add conversational intelligence. He cited a national fitness operator that used ACE to identify the reasons customers were calling before buying AIR to automate recurring inquiries. He said Destination Pet, an existing RingCentral customer, similarly used ACE to identify call drivers and then bought AIR Pro. He said customers can use NiCE's CXone for more complex deployments or RingCentral's RingCX for simpler contact center needs.

Articles.Title: RingCentral Bets on AI Growth as Paid AI ARR Doubles and Margins Hold Firm

stories.Headline: Diamond Restaurant bars AI-generated band flyers to prioritize human artists
stories.Summary:
Diamond Restaurant in Plaza Midwood is refusing to accept AI-generated flyers from bands performing at the venue, saying human creativity should come first. The Charlotte restaurant announced the policy, and the announcement quickly took off online, shared hundreds of times. Employee Ryan Armstrong said everybody came to the conclusion that they wanted to support local artists. He said most of these communities do not want the data centers and the great proliferation of construction using our resources. The policy starts on Sunday, November 22.

The venue's policy applies to bands promoting shows at the restaurant. Owners say they are not telling people what to think about AI, but they want to use their platform to support local artists, musicians and designers who create the work themselves. Armstrong said they thought real artists should be prioritized over this particular function of AI. Charlotte leaders continue a moratorium on new data center development through next October, giving the city more time to study their impact on neighborhoods, natural resources and infrastructure.

Armstrong, who is part of a band named Sand Dollar Starship, said as an artist himself he understands that new tools develop all the time. He said that in the case of AI, we are seeing the development of it abuse artists and intellectual property of many different contributors. Charlotte City Council member Dimple Ajmera said during the October meeting that in the next 11 months, we will have an opportunity to put guardrails in place. She said those guardrails would protect our residents, our neighborhoods and our water and the electricity grid.

The announcement was shared hundreds of times online after the restaurant took its stand. The policy affects bands promoting shows at the restaurant, along with the local artists, musicians and designers the owners say they want to support. Charlotte leaders are studying the impact of data centers on neighborhoods, natural resources and infrastructure during the moratorium. The restaurant's owners say their biggest concern is the effect AI is having on work created by real artists. The policy applies to bands promoting shows at the restaurant starting Sunday, November 22.

The articles say communities across the country are wrestling with the rise of AI. They say Charlotte leaders continue a moratorium on new data center development through next October. They say the moratorium gives the city more time to study the impact of data centers on neighborhoods, natural resources and infrastructure. Ajmera's October meeting remarks came during that moratorium. The articles give no further background on the restaurant or the bands.

The policy starts on Sunday, November 22, and applies to bands promoting shows at the restaurant. The articles do not say how the restaurant will enforce the policy or what happens to bands that submit AI-generated flyers. They do not say how long the policy will last. stories.Headline: Etsy sellers in Canada pull products as Etsy adds AI training to its terms
stories.Summary:
Some Etsy sellers across Canada are removing their products from the platform after the company added language about artificial intelligence model training to its updated terms and agreements. Tsuki Matsuba, a Vancouver-based seller of custom stationery, is pulling her products from Etsy ahead of the new policy, which the company is rolling out next month. Matsuba told CBC News that the change felt like a kick in the teeth for sellers like her. The update to the company's terms and agreements takes effect on Dec. 16 and includes a line allowing Etsy, its third party partners and vendors to use sellers' content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.

The policy change requires sellers who remain on the platform to accept that their content may be used for AI training, and some shop owners are responding by removing their products and original artwork. Artist Tina Nawrocki, who is based in Ottawa, wrote on X that she is closing down her Etsy shop because of what she called the company's new predatory AI practices. The Halifax-based artist known as The Calendork announced it has removed all artwork from its Etsy shop while remaining open, citing the new insane AI policies. Matsuba, who worked in animation for seven years before losing her job, said AI was one of the major factors in that loss, and she fears shop owners are being forced to choose between earning holiday income and staying on the platform under terms that allow their content to be used for AI training.

Etsy's head of customer operations, James Ossman, said in a statement that respecting its sellers' work is central to the way Etsy runs its business. He said sellers' creative work belongs to them, and that Etsy does not use that work to train AI models designed to copy their original work or replace their creativity. Ossman said the company plans to continue discussing the policy change with sellers to clarify what it means and its intent in the terms, and he also said the company should have done more to communicate the changes coming with the updated policies. Matsuba said those discussions will not change her decision to stop selling her products on the platform, because her business is completely AI free and she does not want to participate in developing AI further.

The backlash comes as KPMG reported in 2025 that 88 per cent of tech executives surveyed believe tech companies that embrace AI will develop a competitive edge over those who do not. The same report showed that 68 per cent of respondents expect a moderate to very high return on investment related to AI investments of 10 per cent or more. Etsy has faced criticism on other fronts as well, including its ban on the sale of fur, which the CBC reported may affect Indigenous artisans most. The company says it will keep talking with sellers about the terms, while sellers like Matsuba have already decided to leave before the Dec. 16 date arrives.

Articles.Title: Etsy faces backlash over including AI model training in new policy update

stories.Headline: Harvard's Yu presents CHIEF pathology AI model for bladder cancer analysis
stories.Summary:
Kun-Hsing Yu, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, discussed foundation AI models for pathology image analysis in bladder cancer at the BCAN Think Tank annual meeting, in a UroToday video posted on November 22, 2026. He described his lab's CHIEF model, which was trained on more than 15 million pathology image patches plus an additional 60,000 hosted images from 19 different anatomical sites. The model aligns image findings with text annotations from pathology reports using the CLIP method first proposed by OpenAI. Yu said the model was evaluated for making cancer diagnosis, predicting molecular profiles and survival prediction. He spoke with Ashish Kamat, a urologic oncologist in Houston, Texas, and a professor of urology at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

Yu said a foundation model is a large general-purpose machine learning model trained on broad and diverse data that can be adopted to a wide range of downstream tasks. He cited GPT, Gemini and Claude as families of foundation models developed using vast amounts of human-generated text and image. He said the CHIEF model extracts detailed features from individual image regions and aggregates them into a patient-level representation to capture simple-level patterns. He said several related models using similar approaches have appeared since CHIEF's publication, each with different training data, architectures and combinations of image and language information. He said imaging-based models capture only one dimension of a patient's disease, and that pathology slides, radiology scans, genomic and transcriptomic profiles, medical records, treatment regimen and family history are among the data included in multimodal models.

Yu argued that true clinical impact requires integrating pathology with radiology, genomic, transcriptomic and clinical record data into multimodal models rather than imaging alone. He said this multimodal framework enables discovery of new biomarkers, improves patient prediction and supports translation of insights into clinical care. In bladder cancer specifically, he said this means more accurate risk stratification, better prediction of recurrence and treatment response, and more personalized treatment selection. He said clinical deployment must minimize clicks and cognitive burden rather than add them, and should make clear when a clinician is expected to act on the output or override it. He said accountability requires defining who owns the final clinical decision and monitoring performance shift and unintended harms vigorously after deployment, with a clear process for escalation and correction.

Yu said clinical trust comes from transparency, and that models must communicate the basis and limits of their output and make uncertainty visible to end users while preserving meaningful human oversight. He said responsibility has to be built into the entire AI system, not only added to the end. He predicted pathologists will not be replaced by AI, but that those who adopt it will replace those who don't. He closed by paraphrasing John F. Kennedy, saying we should ask not what AI can do for you but what we can do together to build a better future with AI in medicine.

Kamat said AI and machine learning have seen an explosion in medicine, and noted that niche companies such as Valar Labs have developed AI algorithms that look at tissue and are trained on large data sets as closed platforms. Kamat asked whether pathology AI will remain restricted to certain proprietary platforms or become a general pathology AI available across the globe in the near future. Yu agreed it was a great question and observation, and began to note that several proprietary platforms currently exist. The discussion was part of a breakout session at this year's BCAN Think Tank annual meeting on how AI is beginning to read risk directly from tissue.

Yu's biography lists him as an associate professor in the Department of Biomedical Informatics at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts. Kamat's biography lists him as a professor of urology and the Wayne B. Duddleston Professor of Cancer Research at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, Texas. Related content listed with the video includes BCANTT 2026: AI in Bladder Cancer: What's Real, What's Next, and What to Watch Out For, and sessions on artificial intelligence and machine learning in bladder cancer pathology and clinical decision-making with Hikmat Al-Ahmadie and Alexandre Zlotta. Another related item is Harnessing Artificial Intelligence in Bladder Cancer: Digital Tools for Enhanced Diagnosis and Treatment with David McConkey.

The article was published on UroToday's Bladder Cancer Center of Excellence page, dated November 22, 2026, and the video was posted on November 21, 2026. The page carries a cookie notice with a privacy policy and an I Agree button. The transcript ends mid-sentence as Yu was describing proprietary platforms. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Samsung and Google sell out AI glasses pre-orders within hours of unveiling
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics’ artificial intelligence glasses, called Intelligent Eyewear, sold out in pre-orders that began alongside the product’s unveiling on Nov. 12, with the prepared supply gone within hours. All 16 Intelligent Eyewear models listed on Gentle Monster’s official website are marked as pre-order sold out, and pre-orders underway in the United States are also understood to have sold out across all models. The product was developed in partnership with Google and the fashion eyewear brand Gentle Monster, and the early result is seen as a sign of strong consumer interest that overwhelmed the initial supply. The glasses bring Google’s latest AI model, Gemini, into a lightweight frame of about 41g that includes a built-in camera, speaker and microphone.

Users can carry out a range of AI functions through voice commands alone without taking their smartphones out of their pockets, and the product focuses on everyday convenience. It offers services including real-time foreign language translation, directions to a destination and summaries of complex meeting materials, and it was designed to let people make natural use of AI in the ordinary setting of wearing glasses. Samsung will officially launch the product in the Korean and U.S. markets on Dec. 10 and begin full-scale sales. In Korea it will first introduce the 16 designs developed with Gentle Monster, while in the U.S. it plans a total lineup of 30 models by adding 14 products from the local brand Warby Parker.

The product is priced between 650,000 won, or about $468, and 700,000 won, or about $504, depending on detailed specifications by model. The stated strategy is to target both competitive pricing compared with existing smart devices and value as a fashion item at the same time. The articles do not name who at Samsung or Google is responsible for the launch or what any executive said about it. The articles also give no further context on the wearable market beyond calling the sellout new momentum, and they do not say what happens next beyond the Dec. 10 launch and full-scale sales.

stories.Headline: SoftBank chairman Masayoshi Son drops plan to acquire SK hynix for $1 trillion
stories.Summary:
Masayoshi Son, the chairman of SoftBank Group, recently explored the possibility of acquiring SK hynix to expand his artificial intelligence empire. He approached several major financial institutions in the United States to discuss how he could raise the necessary funds for this massive purchase. The potential deal was estimated to reach a value of $1 trillion, which is approximately 1,400 trillion won. However, the plan appears to have been dropped at an early stage because it was unlikely to be feasible.

The proposed purchase price of $1 trillion was based on a peak market value for SK hynix plus a 40 percent control premium. Currently, the world's second-largest memory chipmaker has a market value of about $577.7 billion, or 777 trillion won. This acquisition would have given SoftBank control over high-bandwidth memory, a critical component for AI accelerators that is currently supplied by SK hynix, Samsung Electronics, and Micron Technology. Such a move would have complemented SoftBank's existing holdings in Arm, SB Energy, Ampere Computing, DigitalBridge, Intel, and OpenAI.

A spokesperson for SoftBank stated that the company reviews many different opportunities but this specific deal is no longer under active consideration. The company did not confirm that Wall Street banks had actually discussed providing the financing for the acquisition. Market observers generally believe that the idea of a trillion-dollar bid was never realistic given the financial requirements. Despite this, industry officials suggest the approach demonstrates that Masayoshi Son intends to control the entire AI value chain.

Son has a long history of using borrowed money and collateral to fund his large-scale investments in technology. He previously used his holdings in Alibaba to help cover the $32 billion cost of purchasing Arm. In 2017, he launched the $100 billion Vision Fund using money from the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. More recently, he pledged shares of Arm as collateral to finance his stake in OpenAI. These actions show a consistent pattern of aggressive financial maneuvering to secure dominant positions in emerging tech sectors.

stories.Headline: IndexBox forecasts growth for thin wafer processing and dicing equipment through 2035
stories.Summary:
IndexBox released a market report on November 21, 2026, regarding thin wafer processing and dicing equipment. This global market is entering a structural growth phase driven by advanced semiconductor packaging demand. The report provides a comprehensive analysis of the industry from 2026 through 2035. It highlights a shift toward thinner wafers and higher die density for heterogeneous integration. This equipment is now a critical enabler for 3D IC stacking and chiplet designs.

The baseline scenario projects a compound annual growth rate of 6.8 percent from 2026 to 2035. The market index is projected to reach 185 by 2035, using 2025 as a base of 100. Advanced packaging represents 35 percent of demand, while power semiconductors account for 25 percent. Memory and logic devices hold 20 percent, and MEMS and sensors represent 12 percent. Wafers for advanced packaging must be thinned to below 50 micrometers.

IndexBox states that the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals and more disciplined procurement behavior. They note that the supply architecture is now more regionally diversified than it was previously. The report claims that the transition to laser and plasma singulation is accelerating to process brittle materials. These technologies are necessary to achieve near-zero kerf loss for silicon carbide and gallium nitride. The analysts suggest that long-term trajectories remain positive despite some cyclical semiconductor spending.

The report identifies Applied Materials, DISCO Corporation, EV Group, SUSS MicroTec, and Tokyo Electron as representative participants. Other key players include Lam Research, ASM International, Plasma-Therm, and Advanced Dicing Technologies. Electric vehicle manufacturers and 5G infrastructure providers are affected by these technological shifts. High-performance computing and mobile applications also drive the need for fan-out wafer-level packaging. These sectors require precise, damage-free singulation that traditional mechanical blade dicing cannot deliver.

The background includes a shift toward wide-bandgap semiconductors like silicon carbide for use in electric vehicles. Eurostat data shows producer unit values for semiconductor manufacture machines were 666,667.00 EUR per piece in 2025. European Union industry output for other special-purpose machinery rose 35.6 percent year-on-year in August 2026. Producer prices for that same machinery category rose 1.5 percent year-on-year in September 2026. Asia-Pacific is the dominant hub for production, while North America and Europe lead system design.

Future growth depends on the ramp-up of AI accelerators and high-bandwidth memory through 2035. The market must overcome high capital costs and qualification cycles that can exceed 18 months. Geopolitical trade tensions and export controls remain potential constraints on equipment sales to certain regions. Technical challenges include managing breakage and thermal issues when processing ultra-thin wafers. The report leaves open how alternative packaging approaches might reduce the need for dicing.
