stories.Headline: AI chip developers shift HBM production to a shared design and manufacturing model
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA unveiled its Custom HBM platform called NVHBM in August 2026 to integrate into the NVLink Fusion lineup for AI accelerators. This new platform will be deployed in NVIDIA's own Feynman GPU and also within AWS's Trainium 4 AI hardware. In October, Marvell presented a system for custom HBM at the OCP Global Summit to discuss new design tradeoffs. This shift moves the industry from a memory maker led model toward a three way division of labor for production. Memory makers like Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron previously controlled both the design and manufacturing of the entire HBM stack.

The new layout moves the memory controller into a custom base die beneath each DRAM stack instead of on the XPU. A narrower die to die physical interface replaces the wide HBM interface at the XPU edge to connect the components. Marvell estimates this change provides up to 25 percent more compute area and room for 33 percent more HBM stacks. Memory interface power could be 70 percent lower, while adaptive power management reduces interface power by 75 percent under normal workloads. These changes shift base die production to advanced logic processes, which increases the importance of TSMC in the supply chain.

Marvell stated that no single company can build custom HBM alone because it requires a coordinated effort from several partners. They argued that the base die, die to die interface, and package thermals must be co designed as one system. Marvell noted that the die to die PHY is a heat hotspot, making package cooling a central design constraint. They suggested using silicon heat paths, copper to copper hybrid bonding, or coolant channels etched into silicon to manage heat. Marvell also mentioned that adaptive power management can reduce interface power by 42 percent during periods of peak traffic.

AI chip developers are evaluating custom HBM because standard HBM must prioritize compatibility, which leaves limited room for individual accelerator optimization. GPU and ASIC designers are now helping define the foundation of HBM, which affects how these critical AI components function. IBM Technology's Kaoutar El Maghraoui explained that some workloads are limited by memory bandwidth rather than by the available computing capacity. This means adding more compute area may not speed up tasks if data movement remains the primary bottleneck for workloads. Marvell cited a Samsung study showing internal thermal resistance accounts for 57 percent of the HBM stack's total resistance.

HBM has traditionally been the home turf for memory makers who controlled everything from DRAM dies to the bottom base die. Marvell estimates HBM now takes up roughly 30 percent of a typical AI accelerator die area in the current market. At 2026 memory prices, HBM accounts for more than half of the total cost of a typical XPU AI accelerator. The roofline model and arithmetic intensity are used to distinguish whether a workload is constrained by compute or memory bandwidth. Samsung's thermal study also found that internal thermal resistance accounts for 13 percent of the total for an adjacent ASIC.

Custom HBM appears to be on the final stretch toward mass production as developers continue to evaluate these new design options. For next generation HBM running above 28 Gbps, Marvell expects the heat flux to exceed 2.0 watts per square millimeter. Marvell relays a projection that internal temperatures in 16 high HBM stacks will exceed the thermal budget by the year 2028. TrendForce will provide more insights on HBM and custom ASICs at the Roadshow Japan 2026 event in Tokyo on December 8. The articles leave open how fast CPO will scale and how a split US China market will reshape 2027 servers.

stories.Headline: KAIST researcher urges metal detectors to stop AI smart glasses cheating on college exam
stories.Summary:
A KAIST artificial intelligence researcher and YouTube creator, Heo Sung-beom, warned in a video posted on his channel on the 16th that test takers could cheat on the college entrance exam using AI smart glasses, and he urged the government to prepare thorough measures before the exam. He said he did not make AI to be used this way and found it sad that some people abuse it before social systems or guidelines are ready. He explained that cheating with AI devices works in three stages, photographing questions with a micro camera, sending them out through communication equipment, and receiving analyzed answers through smart glasses or earphones. He said the biggest problem is that a small number of students abuse technology and may take opportunities away from students who studied hard, and he called it senseless to hold the test without any measures.

Heo proposed a metal detector as the most realistic way to block such cheating, because lenses, smart glasses and earphones all need a battery to run for a long time, and the battery contains metal that a detector should catch. He noted that test supervisors are not professional security staff, so suspicious signals may be missed, and that securing enough equipment and training supervisors in a short time is practically difficult. He questioned thermal imaging cameras, saying very small devices or ones that have not yet built up enough heat may not be caught and that a whole classroom would have to be watched from a distance. He also called for checks of communication devices such as smartphones, smart watches, tablet PCs and portable Wi-Fi at test sites, for unexpected inspections with radio wave detectors, and for later checks of communication records and test paper analysis for suspected cheaters, while warning that investigating every test taker's records could raise legal problems.

The controversy spread after a person identified as A, who passed the tax accountant examination, confessed to cheating on the tax accountant and certified public accountant exams using micro cameras and generative AI, turned himself in to police, and had related electronic devices seized in an investigation. Concern grew that AI cheating could occur in the CSAT, which was to take place on the 19th, and college entrance exam creator Mimiminu, Korean language instructor Yoo Jae-jong and math instructor Jung Seung-je also urged measures to secure fairness, with Jung saying postponement of the CSAT should be considered if no effective measures exist. The government responded, with Cheong Wa Dae holding an emergency meeting on the 15th to discuss a full investigation into suspected AI cheating and ways to strengthen management and supervision of CSAT test sites, and police decided to form a countermeasure team for CSAT cheating. Heo told worried students that cheating is bound to be caught eventually even if it takes time and hoped they would never do it because it could twist their lives, and he told test takers skeptical about studying that people have abused technology in every era and they should go their own way.

stories.Headline: Major tech firms use existing ecosystems to compete in AI office software as models become commoditized
stories.Summary:
Major Chinese companies recently adjusted their organizational structures for AI office business to concentrate resources and use existing advantages in channels and ecosystems. ByteDance integrated Doubao, Feishu, and Volcano Engine in July, while Liang Rubo explained this arrangement at the September Feishu Conference. Tencent incorporated QClaw into WorkBuddy, and Alibaba merged three products into Tongyi Office under the DingTalk team. Baidu integrated internal products into Baidu Dazi, and Kingsoft Office shifted its main focus toward AI.

Tencent WorkBuddy connects to Hunyuan, DeepSeek, Zhipu GLM, Kimi, and MiniMax, while Doubao Work accesses Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, and two Doubao models. Tongyi Office launched ten models in mid-November, including self-developed Tongyi, DeepSeek, Kimi, and MiniMax, after briefly accessing external models in August. Microsoft Copilot adopts both OpenAI and Claude models, and packages AI functions into the E7 plan for 99 dollars per user monthly. Alibaba popularized the data mid-platform concept around 2015, but the company began weakening this specific approach around 2020.

Large enterprises claim that holding massive data provides a competitive advantage, but the author says getting departments to coordinate interests is difficult. These companies also argue that connecting systems to core processes creates customer reliance, though this can make product modification very slow. The author notes that the labor cost saved in some RPA projects is not even enough to maintain the software. Satya Nadella integrated OpenAI capabilities into the Office suite rather than making AI an independent product.

Users of WorkBuddy are partly driven by point subsidies and free traffic from WeChat, though this may not translate into long-term usage. Tencent relies on WeChat and WeCom traffic, while Alibaba uses DingTalk enterprise customers and Kingsoft uses government and enterprise channels. Baidu utilizes its search, cloud disk, and intelligent cloud systems, while Microsoft relies on the customer base from Windows and Office. These companies use traditional software industry tactics, making their AI office products increasingly similar to one another.

The articles state that many people initially thought new AI products would replace industry leaders and allow small companies to rise. However, big companies with existing customer relationships and complete product systems still occupy a favorable position because models are now accessible to all. The author explains that sorting messy data into usable information requires long-term accumulation that cannot be solved by simply switching models. This suggests that AI is currently being used by old companies to complete upgrades to their original systems.

The winner among these five major companies remains unknown because it is too early to tell who will prevail in this competition. The articles leave open whether a balance can be struck between product stability and the flexibility needed for models that update every half year. It remains unclear if a new player, developing outside the attention of leading enterprises, will emerge to re-divide the market. The realization process of technological change is described as more tortuous than initially expected.

stories.Headline: SemiAnalysis finds Apple builds M5 Pro, Max and Ultra as three-die chiplets on TSMC hybrid bonding
stories.Summary:
SemiAnalysis published a die-level teardown finding that Apple's M5 Pro, M5 Max and M5 Ultra are the company's first true chiplet design, splitting the system-on-chip across three separately built dies. The teardown, published on 2026-11-20, reports that the dies are joined with TSMC's SoIC-mH hybrid-bonding packaging instead of solder. SemiAnalysis bought the chips, pulled them apart and measured them rather than relying on a vendor briefing. The CPU chiplet measures roughly 168 mm² and carries 18 cores, four large Thunderbolt 5 PHYs and no efficiency cores. The GPU chiplets are a precise 2:1 scaling of one another at about 300 mm² and 157 mm².

Apple taped out three dies, one CPU die and two GPU dies, a small one and a large one, all on TSMC's N3P process. The M5 Pro pairs the 168 mm² CPU chiplet with the small GPU chiplet of about 157 mm², and the M5 Max pairs the CPU chiplet with the large GPU chiplet of about 300 mm². The M5 Ultra uses two CPU chiplets and two large GPU chiplets and was not measured because the lab had no unit. The large GPU die has 40 GPU cores, 48 MB of System Level Cache and a 512-bit memory interface, while the small die has 20 cores, 24 MB of cache and a 256-bit interface. The CPU chiplet holds 18 CPU cores in three clusters, a 16-core Neural Engine of eight dual-cores, four Display Engines, a 4-lane Display PHY and 16 lanes of PCI-Express, most likely Gen 5, in four 2x2 clusters.

SemiAnalysis said the M5 Ultra's UltraFusion link reaches more than 6x the connection density of the M3 Ultra, which implies hybrid bonding and rules out solder. It said the teardown was inferred, not measured, for the Ultra, reconstructed from a second, larger interconnect on the large GPU die plus Apple's own density claim. It said copper-to-copper bonding can be pitched below 10 µm, versus microbumps stuck at 25 µm, and approaches 3 µm in the most advanced processes. It said the result is the highest quality interconnect you can think of, almost like fusing the metal layers, creating one large coherent chip. It said it is not unlikely that Apple worked on the solution directly with TSMC, and closed with the aside, Can't innovate anymore my ass.

SemiAnalysis said the M1, M2 and M3 Ultra simply took two of the largest dies of a generation and fused them in a classic multi-chip-module arrangement. It said the M3 Ultra used InFO-LSI packaging with a local silicon interconnect and solder-based microbumps, and that measurements show a 25 µm bump pitch. It said the SoIC-mH is the same hybrid bonding behind AMD's 3D V-Cache, but deployed side by side rather than stacked, and that the mH stands for molding horizontally. It said placing the chips side by side avoids the heat trapping of a vertical sandwich, citing the A20 Pro's move to WMCM packaging with memory moved beside the chip. It said the twelve new P-cores, internally called M-cores, are split into two mirrored six-core clusters, each with 8 MB of shared cache and a dedicated matrix engine, and that the S-core cluster is slightly asymmetrical with two S-cores above and four below a shared 16 MB cache.

SemiAnalysis said the CPU die, at roughly 168 mm², is actually larger than a base M5, and that the small GPU die is essentially the large one cut in half, which it suggests shortens development time. It said the four Thunderbolt 5 PHYs outclass the M-cores in size and are not far behind an S-core, and flagged how big analogue SerDes are becoming and how much space the command-and-control area is taking up. It said the 16-core Neural Engine has since been doubled on the M6, and that only the M5 Ultra gets twice the AI hardware because it uses two CPU chiplets. It said it speculates the two-cluster split may be for power management, letting an entire cluster shut off when idle. It said hybrid bonding raises bandwidth and cuts the energy cost of moving data, making it a packaging moat as much as a process one, and puts TSMC's advanced packaging roadmap at the center of Apple's silicon story the way N3P once was.

SemiAnalysis said the first physical analysis of the M5 Ultra will either confirm the two-Max construction or complicate it. It said the other thread worth watching is whether side-by-side hybrid bonding spreads to other Apple products, given the company's apparent shift toward heat-conscious packaging across the A20 Pro and M5 lines. It said the signal for investors is that advanced packaging is becoming a competitive battleground in its own right. It said to watch whether AMD, NVIDIA and the hyperscalers' in-house silicon follow Apple into side-by-side hybrid bonding, and whether TSMC's packaging capacity, not its wafer capacity, becomes the binding constraint on the next generation of high-end processors. It said Apple had access to hybrid bonding for some time, as other TSMC customers did, but waited for the side-by-side implementation.

stories.Headline: A CIO says organizational culture and clear responsibilities, not AI tools, determine enterprise efficiency
stories.Summary:
A CIO friend of a company in Lao Yang's group posted on November 20, 2026, that organizational efficiency cannot be improved by tools alone, and that an agile organization can be efficient even via emails. The same passage said that those who pass the buck all day cannot make good use of the best software in the world even if it is given to them free. Lao Yang wrote the article in Xiangjiang Digital Review, published with authorization from 36Kr, and 36Kr said the views are the author's own. Lao Yang recalled that a CIO friend from a manufacturing group was called out by the general manager that day about arguing over cross-departmental account reconciliation in WeChat groups for three days after adopting AI and buying collaboration software. The CIO replied that the problem was not the system but that no one was responsible for the result of the account reconciliation in the first place.

Lao Yang said the ceiling of organizational efficiency usually lies not in tools but in culture, consensus and collaboration mechanisms, and that technology is advancing while collaboration mechanisms stay stagnant. He said top leaders understand digital transformation as deploying systems, purchasing SaaS and installing models, while efficient organizations have transparent information, decentralized decision-making and clear responsibilities. He said that with these three points even primitive emails, asynchronous, traceable and group-sent for synchronization, achieve high efficiency because everyone knows who to turn to, what to respond and when. He said that with fragmented information and ambiguous rights and responsibilities, AI only makes wrong decisions faster and makes buck-passing reasons more technical. He described an enterprise that deployed an intelligent report system where, when data was wrong, everyone blamed the underlying calibers not being aligned and no one took responsibility.

Lao Yang said the tool did not improve efficiency but gave buck-passing a set of professional terms, and he thought of the word entropy. He said to judge an organization's entropy by one small thing: for a cross-departmental demand from initiation to closed loop, how many groups are created, how many hands it passes through and who makes the final decision. He said the more steps and the more chaotic the groups, the higher the entropy, and that in high-entropy organizations AI is not an antidote but an amplifier. He said enterprises must sort out information flow, rights and responsibilities before talking about tools, and that buck-passing reflects a lack of trust and result-oriented contractual spirit. He said AI and digital tools are levers that amplify executive power in healthy organizations and destructive power in organizations used to shirking responsibilities.

Lao Yang said AI's prediction reports become evidence for departments to attack each other and automated processes become an excuse, with people saying the system judged it automatically. He said the primary premise of AI implementation is a matter-oriented rather than person-oriented data culture, and without the courage and consensus to tell the truth with data, advanced AI tools can only write weekly reports or become an excuse. He said tools are neutral and what the organization turns them into depends on the organization itself. He said email suits teams with high self-discipline and high consensus, while many enterprises stuck in the agricultural era deploy interstellar battleship level collaboration software and AI middle platforms, so employees create small WeChat groups to complain and fill in data no one reads. He said AI implementation failures are often caused not by inaccurate algorithms but by collaboration maturity that cannot support tool complexity, which is production relations failing to adapt to advanced productivity.

Lao Yang said AI implementation should advance in small steps and reject the Great Leap Forward, starting with a small scenario with clear pain points and clear responsibility boundaries, such as financial invoice recognition or automatic classification of customer service work orders. He said light tools should come first and a heavy middle platform at the start is useless except for showing off. He said employees pass the buck mostly because of ambiguous areas in the process, and AI intervention only solidifies these holes with code, deeper and harder to find, while managers use diligence in AI technology to replace laziness in management. He gave the example of an approval process with unclear rights and responsibilities where, after AI intelligent approval, people argue about why AI judged this way and who set the rules, so the buck-passing shifts from people to algorithms and the algorithm takes the blame. He said AI is the accelerator of processes, not the repairman, and business process reengineering must come first, cutting off points that cause artificial buck-passing and clarifying responsibility boundaries with systems and SOPs before AI enters.

Lao Yang said the first step of process reengineering is often to write who on earth is responsible for the result into the system, and execution is the key. He said efficient organizations using emails have every sentence correspond to clear action items and responsible persons, a kind of mental digitalization with a common logic. He said the goal of AI is not to teach employees to operate software but to train the organization's best practices and consensus into the default workflow of AI, and without consensus on what a good solution is, AI solutions are picked on and rejected by departments based on their own interests. He said the highest state is system as code, consensus as algorithm, with 80% of efforts to unify business logic, precipitate knowledge assets and clarify evaluation criteria and 20% for purchasing computing power and training models, solidifying review standards into a reusable knowledge base and review checklist. He said not to let the IT department take the blame for poor organizational efficiency, and suggested that before any major AI or digital project, a team be asked whether it could push the matter forward with only emails and Excel without internet and software, solving people's problems first and then letting AI amplify efficiency.

stories.Headline: Dispatchers and bank staff quietly override AI systems as accountability stays with humans
stories.Summary:
At the end of 2022 a multinational bank approved an AI system to automate routine credit decision-making, and during the pilot phase the system processed applications faster than human staff, made fewer errors, and promised significant cost reductions. The bank's risk management department endorsed it, the compliance department signed off on it, and the CEO publicly promoted the system as strong proof of the bank's march into the future. Six months on, the AI system continued to score users' credit applications and generate recommendations, but most application documents still required manual review, and exceptions were piling up. Measures originally designed as temporary safety safeguards, such as dual-review thresholds and manual confirmation flags, gradually solidified into permanent process steps. Although the AI system was integrated into the bank's workflow, in reality most final decisions were never made by it.

The justifications offered were that the organization was not fully ready, the model needed further optimization, employees required more training, and change is always difficult, yet the technology is already practically viable, the economic benefits are clear, and the AI system received formal and enthusiastic approval from the organization. The only thing it never truly obtained is empowerment, the full backing of the organization to make decisions within clearly defined boundaries. A multinational manufacturing enterprise launched an AI-based demand forecasting system, but its planning department still stuck to old workflows and only treated the AI's forecasts as reference points. A healthcare network introduced an AI-assisted triage system that shortened patient waiting times and improved triage consistency, and clinicians recognized the accuracy of the AI model, yet they still insisted on manually reviewing most of the AI's recommendations. As a result, the triage system was mostly used for archiving rather than supporting decision-making.

The problem is not that the pilot project failed, but that accountability and legitimacy within the organization failed to evolve in tandem to support the application of the AI system. The author calls a legitimacy architecture a consensus within an organization about who has the authority to make decisions and whose decisions can be trusted. Many organizations are continuously raising their level of intelligence, yet they have not reshaped their organizational structures around this change. Previous waves of automated decision-making, such as ERP systems and credit scoring, exposed the same organizational inertia, in which enterprises introduced systems capable of making better decisions yet retained their existing human decision-making authority structures, which often led to the rejection of decisions made by the systems. In the 1990s, when ERP systems such as those from Oracle and SAP emerged, they promised centralized, transparent management and operational optimization across the entire enterprise.

Nestlé USA's experience implementing an ERP system is highly illustrative, because before it the company's various departments operated independently, each responsible for its own production, costs, and supplier contracts. When the ERP system required departments to give up this autonomy and follow unified business processes, employees who were still accountable for local business outcomes naturally had good reasons to insist on making their own decisions. Even though the system generated unified, consolidated forecasts, the accountability mechanisms at the time rewarded local adjustments to or override of the system's recommendations. Tom Davenport of Babson College pointed out that the company treated the ERP system at the time purely as a technology deployment, rather than as a comprehensive management process reshaping. Studies on auto loans show that compared with manual underwriting, algorithmic underwriting not only delivered higher loan profits but also reduced default rates, and the most significant performance gap between the two occurred precisely in segments where loan officers, out of self-serving considerations, fiercely guarded their discretionary power.

Other studies found that loan officers manipulated input data and scoring results to push borderline applications across the approval threshold, in order to earn performance bonuses tied to transaction volume, so it looked like approval authority had been delegated to the model, but ultimate responsibility still rested with the relevant human staff. The airline industry's experience with revenue management systems offers a useful contrasting case, because airlines clarified the scenarios suitable for human intervention, standardized the escalation process for issues, adjusted performance evaluation methods, and established the professional legitimacy of following the system. The system's authority was not established because of the algorithm's perfect performance, but because airlines changed their organizational governance mechanisms for automated systems. Davenport, Erik Brynjolfsson, and others have pointed out this phenomenon before, and the article reveals the root cause behind it: as long as individual employees are still required to take responsibility for the outcomes of system operations, decision-making authority will never truly shift. Enterprises must resolve this disconnect between rights and responsibilities, otherwise employees will continue to bypass AI systems, not out of resistance, but purely out of self-protection.

No amount of training or communication can bridge this gap, and enterprises may successfully implement changes yet permanently relegate the technology to an advisory role, or provide employees with ample psychological safety yet still penalize employees who follow the system's instructions when decision errors occur. Some argue that organizational inertia creates resistance, but in AI applications what is often seen is superficial compliance: dashboards are running, workflows have incorporated the system, and employees are all using it, yet the AI system never truly gains decision-making power. Research on automation complacency suggests that humans tend to defer to machines too easily, but this phenomenon does not apply here, because the company's accountability system makes it professionally risky to blindly follow AI systems. Research on the productivity paradox, while pointing out that information technology investments fail to translate into performance improvements, mostly does not explain the organizational mechanisms that lead to this outcome. Ethan Bernstein's research on transparency shows that employees under surveillance will hide their actual operations to avoid scrutiny, but they also use explicit compliance mechanisms, such as archived exception operations, escalation procedures, and multi-level review processes, as tools to maintain their own control.

In most cases enterprises adopt some kind of AI system and promote it vigorously in internal corporate demonstrations, but in reality whenever AI and humans disagree, humans quietly prevail in the end. Out of prudence, experts always reshape the boundaries of AI systems by adding more review links, slightly lowering trigger thresholds, increasing the number of archived override operations, and enabling new flagging mechanisms for sensitive cases, and individually each of these settings and adjustments is justifiable, but taken together the consequences are catastrophic. UPS's deployment of its ORION route-planning system vividly illustrates this tension, because when the system was first rolled out in 2013, many drivers treated the routes it generated as advisory suggestions, preferring to rely on their own local experience and customer relationships. Over time UPS adjusted its performance evaluation criteria so that drivers were no longer compared against their own past performance but assessed against the routes set by ORION, with the system tracking their compliance with the routes, and as a result following the algorithm became a legitimate part of the drivers' job responsibilities. Recently the author observed the same dynamic at another multinational logistics company that handles high-value cargo transportation for enterprise clients, where during the pilot project an AI route-planning system drastically reduced cargo delays and improved asset utilization, and the company immediately approved the system for adoption.

Dispatchers privately admitted that the system often generated better routes than the ones they devised themselves, but after the full rollout dispatchers kept adjusting routes in their daily work, for long-standing clients, cargo with internal political importance to the company, and drivers they trusted more. At first these adjustments were seen as fine-tuning, but over time the AI system no longer functioned as a decision engine, and its outputs only served as the starting point for discussing subsequent plans. When senior management pushed for full adoption of the AI route-planning system, dispatchers neither argued that the system was flawed nor refused to use it, and instead they added measures: flagging sensitive cargo, adding escalation links, and lowering the thresholds for triggering reviews. One dispatcher explained the logic with disarming candor, saying that if a decision made by the system goes wrong his name is the one signed on the report, and if a mistake is made in a decision he made himself at least he can explain it. This dispatcher was neither troubled by the AI system nor felt a lack of security, he simply accurately interpreted where the responsibility lay.

Research on professional identity threat shows that when practitioners' professional skills face automation substitution, they experience genuine anxiety about their social status, professional value, and future career prospects, and this anxiety affects their behavior, and these behaviors are neither irrational nor trivial. However, these factors cannot explain a phenomenon the author has observed: this pattern persists even when fear and identity th

stories.Headline: Apple builds its M5 Pro, Max and Ultra chips from three dies in a first true chiplet design
stories.Summary:
SemiAnalysis published a teardown on 20 November 2026 finding that Apple's M5 Pro, M5 Max and M5 Ultra are the company's first true chiplet design, built from three separate dies. The analysis rests on physical inspection rather than vendor briefings, because SemiAnalysis bought the chips and had them torn down. The speaker walks through die sizes, core counts, cache allocations and PHY structures measured from the silicon. The M5 Ultra fuses two M5 Max dual-die assemblies with a connection density Apple claims is more than 6x that of the M3 Ultra's UltraFusion. The lab had not yet obtained an M5 Ultra, so its layout is inferred from the M5 Max's second interconnect and Apple's own marketing claims.

Apple taped out three dies, one CPU die and two GPU dies, a small and a large one, all fabricated on TSMC's N3P process. The CPU chiplet is roughly 168 mm², the small GPU chiplet about 157 mm² and the large GPU chiplet about 300 mm². The M5 Pro pairs the CPU chiplet with the small GPU chiplet, the M5 Max pairs it with the large GPU chiplet, and the M5 Ultra uses two CPU chiplets and two large GPU chiplets. The CPU die carries 18 cores in three clusters, four Thunderbolt 5 PHYs and no E-cores, and the GPU chiplets scale cleanly at 2:1, the large one with 40 GPU cores, 48 MB of System Level Cache and a 512-bit memory interface.

The speaker draws a firm line between Apple's earlier multi-die chips and the M5 generation, saying the M1, M2 and M3 Ultra fused two of the largest dies of a generation in a classic multi-chip-module arrangement. He defines a true chiplet architecture by two design targets, optimizing the area of each individual die to improve yield and outsourcing different functions of the SoC onto different chiplets so the final product only works once at least two different chiplets are combined. He acknowledges the definition is contestable, saying everyone is entitled to their own chiplet based opinion, but states it as his position. He calls the GPU chiplets interesting and a bit boring at the same time, because the halving is so exact that the small die reads as a straightforward cut of the large one. He flags the four Thunderbolt 5 PHYs as the standout by area, saying it is crazy to see how big analogue SerDes are becoming and how much space the command-and-control area is taking up.

The speaker says the new interconnect uses TSMC's SoIC-mH, called SoIC-X F2F by TSMC, the same hybrid bonding technology behind AMD's 3D V-Cache but deployed side-by-side rather than stacked, with mH standing for molding horizontally. Standard advanced packaging attaches finished dies to an interposer through microbumps around 25 µm and perhaps down to 18 µm, while hybrid bonding aligns matching exposed copper interconnects surrounded by dielectric and heats them so the copper fuses directly. He describes the result as almost like fusing the metal layers, creating one large coherent chip, and says the pitch drops below 10 µm and approaches 3 µm in the most advanced processes. He says placing the chiplets side by side rather than stacked avoids the thermal problems of a vertical sandwich, citing the A20 Pro's move to WMCM packaging with DRAM moved to the side of the SoC. He says Apple had access to hybrid bonding for some time, as other TSMC customers did, but waited for the side-by-side implementation, and that it is not unlikely Apple worked on the solution with TSMC directly.

The speaker says the last UltraFusion chip, the M3 Ultra, used InFO-LSI packaging with a local silicon interconnect and solder-based microbumps, and that Apple never published the bump pitch but measurements show 25 µm. He says a 6x density increase implies a pitch of about 10 µm or less, squarely in hybrid bonding territory and impossible with solder. He says the left side of the CPU die holds the classic 16-core Neural Engine of eight dual-cores, which he notes has since been doubled on the M6, and that only the M5 Ultra gets double the NPU because it uses two CPU chiplets. He says the twelve new P-cores, internally called M-cores, are split into two mirrored six-core clusters each with 8 MB of shared cache and a dedicated AMX unit, and suggests the split may be for power management so an entire cluster can be shut off. He says the S-core cluster is slightly asymmetrical with two S-cores on top and four below a 16 MB shared cache, each S-core getting a 1 MB slice of L2 cache.

The speaker says the CPU die is larger than a base M5 and that the small GPU die is essentially a cut-in-half version of the large one, which he suggests helps with development time. He says the bottom shoreline of the CPU die is a large IO array running from left to right through an Apple proprietary high-speed PHY for cameras and other sensors, a 4-lane Display PHY and 16 lanes of PCI-Express, most likely Gen 5, arranged in four 2x2 clusters. He says the die also includes an on-die NAND controller and an AES engine in the secure enclave, and that four large Display Engines sit to the right of the M-cores. He says only some media acceleration logic near the die-to-die interface stays the same size across both GPU chiplets. He says the faint striped structure on the CPU die's upper shoreline is the physical layer of the new die-to-die interconnect and matches an identical PHY on the adjacent shoreline of either GPU die.

The speaker's verdict is that hybrid bonding materially improves the M5 series rather than serving as a label, and he closes with the aside, Can't innovate anymore my ass. The open item to track is the M5 Ultra itself, whose configuration is derived from the M5 Max's second interconnect and Apple's density claim, not from a teardown, so the first physical analysis of that part will either confirm the two-Max construction or complicate it. The other thread worth watching is whether side-by-side hybrid bonding spreads to other Apple products, given the company's apparent shift toward thermal-conscious packaging across the A20 Pro and M5 lines. The articles give no date for when the M5 chips shipped or when the M5 Ultra will be torn down. The articles give no statement from Apple beyond its marketing claim on connection density.

stories.Headline: Apple develops autonomous AI agents to perform tasks across apps independently
stories.Summary:
Apple is developing its own autonomous AI Agent to perform tasks across apps and plan workflows independently. The company is the last tech giant to enter this market during the first year of AI Agents. Two job postings related to these agents appeared on the official Apple website in mid-November. Apple wants Siri to evolve from giving verbal commands to taking actual actions on its own. This move follows a trend started by generative AI access for ordinary users in 2023.

The system requires a senior engineering manager to develop assistants with proactive service capabilities that operate computers like humans. It must browse the web, run commands, write code, and coordinate multiple specialized sub-agents to execute multi-step tasks. A senior applied AI engineer must establish personal intelligent evaluation benchmarks and use feedback mechanisms to optimize performance. Candidates are required to use Claude Code and Codex in their daily work. macOS 27.3 Beta 2 adjusts authorization for device control and full disk access permissions.

Bloomberg reports that Apple is developing this autonomous AI Agent to enable independent planning of workflows. Apple's job postings describe a vision where AI can select the appropriate tool for each step of a task. The company emphasizes the need for privacy, security, sandbox isolation, and permission management in these roles. Apple aims for the agent to find ways to complete tasks on its own and become more reliable. The company wants to prevent agents from accessing user data and devices at will.

Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, Tencent, and ByteDance are already pushing AI Agents into real work and life scenarios. Meta's Muse has over 10 million setup users in the US and Canada, with 25 percent using it daily. OpenAI launched Dots in September, which connects to over 4,000 apps and works continuously in the background. Anthropic offers Claude Code and Claude Duet, with the latter currently open for research preview. These competitors have already accumulated millions of users and started generating actual revenue.

Apple relies on a huge ecosystem consisting of the iPhone, Mac, and the App Store. The company is now preparing for the deep involvement of AI within its operating system. Recent updates allow users to authorize specific apps and folders and provide status prompts during AI control. This follows the success of Meta's Muse, which handles travel planning, restaurant reservations, and document sorting. Other agents like Dots and Claude Duet now have their own working environments and external service connections.

Apple considered launching these related products as early as the end of 2027. Development of the autonomous AI Agent is still in the early stage. The company must solve the balance between agent capability and data security together. The articles do not state the exact date the product will be available to the public. It remains open how third-party Agents will be affected by the new macOS permission rules.

The procurement involves the use of hybrid bonding systems to enhance the performance of high-bandwidth memory chips. This technical shift requires the integration of specialized machinery from Besi to achieve higher efficiency in chip stacking. The move is designed to support the development of advanced packaging solutions for the evolving semiconductor market. These tools will allow the company to push the boundaries of memory density and speed.

The report indicates that SK Hynix is taking these steps to maintain its leadership in the high-bandwidth memory sector. While the company has not issued a formal public statement in the provided text, the move suggests a commitment to superior hardware. The acquisition of Besi equipment is seen as a way to outpace other manufacturers in the region. stories.Headline: Suregiant Technology expands capacity to target AI advanced packaging market
stories.Summary:
Suregiant Technology held a pre-OTC-listing earnings presentation on November 18, 2026, to discuss its growth. The company targets high-double-digit growth as its release film enters the advanced packaging market. This material is now used in mass production for the world's top five semiconductor manufacturers. The company is expanding its capacity to meet the rising demand for AI chip packaging. These developments aim to drive revenue and profit to new highs for the firm.

Taoyuan Plant 2 will start official mass production in December, with a scale 2.5 to 3 times Plant 1. The company expects a full-year capacity contribution in 2027 and an OTC listing in mid-December. The tentative public offering price is NT$438 per share for the upcoming listing on the market. Release film entered 2.5D packaging in 2024, FOPLP processes in 2025, and 3D advanced packaging in 2026. The company's first three quarters of 2026 saw earnings per share reach NT$6.35 for investors.

Chairman Yang Yun-pin stated that order visibility extends 2 to 3 years for the company. He noted that customer forecast orders have reached 5 to 6 years for their products. Yang explained that their precision coating experience allows them to provide customized samples to major manufacturers. He said the company does not rely on one customer because end customers are highly diversified. Yang believes long-term demand remains solid as the overall AI and high-end packaging megatrend continues.

Institutional investors noted that AI and high-performance computing demand is expanding the advanced packaging market. Yole Group estimates this market will grow from $46.1 billion in 2024 to $79.4 billion by 2030. First-tier manufacturers are affected as they expand capacity for molding and wafer grinding using these materials. Japanese manufacturers previously dominated this segment, but Suregiant is now capturing share through localized service capabilities. The company's products are already supplied for mass production use in first-tier advanced packaging plants.

Suregiant started in the optoelectronics industry and entered the semiconductor field in 2014 to build material expertise. The company currently focuses on two major product lines, which are release film and grinding tape. Grinding tape has been supplied to the world's top ten packaging plants for more than 12 years. Third-quarter revenue was NT$159 million, which represents an 80.76 percent increase over the previous quarter. After-tax net profit for the third quarter was NT$66.51 million, up 92.72 percent quarter-on-quarter.

A new-generation thick grinding tape is expected to begin contributing to company revenue in 2027. Official samples for a new hydrolyzable tape are expected to be sent to customers in mid-2027. This new tape may begin a gradual ramp-up in 2028 as the company's third growth leg. The articles leave open whether Taiwanese firms can continue capturing market share from Japanese material suppliers. Future performance depends on the ramp-up speed of Plant 2 and the verification of new products.

stories.Headline: Former DeepSeek core member Tony Zhang founds Simplex AI to develop personal computer agents
stories.Summary:
Tony Zhang announced the open source of his personal agent product Linger on November 19. He is a former Project Lead of DeepSeek-VL and a core member of that lab. Zhang founded Simplex AI to develop this new AI technology for personal computers. He started his entrepreneurial journey in 2025 after leaving DeepSeek in March 2024. This move marks the first public case of a DeepSeek core author starting a company.

Linger runs on personal computers to operate software, process emails, and enable multiple AI assistants. It uses PolyStrata, a local inference project created by an 18-year-old developer named VecSzn. Simplex AI, also known as Hangzhou Topology Lingxi Technology Co., Ltd., was established February 24, 2025. The company has registered capital of 1 million yuan and secured 6 million US dollars. GL Ventures led this seed round of financing announced in January 2026.

Zhang Bo said he learned the importance of focusing on one thing from DeepSeek's founder. He told his research team to pursue quality over the number of papers they publish. Zhang hopes to bring AI back to personal computers to change the current data center model. He noted that users currently pay per Token for usage of most large AI models. He wants users to have an AI assistant that keeps working without cloud reliance.

Users on the X platform asked if the product could connect to mobile phones. Some users reported encountering model download problems during the installation of the new software. Linger affects ordinary computer users by reducing the cost of running large AI models. The product allows users to avoid paying Token fees to cloud model service providers. However, users must still bear their own costs for electricity and necessary computer hardware.

Zhang earned a bachelor's degree from Zhejiang University in 2013 and a doctorate in 2019. He worked at Microsoft Research Asia on projects like VQ-Diffusion and Rodin before joining DeepSeek. At DeepSeek, he helped develop the first-generation large language model and the DeepSeek-VL project. He later became a PhD supervisor at the State Key Lab of CAD&CG at Zhejiang University. DeepSeek's core team is stable, with only 6.4 percent of paper contributors having departed.

Simplex AI plans to support mobile phone functions within one month of the Linger release. The team is working to fix a reproduced bug regarding the model download process. Simplex AI also plans to launch a hosted version, though the price is not announced. The articles leave open whether ordinary users can actually use the technology in practice. It remains to be seen if third party developers will verify the enterprise test data.

stories.Headline: Singapore SMEs use artificial intelligence to scale operations and reduce resource limitations
stories.Summary:
The Infocomm Media Development Authority and Singapore Business Federation organized the inaugural SME AI Impact Awards 2026. Thirty winners were named from 290 nominations across 21 different industries. These small and medium enterprises used artificial intelligence to scale their operations. The awards recognized firms for creating their own solutions or deploying customized products. This event highlighted how AI helps smaller firms tackle work requiring bigger budgets.

Oceanus Media Global won the SME Innovation Excellence Award for its AI integrated production pipeline. IYLA Collective and You Tiao Man both received the SME Adoption Excellence Award. IYLA Collective uses Claude tools costing 3,000 dollars a year for its beauty business. You Tiao Man built an AI Operations Co-Pilot using Claude and n8n. These companies are based in Singapore and operate in media, beauty, and food.

SBF chief executive officer Kok Ping Soon said AI provides capabilities previously requiring larger teams. OpenAI international managing director Oliver Jay suggested employees build tools around work they know best. Oceanus Media Global chief executive officer Nick Tan said AI allows co-owning films with partners. IYLA Collective founder Lim Yi Ying stated AI changed what her small team can take on. You Tiao Man founder Audrey Chew noted the tool helps track orders across channels.

The awards affected 30 winning firms that now face fewer resource limitations. IYLA Collective customers can now use a customized product bundle page for National Day. You Tiao Man clients benefit from fewer missed deliveries and better order consolidation. Oceanus Media Global partners with firms from South Korea and Australia on movie projects. These SMEs now compete in areas that once demanded specialist expertise or manual effort.

Oceanus Media Global launched in 2020 and shifted toward original content and hybrid filmmaking in 2024. IYLA Collective sold through its own online store for more than three years before retail. You Tiao Man struggled with six different order formats from Shopify, TikTok Shop, and WhatsApp. IYLA Collective began testing AI tools in early 2025 to analyze sales and content. Oceanus Media Global drew inspiration from Hollywood productions like The Mandalorian and Oblivion.

Oceanus Media Global plans to take on as many as 12 multi-location projects annually. IYLA Collective will launch a customer app built with Claude Code by year end. Lim Yi Ying aims to expand into the region and launch own-brand products. You Tiao Man staff will continue maintaining AI workflows to reduce reliance on external vendors. The articles leave open how other SMEs in the 21 industries will adopt AI.

stories.Headline: Alton partners with XUP to build autonomous robots using AI and hardware manufacturing

The smart mobility company Alton announced a new partnership with the AI autonomous driving robotics startup XUP on November 20, 2026. This collaboration follows a signing ceremony held on November 19 between Alton CEO Kim Shin-sung and XUP CEO Lee Yong-su. The two companies intend to combine hardware manufacturing capabilities with autonomous driving software to create self-driving robots. They aim to lay the necessary groundwork to commercialize these robots for the general market. The agreement requires Alton to provide structural design support and manage the procurement of production components for the robots.

Alton will also offer its manufacturing capacity to help XUP move its autonomous designs into full-scale production. XUP brings specialized technology including vision AI, lidar, inertial measurement units, and RTK-GNSS-based precision positioning. The startup has already created autonomous driving algorithms for unstructured outdoor environments and is building a control platform with a major domestic telecommunications carrier. An official from Alton stated that their experience in sourcing and mass production for electric bicycles provides a core competitive strength. This expertise allows the company to extend its capabilities into various next-generation smart mobility fields, including AI robotics.

The company intends to continue seeking business cooperation with innovative firms through the open innovation program of its parent company, Innox. This move is part of a broader strategy to diversify the business portfolio of Alton into the robotics sector. The company previously reviewed a waste battery recycling business in August as it looked for new growth opportunities. Alton plans to apply network connectivity technology from its shared electric bicycles to these new AI robots. The partnership will pair Alton's network integration and hardware skills with the precision perception and control technologies developed by XUP.

stories.Headline: Ineffable founder David Silver says superintelligence is near and urges safety work now
stories.Summary:
David Silver, a Google DeepMind veteran and founder of the neolab Ineffable, told the Slush audience in Helsinki that AI could become smarter than humans at virtually everything within a few years, and he described the arrival of superintelligence as a matter of when rather than if. He said he believes the technology is close and that people should take the prospect seriously rather than dismiss it. Ineffable has raised a $4.8bn round led by Lightspeed, with Nvidia and Google among the investors, according to the article. Silver previously led the AlphaGo project at DeepMind, the system that beat the world champion at the board game Go.

Silver said the race requires thinking hard about safety, and he argued that the field needs to work out how to keep powerful systems under control before they arrive. He described the goal as building systems that remain answerable to humans and said the industry should not treat the problem as someone else's to solve. The article says Ineffable is working on what Silver calls "magic" superintelligence, and it notes that the company has not published technical details of how it plans to achieve this. Silver also said the singularity, the point at which machine intelligence surpasses human intelligence, is just over the horizon.

Silver is responsible for leading Ineffable and for setting out its safety approach, and he used his Slush talk to call for serious work on the problem rather than slogans. He said he does not think the risks can be waved away and that researchers should be honest about how little is known. The article reports that he compared the current moment to the early days of other transformative technologies, though it gives few specifics of that comparison. He said the company's investors understand the stakes and that the funding gives Ineffable room to pursue the work.

The context is a crowded field in which several labs are racing toward more capable systems, and the article says regulators and researchers are debating how to oversee them. What happens next depends on whether Ineffable publishes more about its methods and whether the safety questions Silver raised get taken up by others in the industry. The article does not say when Ineffable expects to reach superintelligence or what specific safeguards it plans to build. More to follow.

stories.Headline: SK hynix earns SIL 3 certification for its LPDDR5X memory and development processes
stories.Summary:
SK hynix said on Nov. 11 that its LPDDR5X product and its development processes had received Safety Integrity Level 3 certification under IEC 61508, an international standard written to reduce accident risks from failures in electrical and electronic systems. The certification, announced in a report dated Nov. 13 by The Elec, extends the low-power DRAM from vehicles into robots and smart factories. The company had already obtained automotive functional safety certification in January. IEC 61508 defines four safety integrity levels, running from SIL 1 up to SIL 4, and SK hynix's chip was designed and validated to hold safety conditions in real time without interrupting system operations.

The certification lets SK hynix answer functional safety requirements from customers building real-time robotic control platforms and systems-on-chip. Earlier, the company obtained Automotive Safety Integrity Level D, the highest rating under the ISO 26262 automotive functional safety standard, for the same LPDDR5X product. SK hynix also received certification under ISO/SAE 21434 for its cybersecurity management system, which covers threat analysis, security design and verification, and vulnerability management during development and mass production of automotive memory. The article says data security has grown more important as memory is deployed in physical AI systems, because autonomous vehicles and robots act on sensor data and AI results stored in memory.

Kim Jong-hwan, vice president and head of DRAM Development at SK hynix, said that as the physical AI market takes shape it is becoming increasingly important to establish safety and security systems that comply with international standards throughout the memory development process. He said the company will strengthen its memory leadership in the physical AI market by building on safety and security capabilities validated across the automotive and industrial sectors. The article states that if cyberattacks manipulate stored data, vehicles could fail to detect obstacles and brake, while robots could move in the wrong direction and potentially cause accidents. The report does not say what SK hynix plans to do next beyond using the certification to meet customer requirements.

stories.Headline: Samsung promotes three semiconductor executives to president and keeps its dual-CEO structure
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics announced on Nov. 20 its regular executive reshuffle for 2027, involving six appointments: three promotions to president and three changes in responsibilities, about a week earlier than the late-November timing the company had followed over the previous two years. The company retained its dual-CEO structure, with Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun, head of the Device Solutions Division, and President Roh Tae-moon, head of the Device eXperience Division, remaining in their current roles. Both men will step down from their concurrent roles as heads of the Memory Business and the Mobile eXperience Business, respectively. Samsung reported consolidated operating profit of 107.4 trillion won in the third quarter, with the DS Division contributing 106.5 trillion won, or approximately $79.67 billion.

The centerpiece of the reshuffle is the promotion of three semiconductor executives who have helped strengthen the division's technological competitiveness. Hwang Sang-joon, who served as head of Memory Development and the DRAM Development Office, has been promoted to president and appointed head of the Memory Business, and he will continue to lead the DRAM Development Office alongside his new role. Cho Sang-yeon, previously a vice president overseeing Device Solutions America, has been promoted to president and appointed head of the System LSI Business, and he is expected to focus on securing new clients. Lee Jong-myeong, previously head of Process Development at the DS Division's Semiconductor Research Institute, has also been promoted to president and will serve as the DS Division's chief technology officer and head of the institute.

Jun will focus on strengthening the competitiveness of future semiconductor businesses, including foundry, in his capacity as head of the DS Division, while Roh will concentrate on developing new businesses, including robotics, while continuing as head of the DX Division and the RX Business Development Office. Choi Won-joon, previously head of the MX Business Development Office, has been appointed the new head of the MX Business, and he has served as the division's chief operating officer since March 2025 and led the development of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8. Samsung said the appointments were intended to strengthen organizational dynamism and promote generational renewal by placing executives who had driven record semiconductor performance and improved development competitiveness in key leadership positions. The company also plans to finalize and announce regular executive appointments at the vice president level and below, along with an organizational restructuring, in the near future, and it will continue its policy of promoting outstanding employees through appointments throughout the year.

stories.Headline: TSMC restricts advanced chip manufacturing for Chinese designers to comply with new US rules
stories.Summary:
Taiwan's TSMC tightened restrictions on Chinese chip designers around November 19, 2026, by suspending some previously permitted advanced manufacturing orders for those customers. The world's largest contract chipmaker limited affected clients to older technology after new US Commerce Department rules took effect on Thursday. These measures close a remaining route for Chinese firms to produce powerful AI processors, which complicates Beijing's domestic chip development efforts. The company halted orders using manufacturing processes of 16 nanometres and below unless the customers could obtain US export licences. This action follows reports that TSMC and South Korea's Samsung Electronics suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers on Thursday.

Affected Chinese designers are generally limited to 28-nanometre and 40-nanometre processes, provided they avoid advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory. The new US rules remove a compliance route that previously allowed some Chinese companies to access advanced manufacturing without individual licences. TSMC can no longer use its verification process to check if certain Chinese chip designs fall outside of US export controls. Advanced chips are now presumed to be covered by US controls, requiring export licences unless a specific exception or exemption applies. These rules reach beyond AI processors and apply to various advanced manufacturing services provided to mainland Chinese firms and designers.

TSMC stated that it will comply with the new US export rules that strip Chinese chip designers of a key exemption. The company instructed that advanced orders be halted and issued guidance requiring closer scrutiny of customers' operating locations and parent companies. TSMC will now check major shareholders, packaging providers, and shipping routes to ensure full compliance with the updated US government regulations. These checks extend to orders placed through intermediaries or overseas subsidiaries located in Taiwan, the United States, Europe, Japan, and Southeast Asia. The company is implementing these strict verification steps to align with the new requirements set by the US Commerce Department.

Chinese technology giants and independent chip designers developing alternatives to Nvidia processors are particularly affected by these new manufacturing restrictions. Most leading AI chips require 7-nanometre processes or smaller for energy efficiency, while high-bandwidth memory handles the vast data volumes. Advanced packaging is also critical because it integrates chips and memory to boost computing power for complex artificial intelligence applications. A US government list of approved chip designers includes Apple, AMD, Nvidia, and Taiwanese firms MediaTek and Realtek, excluding Chinese firms. Some Chinese AI chip designers had access to 7-nanometre technology before Thursday, though Reuters could not independently verify those specific arrangements.

The background involves China's ambition to develop domestic alternatives to AI chips designed by Nvidia and manufactured by the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. Previously, TSMC could verify the technical characteristics and computing power of certain designs to determine if they fell outside US controls. This verification process served as a loophole that allowed some Chinese designers to access advanced services without needing individual export licences. The US government maintains a list of approved designers to control who can access the most advanced semiconductor manufacturing technology. These geopolitical tensions have led to increasing restrictions on the export of high-end computing hardware to mainland Chinese technology companies.

TSMC will continue to monitor the operating locations and shipping routes of its customers to prevent the evasion of US rules. The company will maintain the suspension of advanced manufacturing orders for Chinese clients who lack the necessary US government export licences. The articles leave open whether Chinese firms will find other ways to produce chips or if other foundries will follow. It remains unclear how many Chinese designers were using the 7-nanometre process before the new rules took effect on Thursday. The reports do not specify if the US government will grant any new exceptions to the affected mainland Chinese firms.

stories.Headline: Baseten releases two open-weight decision models that top the Artificial Analysis Decision Index
stories.Summary:
Baseten released two open-weight decision models called bison-1 and groundhog-1 on November 21, 2026. These tools are built on the Gemma 4 backbone and do not write text for users. Instead, they provide calibrated probabilities for score, choice, and yes or no questions. The company designed these models to handle routing, guardrail pipelines, and ticket triage tasks.

The bison-1 model is a 31B dense model, while groundhog-1 is a 26B mixture-of-experts model with 4B active parameters. Both models increase the context window from 16k to 128k tokens and can accept images. Bison-1 scored 76 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, ranking first among 19 models. This score is one point higher than the 75 achieved by Liquid AI's d1.2-ultra.

Baseten stated that using soft labels in the training mix helped the models report uncertainty more accurately. This method resulted in a Brier score of 0.14, which is the lowest and best on the index. The company noted that bison-1 ranks first on four of six index components. They also reported LongMemEval M scores of 84.8 for bison-1 and 77.4 for groundhog-1.

These new releases join the existing Qwen-based lineup consisting of mammoth-1, elephant-1, and joey-1. Baseten describes this new pair as the first models they have built on an American backbone. The weights for both models are available on Hugging Face under MIT and Apache 2.0 licenses. Users can also access these decision models through the Baseten Model APIs.

stories.Headline: OpenAI releases GPT-Live-1.1 with standby billing for idle voice sessions
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released GPT-Live-1.1, a full-duplex voice model for multilingual conversations, in its API under the model ID gpt-live-1.1 on November 21, 2026, according to MarkTechPost. The model can listen while it speaks and follows GPT-Live-1, which reached the API on September 10, 2026, and has powered ChatGPT Plus and Pro voice since October 15. It accepts audio and text inputs and outputs, supports streaming and function calling, and does not support images, video, structured outputs, fine-tuning or predicted outputs. The release also adds standby, a cheaper billing state for idle sessions, and the model runs only on OpenAI's cloud through v1/live/sessions, with clients connecting over WebRTC or WebSocket.

Live sessions hold a 128,000-token default context window, and instructions can run up to 16,384 tokens. Standby bills idle WebRTC time at $0.02 per minute versus $0.05 active, a 60% lower rate, or $1.20 per hour against $3.00. Standby pauses inference during silence while the connection stays open, the server emits session.paused after the timeout and session.resumed when the user speaks, and the session ID and history are kept. OpenAI warns the first reply after a short utterance may be slower and says the microphone track should stay active during standby, and standby works for both GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1.

Voice sessions are billed by duration, and the GPT-Live-1 model page says billing is per second, while backend model and tool usage are billed separately. The voice model can hand reasoning and tool calls to a backend text model, and OpenAI names GPT-6 Astra for complex issues and Luna for high-volume tasks, though third-party backends also work. The Live conversations guide sets delegation.type to client or responses, where responses mode uses OpenAI models and client mode connects your own backend. Switching an existing Live session requires setting the model to gpt-live-1.1 and starting a new session.

OpenAI says the model speaks with more natural and consistent accents across languages, handles transcription, letters and numbers better, and completes tasks more reliably than GPT-Live-1. OpenAI published no benchmark scores for 1.1, so the quality gains are self-reported with no numbers. The GPT-Live family replaces the usual cascade of speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech, and OpenAI says the model reasons over incoming and outgoing audio together in a single model, handles turn detection and returns ASR transcripts natively. Outbound SIP calling reached all organizations on November 2, so phone agents are supported, and GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1 have separate concurrent-session limits that each apply across inference regions, though the 1.1 page does not publish tier numbers.

stories.Headline: Uzbekistan cybersecurity official Bekzod Muminov urges UN, UNESCO and ITU to lead global AI dialogue
stories.Summary:
Bekzod Muminov spoke at the second International Conference on Cyber Diplomacy on 19 November 2026. He is the Head of the International Relations Department of Uzbekistan's Cybersecurity Center State Unitary Enterprise. Muminov discussed the role of artificial intelligence during panel discussions at the event. He addressed how this technology affects governments and international relations. The official highlighted both the benefits and the risks of these tools.

Muminov stated that the UN, UNESCO, and the International Telecommunication Union should lead the international dialogue. He noted that nations currently have different approaches to regulation, data protection, and technological standards. He also mentioned that countries differ in their access to computing resources. These differences could lead to isolated technological ecosystems if they are not addressed. Such isolation might restrict the exchange of innovation, knowledge, and technology.

Muminov said that artificial intelligence helps governments process large volumes of information and analyze international developments. He claimed it allows for better assessment of economic risks and political risks. He also stated that the technology can improve diplomatic communication. However, he warned that it creates challenges regarding disinformation and information reliability. He noted that it can lead to cyber threats and the manipulation of public opinion.

The official argued that diplomacy must go beyond discussing technological issues to shape international rules. He believes this approach can build trust and prevent new forms of geopolitical tension. Muminov wants the development of artificial intelligence to strengthen cooperation between nations. He believes it should not become a new instrument for technological competition. He views these processes as an opportunity to strengthen positions in the international system.

The articles explain that artificial intelligence enables faster analysis of global developments for various governments. This technology is being integrated into diplomatic efforts to manage risks and communication. The current landscape is marked by a lack of unified global standards for AI. Multilateral platforms are seen as necessary to represent the interests of the international community. These platforms would provide a balanced approach to global technological governance.

The articles do not state what specific actions the UN or ITU will take next. They leave open how nations will resolve their differences regarding data protection and standards. It remains unclear if the international community will successfully prevent the rise of isolated ecosystems. The text does not specify a timeline for creating these new international rules. No further details are provided on the outcomes of the conference.

stories.Headline: Fear Erupts, AI Stocks Tank, but so Do Gold, Silver, Cryptos, Nearly Everything but Treasuries
stories.Summary:
Fear hit the markets on Friday, November 20, 2026, and during the week, and everything sold off, stocks, especially semiconductor stocks, gold, silver and crypto, everything except Treasury securities, which rallied. The Nasdaq fell 5.3% on Friday to 22,618, down 10.0% during the week, down 18.4% from its high on October 6, and down 2.7% since the beginning of 2026. The S&P 500 index fell 3.7% on Friday to 6,910, down 8.6% for the week and down 11.9% from its high in early October. Nvidia's stock plunged 14% on Friday to $125.53 at the close, down 47% from its high on October 6, and the seven-week plunge unwound all the gains since June 2024. The Cboe Volatility Index jumped to 40.03 intraday on Friday and ended the day at 35.89, after being below 20 a week earlier.

The Anthropic IPO seems to have sapped the last bit of energy out of the stock market, and its shares fell 8.5% during regular hours on Friday to $88.91, after falling through the IPO price of $85 a share during the day before recovering a bit. SanDisk fell 16.1% on Friday and was down 73% from its June high, Intel fell 8.0% and was down 64%, Micron fell 13.9% and was down 51%, Qualcomm fell 7.5% and was down 41%, Broadcom fell 12.2% and was down 37%, AMD fell 13.3% and was down 36% from its October high, and TSMC fell 9.5% and was down 35% from its October high. Silver plunged 7.4% on Friday to $41.08 per troy ounce, down 16% during the week and down 66% from its all-time high in late January, unwinding all the gains since July 2025. Gold dropped 4.0% on Friday to $3,539 per troy ounce, down 9% during the week and 37% from its all-time high, unwinding the gains since August 2025. Bitcoin dropped 14% this week to $58,761, where it had first been in March 2021, and since its peak in September 2025 it has dropped by over half.

Wolf Richter wrote in WOLF STREET that there was fear in the markets on Friday and also during the week, and that for months everyone has been talking about the end of the AI bubble. He wrote that the fear now is that it is not just idle talk anymore and that the pieces are starting to line up for all to see. He wrote that Nvidia was at the core of the AI trade and of all the circular financing, selling the shovels into the gold rush and charging more for them than its customers could afford. He wrote that to maintain its revenues, profits and stock price, Nvidia recycled these cash flows and added commitments to help fund its customers so they could afford its shovels at its sky-high prices. He wrote that this system already started unraveling a while ago and that the fear now is that it will unravel entirely.

Richter wrote that fears get exhausted after a while, the profit motive takes over, people jump back into the fray to pick up sold-off stuff, and then there is a bounce, and that there may have been enough fear on Friday to trigger that. He wrote that contrarians use a big jump in the VIX, which doubled this week, as a buy signal for at least a short-term bounce. He wrote that another indication was Friday's after-hours trading, with many beaten-down semiconductor stocks, including Nvidia, trading higher by 2% or 3% or more after hours. He wrote that even the 10-year Treasury yield, which had plunged during the day as Treasury prices jumped on the haven trade, reversed in late trading and headed higher. He wrote that "Nothing goes to heck in a straight line" is the old WOLF STREET dictum, and that we just might see a bounce in tech stocks next week along with some unwind of the massive Treasury rally.

Richter wrote that Nvidia's shares started tanking in early October even before everyone was crawling all over the company for the scandal of a lifetime that keeps spawning new scandals, and that the company is in the process of getting vivisected. He wrote that the x trillions in market value, portfolio value and 401(k) value that have evaporated during this selloff set everyone atwitter, and that on the way up those trillions appeared out of nothing and it was no big deal. He wrote that when a lot of it happens it impacts consumer spending and the economy overall. He wrote that other people have been waiting for this sell-off, cash in fist, to jump in and buy some beaten-up stuff, no matter how dubious, and that this is starting to line up. He wrote that the Nasdaq is still positive, if barely, year-over-year, and is not at the low of the year, which was in late March when it fell to 20,690 briefly before rallying massively again and setting a new high.

Richter wrote that the S&P 500 is still 1% in the green for the year and up 4.7% year-over-year. He wrote that the Nasdaq is down 2.7% since the beginning of 2026. He wrote that the semiconductor stocks had been plunging off their highs for months, interrupted by big bounces. He wrote that gold and silver had already gotten hammered for much of the year after the huge years-long rally topped off by a proper mania ended in late January. He wrote that bitcoin's drop to $58,761 marked six-and-a-half years of massive volatility to nowhere, with no interest and no dividends.

Richter wrote that we just might see that bounce in tech stocks next week, along with some unwind of the massive Treasury rally. He wrote that a dead-cat bounce allows the stock market to breathe. He wrote that fears get exhausted after a while and the profit motive takes over. He wrote that there may have been enough fear on Friday to trigger a bounce. The article leaves open where the selloff will end and whether any bounce would last.
