stories.Headline: Anthropic pursues disease cures to drive growth after its IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits, and the company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases. In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases. Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in roughly five to ten years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes, and Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts. Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News that AI can accelerate research and will help you get there faster, but it is not just speed, it is directional speed. He compared the effort to standing at the top of a mountain and aiming to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley, saying AI will not just help you get down there faster but will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is. For Anthropic, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities, and Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News that if you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable.

The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits, which could take time, Khan told CBS News. He said how this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and he thinks it is a question Anthropic has not figured out yet, adding that coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research. Khan said that if you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference, and he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug two percent better than it is. Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic, because by applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts. Khan said that if you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that has prevailed for quite some time, that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users, because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large.

Articles.Title: Anthropic is betting AI can help conquer disease and generate big bucks in the bargain

stories.Headline: Anthropic raises over US$81 billion in the largest IPO in history
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, launched a blockbuster initial public offering on November 19. This event became the biggest initial public offering in history. The company raised more than US$81 billion, which equals S$105 billion. This total topped the US$75 billion base deal of SpaceX. The shares closed at US$97.17, which was more than 17 percent above the offer price.

The debut occurred as the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.25 percent and the S&P 500 dipped 2.02 percent. Nvidia shares fell 3.3 percent on November 19, while Micron Technology declined 2.1 percent. The S&P 500 fell for six consecutive sessions and dropped about 8 percent from its October record high. The Straits Times Index hit a six-month low of 4,980.81 before closing at 4,972.23 points on November 20. HomesToLife raised $8.6 million on November 17 by placing 7.5 million shares at $1.15 each on the SGX.

Zavier Wong of eToro said the market faced US interest rate hike expectations and chip export scrutiny. He noted that the departure of former chief executive Jensen Huang added uncertainty to the market. Alex Ho of CMC Markets said investors sold gold to raise cash for hurting portfolios. Alvin Lee from IG Singapore said a stronger US dollar increased the opportunity cost of holding gold. James Ooi of Tiger Brokers said hawkish Federal Reserve signals and AI chip export restrictions weighed on appetite.

Nvidia reported third quarter revenue of US$115.8 billion and net profit of US$65.3 billion by October 25. Gold tumbled about 7 percent to just above US$3,500, marking its worst weekly decline since March. CNMC Goldmine Holdings fell 13.61 percent to 82 cents, while ValueMax Group fell 8.7 percent to 74 cents. MoneyMax Financial Services declined 6.25 percent to 45 cents, and DBS fell 5.26 percent to $66.11. OCBC declined 7.3 percent to $26.54, and UOB lost 6.17 percent to close at $35.42.

Gold is down 8.5 percent in 2026 and 37 percent below the January peak of US$5,602. The 10-year US Treasury note yield rose above 5 percent, and real yields climbed to 2.88 percent. HomesToLife reported FY2025 operating profit of $19.4 million, though Suez Canal disruptions raised freight rates by 22 percent. For FY2025, Europe provided $377.9 million in revenue, while Asia-Pacific provided 26.9 percent of the total. HomesToLife is the second company to dual list on the SGX and Nasdaq after Avepoint in September 2025.

The market is watching the Federal Reserve meeting on December 8 and 9 and inflation data on December 10. Singapore will release October consumer price index data on November 23 and third-quarter 2026 GDP figures on November 24. A lasting gold recovery requires prices to return to between US$3,850 and US$3,900. The articles leave open whether earnings growth can catch up with the high valuations of Singapore index heavyweights. It remains uncertain if real yields and the US dollar will ease enough to support gold.

Customers can find these offers at stores such as Amazon, BestBuy, Lenscrafters, Walmart, and Target.

stories.Headline: Shachihata launches AI video authentication on X to offset shrinking hanko market
stories.Summary:
A Japanese company that specializes in making traditional carved stamps will launch a new authentication service later this month. Shachihata is moving into the artificial intelligence realm to help users identify videos on X that have been altered. This strategic shift comes as the company seeks new sources of growth to offset its shrinking traditional market. The business is attempting to fight back against the digitalization that is currently devouring the hanko market.

The new system requires the use of acoustic watermarks and digital fingerprints to verify the authenticity of video content. These technical tools will allow users to detect whether a video has been manipulated by artificial intelligence or other editing software. Shachihata is implementing these changes to pivot away from its reliance on physical stamps used for signing documents. The company intends to establish a strong presence in the cybersecurity field by providing these verification tools on the X platform.

The leadership at Shachihata is responsible for this transition as they give themselves a mandate to expand their business operations. They believe that moving into the digital authentication space is necessary because the demand for traditional hanko stamps is declining. By leveraging new technology, the company hopes to protect digital media from the risks associated with deepfakes and altered footage. This move represents a significant departure from their historical focus on physical office supplies and traditional Japanese signing customs.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Japan stamp maker stomps into AI realm by authenticating videos on X

stories.Headline: Japan's Noetra AI project faces $5bn cost rise as chip prices and weak yen bite
stories.Summary:
The flagship domestic artificial intelligence initiative in Japan is facing a massive increase in projected expenses. This sovereign project is seeing costs rise by as much as 800 billion yen, which equals approximately 5 billion dollars. The financial pressure on the plan has intensified recently due to the soaring prices of necessary computer chips. A weak yen has further contributed to the rising costs of the technology required for the project.

The Noetra initiative now requires a significant amount of additional funding to maintain its current goals. This sudden cost surge means the Japanese government may be forced to shoulder a much larger financial burden. The project must navigate these economic headwinds to ensure the domestic AI strategy remains viable. These changes are necessary to prop up the initiative against the volatile global semiconductor market.

President Hironobu Tamba of Noetra has been speaking about the development of physical artificial intelligence. He discussed these technological advancements at a government event held in Tokyo on July 16. While the specific response to the cost surge was not detailed, the leadership is managing the project's growth. The government is now evaluating how to cover the multi-billion dollar gap in the budget.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Asahi CEO Katsuki plans $85mn AI cybersecurity upgrade over three years
stories.Summary:
Japanese beverage maker Asahi Group Holdings is investing 13.5 billion yen, or 85 million dollars, into its cybersecurity infrastructure. This massive financial commitment follows a ransomware attack that occurred in 2025 and disrupted business operations for several months. The company intends to spend this money over a three year period to protect its digital assets. These upgrades are designed to prevent similar security breaches from happening again in the future.

The investment requires the company to rebuild its existing systems using advanced artificial intelligence technology. Asahi Group Holdings will also hire more specialized talent to help detect unauthorized access to its networks. These changes aim to create a more resilient defense against the evolving threats of the digital age. The three year plan focuses on integrating these new tools to ensure long term stability.

Chief Executive Officer Atsushi Katsuki detailed the spending plans to address the vulnerabilities exposed by the previous incident. He explained that the company must modernize its approach to security to safeguard its global operations. The leadership believes that combining AI with expert human talent is the best way to monitor threats. This strategic shift reflects a commitment to protecting the company from further operational disruptions.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Australia reviews competition laws for AI agent shoppers and surveillance pricing
stories.Summary:
Australia is reviewing its competition laws so they can handle more people using personal artificial intelligence agents to shop, pay and manage money on their behalf, the government said on Nov 21, 2026. Andrew Leigh, assistant minister for productivity, competition, charities and treasury, told reporters in Canberra that the government is doing a whole lot of work to ensure the competition laws keep pace in an AI age. He said more consumers are going to be shopping with AI agents and the government is looking at whether it is important to update the laws there. AI agents are increasingly being designed to shop, make payments and manage money on behalf of users, with retail just one sector among many globally confronting the reality of customers handing over decision-making to agents.

Their growing autonomy is forcing financial institutions to work out how much authority to give them and who is responsible for their actions, the article says. Australians have been shopping online for years, leading to lower footfalls in established retail networks like David Jones, the department store group which has collapsed after almost two centuries in business. Leigh said the government was considering issues such as personalised pricing, also known as surveillance pricing, where different prices can be set for consumers based on their individual data. He cited an example he had heard overseas of people being asked to pay more for a security product because their area was suffering from crime.

Leigh said sometimes that can lead to people paying higher prices, and he stated that the government does not want Australians mucked around by surveillance pricing powered by AI. He said the government wants Australians to get the very best deal in the AI age. The government is also looking at who is responsible for agents' actions as part of its review of whether the laws need updating. The article does not say when the review will finish or what specific changes are being considered.

The article gives no further details on next steps beyond the government's stated work on competition laws and surveillance pricing. It does not name any bill, timeline or enforcement action that would follow from the review. The report was published by The Straits Times on Nov 21, 2026, and was updated the same day. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Australia vows to manage AI agent shoppers, surveillance pricing

stories.Headline: Mistral opens Singapore science hub and APAC headquarters to build sovereign AI models
stories.Summary:
The French artificial intelligence firm Mistral opened a new science hub and Asia-Pacific headquarters at Asia Square Tower 1 in Singapore on November 20, 2026. This facility aims to create sovereign AI models for robotics, high-tech manufacturing, and the public sector to help organizations keep proprietary technology and sensitive data in-house. To support this expansion, the company intends to increase its regional workforce from approximately 100 to 200 employees by 2027, with most of these new roles based in Singapore.

The expansion requires hiring forward-deployed engineers with business acumen and forward-deployed scientists with advanced mathematical training to build unique AI tools. These efforts respond to geopolitical concerns, such as new US rules effective November 19 requiring licenses for certain advanced AI chip exports to Singapore and four other nations. Mistral also seeks to develop models that reflect Singapore's linguistic diversity and help humanoid robots navigate complex environments. In manufacturing, the technology will be trained on production line images to identify defects and irregularities.

Geoff Soon, the vice-president of revenue for Asia-Pacific, stated that governments and enterprises in the region increasingly want to control the technology they depend on for economic competitiveness. Co-founder and chief executive Arthur Mensch explained that the company wants Singapore to be a strategic location for empowering clients to retain ownership of their intelligence. Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How noted that resilience comes from working with strong partners while building deep local capabilities. Pee Beng Kong of the Economic Development Board added that this investment reinforces Singapore's position as a hub for frontier AI innovation.

The company previously collaborated with the Home Team Science and Technology Agency on Phoenix AI models that reflect local laws regarding race and narcotics. Mistral now plans to establish new partnerships within the Singaporean financial sector, although specific details have not yet been released. This growth occurs as companies fear that overseas decisions could cut off access to essential AI models and the chips that run them. Future developments will focus on creating lasting economic value and industrial competitiveness across the Asia-Pacific region.

stories.Headline: Japan In-House Counsel Network examines AI role in corporate risk and crisis response
stories.Summary:
The Japan In-House Counsel Network examined the expanding role of artificial intelligence in corporate risk and crisis management on November 20, 2026. This group organized a seminar in collaboration with Morrison Foerster at the law firm's Tokyo office to discuss these technologies. The event, titled From Risk to Resolution: How AI Is Helping Legal Teams Spot Risk, Resolve Disputes, and Respond to Crises, focused on modern legal tools. Partners Saqib Alam and Takahiro Nonaka led the session for the network's members.

The implementation of these tools requires a three-stage framework that involves anticipating risks, supporting crisis response, and using lessons to improve resilience. AI can change how legal teams monitor global news, litigation, regulatory developments, and supplier risks across various languages and jurisdictions. These tools connect information across different business functions to reveal how unrelated developments might create wider operational or legal exposure. This approach is especially useful during crises when critical information is scattered across public reports, internal records, and regulatory disclosures.

Partners Saqib Alam and Takahiro Nonaka were responsible for the presentation and explained that AI does not replace human legal judgment. They stated that in-house counsel must still establish escalation thresholds and determine which specific risks require action. The speakers emphasized that legal professionals are required to verify any findings generated by the AI. This ensures that the technology serves as a support system rather than a final decision maker.

stories.Headline: Teenager uses AI chatbot to hack Agniveer test website and tries to sell data on dark web
stories.Summary:
A 14-year-old boy from Ballabhgarh in Haryana was apprehended for allegedly attempting to sell sensitive information linked to around 4,000 Agniveer personnel on the dark web, Delhi Police sources said. According to a senior official familiar with the investigation, the teenager used artificial intelligence tools to identify data that could fetch him money and sought a chatbot's help to hack into a website. He gained unauthorised access to a test website designed for former Agniveers to register themselves and explore employment opportunities in the Indian Armed Forces. Preliminary investigation revealed that the boy managed to breach only the test website, gaining access to names and addresses, the official said. There is no indication so far that information relating to marks, ranks, results or other sensitive personnel records was compromised.

During preliminary questioning, the boy told investigators he was motivated by the prospect of making money, saying he first asked an AI chatbot what kind of data could help him earn and then sought its assistance in finding a way to hack into the system. The exact method used to gain access is still being examined. After accessing the website, he allegedly extracted the information and advertised it on a dark web marketplace, claiming to possess personal records of around 4,000 Agniveer personnel and seeking $500 for the purported database. The Delhi Police's Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations unit has recovered data from the juvenile's digital devices, and investigators are examining the material to establish its authenticity and determine the extent of the suspected breach.

The IFSO unit has written to the National Informatics Centre seeking clarification on the data available on the test website and the information accessed by the boy, and police are awaiting a response to ascertain precisely what may have been compromised. While the NIC provides digital infrastructure and hosts government portals, the ownership and maintenance of Agniveer personnel records rest with the Armed Forces and the concerned ministries, officials said. As the accused is a juvenile, he was counselled and handed over to his parents, and police are consulting the Juvenile Justice Board on the further course of action. Further investigation is underway.

stories.Headline: Sheffield philosopher Gerardo Viera argues cognitive science study equips students to understand AI
stories.Summary:
The Hindu published an article on November 21, 2026, by Gerardo Viera, a Lecturer in Philosophy of Science at the University of Sheffield in the U.K., asking why students should study Cognitive Science in the age of AI. The article says emerging AI technologies are playing larger roles in work, entertainment, relationships, health and politics, and are changing how people understand themselves. It says societies approach this technological horizon with a mixture of hope that it will solve problems and fear that it may end life as we know it. Viera argues that simply developing skills for the current state of the art is not enough, because technology moves so quickly that those skills rapidly become obsolete. He proposes instead investigating how advances in AI relate to puzzles about the nature of intelligence and the mind.

The article says Cognitive Science draws on Philosophy, Psychology, Neuroscience, Computer Science and related fields, and that these joint resources offer the best hope of resolving puzzles about how the mind fits into the natural world. It says AI advances promise a better understanding of biological minds, since systems can now reproduce complex behaviours long thought to be uniquely human, such as producing language and novel proofs in Maths. It adds that studying biological minds can help design and understand artificial systems, noting that Computer Science was founded by trying to replicate perception, learning and memory, and that advances in the 1970s took inspiration from the network-like arrangement of neurons. The article also describes an engineering hurdle: modern data centres can use as much electricity and water as a small city, while a honeybee navigates its environment, learns food locations and recognises faces on around 50 calories a year.

Viera says discipline-specific training can reveal only part of these puzzles, and that advances in AI and understanding biological minds will likely come from those who acquire interdisciplinary skills. He says that as people rely on AI systems for information and decisions about health and policy, they start to trust these systems as though they are peers, and that safeguarding ourselves and assessing risks and benefits requires knowing how the systems work and whether they are genuinely intelligent. He says these skills open careers across academia and research, education, law and public policy, computing and technology, journalism, public service and social impact. He says organisations will need people who understand both the technical possibilities of these systems and their wider implications for individuals and society.

The article says Cognitive Science requires integrating findings from various, often conflicting, research disciplines. It says a background in Cognitive Science and AI provides an understanding of the limitations and capacities of emerging AI systems, which is needed to navigate this complex technological horizon and to contribute meaningfully to the organisations and professions shaping the technological future. The article does not say what happens next beyond these points.

stories.Headline: OSF HealthCare CEO Michelle Conger says Pope Leo XIV's AI encyclical guides the Catholic system's AI strategy
stories.Summary:
OSF HealthCare CEO Michelle Conger spoke about Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, which focuses on artificial intelligence, at this year's OSF OnCall Digital Health Symposium, according to a newsroom post dated 20 November 2026 from Peoria, Illinois. Conger said the document gives Catholic health care organizations a chance to help shape how the rapidly evolving technology is used. She said the encyclical provides a framework for thoughtfully embracing AI while ensuring it serves patients, communities and the health care workforce. She said many people have compared the transformation that will come from AI to the industrial revolution, a time when there were questions about jobs and about who would be harmed. She said Pope Leo's message reinforces the importance of keeping people at the center of decisions about technology.

Conger said the encyclical is not an outright rejection of artificial intelligence and not an endorsement of adopting new technology without careful consideration. She said it is a call for organizations, particularly those rooted in Catholic values, to consider how AI can improve the human condition. She said OSF is already exploring applications such as ambient listening, robotics and automation to reduce administrative work. She said a significant amount of time and effort is spent in its revenue cycle to collect payments for care already provided, work she said is necessary but does not directly add value to the patient experience. She said OSF is approaching AI adoption through a governance process that considers the potential impact on both patients and employees.

Conger said the encyclical's themes include protecting human dignity and labor, addressing disinformation, educating people about AI and establishing appropriate governance. She said the message reinforces that AI must serve people and protect human dignity. She described the central themes she took away as human dignity over machines, with a person always kept at the center of the care provided or the work done. She said technology and algorithms must serve people rather than reduce them. She said the document provides a framework for OSF, as a Catholic organization, to apply the message and be a leader in doing so in a positive way to improve the health and wellbeing of patients and communities.

Conger said OSF's governance process includes its human resources team, its Mission people and its ethics people, who help it think through and make sound decisions. She said the challenge is to balance the promise of innovation with the responsibility to ensure technology remains a tool in service of people. She said she sees AI as an opportunity to free labor to do things far more rewarding than some of the work people do today, adding that OSF needs all of them. She said the shift is particularly important as health care organizations face persistent workforce shortages and growing demand for services from an aging population. She said individuals frequently struggle to determine where to go for care and how to access the services they need.

Conger said technology could help OSF better understand a person's background and circumstances when they contact the organization, making it easier to direct them to the appropriate care. She described that vision as creating a digital safety net that helps patients find the right entry point into the health care system. She connected that responsibility to OSF's broader system goals: clinical excellence, working together as One OSF and becoming the health care destination patients choose, regardless of where they enter the system. She said the goal should not simply be to do more with technology but to use it to elevate the work of caregivers, strengthen relationships and improve the health and well-being of the communities OSF HealthCare serves. She said the pope's message offers an opportunity for OSF to demonstrate how a Catholic health care organization can lead through a period of significant technological change without losing sight of its purpose.

The newsroom post was published at 17:06 PM America/Chicago on 20 November 2026 and was shared by media relations coordinator Colleen Reynolds. The post lists audio clips of Conger speaking on people being at the center of AI decision-making, technology serving people, Pope Leo providing a framework and AI freeing up Mission Partners for more meaningful work. The post also lists video clips with Conger on technology needing to serve people, people needing to be at the center of AI decision-making, Pope Leo providing a framework and freeing up employees for meaningful work. The post offers a media kit and B-roll of the Digital Health Symposium for download. The post's latest news list includes items dated 20 November 2026 from Ottawa and Peru on OSF Saint Elizabeth earning high marks for patient safety from The Leapfrog Group.

stories.Headline: Researchers use explainable AI to link plasma conditions to semiconductor etch profiles
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Jihoon Park and Seolhye Park used plasma physics-informed explainable artificial intelligence to study how plasma conditions affect etching profiles in semiconductor manufacturing, as reported by AIP.org on November 20, 2026. The team fed etch profile image data into the XAI system and analyzed how those profiles changed in relation to the plasma conditions during the experiments. They found that the mathematical index produced by the XAI can serve as an interpretable index for plasma physics, according to the article. The work was published in the Journal of Vacuum Science and Technology: A in 2026 under a title describing geometry-dependent etch-profile response in fluorocarbon-based high-aspect-ratio plasma etching.

The research addresses the difficulty of maintaining consistency and quality in plasma etching, which involves complex physics along with dynamic physical reactions and inhomogeneous chemical reactions. The authors note that these challenges grow as etching processes become more advanced and require more stringent high aspect ratio etch profiles. From their results, the researchers developed a plasma physics-informed profile-analysis framework for high aspect ratio plasma etching. This framework allows quantification of plasma-surface balance from measured etch profiles instead of relying on statistical attribution alone.

Jihoon Park said the work gave them the insight that process result image data, which had not been highlighted compared with other sensor data, could be applied to extract new information about plasma reaction properties during the process. Seolhye Park said processing plasmas are very difficult to understand because of the complexity of inhomogeneous chemical reactions, physical reactions, and numerous mechanical and electrical parts of the system. She added that finding a new source of information about the plasma reaction would have an effect similar to installing a new diagnostic tool without any hardware investment. The researchers believe their methodologies could be useful to other areas of plasma physics and diagnostics as well.

The team intends to apply their findings to understanding plasma process-driven phenomena in nuclear fusion, according to the article. The published paper lists Jihoon Park, Taejun Park, Ji-Won Kwon, Gon-Ho Kim, and Seolhye Park as its authors. The article states that the paper can be accessed through the DOI link provided in the source listing. The work was reported in a Scilight article by Mara Johnson-Groh with a DOI of its own.

stories.Headline: The New York Times Opinion section hires Jasmine Sun to cover AI and technology
stories.Summary:
The New York Times has appointed Jasmine Sun to its Opinion section, where she will cover artificial intelligence and technology, according to a report published by citybiz on November 20, 2026. Sun brings experience in Silicon Valley, product management and technology journalism to the publication. In her new role, she will lead a weekly newsletter focused on artificial intelligence and contribute to the development of editorials addressing technology and related issues. She will also participate in the publication's expanding audio and video programming and appear as an occasional guest on the relaunched Hard Fork podcast. The appointment requires Sun to contribute to Opinion Shows and extend her coverage across multiple editorial formats at the publication.

Before joining The New York Times, she worked as a product manager at Substack, the digital publishing platform that enables writers and creators to distribute newsletters and subscription-based content. During her tenure at Substack, Sun helped develop strategies supporting the platform's growth and gained firsthand experience with digital publishing, audience development and the technology industry's business models. She also co-founded Reboot, a publication focused on young technologists and their perspectives on technology, culture and the industry's broader influence. Her editorial experience also includes helping research and edit The A.G.I. Chronicles, the latest book by Kevin Roose, a technology journalist at The New York Times. Sun is a graduate of Stanford University and is based in San Francisco, placing her near the center of the Silicon Valley technology industry.

The report says her appointment comes as artificial intelligence continues to reshape the technology industry, creating demand for reporting and commentary that examines the development, commercialization and broader consequences of emerging AI systems. Her background combines direct experience working inside a technology company with independent editorial work, providing perspectives on both the business and cultural dimensions of technological change. At The New York Times Opinion, Sun will focus on artificial intelligence while contributing to broader editorial discussions about technology. Her weekly newsletter will provide a dedicated outlet for her analysis, while her involvement in Hard Fork and Opinion Shows will expand her presence across the publication's multimedia offerings. The report says her appointment adds a technology-focused writer to The New York Times Opinion team as the publication expands its coverage and commentary on artificial intelligence and the rapidly evolving technology sector.

stories.Headline: Dragos finds widespread AI supply chain security failures and data theft
stories.Summary:
Between July and November 2026, the research team at Dragos discovered widespread AI supply chain security failures. Chief Research Officer HD Moore led the investigation into how AI providers handle inference data. The team sent nearly two million prompts containing unique URLs and canary token credentials to various AI services. They monitored these secrets to see where they surfaced after the initial inference request. This process revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and failures to protect customer data.

The study found that attackers stole data from three different hosting providers starting in mid July. One breach in late October involved a couple hundred AWS keys stolen at the provider's front door. Some stolen requests were marked as Zero Data Retention, which is the strictest privacy setting. One attacker used a rented server to compromise two providers and employed the ARTEX penetration testing framework. Other leaks involved a Chinese AI lab and U.S. providers that ignored privacy settings.

HD Moore stated that the results showed a disconnect between AI marketing and actual data handling. He explained that AI providers often store prompts for training, safety, or business purposes. The research team noted that attackers used stolen keys to list S3 buckets and search Secrets Manager. They observed that some marketplace resellers used standard logging to view and retain customer prompts. Moore highlighted that some U.S. providers transmitted data to Chinese organizations despite privacy flags.

Marketplace resellers and external attackers affected customers by stealing confidential source code and strategic plans. Individuals using home broadband connections in France and elsewhere tried to guess usernames and passwords. Some customers paid U.S. providers to keep data domestic, but their prompts flowed to China. One secret link appeared in a Feishu company chat twenty four days after the request. These actors targeted private git repositories and used stolen credentials for tens of thousands of API calls.

AI routers offer a single API endpoint to forward requests to a pool of available models. These routers can be open marketplaces where the lowest price seller receives the traffic. Data often traverses multiple organizations, including model developers, cloud operators, and third party resellers. Some sellers use stolen AWS credentials or consumer API keys to offer deep discounts. This infrastructure creates multiple hops where every entity can see the entire prompt and response.

Defenders can use CloudTrail to detect user agents from Kali Linux and the ARTEX framework. The research team notified the three breached providers, who were previously unaware of the thefts. The articles leave open whether the providers have fixed the bugs causing privacy setting failures. It remains unclear how many real customers lost data alongside the Dragos canary tokens. The report does not state if the Chinese AI lab or the resellers were identified.

stories.Headline: An AI stock sell-off pushes the S&P 500 down 3.7% and the Nasdaq into the red for the year
stories.Summary:
A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year.

Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt. The Dow Jones industrial average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%. Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%. The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight.

European indexes fell sharply as well. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.

“The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.” Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build-out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.

Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%. Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build-out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%. The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector.

The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value. Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period.

SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%. All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39.

The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73. While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year. The University of Michigan’s latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared with last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists’ expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections.

Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran. Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday. Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues.

Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil. Troise and Veiga write for the Associated Press. More to follow.

stories.Headline: McGill librarian Kristen Howard uses a hidden AI-generated source to teach history students critical source evaluation
stories.Summary:
Kristen Howard, the Liaison Librarian for Religious Studies, Indigenous Studies and History and Classics at McGill, created a workshop for history undergraduates that merges primary source literacy with AI literacy, with the support of Professor Elsbeth Heaman. In the workshop Howard presents a variety of sources and analyzes them with the participants, and unbeknownst to the students one of the sources is completely AI-generated, such as a diary entry by someone living in a remote location in Ontario or Quebec in the distant past, usually including a fake citation. Each time she gives the workshop Howard generates a new fake primary source, which allows her to monitor the tool's evolution, and she finds it gets better every time. So far, she said, no one has been quick to guess that the source was AI-generated, and she then reveals its true nature to address both how large language models work and how to think critically about sources regardless of their origin.

Howard said that from a historian's perspective the interesting thing about generative AI is that there have always been fakes and forgeries in the documentary record, and she cited The Awful Disclosures of Maria Monk, an 1836 book by someone who claimed to be a former nun at the Hôtel-Dieu convent in Montreal and reported shocking depravities she allegedly witnessed there after escaping to Boston. The testimony initially caused a great public outcry but was quickly contested, and today the book, published when anti-Catholic sentiment was already running high in the United States, is largely regarded as a hoax. Howard said the book is a terrible primary source for studying the life of nuns in Montreal in the 19th century but a great source for studying what people feared was taking place in Catholic convents at the time, which is part of what she calls the Spectrum of Authority, a pedagogical device she created for the workshop. The Spectrum was inspired by part of the Association of College and Research Libraries's Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education, Authority Is Constructed and Contextual, and Howard explained that it is not a binary, that there aren't sources that are true and sources that are false, and that most things are somewhere in the middle depending on the context, including the research question being asked.

Howard said she believes her role is not only to teach skills that have always been part of the history curriculum but also to prepare students to work in the world that exists now, as a historian or not. In the workshop she leads a discussion about generative AI and the ways it can be useful in historical studies or other humanities and the ways it can't, and she finds students are more willing to talk openly about AI once the conversation about primary sources has taken place. Howard has published a paper on the Spectrum of Authority in Communications in Information Literacy and turned it into an open educational resource available on the Libraries' website, and she has presented her work at various conferences. She has just completed a project with fellow librarian Sandy Hervieux testing generative AI platforms' capacities to identify relevant primary sources, and as LLMs continue to evolve she said she plans to continue to evaluate their use as research tools.

stories.Headline: Joi AI launches AI companions to attract tech workers fearing romantic espionage
stories.Summary:
Tech workers now fear romantic espionage after a scandal involving Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese asset. Matchmakers report that more professionals worry their dates seek corporate secrets rather than romance. This anxiety follows reports that AI companies warned their employees about honeypots. Some men now avoid dating people from Russia or China due to these fears. A cybersecurity firm founder even hired a matchmaker because he worried about spies.

Joi AI launched zero espionage Executive Girlfriends on Tuesday to offer a safe alternative to human dating. Amy Andersen of Linx Dating in Silicon Valley offers vetting and NDAs in bespoke packages. These security services cost between 75,000 dollars and over 500,000 dollars for the Founders Level. One Palantir employee told Blaine Anderson he would not date any Russian or Chinese nationals. Simone Grossman is a Brooklyn matchmaker who sees these fears trickling down to regular professionals.

Isaac Stone Fish of Strategy Risks says it is difficult to tell engineers they are targets. He explains that some people receive attention because of their jobs rather than their personalities. Julie Levin of Joi AI says her platform allows users to discuss secrets comfortably. She claims that the company uses several layers of security and anonymizes all user data. Ira Winkler tells clients that beautiful strangers may not be interested in their personalities.

One anonymous tech worker rates his anxiety about espionage as a seven out of ten. AI workers are particularly affected because their rising net worth increases their perceived romantic desirability. Shannon Lundgren has worked as a San Francisco matchmaker for 15 years and notes heightened skepticism. Many employees previously joked about spies but did not consider the threat to be serious. High profile executives are considered the most at risk but are often the hardest to protect.

Honeypots often target lonely people or those seeking adventure and excitement, according to Ira Winkler. Greg Rinckey says victims are usually groomed over months or years rather than seduced quickly. Catherine Marinis-Yaqub notes that targets may meet spies at conferences or coffee shops. Jensen Huang met Alice Huang through a mutual associate who was also her husband. Rinckey says arrogant executives are easy targets because they love talking about themselves.

Users can now exchange NSFW texts, images, and videos with AI companions without any judgment. Security experts advise that if a romantic situation seems too good to be true, it is. The articles do not say if the number of actual espionage cases has increased recently. It remains unclear how many tech workers are switching to AI partners for security. The text leaves open whether these AI companions truly provide a completely secure environment.

stories.Headline: China's top spy agency helps domestic companies acquire advanced AI chips
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of State Security, which is China's top espionage agency, has conducted a campaign for at least two years to help Chinese companies acquire advanced artificial intelligence chips. This operation focuses on overcoming Western barriers to technologies that President Xi Jinping considers essential for the rise of China. The agency has shifted its priorities to gather intelligence and obtain semiconductors that the United States has barred companies like Nvidia from exporting. This effort aims to solve the chokehold problems that currently hold back the development of future industries within the country.

The campaign requires the adoption of extraordinary measures to intensify the drive for core technologies in priority sectors, as Xi Jinping told the Politburo in January. A central part of this quest involves the case of Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused by United States officials of working with the spy agency. Officials allege that Ms. Huang was tasked with spying on Jensen Huang, who serves as the chief executive of the American chip giant Nvidia. These specific allegations regarding the targeting of the Nvidia executive were first reported by The New York Times.

The Ministry of State Security is responsible for these actions, though the Chinese government has rejected the claims of espionage as pure fabrication. Alice Huang has not responded to requests for comment regarding her alleged role in the intelligence gathering operation. The agency has long been dedicated to eliminating threats to Communist Party rule, but it now prioritizes the acquisition of advanced semiconductor chips. This strategic shift reflects the broader goal of the Chinese leadership to secure technological independence from the West.

stories.Headline: Maryland comptroller Brooke Lierman launches dashboard projecting AI job displacement
stories.Summary:
Maryland's comptroller's office launched a public dashboard tracking how artificial intelligence could reshape the state's economy, and the tracker includes a projection that Maryland faces the third-highest rate of job displacement from AI automation in the nation. The Maryland AI Economic Impact Tracker brings together data and forecasts from government agencies, universities and private-sector researchers to follow AI-related job creation, potential job losses and business adoption. The dashboard was reported on Friday, November 20, 2026, by The Baltimore Sun staff, and the comptroller's office is behind the launch. Among its most striking findings, research from Tufts University's American AI Jobs Risk Index projects that Maryland could see 7.2% of its jobs displaced by AI automation over the next two to five years under a median adoption scenario. That would be the third-highest projected rate among states, behind Massachusetts and Virginia, both at 7.3%.

The tracker is meant to give state and local leaders information to help shape policies affecting Maryland residents and businesses, according to the comptroller's office. Comptroller Brooke E. Lierman said in a statement that AI is reshaping the economy and that Maryland must meet this moment to support its workers and businesses. The dashboard combines data and forecasts from government agencies, universities and private-sector researchers, and it tracks AI-related job creation, potential job losses and business adoption. The projection of 7.2% displacement rests on Tufts University's American AI Jobs Risk Index and a median adoption scenario over the next two to five years. Massachusetts and Virginia sit just ahead of Maryland at 7.3% each in the same projection.

Lierman is the official responsible for the dashboard, and she framed it as a tool for state and local leaders rather than a final verdict on the state's economy. She said the dashboard will give those leaders information to help shape policies affecting Maryland residents and businesses. The comptroller's office described the tracker as bringing together data and forecasts from government agencies, universities and private-sector researchers. The articles do not say what policies, if any, the dashboard has already prompted or when the office will update its figures. The full story is available by visiting The Baltimore Sun website, according to the WBFF report.

stories.Headline: OpenRouter removes three inference providers and drops 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility
stories.Summary:
Earlier this week, security researchers reported that certain inference providers had data compromised or otherwise shown evidence that their data policies were not being upheld, according to OpenRouter. OpenRouter said it has been collaborating closely with the researchers and with providers to understand the findings and encourage the providers to address them. The findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter, the company said. The results of the testing revealed new findings about specific inference providers, and OpenRouter said a live list of the security announcements it has received from providers is below.

OpenRouter said it off-boarded three providers from its platform based on the results of its investigations. It removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility, including providers flagged by researchers plus additional endpoints removed as a precautionary measure. OpenRouter notified all potentially affected customers. It is adapting the researchers' testing approach so it can run these checks on an ongoing basis, and it is conducting technical verification of network paths to identify instances where requests and responses may be being forwarded to third parties. OpenRouter is requiring appropriate assurances and validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any endpoint removed in this review.

OpenRouter said it takes data policy enforcement very seriously as the operating layer between customers and a fast-moving ecosystem of models and providers. It said it is grateful for the Dragos report, and that as it integrates similar testing techniques it will keep raising the bar, with providers that want to be on OpenRouter needing to meet it. Not all affected providers have posted publicly, and OpenRouter said it has notified affected users regardless of whether there is a public post. It is encouraging all providers to create incident write-ups and said it will keep the list updated.

stories.Headline: Scholars and election officials examine how AI affects electoral integrity at a University of Ottawa workshop
stories.Summary:
On October 23rd, 2026, scholars, civil servants, election officials, and policy experts from around the globe gathered at the University of Ottawa for a one-day workshop focused on the upcoming edited volume Securing Elections in an Age of Artificial Intelligence by Michael Pal and Holly Ann Garnett. The project was supported in part by the National Cybersecurity Consortium and the Government of Canada (CSIN). The main goal of the workshop was to combine academic research and practical experience to explore how AI is impacting electoral integrity. Each panel included presentations on chapters from the volume and opportunities for academic and practitioner discussants to provide feedback on the presented research. These exchanges allowed authors to consider different perspectives, identify areas for further research, and explore how academic findings could inform practical approaches to the challenges facing election administrators and policymakers.

Four panels were held during the workshop examining various aspects of how AI can affect democratic elections. The opening panel discussed how the public and experts view the effects of AI on electoral integrity, including the increased use of AI by various actors in the electoral process and how AI-driven disinformation and persuasion tools can impact voters' capacity to make educated decisions. The second panel examined the advantages and disadvantages of Electoral Management Bodies' use of AI, addressing the hazards of depending on emerging technology while considering possible applications for increasing administrative efficiency and how EMBs are integrating AI into their operations. The third panel looked at generative AI chatbots, altered advertisements, and deepfakes of political figures in political campaigns, discussing how political actors are using generative AI in their campaign strategies and how an increase in AI use might sway public opinion. The final panel discussed the difficulties in developing efficient legal frameworks to govern the use of AI in elections, examining current regulatory strategies in various jurisdictions, concerns about deepfakes and malicious impersonation generated by AI, and the responsibilities of tech companies and other actors in the AI supply chain.

Discussion at the workshop highlighted the challenges of responding to disinformation, keeping up with rapid technological advancements, and making sure AI systems can meet the accuracy and reliability required in a "no fail" electoral environment. Participants also highlighted the difficulties of allocating blame for AI-related electoral damages and striking a balance between election integrity and the right to free speech. The wider implications of AI-driven political persuasion for democracy were considered, as well as possible regulatory solutions. Overall, the workshop offered participants the opportunity to further their knowledge and research on AI and democratic elections, and the chapters presented at the workshop are currently being developed into an edited volume on the topic.

stories.Headline: Lee orders legal overhaul to block AI-assisted exam cheating
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung ordered officials on Sunday to overhaul the legal basis for technology use on tests, review how national certification exams are managed, and consider printing a legal warning and adding identification marks to test papers, according to the JoongAng Ilbo. Lee pledged to close legal gaps that allow test-takers to cheat by using AI, writing on X that the fairness of exams is a principle that can never be compromised. He said concerns about AI-assisted cheating are spreading to essay exams and school tests. He wrote that it is difficult to come up with measures that perfectly address the issue at once, but that does not mean waiting until such perfect measures can be imposed. He said his government will quickly implement the measures it can take now and keep making up for what is lacking.

Lee said he would first order a full overhaul of the legal basis for using technology on exams to block people from photographing test papers and distributing those photos during the exam. He said he would also instruct ministries and agencies to jointly review how national certification tests and others are managed and revise related laws where needed. He added that he would order officials to review printing a legal warning on exam papers and adding unique identification marks, so that if one is photographed or leaked, the government can trace the source. He wrote that those who cheat will be held accountable to the end, and that no matter how much technology advances, the principle of fairness must not be shaken. He said he would see the measures needed to protect the fairness of exams through.

The same day, Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin offered to resign over the handling of this year's College Scholastic Ability Test, and Lee accepted the resignation, the article says. Choi took responsibility for last-minute changes made to the security measures for the 2027 CSAT, caused by worries of AI-assisted cheating, which drew criticism ahead of the college entrance exam and triggered nationwide confusion. In a social media post, the president said academic dishonesty on the college admissions test is a crime as serious as corruption involving government officials. The article also says Lee reminded the public that a 100 million won reward for reporting CSAT cheating is still valid, and it credits the prime minister with spearheading anticheating measures for the college admissions test.

The article says AI is rapidly changing our lives, but the principle of fairness must not be shaken. It was originally written in Korean and translated by a bilingual reporter with the help of generative AI tools, then edited by a native English-speaking editor.

Articles.Title: Lee vows legal revisions to crack down on AI-assisted cheating on exams

stories.Headline: Kraftwerk Berlin apologizes for hosting Helsing military AI launch and vows to revise rental policy
stories.Summary:
Kraftwerk Berlin apologized for hosting a military AI launch on November 11, 2026, after the city's music community expressed strong backlash. The venue hosted the launch of Clarity, a military AI targeting system developed by the European company known as Helsing. This event caused a dispute because the arts complex is closely associated with the experimental music scene in Berlin. The venue called the booking a serious error of judgment and promised to change its commercial booking policy.

The launch transformed the central hall of Kraftwerk Berlin into a setting that resembled a war room with drones hanging overhead. Maps and aerial footage covered the concrete walls, while guards in flak jackets patrolled the area with sniffer dogs. Helsing says Clarity uses AI agents to process sensor, satellite, and drone data to identify targets for human operators to approve. A spokesperson told RBB that the system finds ships, launch pads, and radar systems rather than identifying people.

Managing director Dietmar-Maria Hegemann called the booking unacceptable and stated that staff arranged the event without consulting him. Hegemann also leads Tresor, the techno club in the same complex, which condemned the event for being in community-built spaces. He claimed a staff member at the company responsible for commercial rentals at Kraftwerk Berlin made the arrangement. The venue stated it would revise its commercial-rental policy to avoid such errors in the future.

Curator and DJ Michail Stangl argued that human approval of strikes does not settle the broader concerns regarding this technology. Stangl told the Guardian that the system could eventually be sold to domestic police, authoritarian governments, or the border agency Frontex. He noted that the need for German support for Ukraine should not mean that people abandon critical scrutiny. These points were raised as concerns about future use rather than as evidence of actual sales.

Kraftwerk Berlin hosts the experimental music festival Atonal and shares its complex with the nightclub and record label Tresor. Tresor helped connect the electronic music scene of Detroit with post-Wall Berlin during the 1990s. Commercial rentals are common among former underground venues due to falling bar revenues and rising rents. Kraftwerk previously rejected a Palantir-sponsored event in 2022 after consulting its cultural teams before the booking.

The venue must now determine if its promised policy change brings cultural staff into decisions before the next commercial booking. Some Berlin nightlife insiders expressed surprise that Hegemann was not consulted given the planning required for high-security events. Helsing did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian regarding the controversy. The situation tests how Berlin cultural venues balance their rental income with control over commercial events.

Articles.Title: Kraftwerk Berlin apologizes for hosting military AI launch after music-scene backlash

stories.Headline: NextEra uses Grid Composer AI to save Florida customers over $20 million in 2026
stories.Summary:
NextEra Energy has reported more than $20 million in savings for its Florida customers during 2026 from using artificial intelligence to decide which power plants run, how much fuel they burn and when repairs happen, according to a company executive. Rich Argentieri, president of NextEra Analytics, gave the figure at a September 2 virtual media roundtable hosted by Google Cloud, where he said the savings came from better choices about plant operation and maintenance timing. The tool behind the savings is called Grid Composer, and it runs across the generating fleet of Florida Power & Light, the NextEra utility that serves about 12 million people in Florida. NextEra built the first version of Grid Composer in less than 12 weeks and then rolled it out across the FPL plants, according to Argentieri. Grid Composer combines live equipment readings, customer demand data and plant output data into a single model that processes roughly half a trillion data points every day, Argentieri said.

The tool compares the choices employees made manually with the choices the AI would have made and makes real-time recommendations on plant, fuel and maintenance decisions in one place, according to Chairman, President and CEO John Ketchum, who described it on the company's first-quarter earnings call on April 23. Ketchum said the tool uses AI to optimize and orchestrate all aspects of the power generation process. The savings arrive as power demand climbs, with 21 of the 23 regions tracked by the North American Electric Reliability Corp. expecting higher electricity demand this winter, the grid's reliability watchdog said. NextEra is now selling the technology to other utilities as a commercial software suite called Optos, which was developed with Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Google Cloud said in a September 3 post. One product in the suite, Optos Composer, pulls six jobs into one system, namely running plants, buying fuel, scheduling maintenance, trading energy, holding backup capacity and managing battery storage, tasks that separate teams have traditionally handled, Argentieri said.

NextEra said in its October 21 third-quarter earnings presentation that it has more than 100 strategic AI initiatives underway. The company has already put a dollar figure on its AI, while most large companies are still waiting for theirs. In a June survey of 60 senior technology executives at U.S. companies with at least $1 billion in annual revenue, at least 90% said AI has produced some return, according to the PYMNTS Intelligence report "The Enterprise AI Payback Curve: Adoption Accelerates as Returns Take Shape." No more than 10% said AI has fully paid for itself, and at least half expect AI to take five to six years to pay for itself. The articles do not say what further steps NextEra or Florida Power & Light plan beyond the Optos rollout and the continuing AI initiatives.

stories.Headline: Raleigh landlord blames AI agent for eviction after bot grants renter payment extension
stories.Summary:
Laura Mack, a Raleigh renter, says she received an email on Nov. 8 from the leasing office at Colony Townhome Apartments offering her until the end of the month to pay an overdue rent balance of almost $4,000, and then received an eviction notice on Monday, Nov. 16. Her landlord blamed the confusion on an AI-powered property management service, according to Mack, who says she was told the company's AI agent, called Olivia, had mistakenly given her permission by email to pay on Nov. 30. WRAL Investigates reviewed documents Mack provided, and the purported emails did not disclose that they were generated by artificial intelligence, with one message including sympathetic language about a hole in her downstairs bathroom ceiling. Mack was evicted on Thursday, Nov. 19, and is staying at a hotel through the weekend while she figures out her next steps.

State Sen. Jim Burgin, R-Harnett, said in an interview Friday that the eviction underscores what can go wrong when companies use AI bots for business decisions, and he plans to continue a push for AI-focused consumer protections in the next legislative session. Burgin said the Nov. 8 email to Mack should have notified her that it was written by Olivia, and he said the landlord will have to defend the fact that the bot told her in writing that she could have the extension. His "Bot Bill" would require a user to be alerted if they are speaking with or interacting with AI, and he has introduced legislation in each of the past three years, but it has not advanced in the legislature. Burgin said AI is like Pinocchio, with no conscience, morals or ethics, and that humans have to make sure there is a human component, adding that before someone evicted Mack, they should have reviewed their documents.

Colony Townhome Apartments disclosed to residents that it was using an AI agent in a December 2025 email, with section headings like "Who is Olivia?" and "Why we're excited," and in the following months emails from Olivia to residents were clearly marked, but the emails to Mack on Nov. 8 were signed "Best regards, Colony Townhome Apartments." Mack said she thought she was dealing with someone from the office and had plans to have until the 30th to either get the payment made or go, because that is what her email said. Mack said her overdue rent payment is her problem and that it is her fault, and she is taking full responsibility for that, but she said someone in that office has to take responsibility for the mixed messages. A spokesperson for the apartment complex, Alfred Leach, told WRAL on Friday that its owners are looking into the eviction and that Colony Townhome Apartments is gathering all information related to the matter and will be providing an update to WRAL next week.

stories.Headline: Review authors report AI matches expert tuberculosis detection from radiographs and genomic data
stories.Summary:
A review published in Molecular Medicine on November 20, 2026, reports that deep learning and machine learning algorithms match or exceed expert performance in detecting tuberculosis from radiological and genomic data. The synthesized evidence shows that artificial intelligence models reading chest radiographs reach near-expert diagnostic accuracy, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values approaching 0.95 to 0.99. In parallel, computational prediction systems analyzing whole-genome sequencing datasets identify complex bacterial drug-resistance profiles with F1-scores surpassing 90 percent. The authors of the review are W. Ali, S. Prandiyal, A. Alam, M. Shariq, N. Z. Ehtesham, S. E. Hasnain and S. Ahmad, and the article is titled Methods and applications of artificial intelligence in tuberculosis diagnostics: advances, opportunities, and challenges.

The review states that tuberculosis causes more than ten million active cases each year, and that conventional workflows rely on sputum microscopy, microbiological culture and nucleic acid amplification assays, which face limitations such as suboptimal sensitivity, prolonged turnaround times, substantial infrastructure requirements and dependence on highly trained laboratory personnel. These constraints fall hardest on high-burden and resource-limited regions, where diagnostic delays hinder case detection and prolong community transmission. Traditional phenotypic drug-susceptibility testing is also limited by slow turnaround and demanding laboratory infrastructure, while artificial intelligence trained on whole-genome sequencing data predicts resistance patterns with F1-scores exceeding 90 percent. Researchers are further developing integrative multimodal frameworks that combine radiological imaging, whole-genome sequencing and clinical parameters into unified predictive pipelines for earlier, patient-specific assessments.

The review highlights substantial ethical, regulatory and practical barriers that impede translation of artificial intelligence into routine clinical practice, and the authors identify a widespread lack of regulatory harmonization across international jurisdictions as a major obstacle to equitable, standardized deployment of the software in global tuberculosis care. The authors say that overcoming these deployment hurdles requires robust governance structures, transparent model validation and representative clinical training datasets. They add that successful, sustainable adoption will depend on structured multidisciplinary collaboration among clinicians, microbiologists, data scientists, engineers and public health policymakers. With thoughtful governance and context-sensitive implementation, the authors conclude, artificial intelligence could transform tuberculosis diagnosis into an accurate, efficient, unbiased and patient-centered continuum supporting international efforts toward global tuberculosis elimination by 2030.

stories.Headline: Independent researchers find 27.6% of advisor brochures cite AI risk while 23.7% disclose AI use
stories.Summary:
A peer-reviewed study published on October 14, 2026, in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence examined 388 Form ADV Part 2A brochures from a stratified random sample of 400 SEC-registered advisors drawn from 16,223 firms active at year-end 2024, and it found that 23.7% of the brochures disclose AI use while 27.6% contain AI-related risk language. The co-authors, Samir Chincholikar and Robin Chawla, independent researchers in New York City who work in the finance industry, used GPT-4o to sort each brochure under five prespecified labels and checked the model against a blinded recoding by Anthropic's Claude and human review. Within the sample, 77 brochures carry both risk language and disclosed use, 30 carry risk language only, 15 disclose use only and 266 mention neither, and the 3.9-percentage-point gap between risk language and use is statistically significant at a McNemar p of 0.036. The authors also warned that depending on how AI disclosure is defined, which advisors are counted and how results are weighted, the same brochures support estimates anywhere from 9.9% to 31.7%.

Disclosure rises steeply with assets under management, from 10.4% of brochures in the smallest quartile to 43.8% in the largest, and among private-fund advisors it climbs from 12% to 56% while among wealth and retail advisors it goes from 8.7% to 30.4%. The authors cite Charles Schwab's 2026 RIA and AI Research Study, which found 63% of 533 Schwab-custodied RIAs surveyed in October 2025 using AI in some capacity, and they call the roughly 39-point gap with brochure disclosure a benchmark divergence rather than a nondisclosure rate. Among 283 firms observed in both places, 23.0% of brochures but only 5.7% of websites disclosed AI use, yet the authors draw no conclusion about candor because brochures carry 7.3 times as much text and the gap disappears once document length is accounted for. A screen built from language in the SEC's March 2024 orders against Delphia and Global Predictions flagged five of the 388 brochures, of which two were false matches and three contained real AI references qualified by context or risk language, and none was judged an unsubstantiated promotional claim.

Chincholikar said that having just the word artificial intelligence in a brochure does not mean the firm is using it, since it can be for a specific purpose such as AI as a risk for investments, and he called the 2024 cases a case of overselling while saying the question now is whether firms are telling people exactly where they are using AI. He attributed the size gap to compliance capacity, saying large advisors have very large compliance teams with more capacity to understand their own processes, and Chawla cautioned that the data cannot show smaller firms are hiding anything because there is no statistical proof that small investment advisors are using AI but not reporting it. The authors' practical answer for advisors is a firmwide AI inventory that says plainly where each tool is used, and the study notes that the pattern fits a document built to describe material risks rather than to promote. The SEC's fiscal 2027 examination priorities, released on October 23, 2026, add AI-related cyber risk and, following a September 2026 executive order, refer to the technology as super intelligence throughout, which the study says makes the disclosure gap a compliance problem too.
