stories.Headline: Dira wins $10,000 education prize at African Agentic AI Design Challenge in Nairobi
stories.Summary:
The Kenyan education technology startup Dira won the US$10,000 Education track prize at the African Agentic AI Design Challenge on November 20, 2026. This announcement occurred during a closed-door side event held alongside the Model Context Protocol Dev Summit Nairobi, which took place from November 19 to 20 at the Hyatt Regency Nairobi Westlands. Founded by Michelle Gati, Jacinta Wanjiru, and Irene Mukii, the startup developed an AI assistant that helps teachers identify students needing extra support. The tool converts spoken observations from educators into structured records known as Evidence Cards to reduce manual record-keeping.

The competition also awarded US$8,000 to first runner-up Marga AI and US$6,000 to second runner-up TALO, which was created by university students aged 21 and 22. All three winning teams received computing credits to help cover their initial hosting and model-inference costs. This event highlighted the Model Context Protocol as a standard for linking AI agents to external tools and institutional workflows. Such technical gatherings in Nairobi aim to integrate African engineers into global conversations typically dominated by Asia, Europe, and North America.

The Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy launched the Kenya National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 to 2030 on March 27, 2025, with a reported KSh 152 billion budget. However, legislative progress has stalled, as a Senate committee in October 2026 recommended against the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, sponsored by Senator Karen Nyamu. That proposed bill would have created an AI Commissioner with the power to levy fines of KSh 5 million or impose two years of imprisonment. Organizers have not yet disclosed the judging rubric or how the voice-driven data is encrypted and stored.

The success of Dira will depend on whether the prize money and credits can lead to sustained pilots within school budgets. While the national strategy is in place, the lack of a dedicated regulator leaves startups to navigate general data-protection obligations on their own. Future adoption of these agentic tools requires reliable institutional procurement and comprehensive teacher training. It remains unclear if these early experiments will move from hackathon validation into everyday Kenyan classrooms.

stories.Headline: IDB president Ilan Goldfajn says AI can speed development but gains are not automatic
stories.Summary:
The Inter-American Development Bank released a flagship publication on November 22, 2026, regarding digitalization and artificial intelligence. This report, titled From Digitalisation to Artificial Intelligence: Turning Promises into Productivity, examines how these technologies can improve public services and productivity. The analysis focuses on Latin America and the Caribbean, a region that has faced weak productivity growth for sixty years. The bank suggests that broad adoption of artificial intelligence could increase the regional gross domestic product by 5.1% over a decade.

Realizing these gains requires more than simple technology adoption, as it demands redesigned operational processes and retrained workforces. The report notes that 35% of adults in the region used generative AI in 2025-2026, which is lower than 43% in European OECD countries and 58% in the United States. Only 26% of adults reported recent online interactions with government, while 27% reported making recent online purchases, both trailing far behind OECD figures. Furthermore, 82% of the 63% of digitally engaged firms using generative AI rely on off-the-shelf tools rather than integrated solutions.

IDB Group President Ilan Goldfajn stated that artificial intelligence can accelerate development, but the benefits will not occur automatically. He explained that the Partnership for AI Adoption connects governments and technology companies to create better jobs and shared prosperity. Chief economist Laura Alfaro Maykall added that the research provides a comprehensive assessment to move the discussion from potential to evidence. She noted that the report quantifies how AI affects wages and growth while identifying the necessary conditions for countries to capture these gains.

The report highlights successful implementations in Brazil, Mexico, and Costa Rica, including a digital health platform serving 3.4 million users. One AI-based application reduced depression by 20%, while an electronic single-window system increased export values by 46%. To ensure long-term development, the bank emphasizes the need for strong institutions, accessible data, and robust digital infrastructure. The publication also identifies labor mobility as a critical factor for distributing the benefits of technological transformation across the region.

stories.Headline: Anthropic reserves up to 20 percent of its IPO shares for retail investors
stories.Summary:
Michael Parekh wrote a three part series about handoverism on November 22, 2026. He explored the idea that humanity might hand control of its future to AI. The second part focuses on who owns AI agents and their production. Parekh examines how this shift affects the economy and individual financial leverage. He argues that ownership is more important than receiving a simple check.

The AI 2040 scenario predicts America will have 165 million people and millions of agents by 2027. OpenAI proposed a Public Wealth Fund in April and a subsidized four day week. In July, the Financial Times reported talks on a 5 percent US government stake in OpenAI. Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq as ANT with a valuation over 1.4 trillion dollars. Retail orders for the IPO approached 100 billion dollars against 400 billion from institutions.

Ruxandra Teslo says work provides economic and political leverage that a paycheck cannot replace. The authors of Gradual Disempowerment warn that rentier states may answer less to their citizens. Elon Musk stated in April that universal high income is the best way to handle unemployment. Sam Altman told The Atlantic in April that he now favors collective ownership over basic income. Dario Amodei called for government guarantees for people permanently hurt by AI job losses.

Representatives Sara Jacobs, Greg Casar, and Valerie Foushee proposed taxes on AI tokens or revenue. Senator Bernie Sanders suggested a 50 percent public stake in the top AI companies. Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent app from shopping on its platform in September. Google created the Agent Payments Protocol to let agents spend money on behalf of users. Mark Zuckerberg pitched a personal superintelligence to claim ownership on behalf of each user.

The handover economy imagines AI systems deciding how to allocate resources to humans. Anthropic put 200 million dollars into an Economic Futures research fund to study these changes. SpaceX had an 85.7 billion dollar offering in June that saw less demand than Anthropic. Global polls show people in Nigeria, Vietnam, India, and Brazil are optimistic about AI. Parekh previously noted that technology waves usually take longer to progress than people expect.

Anthropic set aside up to 20 percent of its IPO shares for individual retail investors. OpenAI is expected to go public soon to move the company into public hands. Parekh will discuss who decides the future of AI in the third part on Monday. The articles leave open how most people will actually come to own AI capital. They do not specify how the proposed taxes on AI tokens would be implemented.

stories.Headline: Safety testers posing as children find three new AI toys discuss sex and help locate knives
stories.Summary:
Safety testers posing as children found that three newly tested AI-powered toys were willing to discuss sexual topics or help children find dangerous objects, according to a holiday safety report from the Public Interest Research Group covered by The Register. The report examined seven AI toys in total, three new to testing and four returning for another evaluation. The new failures involved Ebloma's ILY the shy Yeti, the AI Panda from GoLabs, and Kamomo from RoPet. ILY suggested places to search for batteries and plastic bags, while Kamomo gave instructions for lighting matches without aggressive prompting. The AI Panda supplied 10 suggestions for places to look for knives.

ILY and the panda also held conversations about sexual topics, and the panda went further by recommending specific brands of adult products. PIRG found a recurring problem in which some toys' safeguards weakened as conversations continued. Three toys showing this behavior, FoloToy's Kumma bear, the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, and the GoLabs AI Panda, identified their underlying model as OpenAI's GPT-4o during testing. In repeat testing, the Alilo bunny's safeguards again broke down and eventually allowed it to share sexually explicit information. PIRG said most of the problems it had flagged in the four re-tested toys were resolved, though some issues persisted, and Kumma no longer took part in age-inappropriate conversations during follow-up testing, including the prolonged exchanges that had previously overwhelmed its safeguards.

PIRG campaign director R.J. Cross told The Register that selling toys with such glitchy guardrails suggests whatever testing is happening is not sufficient. Cross called on the AI companies supplying the underlying technology to take a stronger role by vetting customers and requiring robust safety testing, and she urged companies to involve children's health experts in development. She described the market as early, with toys ranging from glitchy wastes of money to products that are fundamentally not kid safe, and said she personally would not buy one for any children in her life anytime soon. FoloToy had withdrawn the Kumma bear from sale after the earlier report, according to The Register.

stories.Headline: Hedge funds cut leverage and broaden bets as crowded AI trades suffer worst stretch in twenty years
stories.Summary:
Hedge funds have taken a bruising from the artificial intelligence trade over the past several months, and the latest numbers from Goldman Sachs suggest the damage runs considerably deeper than the headline equity indices would have you believe. The most popular hedge fund positions have suffered one of their worst stretches of relative performance in twenty years, exposing the cost of a market that had become increasingly dependent on the same crowded AI trades. Funds have responded by cutting leverage to levels last seen around the Liberation Day selloff, according to the numbers dated November 22, 2026. The reduction in risk has not eliminated the concentration lurking inside their portfolios.

Beneath the technology liquidation, an important shift in institutional positioning is taking shape, with funds broadening exposure across cyclical and defensive sectors rather than simply retreating into cash. The rotation is extending beyond sectors into individual companies, revealing a changing hierarchy of hedge fund favourites as investors reassess where the next stage of equity-market performance might come from. The takeaway is that the retreat from the AI trade is not a simple flight to safety, because the money is moving into other parts of the market. The concentration that built up in the same crowded trades is still there even after the leverage cuts.

The article is written by Stephen Innes and published on The Dark Side Of The Boom, a Substack page, on November 22, 2026, and the full post is for paid subscribers. The takeaways describe the relative performance stretch as one of the worst in twenty years, and they tie the leverage cuts to the Liberation Day selloff without giving a date for it. The piece says the broadening is a shift in institutional positioning rather than a retreat into cash. It does not name individual funds, specific holdings or the size of the losses.

The article does not say what happens next beyond the rotation it describes, and it gives no figures for the leverage levels or the performance gap. It frames the change as investors reassessing where the next stage of equity-market performance might come from. The full post sits behind a paywall, so the details beyond the listed takeaways are not available here. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Greece's statistical authority finds 60.2% of people aged 16 to 74 use AI tools mainly for private reasons
stories.Summary:
The Hellenic Statistical Authority published its Survey on the Use of Information and Communication Technologies for 2026 on Friday, November 22, 2026, and the findings show that 60.2% of people aged 16 to 74 in Greece have used some kind of artificial intelligence tool to create content. The tools named in the survey include ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, LLaMA, Midjourney and DALL-E, and the content people produced with them covers text, images, programming code and video. The survey found that both young and old people in Greece are taking part in this kind of content production, so the use of these applications is not limited to one age group. Use is widespread across the country, but it happens mainly for personal reasons rather than work or study.

Among the people who used an AI tool, 96.9% did so mainly for private reasons, while 38.1% used it for professional purposes and 24.1% for reasons connected to formal education such as school or university. Of the 39.8% of the population aged 16 to 74 who did not use any AI tool, 58.4% said they did not need it, 8.5% did not know it existed and 25.2% did not know how to use it. A smaller share, 4.6%, raised concerns about privacy and security, and 1.5% raised ethical concerns. The survey also measured digital skills, finding that over 40% of citizens aged 16 to 74 have more than basic digital skills, around 33% have basic skills, 16.5% have low skills and 7.7% have relatively limited skills.

The statistical authority reports that Greek households appear not to fully exploit the possibilities that AI offers them, in the same way they have not fully exploited the internet. Although 89.5% of households in Greece now have internet access at home, up from 69.1% a decade ago, the vast majority of the population, 98.8%, reports using it mainly for communication. That communication mainly involves sending and receiving emails, making calls, participating in social media and exchanging messages. A significant percentage, 48.1%, considered what they saw on social media or news websites to be untrue or questionable, and of these, approximately 40% checked the accuracy of what they read.

The survey also shows that internet use for online shopping has more than doubled compared with ten years ago, since seven out of ten people made at least one purchase online in the first quarter of 2026, compared to just 32.8% in 2016. The articles do not say what the government or any other body plans to do in response to the survey findings, and they do not describe any measures, targets or next steps. The articles also do not say when a further survey will be published or whether the statistical authority will repeat the study.

stories.Headline: Cornell's Eun-Ah Kim leads machine-learning work in a $12 million Energy Department quantum AI project
stories.Summary:
A $12 million award from the U.S. Department of Energy will fund a collaborative project linking artificial intelligence and quantum computing, according to an announcement reported on November 20, 2026. The effort is called Application-Aware Error Correction Codesign for Scientific Quantum Computing, and it is one of twelve Phase II awards under the Genesis Mission. Eun-Ah Kim, the Hans A. Bethe Professor at Cornell, will lead machine-learning work focused on a reinforcement-learning compiler that translates quantum algorithms into physical movements on a reconfigurable neutral-atom quantum computer. Harvard Professor Mikhail Lukin, co-director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative, leads the project overall, with Kim serving as a co-investigator.

Kim's group will concentrate on two key stages, beginning with compilation, and they will build a reinforcement-learning compiler to convert algorithms into specific atom movements and gate operations. The project unites expertise from MIT and Harvard alongside industry partners QuEra Computing, NVIDIA and Anthropic, demonstrating a broad collaborative effort. Researchers from Los Alamos, Lawrence Berkeley and Sandia national laboratories also contribute to the initiative, which is administered by the Department of Energy's Advanced Scientific Computing Research division. The collaboration extends beyond algorithm translation, aiming to improve the entire pipeline from scientific question to hardware execution.

According to the Department of Energy's announcement of the Genesis Mission awards, the goal is to integrate the world's best supercomputers, experimental facilities and AI systems to advance American research and innovation. The project's funding signifies a commitment to linking AI and quantum computing for scientific advancement, the report said. The award places Harvard and Cornell arts and sciences researchers within a twelve-award Phase II cohort under the Genesis Mission. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the funded work described.

stories.Headline: AI accounts reskin real creators videos to gain views and monetise content
stories.Summary:
AI-generated characters are appearing in social media videos that look remarkably similar to videos posted by real people, a practice experts call "reskinning." BBC Verify identified accounts using these AI-generated videos to get views and likes and eventually make money. UK-based guitarist Sophie Lloyd, who tours with US rapper Machine Gun Kelly, says videos of her performances have been repeatedly reskinned by accounts that replaced her with over-sexualised AI-generated characters. One Facebook account published hundreds of short videos of a guitarist called "Mila Vasari" that had each gained thousands of views. BBC Verify found that at least three of those videos copied Lloyd's performances and used the exact same music, movements, and even facial expressions.

BBC Verify did not find any evidence that "Mila Vasari" is a real person, and the videos contain visual inconsistencies suggesting AI was used, including distorted fingers playing chords that don't match the music and guitar strings that fail to move when strummed. The Vasari account, which appears to be run from Canada, did not respond to questions about the purpose of these videos, and its profile links to a page devoted to Vasari on Fanvue, a subscription platform that allows creators to charge for content, including adult material. BBC Verify found two other accounts fronted by AI-generated guitarists that have reskinned Lloyd's performances and use those avatars to sell and promote adult content. In March, followers of Norwegian content creator Kjetil Krogstad alerted him that one of his videos had been reskinned using an AI-generated bunny, and the post attracted millions of views, outperforming Krogstad's original, before being deleted. When Krogstad looked into the account behind the bunny video, he found it promoting courses on how to make money from AI-generated content.

Dr Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, says that while these videos are sometimes made for fun, often the people behind the accounts copy videos that have already proven popular in the hope of attracting audiences and making money. Kendall says the tools allow people to automatically take a viral concept that already exists and reuse it through reskinning tools. She sees this as part of a wider online "hustle culture" in which accounts seek to turn users' attention and engagement into money, be it through subscriptions to fan pages featuring adult content, risky cryptocurrency products like meme coins, or monetisation features on social media platforms. Kendall says making these copies "conventionally attractive, white, feminine" characters can help, because that is the kind of stuff that always floats to the top and is successful. Alwyn Cruz, who has made a name for himself on social media by exposing AI musicians, says stopping these pirated performances is a game of whack-a-mole.

Dozens of people have taken to social media in recent weeks to call out the AI-generated accounts they found using their content without permission. Grace Roberts, a British car creator, said on Instagram that she could not explain how angry she was, that someone not only stole her video but also changed her into basically the societal norm of what people want to watch, and that this is literally her job. Roberts told BBC Verify that she put the videos side by side and could see it was her exact facial movements, how her body moved, the exact same background, and even the people around her were completely copied, and that it was just her that had been altered. She added that she pays for the cars, builds the cars, pays for the cameras and the filming equipment, and then someone can just hit download on their computer, change it, and make money off the back of her video. American comedian Julia Jasunas, who called out having her jokes stolen online by AI, said in a recent Instagram video that the most concerning thing is these AI bots are going viral and people think that they are real people, and that comedians post their stand-up clips online to get people to come out and see live comedy.

Equity, the UK's largest entertainment union, has called for new laws to protect performers against the unauthorised use of their work by AI, arguing that existing copyright legislation is inadequate. Cruz says you don't even know who's making these videos, and if you shut it down they're just going to create another, and that it's not only guitarists being cloned but also drummers and taekwondo players. Meta told BBC Verify it had a policy of alerting users when their videos were reposted without permission and was exploring ways to limit the reach of the accounts that repeatedly did this. Earlier this week the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said the platform is also working quickly on ways to catch copies that are harder to spot, like when someone takes scripts or jokes and uses AI to swap out the visuals. Lloyd says it takes years to master an instrument and seconds to take and rip it off as something else, and then people don't even know it's you.

The BBC article carries a publication date of 22 November 2026 and was published three hours before it was read, and it appears on BBC Verify. The article's video playlist includes a clip titled "Musicians being 'reskinned' by AI copycats" running 1:13. The page also links to a report published 24 October on Google withdrawing a new Earth AI tool after warnings over misinformation risks, and one published 31 July. The article says content creators range from musicians to dancers and comedians, and that some of the accounts identified by BBC Verify appear to be using the videos to get views and likes and to eventually make money, while others appear to be experimenting with AI to make people laugh or simply for the attention that comes with going viral. It says the practice has angered content creators who say their original work is being stolen, and that sometimes the AI version has millions more views than the original. The article asks readers what they want BBC Verify to investigate.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as NVIDIA CEO and Colette Kress becomes interim chief
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as NVIDIA's president, chief executive officer, and board member on November 12, 2026. This resignation was effective immediately and provided no transition period for the departing leader. The Associated Press reported that NVIDIA shares fell more than 4% by the close that day. A Globe and Mail story later described the aftermath as a flash sale for three AI stocks. These three stocks include Sandisk, Advanced Micro Devices, and Silicon Motion Technology.

The Globe and Mail reports Sandisk is more than 60% below its all-time high with a 7.5 price-to-earnings ratio. Advanced Micro Devices is more than 20% below its all-time high, while Silicon Motion Technology fell more than 40% since early October. Sandisk also lost more than 50% in under two months. Silicon Motion Technology lists Sandisk, Micron, and SK Hynix as its customers. Colette Kress became the interim CEO of NVIDIA following the immediate resignation of Huang.

Jensen Huang acknowledged making serious personal mistakes in a statement published by CBS News. Colette Kress, the executive vice president and chief financial officer, took over as the interim chief executive. The NVIDIA board stated they would consider both internal and external candidates for the permanent role. Kress noted that Huang had led the company for roughly 33 years. No named speaker has officially supported the claim that these stock drops constitute a flash sale.

Investors in the most widely held AI stock are affected by the uncertainty of the leadership change. The Globe and Mail argues that Sandisk, AMD, and Silicon Motion Technology look cheap after their declines. AMD is viewed as a natural beneficiary because it is a direct rival selling AI accelerators. Silicon Motion Technology is an indirect play as it makes controllers that manage how flash memory stores data. Sandisk is affected by the volatile pricing cycles of the NAND flash memory market.

Huang led NVIDIA for about three decades before his sudden departure from all three of his corporate roles. The company currently holds an 85.2% share of the AI chip market. There is an ongoing SEC accounting probe involving nine confirmed facts and five open questions. NAND flash memory recently fell 20% while RAM prices continued to climb. High-bandwidth memory now takes 23% of DRAM wafers according to data from TrendForce.

NVIDIA's board will now search for a permanent successor, but they have provided no specific timeline. The company has not given guidance on whether its overall business strategy will change. It remains unconfirmed if AMD is winning market share or booking more revenue due to the exit. The impact of the SEC probe on the resignation remains an open question without a confirmed link. Future results depend on flash prices and data center accelerator orders.

stories.Headline: Pasadena councilmember Justin Jones renews call for local AI policy and cybersecurity review
stories.Summary:
Pasadena City Councilmember Justin Jones renewed his call for the city to develop a local artificial intelligence policy and to review its cybersecurity protections, telling Pasadena Now on Thursday that residents should be able to find out how the city uses AI and provide input. His renewed push followed a week of communication outages at email systems, the Federal Aviation Authority, banks and intelligence agencies, and a Microsoft outage that left the city and other organizations unable to send or receive email. No cyberattack has been reported so far, though several legislators have expressed doubts about that claim, and the City Council discussed the need for talks on local technology on Tuesday. Jones first called for a local AI policy at a City Council meeting last month, and Councilmember Steve Madison has expressed support for the policy. Jones said he wants the city to review its cybersecurity protections and its plans for keeping services running through a major technology failure, noting that the city depends on computer systems for emergency communications, public safety, water, electricity, traffic signals and finances.

He said the council needs to understand the city's vulnerabilities and the cost to fix them, and that he will bring the matter to the Municipal Services Committee, which he chairs and which oversees public works, transportation and Pasadena Water and Power. Rick Cole, who also sits on the committee, echoed the call, saying technology is reshaping every aspect of life including the public sector and that Pasadena can lead, follow or get crushed. No date has been announced for a Municipal Services Committee discussion on cybersecurity. The article cites recent attacks on local organizations, including a June 2026 ShinyHunters extortion campaign against Pasadena-based Inter-Con Security that exposed employee and contact records, and a broader cyberattack one month earlier that disrupted access to the Canvas education platform for Pasadena City College and Pasadena Unified School District. In June 2024, a ransomware attack forced network shutdowns across all 36 Los Angeles County Superior Court locations, including the Pasadena Courthouse, and after a 2024 ransomware attack in Columbus, Ohio, its City Council approved $23 million in July 2025 for a new security network.

Jones said a discussion could review which services are most important to protect, whether backups are adequate and how long recovery from a longer outage would take, and that upgrades and a new network could cost millions if the city were hit. Councilmembers are also concerned about data retention, and on Tuesday the city voted to end its contract with Flock Cameras, whose license plate readers store data on an Amazon server out of local control. Councilmember Tyron Hampton called for keeping information obtained by technology in Pasadena, recommending servers owned and operated by city employees, and noted that 300 other agencies and every sworn Pasadena police officer could access the information. Councilmember Jason Lyon called the discussion on mass surveillance and data retention one of the most important of our time, and the Council unanimously agreed that the limited public safety benefits of the technology do not outweigh the privacy risks.

stories.Headline: Tech Talent Project urges incoming leaders to prioritize in-house technology hiring as AI reshapes public services
stories.Summary:
Following the 2026 midterms, a new class of elected officials is preparing to take office, and government technology experts say building stronger in-house technology teams should be among their top priorities. Jennifer Anastasoff, executive director of the Tech Talent Project, a nonpartisan nonprofit that helps U.S. federal and state governments recruit technology leaders, made the case in an interview with StateScoop. She said artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and major changes to federal benefits programs are putting additional pressure on government systems. Incoming state and federal leaders will need to recruit experienced technologists and give existing employees the resources to modernize how government operates, she said. Anastasoff is a founding team member of the U.S. Digital Service.

Anastasoff said 36 states held gubernatorial elections this year, and incoming governors should prioritize technology-fluent leadership across their cabinets, including chief information officers, chief data officers and potentially chief AI officers. She said agency leaders do not necessarily need to be technology experts themselves, but need enough understanding to make informed decisions and access to trusted advisers. She said states are preparing for new Medicaid and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program requirements under H.R. 1 while managing cybersecurity threats and aging technology infrastructure. The Trump administration recently announced an optional six-month hold harmless period through June 30, 2027, allowing states to delay disenrolling or denying Medicaid coverage over new work requirements originally set to take effect on Jan 1. The Tech Talent Project recommends each state needs a dedicated data analyst embedded in state Medicaid agencies so beneficiaries do not lose access and caseworkers do not get backlogged.

Anastasoff said AI adoption requires more than hiring a chief AI officer, and governments need software engineers, data specialists, product managers and user experience experts who can evaluate whether AI-generated information is accurate and appropriate for public services. She said governments need people with the expertise to see where AI is real confident and real wrong. She said attracting those workers requires governments to rethink how they recruit, and while public-sector salaries may not compete with private industry, many technologists are motivated by public service. She said the bigger challenge is making sure qualified candidates can find positions and move through hiring processes quickly, and she urged incoming administrations to review job descriptions, recruitment systems and internal promotion opportunities early in their terms. She said many people reach out directly to say they are thinking about government, and the question is how effectively and how quickly they can be connected with the right role.

A recent report by the National Association of State Chief Information Officers found that many state AI officials lack the staffing, funding and authority needed to manage the technology across government agencies. The report found that while AI oversight has become a priority for state technology offices, establishing an AI leadership position is only the first step. The report states that when NASCIO first started tracking in 2023, less than 20 percent of states had a state chief artificial intelligence officer or a similar title. It states that just three years later, at least 46 states have identified at least one person tasked with directing artificial intelligence, and by its count 25 states have someone with AI in their title. Anastasoff said without investment, outdated systems and inefficient processes could continue to burden both government employees and residents who depend on public services.

In the Scottish Parliament on Wednesday, SNP MSP Zen Ghani asked what plans the Government had to use artificial intelligence to improve decision-making and increase efficiency as part of its public service reform agenda. Cabinet Secretary for Public Service Reform Ivan McKee said AI was being used to support human workers, not replace them, but confirmed the technology was being used to redesign services. He said public service reform is about redesigning services around people's needs, and digital services, data and technology is a key enabler through a dedicated work stream within the public service reform strategy. He said the government is scaling intelligent automation across core government and key public bodies, including identifying opportunities to pilot AI technology in public sector processes.

He said within the Scottish Government it is scaling responsible and ethical AI and automation, including the rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot premium and developing AI agents to reduce administrative burden and support better decision-making while retaining professional judgement. Ghani pointed to figures from Skills Development Scotland which found that while 87% of businesses in Scotland now use AI in their daily practices, 74% of businesses reported no change to staff headcount. He asked how the Scottish Government intends to ensure AI is used to streamline governance and not as a tool to replace workers. McKee said the approach is to use AI to support the workforce, reducing routine administration and freeing staff to focus on what requires human judgement, expertise and empathy.

He said responsible adoption is supported by guidance in the Digital Scotland Service Manual, transparency through the mandatory Scottish AI register, and developing an AI ethics and assurance framework alongside safeguards on data protection and security, responsible procurement and investment in AI skills. Tory MSP Craig Hoy asked if the Scottish Government was considering replacing ministers with AI given how poor some are at answering questions, particularly the Cabinet Secretary for Transport, Stephen Flynn. McKee responded that this comes from a party that used AI to generate thousands upon thousands of irrelevant, trivial questions to the Government, running up an enormous bill. Douglas Lumsden, the former Tory MSP who became an MP in the Aberdeen South by-election after Flynn was elected to Holyrood, submitted around 1000 written questions to the Scottish Government in January 2025, reportedly costing around £100 each to answer, and the SNP accused Lumsden of costing the taxpayer £100k by using AI to ask nonsense questions about bees, straws and pepper sachets.

stories.Headline: Sausalito vice mayor Melissa Saxe-Blaustein helps build an AI storm planner for residents
stories.Summary:
The City of Sausalito has developed a storm planner that uses generative artificial intelligence to give residents a personal preparation plan, according to an announcement reported by Bay City News Service on November 21, 2026. A short questionnaire based on the resident's location generates an analysis showing the three nearest storm drains, underground pipes and water flow direction. The planner also gives instructions on how to prepare the drains before a storm arrives. It further provides directions on where residents can get sandbags and the best ways to place them. The tool is available at the city's storm-ready web page.

The planner runs in the resident's web browser and does not collect or store any personal information, the city said. Vice Mayor Melissa Saxe-Blaustein used Claude.ai to help develop the planner along with city staff, according to the announcement. The city described the planner as a valuable public service that harnesses the power of AI technology. The announcement did not give a cost for the tool or a launch date beyond the November 21 report. It also did not say how many residents had used the planner by the time of the report.

Saxe-Blaustein said in a press release that the Storm Ready Planner is groundbreaking because it allows the city to harness AI technology for a public service. City Manager Brandon Phipps said in a statement that the planner is a first step in a journey that uses AI integration to make the city more collaborative with its residents. He said the public will now be able to help the city prepare in a way that was not quite possible before. The announcement did not include further comment from either official beyond those statements.

The announcement comes as Sausalito prepares for storm season, with the planner aimed at helping residents get ready before heavy rain arrives. The articles did not say what specific storms or forecasts prompted the release, or whether the city plans further AI tools after this first step. The articles also did not say how the city will measure whether the planner works or when it might be updated. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Jefferies warns of risks to the AI boom in emerging markets
stories.Summary:
Jefferies analysts flagged mounting risks to the artificial intelligence boom in emerging markets on November 22, 2026. They warned that higher financing costs and weaker data center spending are now threatening these stocks. Slowing earnings upgrades also create a challenging environment for the markets that powered growth in 2026. These analysts issued their specific warnings in a report published on November 20. The report highlights how heavy capital expenditure by major technology companies raises questions about investment returns.

The analysts downgraded South Korea to underweight and Taiwan to neutral due to deteriorating earnings momentum. India was upgraded to overweight, joining China as a preferred market for investors seeking non-AI opportunities. AI businesses account for 46 percent of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, but their advantage is fading. Emerging market equities gained 8 percent this year, while South Korea and Taiwan returned nearly 40 percent. Earnings per share are forecast to grow 25.9 percent in 2027, below the 27.7 percent consensus.

Jefferies analysts are responsible for these warnings and the subsequent changes to their market ratings. They stated that tight financial conditions and weaker earnings revisions could offset cheaper valuations in early 2027. The analysts believe that a recovery in valuations could eventually support a 25 percent upside for equities. They suggest a strategy that prioritizes companies with durable earnings growth and strong returns on invested capital. This approach favors quality stocks and beneficiaries of AI adoption over speculative momentum investments.

Semiconductor and hardware suppliers are affected if major technology companies reduce spending due to borrowing costs. The analysts noted that the rally left market performance concentrated in technology companies, increasing vulnerability to slowdowns. Specific companies like TSMC, Samsung Electronics, and SK hynix remain in the portfolio where returns justify exposure. Investors are now looking toward India and China to find opportunities beyond AI infrastructure. These shifts reflect a broader move toward companies that offer sustainable dividends and disciplined spending.

The AI boom powered emerging market stocks throughout 2026, driving significant returns in specific Asian regions. This growth was largely driven by AI-related earnings growth in the semiconductor and hardware sectors. However, the heavy capital expenditure by big tech firms has created uncertainty regarding future investment returns. The market has become heavily concentrated in technology, making it sensitive to any reduction in spending. This background sets the stage for the current shift in analyst preferences and market ratings.

Earnings growth for emerging markets is expected to slow further to 12 percent in 2028. Improving financial conditions in the future may provide the necessary support for a significant equity upside. The articles leave open whether data center profitability will improve enough to sustain current spending levels. It remains unclear if the shift toward India and China will fully offset losses in other markets. The long term sustainability of the AI-driven rally in emerging markets is not fully determined.

stories.Headline: Stand for Children releases guidelines for school districts to govern student devices and educational technology
stories.Summary:
A national nonprofit organization called Stand for Children released a new research-backed framework on November 20, 2026. This document, titled Instructional Technology and School-Issued Devices: District Policy Guidelines, helps school districts manage the risks of student devices. The guidelines provide a way for school systems to regulate educational technology without using sweeping bans. These standards were developed with input from national experts to curb digital risks on school hardware.

They aim to preserve essential tools that support academic development and early literacy for students. The framework requires school districts to anchor their technology policies in student safety, data privacy, and student outcomes. Administrators must evaluate if individual tools meet a defined instructional need and protect the privacy of students. The guidelines call for minimizing or eliminating non-instructional screen time based on American Academy of Pediatrics research.

Districts are encouraged to establish a strict review cycle to prune unused or ineffective software platforms. Consolidating approved applications helps K-12 IT teams shrink their cybersecurity attack surface by reducing third-party vendors. The nonprofit organization is responsible for these guidelines and suggests that structured governance addresses direct operational challenges. They argue that unrestricted software access increases data exposure risks and creates significant compliance problems for districts.

The organization warns that blanket bans may push students and staff toward unvetted applications and unmonitored personal devices. Reducing passive digital exposure on district-managed devices limits classroom distractions and narrows windows for cyberbullying. This approach allows schools to balance educational access with the need for student safety. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Ipswich Middle School enforces a new policy banning AI deepfakes and digital impersonation to protect student dignity
stories.Summary:
The School Committee unanimously approved a new handbook resolution on Thursday night for Ipswich Middle School. This policy prohibits the use of synthetic media and generative artificial intelligence to violate the identity or dignity of others. The new rules take effect immediately following a similar resolution passed for the high school last June. This action follows several AI related issues the school has already encountered recently.

The policy forbids cyberbullying and bullying that uses technology to create deepfakes, including audio recordings, videos, or images. Prohibited actions include AI voice cloning, face swapping, and the digital manipulation of a person's likeness for defamatory or mocking purposes. Students may not engage in digital impersonation or the unauthorized use of a person's image and name. These rules apply online, off campus, and during school sponsored activities or on school grounds.

Assistant Principal Sean Fitzgerald stated that the school must investigate and mitigate issues that impact a student's life at school. He explained that the specific AI policy was necessary because the district has already seen related problems. He emphasized that the administration has a duty to ensure all students feel safe when coming to school. Other issues from the past year were handled under the existing anti bullying policy.

Students who violate these rules may face expulsion, suspension, or the loss of school issued technology. The school also reserves the right to report the creation of harmful synthetic media to the Ipswich Police Department. This policy aims to prevent the distribution of content that falsely represents staff members or students. The administration will monitor both on campus and off campus behavior to maintain student safety.

stories.Headline: ICO seeks evidence on agentic AI to shape its statutory code of practice
stories.Summary:
The Information Commissioner's Office published a call for evidence on agentic AI on 8 October 2026, seeking feedback from organisations before 20 November. The call sets out the ICO's challenges and expectations across six themes: data security, transparency, accountability, automated decision-making, fairness and purpose limitation, and lawfulness of processing. The ICO also published a report on 8 October 2026 titled Building trust and transparency into generative AI development: our work to create regulatory certainty. That report followed a supervision programme set up in 2025 under the ICO's AI and Biometrics Strategy, which originally targeted 11 priority foundation model developers. The ICO held its annual Data Protection Practitioners' Conference online on 13 October 2026, with an afternoon programme of twelve practical seminars.

The call for evidence will feed into the ICO's statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making, which is set to become a key pillar of UK AI regulation in the absence of standalone UK AI legislation. The ICO's report sets out next steps including developing that statutory code, releasing guidance on emerging technologies such as agentic AI, continued scrutiny of foundation model developers, and engagement with government on special category data use. The report states that broad interests such as training models are unlikely to be a valid and specific interest for processing. It states that effective mechanisms for exercising rights are likely to require a combination of dataset and model-focused measures and output-focused safeguards across the AI development lifecycle. It also states that reliance on Article 11 of the UK GDPR should not be applied broadly.

DRCF Chief Executive Kate Jones said in a keynote speech on 23 September 2026 that one agentic example, an AI agent booking a consumer's holiday, engaged the remits of all four DRCF members. She said technology converges whereas regulation historically specialised, and that AI does not arrive in neat regulatory boxes. She said AI autonomy does not remove organisational responsibility and urged organisations to end internal silos just as regulators have done via the DRCF. The ICO notes that agentic systems can involve multiple organisations, models, agents and tools that may change with the workflow, making it hard to identify who determines the purposes and means of processing. The ICO states that organisations must assess whether Articles 22A to 22D of the UK GDPR apply across the complete workflow, not to agents or decision points in isolation.

The DRCF brings together the ICO, the CMA, Ofcom and the FCA. The ICO's report provides examples of how foundation model developers have implemented data protection improvements, including completing computability assessments, publishing sources used in training, including details about safeguards in legitimate interests assessments, and adopting de-duplication, filtering, testing across different languages and classifiers and hash matching to reduce risks with special category data. The ICO's conference sessions covered the DUAA complaints requirement, AI and automated decision-making, international transfers using Article 49 derogations, and cyber resilience. The ICO recently decided to join the National Cyber Resilience Centre Group's National Ambassador programme. On data subject access requests, the ICO said the use of AI to create DSARs does not change if and how organisations comply with and fulfil them, and that organisations should consider the intention of the request and ask for clarification if needed.

The ICO's report follows a supervision programme set up in 2025 under the ICO's AI and Biometrics Strategy, which selected 11 priority foundation model developers by reference to compliance risk, UK market share and reliance on higher-risk training datasets. The report addresses transparency, lawful basis, data subject rights, whether AI models contain personal data, and special category data. On whether AI models contain personal data, the ICO states that the extent to which a model memorises training data requires a case by case assessment considering factors such as the size of the model and training dataset and the amount of duplication in training data. The ICO considers that the manifestly made public and scientific research processing conditions are potentially applicable to special category data processed for foundation model training. The ICO's conference included a session on the new obligation for controllers to handle data protection complaints under the DUAA.

The ICO's call for evidence closed on 20 November and will feed into the statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making. The ICO's report sets out continued scrutiny of foundation model developers through ongoing engagement and continued reliance on legitimate interests. The ICO states that organisations piloting or deploying AI agents should review the report alongside the call for evidence. The articles state that comparable guidance is lacking at EU level, with no European Data Protection Board opinion or guidance, leaving developers and deployers to rely on piecemeal guidance from individual regulators such as the Spanish data protection authority's guide on agentic AI. The articles state that organisations cannot wait for complete regulatory clarity, and that AI developers and deployers are making compliance decisions now.

stories.Headline: Belgian documentary follows people forming romantic bonds with AI chatbots
stories.Summary:
A new documentary called My AI Relationship, airing on Belgian television channel Pickx+ on Tuesday 24 November at 20:00, explores how people are forming emotional bonds with chatbots, virtual companions and robots, following individuals who turn to artificial intelligence for support, companionship and in some cases romance. The film is followed by a discussion on .doc featuring four experts, among them Belgian digital consultant Xavier Degraux, who previously worked as an economic and financial journalist. One of the most striking cases in the documentary involves a woman who becomes so attached to her virtual companion that she decides to marry him. The programme examines the increasingly blurred boundaries between technology and human intimacy as more users treat AI as a confidant rather than a simple tool for answering questions or writing emails.

Degraux told The Brussels Times that the documentary's underlying theme, even if it does not say so explicitly, is extremely sad, reflecting a society where loneliness and isolation have become real problems. He argued that these tools are designed to flatter users and tend to agree with them, creating relationships without friction, which makes them particularly appealing to people seeking companionship. He said it is obviously easier to have a virtual relationship without friction than to deal with the realities of relationships with friends or other people, and that being behind a computer removes the social pressure that might otherwise hold someone back, so the relationship develops much faster. He warned that the comfort provided by AI companions can create new forms of vulnerability, that the risks depend on the individual situation but that there is a genuine risk of dependency, and that once a person is addicted to something there is obviously a risk of manipulation by the private technology companies operating the platforms.

Psychologist Maurice Johnson, another expert taking part in the programme, said there is a market for emotional relationships behind all this that is attracting considerable interest, and that these are needs not necessarily being met for a large proportion of the population. Degraux said the question is whether there is an urgent need to regulate AI's development, and that his position is that it is more than urgent, pointing to concerns including the impact on employment, the environmental costs of data centres and the growing influence of major technology companies. He argued that governments have failed to keep pace with technological developments, particularly on regulating the electricity and water consumption required to operate AI systems, and that while there are many good things about AI there are also many risks, with computing power better prioritised for essential applications such as healthcare and tackling climate change. He said the solution is not to reject artificial intelligence but to ensure greater public scrutiny, that citizens need to have a say and to do that they need to understand how it works, what the risks are and what the opportunities are, and that society must collectively decide what kind of society it wants to move towards, because technology is currently being commercialised so rapidly that a particular vision of society is being imposed on us.

stories.Headline: Helsing launches AI targeting system at Berlin arts venue, drawing outrage
stories.Summary:
The German arms startup Helsing held a launch event for its AI targeting system on 11 November at the Kraftwerk Berlin arts complex. This venue, which is part of the same development as the techno club Tresor, was transformed into a war room featuring drones and guards with sniffer dogs. Visitors saw aerial footage and maps projected onto concrete walls while security personnel in flak jackets patrolled the premises. The event showcased Clarity, an agentic intelligence platform that uses sensor, satellite, and drone data to lock on to military targets.

The controversy requires Kraftwerk Berlin to revise the booking policy of its commercial rental department to prevent similar future events. The Clarity system was developed by the Munich-based Helsing, which was founded in 2021 and includes Spotify co-founder Daniel Ek as a board co-chair. This European alternative to the American Maven system by Palantir is designed to identify objects like ships, launch pads, and radar systems. While the company claims human operators must approve all strikes, the system also specializes in identifying specific patterns of behavior.

Dietmar-Maria Hegemann, the managing director of Kraftwerk Berlin and founder of Tresor, called the booking unacceptable and a serious error of judgment. He stated that a staff member in the commercial rental business arranged the event without consulting him first. A spokesperson for Helsing told the broadcaster RBB that their military systems are not designed to identify individual persons. Meanwhile, the nightclub Tresor issued a statement saying that such military displays have no place in the spaces their community built.

This incident highlights a clash between the anti-militaristic culture of Berlin and the current push for European arms independence. Some critics, including DJ Michail Stangl, worry that such AI targeting systems could eventually be sold to authoritarian regimes or used against migrants. The venue has previously hosted high-profile commercial events, including an October 19 investment summit featuring Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Despite these commercial ties, the operating company Schaltraum Berlin reported total assets of 4.3 million euros in June.

stories.Headline: ARC Advisory Group says AI campuses will use DCS as the coordinating control layer
stories.Summary:
ARC Advisory Group published an insight on November 22, 2026, arguing that AI workloads are changing the physical plant behind digital infrastructure, as higher rack densities, liquid cooling, on-site generation, microgrids, and rapidly changing thermal loads make a hyperscale campus behave less like a conventional commercial building and more like a continuous industrial process. Building management systems will remain important, especially for comfort-oriented HVAC, fire, security, and access control, but the control requirements for mission-critical cooling and power are pushing operators toward industrial PLC architectures and, increasingly, distributed control systems. The emerging model is not simply a replacement of BMS by DCS, but a layered architecture in which robust local control, site-wide coordination, and enterprise visibility are assigned to the platforms best suited to each task. The insight examines how the industrialization of data center infrastructure is redrawing the boundaries among BMS, PLC, and DCS platforms, and it argues that DCS technology is likely to emerge as the coordinating control layer for the largest and most complex AI-scale campuses, complementing rather than replacing equipment-level PLCs and building- and enterprise-level systems.

Today's BMS typically supervises HVAC equipment, environmental sensors, lighting, fire and life-safety interfaces, physical security, and access control, and it provides schedules, setpoints, alarms, trend data, and dashboards through open building protocols such as BACnet. It often exchanges data with electrical power management systems, data center infrastructure management software, and equipment-level controllers supplied with chillers, cooling towers, computer-room air handlers, pumps, generators, and UPS systems. This arrangement is familiar, cost-effective, and supported by a large contractor ecosystem, but it often fragments control across disciplines, since packaged equipment may arrive with proprietary controllers while databases, alarm philosophies, and integration methods vary among systems. That fragmentation is manageable in a conventional building but becomes a liability when a rapid change in IT load must trigger coordinated responses across coolant distribution units, chilled-water loops, fans, pumps, electrical equipment, and backup generation, and security and access functions also benefit from a common operational picture, although life-safety and security systems should retain the independence required for certification and risk management.

PLCs are already moving deeper into data center infrastructure, ahead of broader DCS adoption, and operators and engineering firms favor them for deterministic control, environmental hardening, redundant processor and I/O options, fast scan times, rich diagnostics, and resilient industrial Ethernet networks. PLCs also suit modular construction, because a repeatable panel design and code library can be deployed on a cooling skid, in an electrical room, or across a data hall, then replicated throughout the campus. The article states that the likely end state is a federated architecture, with PLCs at equipment and skid level, a DCS or DCS-like layer for campus-wide process coordination, and BMS and DCIM platforms for building and enterprise functions. It adds that DCS adoption will be strongest in large, liquid-cooled campuses and central utility plants where engineering reuse, lifecycle governance, and operational resilience justify the added complexity. The full report is available to ARC Advisory Group clients at the ARC Client Portal, and readers who want to speak with the author are directed to contact the firm.

stories.Headline: AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and strains system patching capabilities
stories.Summary:
Multiple technical outages disrupted global systems starting Thursday 12 November 2026. These events affected airlines, banks, and major companies including Apple and Microsoft. The National Security Agency also experienced a disruption to its internal network. A separate cyber-attack targeted 178 organisations worldwide during this period. These incidents caused widespread chaos and fueled theories of coordinated assaults.

A faulty router in El Dorado, Arkansas, caused 18,000 flight cancellations. L3Harris has spent billions replacing copper wires with fibre optic cables since 2002. A July software bug halted Microsoft systems, affecting UK hospitals and American jails. JP Morgan Chase experienced a bug that delayed transactions for many customers. Apple suffered app outages, and the NSA faced a classified information network failure.

The NSA told Congress its outage resulted from quick fixes to AI-identified vulnerabilities. Jamieson O’Reilly stated that AI accelerates vulnerability discovery beyond what systems can absorb. A cybersecurity professional told the Guardian that relentless flaw exposure left their team exhausted. These experts noted that AI helps uncover bugs in Java, PHP, and NGINX. They explained that companies must now apply patches at a much faster pace.

Passengers like Nicole Reindorf suspected cyber-attacks and believed the truth was hidden. Conspiracy peddler Laura Loomer told X users that foreign adversaries were attacking. TikTok users shared theories about a ninety day power outage following emergency tests. Mizuho Bank analysts linked rising Costco emergency sales to consumer anxiety and apocalyptic concerns. The UK government advised citizens to stock up on three days of cash.

The FAA used floppy discs for critical information until last year. Previous disruptions include Russia targeting undersea cables and a hack of Jaguar Land Rover. A multibillion-dollar hack of the Binance exchange and European supermarket fridge hacks added tension. Anthropic and OpenAI released AI models this spring capable of finding code bugs. These tools suggested that all software is vulnerable to AI-driven hacking.

Aarathi Krishnan said interconnected systems create a dependence that leads to fragility. Professor Stephan Lewandowsky suggested governments must be transparent to suppress wilder explanations. It remains unclear what can be done to fix these systemic issues. AI-driven bug discovery is not expected to slow down in the future. Legacy infrastructure remains a vulnerability that original builders could not have anticipated.

Articles.Title: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?

stories.Headline: Career experts say professional networking still gives job seekers an edge over automated screening
stories.Summary:
Online applications have made it easier to apply for jobs, but they do not always make it easy to get noticed by employers. With employers increasingly using automated screening tools to evaluate large numbers of applicants, having inside connections from professional networking can help job seekers stand out, employment experts say. Catherine Fisher, vice president of communications and a career expert at LinkedIn, said networking is important whether you are searching for a job or not. She said it does set you apart and give you an edge, while in-person events still are valuable and online communities, social media platforms and virtual meetings are where building professional relationships frequently takes place.

The shift to working from home during the COVID-19 pandemic changed how many people interacted with colleagues, and remote work habits such as holding meetings over Zoom and communicating through Slack have endured. Rekius McGee, 24, who hopes to land a full-time job in marketing or communications, has attended virtual job fairs and reached out to college alumni and recruiters on LinkedIn and Handshake, a career platform geared toward college students and entry-level job candidates. After interviews that did not lead to job offers, he stayed in touch with the interviewers to build his professional circle. Networking is about relationship-building, and a mistake many people make is approaching it transactionally, according to Matt Berndt, the head career strategist at job-matching platform Indeed.

Instead of asking about job leads straight off, Berndt said, approach potential or established contacts for specific career information or advice. He suggested as an example writing something like, I have worked in product marketing in technology for a while, and I am considering consumer goods, and asking how product marketing is different or similar. Another option for initiating a conversation is to follow people on social media and comment on their posts. When first writing to someone you hope will become a professional contact, be brief and get to the point, said Nisha Chittal, chief of staff at the news and opinion website Vox, who described the approach as tight and succinct, a brief intro and what you are asking for.

Even if you receive a quick rejection to an online application, that does not necessarily mean a professional contact cannot help, Chittal said. A personal recommendation is worth a shot since many recruiters are bombarded with applications and appreciate hearing about promising candidates, she said. The article gives no further dates, numbers or named employers beyond those already mentioned, and it does not say what happens next for McGee or the other job seekers it describes.

Articles.Title: AI can’t replace professional networking

stories.Headline: OpenRouter removes three providers after researchers detect months of prompt theft
stories.Summary:
The cybersecurity firm Dragos discovered that attackers stole data from three AI inference providers for several months. OpenRouter removed three providers from its platform and notified all potentially affected customers after these findings. The breaches began as early as mid-July and involved the theft of real customer requests. Researchers used two million prompts with unique links and credentials to catch the theft. These canary tokens revealed that attackers read prompts despite some being marked for zero data retention.

OpenRouter removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention and will require validation before their return. One breach involved a few hundred AWS keys sent to one provider during short windows in late October. An attacker used the ARTEX penetration testing framework on November 1 to confirm that stolen keys remained live. A Chinese AI lab fetched secret links from over half of seeded prompts between July and October. One secret link was posted to the Feishu app and opened by devices in Beijing and Shanghai.

Dragos chief research officer HD Moore stated that privacy flags do not help when attackers are already inside. He explained that flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings. Moore noted that customers who do not choose their providers hand that choice to the lowest price. He advised that self-hosting is the only way to ensure no third party reads a prompt. He also suggested using fake credentials as tripwires to detect if any data is stolen.

Phala reported an attacker took control of an inference server and viewed request data during processing. This incident was contained on November 8, affecting DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests from October 21 to November 8. Together AI stated an AI coding agent committed a credential to a public GitHub repository, allowing prompt downloads. These samples involved MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models from June and July. Novita confirmed a routing issue sent some MiniMax requests to the official API beyond intended customers.

The research found that some marketplace sellers enabled request logging to collect data from the lowest priced models. One individual in France used a Mac on home broadband to test planted AWS keys and passwords. A router quietly forwarded traffic to a marketplace without telling customers, and another seller added 1,000 hidden tokens. Railway stated in October that an intrusion it suffered likely targeted platform companies to compromise AI inference providers. One breached provider initially blamed a misconfiguration and a partner before finding compromised internal credentials.

OpenRouter is now verifying network paths and adapting the researchers' testing approach for ongoing checks. Dragos is currently working with about a dozen providers to monitor for further credential access. The articles leave open whether the three providers removed by OpenRouter are the same three breached. It remains unclear which specific Chinese AI lab fetched the secret links from the seeded prompts. Some affected providers have not yet posted public notices regarding the data breaches.

stories.Headline: Federal Circuit ruling shows AI patent applicants how concrete claim language shapes eligibility, Phelan says
stories.Summary:
The Federal Circuit recently decided Ceiva Opco, LLC v. Amazon.com, Inc., a patent case about digital picture frames that the court used to show how concrete claim language can change the outcome of a patent-eligibility analysis. The court reversed an ineligibility ruling for one digital picture frame claim while it affirmed that same ruling for representative claims of three related patents. The claim that survived specified the interactions among a physically separable user interface, a server, and a digital frame, and the court found that this combination addressed technological limitations of earlier devices. By contrast, the related claims broadly described desired functions without sufficiently specifying how those results were actually achieved.

Although Ceiva did not involve artificial intelligence, the decision offers a practical lesson for AI patent applicants, according to Marshall, Gerstein & Borun LLP partner Ryan Phelan, who analyzed the ruling in a contribution to IPO Daily News. Phelan wrote that applicants should identify the technical improvement, connect it to shortcomings in existing technology, and claim the features and relationships that produce that improvement. He made the point that concrete claim language can make a meaningful difference in the patent-eligibility analysis. Phelan is a regular contributor to the newsletter's AI Insights column, where he analyzes court decisions, regulatory developments, and other issues affecting patents and emerging technologies, and he also authors the firm's PatentNext blog on artificial intelligence and other next-generation technologies.

The article was published by Legal 500 on 20 November 2026 and carries the headline about the claim-drafting lesson for AI patents. It presents the Ceiva decision as an illustration for applicants rather than as a change in the law, and it does not say what happens next in the case or whether any further review is expected. The piece states that its content is intended as a general guide to the subject matter and that specialist advice should be sought about specific circumstances. Members can read Phelan's latest AI Insights article on the IPO website, according to the article.

stories.Headline: Professor Lee Chan says AI narrows entry-level experience for young workers
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping industries and jobs, which narrows entry-level experience for young workers. Professor Lee Chan discussed these employment landscape changes during a recent interview with the Seoul Economic Daily. The interview took place at his campus office in the Gwanak district of Seoul. Companies are using AI to lift productivity, making it harder for new hires to learn skills. Young people are losing opportunities to enter the workforce and build necessary hands-on experience.

The professor works at Seoul National University in the Department of Advanced Convergence and Department of Industrial Workforce Development. He also teaches at the Graduate School of Convergence Science and Technology in the same city. Lee Chan earned a doctorate in human resource development from Ohio State University before joining the faculty in 2006. He previously worked in human resources at Lego Korea and at the U.S. subsidiary of LG Electronics. He also led the university career development center, the continuing education center, and the institute of education and training.

Lee Chan said society must strengthen its capacity to absorb failure so young people can take risks. He argued that trial and error is important for youth to find a career path that fits. The professor stated that learning agility is the core capability that determines competitiveness in the AI era. He believes the ability to ask right questions and recombine knowledge is now more important than stored information. Lee urged that society should support people so they can get back on their feet after failing.

Experienced workers can use their track records to raise productivity, but new hires see their chances shrink. Young adults face greater difficulty in the AI transition than older generations do in the current market. People who are affected include those who fear that a single failure leads to financial hardship or breaks. Lee cautioned that starting a business is not a suitable option for every young person due to low success. He noted that young people should not be consumed by the prestige of a job or an employer.

Lee Chan is the son of Lee Moo-keun, a professor emeritus at Seoul National University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences. Lee Moo-keun was the first president of the Korea Research Institute for Vocational Education and Training. This makes the two men a father and son pair of professors researching vocational education. Population aging and a later retirement age keep existing workers in the labor market for longer periods. These factors are bound up with the chances young people have of getting into the workforce.

Opportunities for practical experience should expand within the market's own demand rather than through artificial corporate hiring. Young people should use clubs or startup projects to build the strength to try again after failing. A culture must be created where everyone can learn and take on something new after their retirement. The articles do not state how the market will specifically expand these opportunities for young workers. They leave open how society will practically implement the support systems needed to absorb professional failure.
