stories.Headline: Teachers at WHS debate how to regulate student AI use as departments split on its value
stories.Summary:
For the past four years, educators have scrambled to change curriculums around the emergence of AI in a way that reduces the ability to potentially cheat with AI tools. As the use of AI in schools becomes more prominent and commonly used, debates surrounding the topic have increased. Reports analyzing various advantages and harms to AI in school prompt further conversations on what the role of AI should look like. In a survey by Pew Research Center about 32% of K-12 educators say there is an equal mix of benefit and harm using AI tools in an education background. At WHS, departments share different needs for AI, and in certain subjects teachers argue AI creates a lack of critical thinking, especially in an academic setting.

History Department Head David Schmirer said AI is literally taking away your power to be able to think for yourself. Schmirer said the ability to make critical decisions and choices as you get older is going to become a lot more difficult. Math teacher Emily Grant said AI can be useful in math when students use it to understand how to do problems and not to just get the answers. Grant said if students put in a problem and ask for AI to make a similar problem and show the steps, that can be a really helpful way to learn the material. English Department Head Peter Galalis doesn’t believe there will ever be a use for AI in English classes.

Galalis said writing is a human practice, and it always is going to be. Galalis also points out that writing at a professional level means there are certain legal barriers to producing something written by AI, because AI isn’t protected under copyright. Galalis said it’s going to continue to be really important that human writers produce and own their own words, because what you produce with a chatbot is not the same as something that you’ve written. Galalis argues that the physical act of writing something human can’t be replaced by generative AI. Galalis said writing is something we don’t do just to produce more words for other people to read, and if you outsource that to a chatbot, you rob yourself of those opportunities.

Math Department Head Kanchan Kant believes policies should adapt to focus on teaching what will be helpful for students seeking a math degree in the world of AI. Since AI will have an impact on careers in math, Kant believes a specific part of math jobs will no longer be focused on writing proofs, but instead critiquing what already exists. Kant said if critiquing AI’s work is a part of what our students will end up doing, we should be preparing them for that. Schmirer said AI’s capability and availability has increased so rapidly that it’s really difficult for any teacher at the school to keep up with it. In the history department, Schmirer comments that teachers are allowed to choose their own pathway regarding AI usage.

While some teachers attempt to sway students away from AI by giving students zeroes on assignments completed with AI, Schmirer’s method is to inform students on just how harmful AI can be and encourage them to use their own thinking. Schmirer said ultimately all we can do is appeal to students to make good choices, just like we do in other areas of life. The in-class essay, rather than a take home essay, is becoming increasingly popular as a way to remove AI from the equation. Some teachers assign print-out readings rather than the typical online readings that teachers worry will be copy and pasted into an AI tool. Research shows that reading off a paper, annotating, and taking notes by hand is more helpful in successfully absorbing information than reading a screen.

One anonymous student was given a zero on a homework assignment after it was flagged by an AI detector, and later met with their teacher over the issue to defend their academic integrity, where the student was able to receive full credit. The anonymous student said they were very confused and thinking maybe there was a glitch or something like that. The anonymous student said it should be a bit more holistic with teachers meeting with students before assigning a grade for AI use. Up until last year, take-home essays were common, if not expected, in WHS humanities classes. Junior Archie Baker said they started here in 2024, so in freshman year and sophomore year it was almost entirely take-home essays, which they appreciate a lot more.

English teacher Phillip George said in his first year teaching here in 2023, he thinks he had something like 16 instances of catching students cheating using online resources, and that shocked him. George said that forced him after that first year to start revising his approach. George used the analogy of marathon runners and sprinters, and said now he’s making them sprint, and they are sprinting for at least an hour. George said the in-class essay is great for authentically assessing student thought and writing, but it is very narrow in scope. George said it eliminates the opportunity for revision, improvement, and the drafting process, which is usually so essential to writing, and it limits the kind of time under tension that students experience.

Junior Archie Baker said during an in-class essay they feel much more rushed, and they can’t refine their thoughts, so they just write it and then that’s it. Baker said they’re trying to develop ideas but can’t get as in-depth or as nuanced as they’d like to. George said what is lost is a sense of intellectual endurance, and the reward for the virtue of prolonged thought and hard work. Schmirer said he’d rather get less than good work from a student that’s their own work and that they put time and effort into than something that is just simply not their own at that point. Schmirer describes it as a fluid situation where teachers react in the interest of educating students and preparing them for their futures as new advancements in AI continue to present themselves.

stories.Headline: Masayoshi Son reportedly explores a $1 trillion SK hynix acquisition to secure AI memory supply
stories.Summary:
SoftBank Chairman Masayoshi Son reportedly considered acquiring SK hynix for about $1 trillion and approached Wall Street financial institutions about possible financing, according to The Information, which reported the news on the 20th, local time. The proposed acquisition shows Son's strategic ambition to gain control of a critical supply chain for the artificial intelligence industry. The plan envisioned securing high-bandwidth memory, which has emerged as a bottleneck in AI computing, in addition to semiconductor design, AI models and data centers. SoftBank is the largest shareholder in British chip designer Arm and has made a major investment in OpenAI. Son's portfolio also includes SB Energy, a data center and power infrastructure company, and chip designer Ampere.

SK hynix currently has a market capitalization of about $577.7 billion, about 777 trillion won, and the $1 trillion figure appears to reflect a customary acquisition premium added to the company's market value. SoftBank Group's standalone cash position at the end of September 2026 was 5.3934 trillion yen, about $34.3 billion, a figure that includes cash, short-term investments and bond investments. In October, SoftBank made an additional $10 billion investment in OpenAI, financing it by issuing $10 billion in dollar-denominated bonds and 1 billion euros in euro-denominated bonds. SoftBank also raised the loan limit on borrowing secured by its Arm shares to $25 billion and used the facility while repaying a large short-term bridge loan early. SK hynix's largest shareholder, SK Square, holds a 20% stake.

SoftBank said Son is not currently actively considering the deal. SK hynix said in a statement that it had no knowledge of the reported acquisition. SK hynix's position is that a foreign company's acquisition would require prior government approval because it is a key company in Korea's semiconductor industry. The Information noted that it was unclear how SoftBank could finance a $1 trillion deal as its financial burden has grown because of investments in OpenAI and other commitments.

According to Counterpoint Research, SK hynix's share of the HBM market is declining but it remains in first place with 50% as of the second quarter of this year. SK hynix has played a key role in the supply chain for HBM used in Nvidia's AI accelerators. Industry observers see little chance of the acquisition going through because it would have to overcome financing, corporate governance and industrial security barriers at once. In a September report, the U.S. think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies said the concentration of HBM production in Asia was heightening supply chain security concerns for the United States and its allies. Sujai Shivakumar, Director General of the CSIS Renewing American Innovation program, said production and investment decisions by a small number of companies, including SK hynix, Samsung Electronics and Micron, have a significant impact on global memory supply, and that HBM shortages are becoming a supply chain security issue, not just a pricing issue.

In January 2026, President Donald Trump determined under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act that imports of semiconductors and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, among other products, threatened national security. Japan and the Netherlands control exports of advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment through licensing systems. Korea has a system for reviewing the effects of foreign acquisitions and mergers involving companies with core national technologies on national security and the national economy, and can suspend or prohibit deals when necessary. HBM stacks multiple dynamic random-access memory chips vertically to increase data transfer speeds and bandwidth, making it a critical factor in the performance of AI accelerators. As generative AI models have grown and the amount of data graphics processing units must handle has surged, memory bandwidth has become as important as computing power.

Even if SK hynix joined Son's portfolio, the chairman would still have to rely on other companies in key areas such as GPUs, AI accelerators, foundries and advanced packaging. Son's consideration of the SK hynix acquisition is seen as reflecting a belief that competitiveness in the AI industry is determined not by any single chip or model, but by an ecosystem combining design, memory, computing, data centers, power and software. The articles do not say whether Son or SoftBank will revisit the plan. The articles do not say what price or structure any future approach might take. The articles do not say when, or whether, Korean government approval would be sought.

stories.Headline: Samsung orders more Protec bonding equipment for HBM expansion
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics placed an additional order with Protec for temporary attach bonding equipment as it expands high-bandwidth memory production capacity, and Protec disclosed the contract on Nov. 20. The order is worth 23.41 billion won, which represents 10.2% of Protec's consolidated revenue in 2025. The contract period runs from Nov. 19, when Protec received the purchase order from Samsung, through Sept. 30, 2027. Protec had previously supplied the same equipment to a Samsung mass-production line in 2025, and the initial order placed in September 2024 was worth 24.38 billion won.

Temporary attach bonding equipment is used to precisely align and temporarily attach chips at designated positions before final bonding, and the newly ordered tools will be installed at Samsung's Cheonan facility, a key advanced packaging site. Samsung began construction of its fifth advanced packaging line at its Onyang Campus in Asan, South Chungcheong Province, on Nov. 12, and that line is scheduled to begin operations in June 2028. Samsung plans to invest a total of 46 trillion won in the Onyang Campus in phases, and the expansion of its advanced packaging capacity could lead to additional orders for Protec. Protec's mainstay equipment has traditionally been dispensers that uniformly apply liquid materials during semiconductor packaging processes, and the company began supplying semiconductor die bonders in 2020.

Protec expanded into advanced packaging bonding equipment following its Samsung order in 2024, and annual bonding equipment revenue, previously between 5 billion won and 10 billion won, increased to approximately 30 billion won in 2025. Protec reported consolidated third-quarter revenue of 78.2 billion won and operating profit of 24.4 billion won, up 53.1% and 57.2% respectively from a year earlier. Its operating margin reached 31.2%, and cumulative operating profit for the first three quarters totaled 63 billion won, exceeding the 46.3 billion won recorded for full-year 2025. The articles do not say what Samsung or Protec executives said about the order, and they do not state what happens next beyond the scheduled line start and the possibility of further orders.

stories.Headline: Deloitte analyses legal risks of generative AI for businesses across IP, data protection and contracts
stories.Summary:
The articles do not contain a specific news event, so this is not a breaking story. Deloitte published an analysis on 22 November 2026, in collaboration with the Deloitte AI Institute, of the legal implications of Generative AI for corporations, covering intellectual property, data protection, contracts and Generative AI policy. The article notes that enthusiasm for AI adoption is being fuelled in part by Generative AI, and it cites the EU AI Act, Article 28b (4), which defines Generative AI as foundation models used in AI systems specifically intended to generate, with varying levels of autonomy, content such as complex text, images, audio, or video. It says a legal executive's role is to advise stakeholders, including business leaders, executive peers and the board, on the risks of business applications of Generative AI, and that regulatory frameworks in this area are emerging and quickly evolving.

On intellectual property, the article says AI can process vast quantities of data and, without much noteworthy human intervention, transform it into an AI-generated output, and that discussion of how to treat rights in both the training input and the AI output is still in its early days. The report focuses on copyright law, but the same concepts are likely to apply to other sorts of protected IP. Generative AI systems ingest and generate large amounts of data, including images, text, speech, video, code, business plans and technical formulae, and training, testing, uploading, analysing, consulting or otherwise processing such input and output data requires various levels of protection. The report addresses challenges organisations face when using personal and confidential data in Generative AI systems, and measures to mitigate the relevant legal risks.

The article says several common personal data principles and protections across jurisdictions are highly affected by Generative AI systems, and organisations should pay specific attention to transparency, data minimisation, lawfulness, sensitive data and individual rights. Given the legal risks of using Generative AI in a business context, it says careful consideration of contract terms is important when licensing or otherwise entering into a contract relating to a Generative AI solution, with key points from liability to AI regulations likely to require attention. It says adoption of this powerful, differentiating technology demands attention to risks that could imperil an enterprise's brand, reputation, stakeholder trust or compliance with legal and regulatory obligations.

The article also links to related Deloitte material, including a piece asking who is responsible for mistakes when AI acts on its own, which says embedding legal oversight and clear accountability into agentic AI from the outset lets businesses harness autonomous technology with confidence and control. It points to a piece on scaling Generative AI deployment, which says scaling responsibly requires navigating legal, ethical and regulatory complexities. It cites Deloitte's 2026 Global Tax Policy Survey, with insights from 1,010 tax and finance leaders across 28 jurisdictions on tax transparency, digitalisation of tax including AI, sustainability, international tax reform including OECD Pillar Two, and trade and tariffs. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Reticket founder Aniket Chaudhary says ticket scalping in India still relies on scripts and fake accounts rather than AI
stories.Summary:
Raye’s registration for her concert at London’s Royal Albert Hall attracted 1.8 million sign-ups for just 5,000 seats, and she wrote on X that scalpers using AI bots created hundreds of thousands of fake registrations. She said she had never witnessed bots on this scale, and her team decided to manually review registrations. When Coldplay came to India last year, BookMyShow saw nearly 13 million fans vying for 150,000 tickets. A large number of tickets appeared on resale platforms such as Viagogo and Gigsberg with astronomical markups, and the culprit was bot-driven ticket scalping, where operators used bots trained to mimic human behaviour to bypass checks.

India’s live and concert market is worth ₹20,000 crore. Reticket uses zero-knowledge Transport Layer Security through Reclaim Protocol to obtain cryptographic proof that booking details came directly from the issuing platform’s servers and were not altered. The verification checks the event, payment, and booking status, each ticket can be listed only once, and a listing is locked when a buyer begins payment. Reticket holds sellers’ payouts until 72 hours after the event, and where a transfer or wristband delivery is delayed, sellers must set up a refundable UPI mandate deposit ranging from ₹499 to ₹4,999 to compensate the buyer. Reticket caps resale prices at the amount originally paid by the seller.

Aniket Chaudhary, Founder of secondary ticket marketplace Reticket, said most ticket scalping in India still runs on old methods: scripts that check out faster than a human can, lots of accounts on different phone numbers, and people hired to wait in online queues, none of which needs AI. He said anyone can now make a booking confirmation that looks exactly like a real one in about a minute. He explained that the bigger problem is real tickets, since more scams involve someone holding a genuine ticket than an AI-made fake. He said Reticket’s verification already works without any formal tie-up because sellers prove ownership from their own accounts, but the original platforms can do things Reticket cannot. He said that soon many people will simply ask an AI assistant to book tickets for them, and that is completely fair.

Anuj Gupta, Founder and CEO of AI research lab KiteFishAI, said the real issue is that ticketing systems were originally designed around human interaction, while automated systems can operate at a completely different speed and scale. He cautioned that a bot written with the help of ChatGPT is not necessarily an AI agent. He argued that ticketing platforms need to treat tickets as verifiable digital assets rather than images or documents, and that every ticket should be associated with a valid transaction and a unique cryptographic identifier that can be verified against the issuing platform. He said the distinction should be based on identity, authorisation, transaction behaviour, and intent rather than simply whether a browser or an AI agent is involved. Events discovery platform MeraEvents identifies bulk registrations, duplicate accounts, unauthorised resale, and copied booking confirmations as potential risks, but cautions that automation alone does not establish AI involvement.

Earlier, scalper bots could be blocked by simple IP blocks and “traffic light” tests, but now scalpers use thousands of generated digital identities, continuously scraping through resale demand and seat availability to adjust markups. Conventional bots can refresh availability, navigate online queues, select seats, and submit checkout requests using predefined instructions. Fake booking confirmations can reproduce familiar logos, booking IDs, and QR codes, supported by convincing descriptions and conversations with supposed buyers. A screenshot or PDF cannot establish that a seller still owns a ticket or has the right to transfer it. MeraEvents notes that event organisers need to communicate official booking channels, establish transfer and entry rules, and coordinate with ticketing and on-ground teams when discrepancies arise.

Primary ticketing platforms could notify resale marketplaces when a ticket has been scanned or transferred, and could also reissue tickets to buyers, invalidating the seller’s original copy and making double-selling harder. Dynamically refreshing QR codes, digitally signed ticket credentials, and controlled transfers could also make screenshots and duplicate tickets harder to reuse. Chaudhary argues that linking purchase limits to verified individuals rather than accounts could make bulk buying harder. Gupta argues that platforms should not automatically treat all automation as malicious, which could require systems that establish which customer an agent represents, what actions it is permitted to perform, and whether a specific transaction has been authorised. Without those checks, the same tools that help a fan book a ticket could also be used to coordinate purchases across multiple accounts.

Articles.Title: From Raye to Coldplay, How AI Scalpers are Pricing You Out of Concert Tickets - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Reco predicts AI agent security will merge with SaaS posture management in 2027
stories.Summary:
Reco, a security vendor, published five predictions on 19 November 2026 about how enterprises will manage AI agent security in 2027, arguing that agent security will merge with the established SaaS Security Posture Management market, known as SSPM, rather than remain a separate category. The company expects security teams to treat AI agents, model context protocol connections and AI-driven workflows as the same governance challenge as users, applications and OAuth permissions. Gal Nakash, Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer at Reco, said the distinction between SSPM and agent security will blur because agents increasingly operate inside the same SaaS platforms that SSPM products already monitor. He said enterprises will increasingly expect SaaS security platforms to account for agents, MCP connections and AI-enabled workflows alongside users, applications and OAuth grants.

The second prediction is that agent security posture management will move closer to runtime enforcement, so that findings such as unnecessary access rights or risky connections may trigger direct action while an agent is operating rather than being left as alerts for later review. Possible responses include blocking a tool call, requesting approval, quarantining an agent or restricting access to certain systems, which Nakash said means more platforms will use posture context to make decisions while an agent is acting. For Chief Information Security Officers, that could mean defining more clearly which actions can be blocked automatically and which still require human sign-off. Reco also argues that AI-assisted integration work will become central to maintaining visibility, because the number of enterprise applications, agent platforms, MCP servers and AI-enabled features is growing too quickly for vendors to build and maintain connectors manually.

Nakash also expects large software vendors including Salesforce, Microsoft, ServiceNow and Anthropic to strengthen governance features for agents running on their own platforms, but Reco argues that native controls will not remove the need for an independent cross-platform view. He said those tools will raise the baseline but cannot fully address agents that connect across applications, identities and vendors. The final prediction is that AI itself will play a larger role in investigating and remediating agent risk, tracing permissions, mapping connections, identifying likely causes of risk and recommending specific changes to access rights. Nakash said using AI to summarise alerts will no longer be particularly differentiated, and that platforms will increasingly use AI to investigate why an agent represents a risk and, in lower-risk situations, carry out remediation automatically.

That leaves enterprises with a governance question about how much authority to give the security agent itself, especially when it comes to revoking access or making changes without direct human involvement. The cross-platform concern is becoming more relevant as enterprises test autonomous workflows that depend on several identity systems, APIs and software layers at once, and security teams may need to understand how an agent's relationships change across the wider estate rather than only whether it is controlled inside one application. Reco's predictions cover 2027, and the article does not say what happens next beyond those expectations.

stories.Headline: Unauthorized party downloads stored prompt samples from Together AI
stories.Summary:
An unauthorized party downloaded stored prompt samples from Together AI during June and July of 2026. This security incident occurred after an AI coding agent named xorl committed a private repository credential into a public GitHub repository. The leaked data consisted of prompt samples from the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models. These specific samples were primarily collected on June 24, July 4, July 8, and July 14, 2026.

The company is now implementing several changes to strengthen its development workflows and customer data controls. These updates include using keyless access or short-lived credentials and checking all pull requests for sensitive information. Together AI has also made zero data retention the default setting for all new accounts. The organization is currently reviewing the affected data to identify which customers require direct notification regarding their exposed information.

Together AI apologized for the incident and stated they are working with law enforcement and an external forensic firm. They noted that the unauthorized party searched the samples for other credentials, though five tested keys were only canary credentials from a Dragos security experiment. The company claimed they have found no evidence of additional prompt leakage beyond this specific event. They advised customers who handle sensitive data to enable zero data retention in their account settings.

stories.Headline: Salesforce leads US-backed Super Intelligence export consortium under Commerce program
stories.Summary:
Salesforce was selected by the U.S. Department of Commerce to lead a government-backed Super Intelligence export consortium, according to a Simply Wall St report dated November 22, 2026. The designation comes under the new American SI Exports Program, which was created to promote governed Super Intelligence technology packages globally. Salesforce is expected to coordinate with public agencies and private partners to support international adoption of U.S. Super Intelligence systems. The report says the export role should be weighed alongside other business fundamentals and risks before any investment decision, and it notes three warning signs worth knowing about at Salesforce.

The export designation puts Salesforce closer to governments that are standardising on governed data, model choice and agents, the report says. That aligns with its existing subscription and workflow platforms and can support more usage based AI revenue if public sector customers route more services through Agentforce, Data Cloud and related tools. Salesforce earns most of its money by selling customer relationship management software that helps organisations handle sales, service and marketing, and the report describes it as a large US$148.7b software provider to enterprises across the US, Europe and Asia Pacific. The consortium role lines up with the view that Salesforce wants its data products to be the context layer for AI and that Agentforce style bundles can support higher contract values, while raising the stakes on previously highlighted risks around security and reliability because more government workflows would run through those same agents.

The report says the clearest near term checkpoint is how much SI related business Salesforce reports in upcoming earnings, especially any disclosure of American SI Exports Program deals inside its public sector segment. Investors can track references to Super Intelligence packages and governed AI agents in fiscal 2027 and 2028 guidance updates, according to the report. The article was produced with the assistance of AI automation based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St, and it states that it is general in nature and not intended as financial advice. It also says Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned.

stories.Headline: Asia-Pacific business leaders call for increased cooperation to turn AI into economic gains
stories.Summary:
Global business leaders gathered at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, on Tuesday to discuss artificial intelligence. These executives called for increased cooperation across the Asia-Pacific region to turn technological advances into real economic opportunities and productivity gains. They emphasized that the next phase of adoption depends on how effectively companies translate deployment into better decisions and measurable customer value. The goal is to achieve tangible improvements in business performance rather than pursuing automation for its own sake.

Robin Li, the cofounder, chairman and CEO of Baidu, noted that while investment in cloud resources and computing power has risen, many firms have not seen higher profits. He warned that AI could become a bubble if companies fail to identify specific scenarios where the technology is truly suited. Yang Ting, the vice-president of Agilent Technologies and general manager for Agilent China, explained that her company integrates AI into laboratory workflows to improve data quality. Fang Ling, the president of Alstom's Asia-Pacific region, stated that rail technology requires combining AI with deep engineering expertise and rigorous validation for safety.

Poh-Yian Koh, the president of FedEx China, argued that scaling AI responsibly requires high-quality data, connected systems, and clear governance. He suggested that employees must combine AI-driven insights with their own professional expertise and sound judgment to be effective. These leaders viewed China's AI Plus initiative and its diverse industrial scenarios as key opportunities for multinational companies to develop solutions. They urged APEC economies to share practical experiences and expand digital skills to make these applications more accessible across various industries.

stories.Headline: MBZUAI releases PAN 2 world model to enable simulative reasoning for AI agents
stories.Summary:
The Institute of Foundation Models at MBZUAI released the PAN 2 world model on November 17, 2026. This open 29-billion-parameter model allows agents to practice simulative reasoning by imagining and rendering plans. It generates up to 20 seconds of video from text actions and optional images. The model was published on Hugging Face at the IFM/PAN2 repository. It uses Generative Latent Prediction to help agents act on the best simulations.

The system requires Python 3.14, PyTorch 2.12.1, flash-attn 4, and CUDA 13.2. It combines a Qwen3.5-9B conceptual reasoner with a 29B MMDiT diffusion backbone and Wan 2.2 VAE decoder. Videos are rendered at 704 by 1248 pixels at 24 frames per second. Users must download weights from IFM/PAN2 and models from Qwen and Wan-AI into HF_HOME. Default settings use 50 steps and a CFG of 2.5 for 241 frames.

MBZUAI researchers stated that the model handles symbolic planning through language and pixels through diffusion. They noted that the perceptual backbone was trained on hundreds of millions of videos with structured annotations. The team admitted that long plans often fail, with two in three containing a missed step. They warned that appearance drifts across clips and the model may shortcut physics. MBZUAI requested that users report any misuse to the pan@ifm.ai email address.

Robotics teams comparing PAN 2 to Figure or Unitree demos are affected by these physics limitations. The model is suitable for agent plan scoring but weak for marketing clips due to caption requirements. It is considered entertainment-grade physics and should not be confused with lab instruments. Users needing verifiable numeric benchmarks are advised to pair it with NVIDIA Nemotron for Science. The model is not a replacement for NVIDIA Isaac Sim or production digital twins.

The model follows research threads including VibePrevisBench 4D scenes and embodied AI exposure benchmarks. It is based on the Critique of World Models paper and the GLP framework. The model card includes 300 single-action tests and 100 multi-step tasks with 456 steps. Performance was measured using Physics-IQ Verified, PhyGround, RBench, and 1,400 human pairwise judgments. The system uses a Bradley-Terry model centered at 1500 Elo for these comparisons.

Next, builders should run the pan2-guardrail as a sidecar container to prevent deepfakes and misinformation. Users can fork the model in air-gapped labs or use it for short agent planning. Continued pretraining is possible for labs with proprietary teleoperation logs using provided YAML configs. The articles leave open whether the model can run on consumer GPUs without heavy quantization. They also leave open how it compares to DeepMind world models in specific benchmarks.

stories.Headline: CERT-In warns agentic AI frameworks divert funds by altering payment records
stories.Summary:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team issued an advisory on November 20, 2026, warning that hackers are manipulating business records and payment approval workflows in order to divert funds. These attacks use open-source agentic AI frameworks to automate reconnaissance and intrusion across government, enterprise, and service provider systems in India. CERT-In observed that unauthorised financial transactions are not limited to BFSI entities, because they also affect technology service providers supporting government-linked payment processes. The agency further noted that platforms handling vendor or partner payouts are affected as well, and it described the use of an AI-driven agentic offensive framework against enterprises, service providers, government organisations, and academic and research institutions.

Threat actors alter business records or approval processes to steal money through legitimate payment processes, rather than targeting payment APIs directly. This approach allows transactions to pass the usual application and approval checks, even when records have been changed without authorisation, without immediately raising suspicion. The agentic offensive frameworks conduct automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems and rapidly prepare exploitation methods, according to the advisory. They use multiple agents or automated workers for parallel intrusion tasks, which shortens the attack stages, and the advisory was published by TechGig on November 22, 2026.

CERT-In recommended that organisations identify service provider systems and accounts that can approve payments or access sensitive information. It also urged them to recheck payment instructions and business records against independent authoritative records. The agency advised organisations to establish agreements with service providers covering incident detection, access to logs, investigation, and timely notification of shared compromises. The advisory places responsibility on organisations to verify payment-related records independently and to secure their arrangements with the service providers they rely on.

The advisory covers government, enterprise, and service provider systems in India, and it states that unauthorised financial transactions extend beyond BFSI entities to technology service providers and payout platforms. CERT-In attributed the attacks to open-source agentic AI frameworks that automate reconnaissance and intrusion, and it said the offensive frameworks target enterprises, service providers, government organisations, and academic and research institutions. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the recommendations the agency issued to organisations.

stories.Headline: Google Antigravity guide matches AI models to coding task complexity
stories.Summary:
Google's Antigravity platform gives developers a selection of AI models, including Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Neon, Argon and Carbon, alongside Claude Sonnet and Claude Opus, according to a TechGig guide published on November 22, 2026. The platform also features Orchestrator, which allows two AI models to collaborate on a single task. The guide says the choice of model depends on the complexity of the development task, with simpler models suited to routine work and more capable ones reserved for demanding problems. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is recommended for quick changes, routine coding and simple debugging, while Gemini 4 Neon is better for difficult debugging and complex coding tasks.

Antigravity groups its models into categories it calls Everyday Workers, such as Gemini 4, Orchestrators, which pair models together, and Alternative Models from Anthropic. Orchestrator uses one model for planning and another for implementation, typically Gemini 4 Neon for planning and Gemini 4 Hydrogen for execution. Gemini 4 Carbon is Google's heavyweight option for complex software architecture and major migrations. Claude Sonnet and Opus offer alternative approaches when Google's models are not producing the desired results, particularly for frontend work or in-depth analysis. The platform also lets developers adjust thinking levels for models, from Low for speed to Extra for demanding tasks.

The guide recommends a workflow that starts with Hydrogen for small tasks, moves to Neon for complicated problems and uses Orchestrator for substantial feature development. Developers should prioritise specific prompts, define what should not change and ask for investigation before implementation, according to the article. It also advises working in manageable steps and varying approaches when a prompt fails. The article says developers can optimise their AI-assisted development workflows and resource usage by selecting the appropriate model for each coding task.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: 46 per cent of firms deploying AI agents in production report higher operating costs than expected
stories.Summary:
A G2 report published in October 2026 found that 46 per cent of companies deploying AI agents in production report higher operating costs than they expected, according to TechGig. The overruns stem from three main factors, which are integration work that was not covered in the initial budget, insufficient support after agents go live, and a lack of visibility into costs on a per-agent basis. Gartner's September 2026 forecast projects that global spending on AI agents and assistants will reach US$29 billion in 2026, which shows the growing financial stake in these deployments. The report was covered by TechGig on 22 November 2026.

Several studies point to operational friction as a driver of these costs. MIT NANDA's "The GenAI Divide" from 2025 found that only 5 per cent of organisations successfully implemented generative AI for specific tasks. MuleSoft and Salesforce's Connectivity Benchmark from 2025 surveyed 1,050 IT leaders and found that 95 per cent faced integration challenges when adding AI to existing processes. Deloitte's "State of AI in the Enterprise" from 2026 reported that only 21 per cent of respondents had a mature governance model for AI agents. Together these studies suggest that AI models often struggle when they interact with real-world systems, data, rules and processes.

The report says buyers should demand specific provisions from vendors before signing contracts to avoid cost surprises. These include cost visibility per agent, per session and per call, with execution details that can be recorded and queried through a console and an API. Buyers should also insist on a spending cap per agent that halts execution when the cap is reached, even when the agent runs on the buyer's own provider key. Using one's own provider key, such as for Anthropic, OpenAI or Google, with no vendor markup on tokens, ensures transparent billing directly from the provider. Vendors should also provide regular reports on AI costs and points of attention to decision-makers before the bill arrives.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond these recommendations for buyers and vendors.

stories.Headline: Researchers introduce VEX framework to help AI agents learn computer use from tutorial videos
stories.Summary:
Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li, and Chao Zhang introduced a new framework called VEX on November 22, 2026, to improve how computer-use agents learn. This system allows agents to learn directly from the audio and visual information found in tutorial videos instead of relying on simple screenshot trajectories. The agents follow a specific watch-act-rewatch paradigm to extract guidance from spoken explanations and visual demonstrations before executing tasks. After performing the actions, the agent verifies its own progress by rewatching its execution as a video to ensure accuracy.

The researchers instantiated this framework as video-SALMONN-VEX, which is a 9B-scale agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture using a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. To enhance performance, they developed Action-Grounded Guide Optimization, a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for predicting future actions. The team augmented the AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym benchmarks with more than 24,000 real-world tutorial videos to provide better training data. These technical changes allow the agent to unify external learning from demonstrations with internal reflection on its own behavior.

The authors reported that video-SALMONN-VEX achieved a 22 percent relative increase in task success over the Qwen3.5 backbone when tested on OSWorld. They also found that the guidance generated by their system improved the performance of Gemini-3.5-flash by 10 percent relatively on the same benchmark. The researchers stated that these results demonstrate the strong potential of using audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning. By integrating these capabilities, the agents can better perceive graphical user interfaces and reason over complex instructions to execute tasks.

stories.Headline: SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
Shibin Zhao, Hao Tan, Fan Yang, Haixin Wang, Feilong Chen, Yidong Ma, Chaoyang Zhao, Ming Tang and Jinqiao Wang posted a paper titled SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models to arXiv on 22 November 2026. The paper addresses the limited 3D spatial reasoning of Multimodal Large Language Models, which show promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding. The authors report systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion and find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels, such as distance estimation versus route planning, require geometric representations of different granularities. That finding reveals that a fixed fusion scheme cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements, which the authors say earlier approaches either used across all tasks or adopted regardless of task-specific needs.

To bridge this gap, the authors propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations. SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. The authors further introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse, and gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements.

The authors report that experiments demonstrate SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Computational Geometry, and the source code is publicly available at a URL given in the abstract. The abstract presents the work as a response to the gap left by recent studies that explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. Those approaches, the authors write, either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements.

The paper appears on arXiv with the identifier 2611.22415, and the listing offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, with the abstract page naming all nine authors. The articles give no further details on the benchmarks beyond VSI-Bench, no training details beyond the gating network and the regularization loss, and no publication venue beyond the arXiv posting. The articles also say nothing about planned follow-up work, so what happens next is not stated.

stories.Headline: Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data
stories.Summary:
Zhen-Yu Zhang, Jerry Huang, Gang Niu, Takashi Ishida and Masashi Sugiyama posted a paper to arXiv on November 22, 2026 describing a method for personalizing large language model alignment with multidimensional user preference data. The paper is titled Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data and carries the identifier 2611.22210. The authors note that preference alignment has become a central tool for aligning large language models with human values and desired behavior. They add that the online variant of preference alignment can advance model capabilities beyond what static data alone offers by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback.

The paper states that costly, time-consuming annotations limit the scalability of online preference alignment, which makes sample efficiency essential. Existing methods typically try to improve sample efficiency by expanding coverage of the response space or by selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. The authors argue that although these methods are effective, they quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the language model, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user. They give the example that a pair can appear highly uncertain to the model even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering.

In response, the authors propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization, or MPG-DPO, which uses low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user's historical comparisons to build a personalized preference cone that guides response selection for online preference alignment. The method first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet show the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis in the paper shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple language model families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.

The paper appears on arXiv, which describes arXivLabs as a framework allowing collaborators to develop and share new features directly on the website. arXiv states that individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have embraced and accepted its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv is committed to these values and only works with partners that adhere to them. The page also invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community. The articles do not say what happens next with the method beyond the reported experiments.

stories.Headline: Optimal Deep Nonparametric Regression with Uniformly Bounded Lipschitz Constants
stories.Summary:
A paper posted to arXiv on November 22, 2026 by Jiaxin Shi, Ziyuan Chen, Jian Huang and Hansheng Wang sets out a sharp approximation theory for deep ReLU networks held under a split spectral norm product constraint. The authors write that weight norm constraints are widely used to control sensitivity to input perturbations by bounding the Lipschitz constant of neural networks. They add that existing approximation results under fixed bounds on standard norm products are not sufficient to establish optimal statistical rates. Their theoretical result shows that sufficiently smooth Hölder functions can be uniformly approximated to arbitrary accuracy as network depth increases, with the norm-product bound held fixed.

The paper then proposes a penalized least squares estimator for deep nonparametric regression. The authors state that the resulting estimator has a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant while still reaching the optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor. As applications, they establish optimal prediction rates for two-stage learning and give robustness guarantees under adversarial input perturbations. Numerical studies reported in the abstract show the penalized estimator has well-controlled sensitivity to input perturbations and prediction accuracy comparable to classical deep network methods. The work is listed under machine learning in statistics, machine learning in computer science and statistics theory in mathematics.

The abstract names stability under input perturbations as necessary for deep neural network estimators in many applications involving noisy covariates or estimated features. It presents the fixed norm-product bound as the setting in which earlier approximation results fell short of optimal statistical rates. The authors describe their contribution as a sharp approximation theory together with an estimator that keeps the Lipschitz constant uniformly bounded. The abstract does not give the size of the logarithmic factor, the constants involved or the specific numerical results of the studies.

The paper is identified on arXiv as 2611.23979, and the posting page offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. The abstract does not state where the work has been published or accepted, nor does it give a date for any later version. It also does not say what experiments or applications will follow from the results. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Peking University researchers develop AI-driven cross-scale simulation for lithium batteries
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the School of Advanced Materials at Peking University and other institutions published a study on November 22, 2026. This team of scientists including Qiliang Zhang, Juntao Zhao, and Chuying Ouyang developed an AI-driven cross-scale simulation for lithium batteries. The project received support from the AI for Science Preferred Program and the National Natural Science Foundation of China. These experts worked across several locations including the Shenzhen Graduate School and the Fujian Science and Technology Innovation Laboratory.

The new simulation method addresses the high computational costs that often hinder the development of energy storage. It aims to fix the insufficient dynamic feedback mechanisms that currently limit the accuracy of battery modeling. The research was funded by the Advanced Materials National Science and Technology Major Project under number 2025ZD0618801. Additional financial support came from the National Natural Science Foundation of China through grant number 12426301. This technical approach integrates artificial intelligence to bridge different scales of material behavior.

The authors of the study, who include Genming Lai and Zekai Liu, declared that they have no competing financial interests. They presented their findings in the journal ACS Nano to show how AI can improve battery simulations. The researchers explained that traditional methods are too expensive and lack the necessary feedback for real-time analysis. By using these new tools, they believe the industry can design more efficient lithium batteries more quickly. This work represents a collaboration between Peking University and the Laboratory of Computational Materials Physics.

stories.Headline: Analyst Jim Handy warns Samsung and SK hynix face a memory price collapse if AI spending slows
stories.Summary:
Jim Handy, founder and general director of Objective Analysis, warned in an interview with The Korea Times that Samsung Electronics and SK hynix could face a sharp memory price decline if hyperscalers reduce their AI spending. He said memory prices could eventually return to 2024 levels as demand weakens. The warning came as shares of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix fell about 33 percent and 34 percent, respectively, over the past three months until Friday. Handy said a downturn could push chipmakers' gross margins from above 80 percent to near zero within roughly two quarters.

Google, Meta, Amazon and OpenAI are spending roughly 40 percent of their revenue on capital expenditures, including AI computing infrastructure, according to Handy. He said such spending is sustainable only if AI demand keeps growing fast enough to justify the investment. Samsung Electronics posted the world's highest quarterly operating profit in the third quarter, helped by higher orders for high-bandwidth memory and other high-end chips as AI server demand increased. Handy said production levels are limited by demand projections made two years earlier, which he said were lower than subsequent demand.

Handy said he does not think AI demand is growing that quickly, so the hyperscalers are likely to slow their spending at some point, and that will cause memory prices to collapse. He said the growth is temporary and prices will fall back to where they were in 2024. Many Korean analysts have focused on rising production levels as the main threat to prices, but Handy argued the more serious risk could come from the demand side if AI investment fails to maintain its current pace. For Samsung and SK hynix, he said, the key risk is no longer simply whether they can keep up with AI-driven demand, but whether that demand will remain strong enough to absorb the enormous amount of capacity and investment being built around it.

stories.Headline: AI chip demand creates structural high bandwidth memory shortage for top suppliers
stories.Summary:
A high bandwidth memory shortage occurred by November 21, 2026, as AI demand strained global silicon supplies. Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron caused this shift by dedicating more wafer capacity to HBM. This structural problem emerged because AI accelerators require far more memory bandwidth than ordinary DIMMs provide. The shortage is not a temporary inventory issue but a result of zero sum reallocation. Every wafer used for AI memory stacks is one that cannot become conventional DDR5.

TrendForce reports HBM took 23% of DRAM wafer input in 2026 and will reach nearly 30% by 2027. HBM requires three to four times the wafer capacity of general purpose DRAM to produce. HBM4 prices are at least 2.05 dollars per gigabit in 2026 and 3.00 to 5.50 dollars in 2027. Conventional DRAM contract prices are expected to rise 10% to 15% quarter over quarter in Q4 2026. Samsung is building an Onyang hub for HBM4E with operations moving up to June 2028.

SK hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung stated that customer demand will exceed supply capacity even beyond 2030. Sales chief Kim Ki-tae noted that customers request more than twice the volume the company can supply. Samsung chairman Lee Jae-yong outlined plans for the Onyang complex, which costs 46 trillion to 56 trillion KRW. Micron announced high volume production of HBM4 for the Nvidia Vera Rubin platform to meet demand. These leaders agree that the supply chain cannot flex quickly to resolve the current structural imbalance.

Nvidia, AMD, and Google are primary buyers, with Nvidia's RTX Spark offering up to 128 GB of unified memory. Consumers of phones, PCs, and standard servers are affected by higher prices and longer lead times. Paul Triolo said securing advanced packaging and logic memory interfaces is the top priority for South Korea. Takashi Yunogami noted that TSMC holds a near 80% monopoly on the critical 2.5D packaging market. Douglas Fuller argued that industrial policy should prioritize dynamic efficiency and technological learning over short term costs.

HBM stacks several DRAM dies using through silicon vias and mounts them beside accelerators on a shared interposer. Counterpoint Research put SK hynix at 50% of HBM revenue in Q2 2026, down from 64% previously. Samsung rose to 33% and Micron held 18%, while Samsung's HBM4 revenue tripled in Q3 2026. SK hynix reported Q3 2026 revenue of 104.62 trillion KRW and an operating profit of 83.33 trillion KRW. China has raised its share of domestically supplied semiconductor equipment to between 20% and 30%.

SK hynix has sold out its HBM and related DRAM through 2029, while Micron covers only partial demand. Samsung continues pouring money into packaging capacity to catch up with its rivals in the HBM3E cycle. New capacity from China's CXMT and other major fabs may not add meaningful output before around 2028. The articles leave open whether Samsung's massive Onyang investment will create a memory glut after 2028. It remains uncertain if South Korean firms can break the TSMC monopoly on 2.5D packaging technology.

stories.Headline: Together AI adds Qwen3 TTS model to its serverless inference platform for real-time voice agents
stories.Summary:
Together AI launched the Qwen3 TTS open text-to-speech model on its serverless inference platform on November 20, 2026. This addition provides developers with a tool for real-time voice agents that separates speaker identity from delivery style. The system allows users to control emotional tones through plain language instructions without changing the chosen voice. This capability targets the growing demand for agentic deployments in customer support and experience automation.

The service costs 20 dollars per 1 million characters and offers nine preset voices for native speakers of English, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. These voices support 10 languages, including French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, and Spanish, with first audio delivered in as little as 97ms. Developers can use a WebSocket API or HTTP streaming, and they can preview custom text using the VoiceFinder tool. The underlying Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B model was developed by the Qwen team at Alibaba Cloud.

Together AI designed the serving stack to prioritize production voice performance and low latency for enterprise users. The company aims to provide a flexible alternative to proprietary ecosystems that often force developers into model lock-in. By offering a library that spans voice, code, and language, the platform supports organizations that prefer a mix of vendor and in-house solutions. This strategy positions the company to capture a larger share of the AI platforms market.

stories.Headline: Together AI launches free storage accelerator to speed data pipelines for GPU clusters
stories.Summary:
Together AI launched the Together Storage Accelerator on November 19, 2026, to speed up data pipelines for GPU clusters. Authors Pavneet Ahluwalia and Vinamra Jain introduced this distributed caching layer to stop compute resources from sitting idle. The tool provides fast and free data caching for every Together GPU Cluster to alleviate repeated data reads. It targets the problem of data living far from GPUs in object storage or on the Hugging Face Hub. This new service is now included at no additional cost for users of Together GPU Clusters.

The system requires no application changes, new SDKs, or rewritten data loaders to function for the user. It works with Hugging Face Hub and S3 compatible storage like Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, and Together AI's T4. T4 is an in data center object storage solution that is currently available in a limited preview. Users can enable the tool from the cluster settings page or use a single command to get started. The system uses encrypted credentials stored in a secrets vault to handle authentication for the user.

The authors stated that GPUs are only as fast as the data pipelines that feed them during training. They explained that cold starts pay a WAN tax because cross cloud or cross region reads are slow. This tax includes egress from AWS which can run up to 0.09 dollars per gigabyte of data. The authors noted that the tool provides resilience to outages because cached data serves even when upstream fails. They claimed that the tool dramatically accelerates AI data pipelines while also cutting data egress bills for users.

AI teams are affected because they often pull the same checkpoints across hundreds of nodes, which compounds waste. These teams face slow reads, high costs, and failed jobs when the origin source throttles their data requests. Measured results from October 28, 2026, show that warm reads on an H100 node are about 20 times faster. A 2 GiB object from Cloudflare R2 dropped from 12.7 to 15 seconds down to 0.64 to 0.72 seconds. Small files saw latency drop from 320 to 680 milliseconds down to 5 to 8 milliseconds.

The technology is powered by ASTRA, which stands for Accelerated Storage Transport and Retrieval Architecture, used for their inference fleet. A 70 GB checkpoint pulled by 200 nodes now requires only one origin fetch instead of 200 fetches. Cold reads through the system cost nothing extra and ran within about 5 percent of a direct download. The system achieves local speeds of up to 3.4 GB per second per node on a Together GPU Cluster. Origin speed varies by region, as Hugging Face downloads ran 5 times faster from us-central than ca-west.

Users can now point the accelerator at existing S3 or R2 buckets without migrating any of their data. Those wanting warm data to live permanently next to GPUs can switch to T4 with one config change. Together AI will share a deeper technical look at the ASTRA technology in an upcoming engineering post. The articles leave open the specific date for the general release of the T4 object storage solution. They also do not specify the exact technical details of the ASTRA architecture in this current announcement.

stories.Headline: South Korea surpasses one trillion dollars in annual exports driven by AI chip demand
stories.Summary:
South Korea surpassed one trillion dollars in annual exports for the first time this year on Thursday, driven largely by a boom in artificial intelligence chips. This milestone makes the nation the fourth country ever to reach this threshold, following the United States and Germany in 2006 and China in 2007. The achievement occurred despite significant global trade headwinds, including higher tariffs from the administration of President Donald Trump and ongoing conflicts in the Middle East. This growth follows a previous record of 709.3 billion dollars last year, which narrowed the gap with Japan's 738.3 billion dollars. The surge was led by semiconductor exports, which rose 193.1 percent to 396.8 billion dollars between January and October, representing 42.7 percent of total exports.

This demand for memory chips used in data centers benefited major companies like Samsung Electronics Co. and SK hynix Inc. The cumulative trade surplus for the first ten months reached 294.9 billion dollars, more than triple the 2017 record of 95.2 billion dollars. Consequently, the economy is expected to grow by more than 3 percent in 2026, the first such expansion since 2021. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan credited the workers and businesses for this success and promised continued government support for exporters. He stated that the government would help companies overcome various challenges in financing, logistics, and trade to maintain this growth. Meanwhile, Professor Lee Jae-min of Seoul National University School of Law called the event historic but warned about potential trade restrictions.

He noted that managing these risks is essential to ensure the sustainability of growth driven by semiconductors and artificial intelligence. While shipbuilding, defense, and biohealth industries grew, automakers and electronics manufacturers faced pressure from Chinese rivals and American tariffs. Experts warn that a heavy reliance on semiconductors makes the economy vulnerable to price drops or a slowdown in global AI investment. To mitigate these external shocks, the country must develop new markets and diversify its export industries beyond traditional heavy manufacturing. South Korean companies are currently reviewing their supply chains and overseas production plans to adapt to these uncertainties.
